### How much does a game fence cost in Waco?

### Do you charge extra for after-hours emergency calls?
Yes, after-hours and weekend emergency calls carry a $150 to $250 trip fee on top of the repair, depending on how far out you are. If cattle are out on a road we treat it as a priority call and we'll usually have wire back up the same night.

### How tall does a game fence need to be for deer?
Whitetail need a fence at least 8 feet tall to be reliably contained, and Texas high fence rules apply if you're managing deer behind wire. We build game fence at 8 feet with fixed knot wire, which also does a good job slowing feral hogs.

### How long does it take to fence 10 acres?
A 10 acre perimeter is roughly 2,600 feet of fence. With normal clearing, a crew typically finishes barbed wire in 3 to 5 working days, while game fence or pipe fence takes longer because of the heavier posts and wire.

### Do you clear brush along the fence line?
Yes, we clear cedar, mesquite and brush along the fence line as part of most jobs, and we price it separately so you can see the cost. A clean line makes for a straighter fence and a lot less maintenance down the road.

## How to Pick the Right Fence
Most people call knowing the animal but not the fence. That is the right order, because the animal decides almost everything else.

- Cattle on open pasture. Five-strand barbed wire is still the cheapest fence that does the job, at $2.50 to $5.50 per foot.
- Horses. Barbed wire and horses are a bad combination in a small trap. No-climb mesh or pipe costs more up front and saves vet bills later.
- Goats and hair sheep. Anything with a gap they can get a head through will eventually hold a stuck goat. Four-inch mesh is the answer.
- Deer and exotics. Eight feet or it does not count. See game and high fence.
- Frontage and headquarters. Pipe and a built entrance are what people see of your place from the road.
- Working cattle by yourself. A fence does not sort cattle. A corral and working pen does.

Two things on the list are not fence at all. Fence line clearing is the cedar and mesquite work that has to happen before a post goes in, and it is priced separately because it varies far more than the fence does. Fence repair is the around-the-clock call when a tree comes through the line or the cattle are already on the county road.

## What Every Job Includes
The same four things, whether you are fencing five acres or five hundred:

- A walked line. We measure your actual fence line, not a satellite photo. Corners, creek crossings, and rock all move the number.
- A written per-foot price. Clearing, gates, and braces are broken out as their own line items, so you can see what you are paying for and phase the job if you want to.
- Corners set to carry the load. H-braces and pipe corners in concrete. A mile of stretched wire pulls thousands of pounds, and weak corners are why cheap fences lean inside three years.
- One crew accountable for the whole perimeter. When the high fence, the pipe frontage, and the entrance are all ours, the heights match and the braces tie together.

We run a 24/7 line for storm damage and cattle-out calls, and the estimate is free whether you hire us or not.

## What a Game Fence Costs Around Waco
Straight talk on price: most 8-foot game fence in Central Texas runs $4.50 to $10 per linear foot installed. That's about $25,000 to $50,000 per mile. Where you land in that range comes down to wire class, post spacing, how rocky your ground is, and how many corners and gates the layout needs.

Fixed-knot high-tensile wire costs more up front than hinge-joint, but it holds tension longer and stands up better when a buck hits it at a dead run. On rocky Bosque County hillsides, drilling post holes takes more time than it does in Falls County bottomland, and the bid reflects that. Clearing is always extra, and heavy cedar can add real money, so we price it as its own line item.

A few things that move the number:

- Wire type, with fixed-knot at the higher end and hinge-joint at the lower end
- Terrain, since rock, creek crossings, and steep grades slow the crew down
- Corners and gates, because every brace assembly adds material and labor
- Clearing, from light brush to solid cedar breaks

For a deeper breakdown, read our ranch fence cost guide, then call (254) 870-8898 and we'll put a real number on your line.

## How We Build an 8-Foot High Fence That Lasts
A game fence lives or dies at the corners. We set pipe corner posts and H-brace assemblies in concrete, because a mile of stretched net wire puts thousands of pounds of pull on every end post. Skimp there and the whole fence leans inside a few seasons.

Line posts go in on 15 to 20 foot centers depending on terrain, driven or set deep enough to handle our Central Texas clay that swells and shrinks with every wet and dry spell. Then we stretch 8-foot net wire in long runs, keeping the bottom tight to the ground so hogs and fawn-sized animals can't work their way under.

Many landowners pair a game fence with pipe fencing at the headquarters and a custom ranch entrance gate up front. We build all three, so the heights match, the braces tie together, and one crew is accountable for the whole perimeter.

## High Fence and Your Wildlife Management Exemption
Plenty of our game fence calls start with a tax question, not a deer question. If you're moving land from an ag exemption to a wildlife management valuation, or you're building a managed whitetail or exotics operation, a high fence is often part of the plan. It lets you control your deer density, protect your genetics, and keep your neighbor's spikes off your protein feeders.

We're fence builders, not appraisers, so your CAD office or wildlife biologist should drive the exemption paperwork. What we bring is a fence that actually holds what your management plan says it holds. An 8-foot perimeter that's tight, braced, and gapped correctly at gates and water crossings is what makes the rest of the program work.

If you're weighing a full high-fence perimeter against improving your existing low fence, we'll walk it with you and give you honest numbers on both. Sometimes the right answer is high fence on three sides and upgraded barbed wire where a creek or bluff already does the work.

FAQ

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does a game fence cost per foot in Waco?
Most 8-foot game fence around Waco runs $4.50 to $10 per linear foot installed, or roughly $25,000 to $50,000 per mile. Fixed-knot wire, rocky ground, and extra corners push you toward the top of that range. Clearing the fence line is priced separately. We give you an exact written number after we walk your property.

### How tall does a game fence need to be for deer?
Eight feet is the standard for whitetail in Texas, and it's what we build. A healthy buck can clear a 6-foot fence without much effort, so shorter fence won't hold deer you're trying to manage. For jumpers like axis, 8 feet with tight bottom wire is the right spec.

### Will a high fence help me qualify for a wildlife management exemption?
A high fence by itself doesn't qualify you, but it's a common part of a wildlife management plan because it lets you control deer numbers and habitat use on your acreage. Your county appraisal district and a wildlife biologist handle the plan and paperwork. We build the 8-foot perimeter that makes the plan enforceable on the ground.

### How long does it take to build a mile of game fence?
Figure 3 to 5 weeks for a mile on typical Central Texas ground, and longer if there's heavy cedar clearing or a lot of rock drilling. Corners, gates, and creek crossings are what eat the calendar, not the straight runs. We give you a schedule with the written estimate so you can plan around it.

### Do you clear brush and trees along the fence line?
Yes. We clear a working lane along the line before we build, usually 10 to 15 feet wide, so the crew can stretch wire properly and you can maintain the fence later. Clearing is billed separately from the fence itself because it varies so much, from light brush at a few hundred dollars per quarter mile to heavy cedar that costs considerably more.

## Pipe vs Wood: Why Ranchers Around Waco Switch
Wood fence looks good the day it goes in. Then Central Texas gets to work on it. Blackland clay swells and shrinks with every wet spring and dry summer, posts rot at the ground line, and a 1,200 pound cow scratching herself will loosen a wood post in one season.

Here's the honest comparison from a crew that builds both:

- Lifespan: welded pipe goes 40 to 50 years. Wood posts around here give you 15 to 20 before you're replacing them one by one.
- Upkeep: pipe needs paint every decade or so. Wood needs constant post swaps, re-nailing, and staining.
- Strength: drill stem shrugs off cattle pressure, feed trucks backing up, and storm-thrown limbs.
- Cost over time: pipe costs more per foot up front, but spread over its life it's usually the cheaper fence you'll ever build.

That's why so much of our corral and entrance gate work is tear-out jobs, pulling rotted wood and replacing it with pipe that the next owner won't have to touch.

FAQ

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does pipe fence cost per foot in Waco?
Welded 2-3/8 inch drill-stem pipe fence runs $12 to $28 per linear foot in the Waco area. A 2-rail perimeter fence sits at the low end around $12 to $16, a standard 3-rail cattle fence runs $16 to $22, and heavy 4-rail corral fence runs $22 to $28. Rocky ground, extra gates, and short broken-up runs push the price up. Call (254) 870-8898 and we'll put an exact number in writing for free.

### How long does a pipe fence last compared to wood?
A welded drill-stem pipe fence lasts 40 to 50 years with little more than an occasional coat of paint. Wood posts in Central Texas clay typically rot out in 15 to 20 years, and you're usually replacing individual posts well before that. Over the life of the fence, pipe almost always costs less per year than wood.

### Can you add cattle-tight net wire to a pipe fence?
Yes, and it's one of our most requested combos. Net wire runs $3.50 to $8 per foot depending on wire gauge and height, hung under a pipe top rail. That setup holds calves, goats, and sheep that would slip through barbed wire, while the pipe carries the strength up top.

### Do you build corrals and working pens?

## Net Wire and Field Fence Installation in Waco, TX (https://brazosridgefence.com/net-wire-fence-waco/)

> Net wire and field fence around Waco, $3.50 to $8 per foot. Fixed-knot and hinge-joint woven wire for goats, sheep, horses, and calves. Free estimates.

Our Services

# Net Wire and Field Fence Installation in Waco, TX
Woven field fence that holds what barbed wire lets through. Fixed-knot and hinge-joint in 32, 39, and 47 inch heights, stretched tight and braced to stay that way.

Call Now — (254) 870-8898 Get a Free Estimate

If barbed wire is not holding what you are running, net wire is usually the answer. Brazos Ridge Fence Co. installs woven field fence across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, from a 32-inch cattle-tight perimeter to 47-inch fixed-knot that keeps goats in and coyotes out. Most net wire around Waco runs $3.50 to $8 per linear foot installed, depending on wire class, mesh spacing, and how rough the ground is.

Net wire is a different animal from barbed wire to build. It comes in 330-foot rolls that weigh a few hundred pounds, it has to be stretched evenly across the full height or the bottom goes slack first, and it pulls harder on a corner than five strands ever will. Our guide on barbed wire vs net wire covers which one fits your livestock. This page covers what we build, how we build it, and what it costs.

What We Handle

## What's Included in Every Job

### Fixed-Knot and Hinge-Joint
Fixed-knot wire holds tension for decades and shrugs off an animal hitting it at speed. Hinge-joint costs less and gives a little. We quote both so the difference shows up in dollars instead of adjectives.

### 32, 39, and 47 Inch Heights
Height comes from what you are keeping in. Thirty-two inches for a cattle-tight perimeter, 39 for calves and sheep, 47 where you have goats or predator pressure. Barbed strands on top add height cheaply.

### Graduated Mesh Spacing
Openings tight at the bottom and wider toward the top, so a calf or a kid cannot slip under while the fence stays affordable across the full height. Six-inch stays where the stock warrants it.

### Class 3 Galvanized Wire
Class 3 coating carries roughly three times the zinc of Class 1. On a fence you intend to build once and leave alone, it is the cheapest real upgrade on the bid.

### Proper Stretching and Bracing
In-line strainers, dead-men on the long runs, and H-braces sized for the pull. Net wire that sags along the bottom was almost always stretched wrong rather than built wrong.

### Barbed Top and Bottom Wire
A barbed strand above keeps cattle from leaning the fence over, and one below keeps hogs from rooting under it. Both are cheap insurance on a woven fence.

## What Net Wire Fence Costs Around Waco
Most net wire and field fence in Central Texas runs $3.50 to $8 per linear foot installed. That works out to roughly $18,000 to $42,000 per mile. Where you land depends on four things, in about this order of importance.

- Wire type. Hinge-joint field fence sits at the bottom of the range. Fixed-knot high-tensile sits at the top, and it is worth the difference on any fence you expect to outlive your truck.
- Height and mesh. A 47-inch roll with 6-inch stays uses considerably more steel than a 32-inch roll with 12-inch stays, and the price follows the steel.
- Posts. T-posts on 12-foot centers are the economical build. Pipe line posts cost more and are the right call on a fence you are tying into a pipe frontage.
- Ground. Rock west of the Bosque River means drilling instead of driving. Blackland clay near Marlin means setting corners deep enough that summer cracks do not work them loose.

Corners, gates, and clearing are quoted as separate line items rather than smeared across the per-foot number, so you can see what the fence costs and what the site work costs. Our ranch fence cost guide puts net wire side by side with barbed wire, pipe, and game fence if you are still deciding.

## Fixed-Knot vs Hinge-Joint: What You Are Actually Paying For
Hinge-joint field fence is what most people picture when they hear "net wire." The vertical stays wrap around the horizontal line wires, and that joint is designed to flex. When a cow leans into it, the fence gives and springs back. When a cow leans into it every day for six years, the joint stops springing back and you get a permanent belly in the fence.

Fixed-knot wire uses a separate piece of wire tied at every intersection. Nothing hinges, so nothing works loose. It is high-tensile steel, which means it holds tension through heat and cold instead of going slack every August, and it takes an impact without deforming. It is the same construction we use on 8-foot game fence, for the same reason.

The practical rule: if the fence is a cross fence you might move in five years, hinge-joint is fine and the savings are real. If it is a perimeter, or it is going somewhere you do not want to walk again for twenty years, buy fixed-knot. The wire is maybe a third more; the labor to build it is identical, which is why the total difference is smaller than people expect.

## Stretching Net Wire on Rolling Ground
Flat ground is easy. Almost nothing around here is flat. Net wire has to follow the contour of the land without leaving a gap at every low spot, and the way you get that is with more posts through the dips and rises, not with more tension.

We stretch in runs between braced ends, pulling the whole roll evenly with a stretcher bar rather than yanking on individual wires. Pulling one line wire tight and the rest loose is how you get a fence that is tight at the top and useless at the bottom, which is exactly where goats, calves, and hogs test it. On long runs we set in-line braces so no single stretch is carrying more than it should.

Where a line crosses a draw or a creek, we build a water gap that is meant to be rehung rather than a stretch of fence meant to hold. Anything else washes out the first real rain and takes a hundred feet of good fence with it. On the rocky ground west of Valley Mills and Meridian, post holes get drilled; our notes on setting posts in rocky ground and setting posts in clay explain why the same fence gets built two different ways depending on which side of the river you are on.

## What Net Wire Holds That Barbed Wire Does Not
Barbed wire works by discomfort. An animal touches it, decides against it, and stays put. That works well on mature cattle and works poorly on anything smaller, faster, or more determined.

Net wire works by physically not having a hole. That matters for goats and sheep, which will walk through a five-strand fence without slowing down; for young calves, which slip under the bottom wire and then panic on the wrong side; for horses, where the safety argument runs the other direction and no-climb mesh is what you want instead of barbs; and for keeping things out, including coyotes and, with a tight bottom, feral hogs.

Plenty of places end up with both. A cattle perimeter in barbed wire, a net wire trap near the house for the smaller stock, and a hot wire offset where the bulls lean. We build all of it, and we would rather tell you which sections genuinely need woven wire than sell you woven wire around the whole place.

FAQ

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does net wire fence cost per foot around Waco?
Most net wire and field fence runs $3.50 to $8 per linear foot installed, or roughly $18,000 to $42,000 per mile. Hinge-joint on T-posts sits at the low end; 47-inch fixed-knot on pipe posts sits at the high end. Clearing and gates are quoted separately. We give you an exact written number after we walk the line.

### What height of net wire do I need?
It depends on the animal. Thirty-two inches is a cattle-tight perimeter and will not hold much else. Thirty-nine inches handles calves and most sheep. Forty-seven inches is what you want for goats, for predator pressure, or anywhere you plan to add barbed strands on top for extra height. Deer and exotics need 8 feet, which is a game fence rather than field fence.

### Is fixed-knot really worth the extra money?
On a perimeter, yes. Fixed-knot holds tension through Texas heat and cold instead of going slack, and it takes an animal hitting it without permanently deforming. The wire costs about a third more but the labor is identical, so the difference on the total bid is smaller than people expect. On a temporary cross fence, hinge-joint is a reasonable way to save money.

### Can you put net wire on my existing fence posts?
Sometimes. If the posts are sound and spaced right, we can pull the old wire and hang net wire on them, which saves real money. What almost never carries over is the corners. Net wire pulls far harder than barbed wire, and old corner assemblies built for five strands will lean the first season. We look at the corners first and tell you honestly what can be reused.

### Will net wire keep hogs out?
It helps a great deal, but hogs go under rather than through. A tight bottom wire, a barbed strand run low, or a buried apron is what actually stops them. Our post on feral hog fence damage covers what works and what people waste money on.

# Horse Fence Builder in Waco, TX
Fence built so a spooked horse hits something solid instead of something sharp. No-climb mesh, welded pipe, and pipe-top-with-mesh across Central Texas.

Horses are the one animal where the cheapest fence is genuinely the wrong fence. Brazos Ridge Fence Co. builds horse fencing across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, from a five-acre trap behind the house to a full boarding operation. As a general Central Texas market range, expect $6 to $28 per linear foot installed, depending on whether you are running no-climb mesh, welded pipe, or the pipe-top-with-mesh combination most people land on.

The reason horse fence costs more is not upsell, it is anatomy. A horse that hits a fence at speed does not bounce off it the way a cow does, and a horse that gets a leg through a fence will fight until something tears. Our post on the best fence for horses makes the case in detail. This page is what we build and what it costs.

What We Handle

## What's Included in Every Job

### No-Climb 2x4 Mesh
Woven mesh with openings too small for a hoof to pass through. It is the safest wire fence you can put a horse behind, and it will not let a foal roll under the bottom either.

### Welded Pipe Fence
Drill-stem pipe in three or four rails. Nothing to cut, nothing to break, nothing that rots. It is the most expensive option and the one people never regret on a frontage or a stallion pen.

### Pipe Top With Mesh Below
A pipe top rail gives the horse a visible line to respect, and no-climb mesh underneath closes the gaps. This combination is what most Central Texas horse places end up with.

### Heights That Match the Horse
Sixty inches is the working standard. We go taller for stallions and for traps small enough that a horse can build up speed toward the fence, and we set the bottom close enough to the ground that a leg cannot go under.

### Gates That Swing Clear
Wide, smooth-latching gates hung on posts set in concrete, sized for a tractor and a trailer. A gate that drags is a gate somebody eventually leaves open.

### Cross Fencing and Traps
Rotating even two pastures beats grazing one flat, and a small catch trap near the barn saves an hour every time you need to bring one in. We lay both out with the arena and run-in shed in mind.

## Why Barbed Wire and Horses Do Not Mix
This is the conversation we have most often, usually with somebody who has just bought acreage that came with an existing cattle fence. The fence is not wrong for cattle. It is wrong for what is standing behind it now.

A cow leans into barbed wire, feels the barb, and backs off. A horse spooks, runs, and either goes through the fence or gets tangled in it. The damage from a tangled horse is not a scratch. It is a wire wrapped around a pastern, a horse that fights the wire until the wire wins, and a vet bill that will pay for a good deal of fence. The risk goes up as the trap gets smaller, because a horse in a five-acre pen can hit a corner at a dead run before it has anywhere to turn.

The other issue is visibility. A single strand of wire is nearly invisible at dusk to an animal built to run first. A pipe top rail, a wide top board, or a strand of sight-wire tape gives the horse something to see. That is why the pipe-top-with-mesh build shows up so often around Waco: the pipe is the part the horse sees, and the mesh is the part that closes the gaps.

## What Horse Fencing Costs in Central Texas
The range is wide because the builds are genuinely different from one another.

These are general Central Texas market ranges; the written estimate after we walk your line is the real number.

- No-climb 2x4 mesh on wood or T-posts: $6 to $10 per foot. The economical safe option, and the right call for perimeter and larger pastures.
- No-climb mesh with a pipe top rail: $12 to $18 per foot. Visibility plus containment. This is the most common build we do for horse places.
- Full welded pipe, three or four rail: $12 to $28 per foot. Priced by pipe diameter and rail count. See our pipe fence cost breakdown for the detail.

Two things move those numbers more than anything else. Gates, because a horse operation needs more of them than a cattle place and they need to be wider. And corners, because every change of direction is a brace assembly, and a small trap with six corners costs more per foot than a straight quarter-mile run. If you are pricing a whole place, the ranch fence cost guide shows how horse fence compares with the rest.

## Building for Small Acreage South and West of Waco
A lot of our horse work is on places between two and forty acres, out toward Lorena, Hewitt, Woodway, and China Spring. Small acreage changes the math in ways that surprise people.

The perimeter is a smaller share of the total, and the gates, cross fences, and catch pen are a bigger one. Fence per acre goes up sharply as the place gets smaller, which is why a five-acre place can cost nearly as much to fence as a twenty-acre one. Our guide to small acreage fencing around Waco runs the numbers.

Ground matters too. These places are mostly Houston Black clay, which grows good grass and holds a post poorly once August opens cracks in it. We set corner and brace posts deep and tamp in lifts rather than trusting a collar of concrete at the top, because on a small place every corner is close enough to the house that you will watch it lean. Our note on setting posts in clay soil covers the why.

## Arenas, Round Pens, and Barn Lots
Fence around a working area is a different spec from fence around a pasture. In an arena or round pen, the horse is close to the rail and moving, so nothing can protrude on the inside face. We weld rails on the inside of the posts and grind the joints, so there is nothing for a knee or a stirrup to catch.

Barn lots and turnout traps get the same treatment plus attention to the corners, which is where a horse gets pinned. Rounded or filled corners are worth the extra material in any pen small enough for one horse to run another into one.

If you are also running cattle, we build the corrals and working pens for that side of the operation, and a horse-safe fence line where the two share a boundary. One crew, matching heights, braces that tie together.

### What is the safest fence for horses?
No-climb 2x4 woven mesh with a visible top rail. Welded pipe alone is also very safe and lasts longer, but costs more and gives a horse nothing soft to hit.

### Can I put horses behind the field fence that is already on the place?

### Do you build arena and round pen fencing?

## Goat and Sheep Fence Installation in Waco, TX (https://brazosridgefence.com/goat-sheep-fence-waco/)

> Goat and sheep fencing around Waco, $3.50 to $8 per foot. Four-inch mesh, tight bottoms, and offset hot wire that holds goats in and keeps coyotes out.

Our Services

# Goat and Sheep Fence Installation in Waco, TX
Fence sized for the animal that finds every hole. Four-inch mesh, a bottom tight to the ground, and hot wire where the goats have already made their point.

Call Now — (254) 870-8898 Get a Free Estimate

There is an old line about goats and fence: if it will not hold water, it will not hold a goat. It is closer to true than most people find comfortable. Brazos Ridge Fence Co. builds goat and sheep fencing across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, mostly in the cedar and limestone country west of the Bosque River. Expect $3.50 to $8 per linear foot installed.

Sheep and goats fail fences in two different directions. Goats go through, over, and under, and they will spend all day working on it. Sheep mostly stay put until a coyote gives them a reason not to, which makes predator exclusion the bigger part of the job. A fence built for one is not automatically right for the other, and our guide on the best fence for goats and sheep walks through the difference.

What We Handle

## What's Included in Every Job

### Four-Inch Mesh
Four-inch openings are small enough that a horned goat cannot get its head through and then panic. Six-inch field fence is exactly the wrong size, and it is how most stuck goats happen.

### 47-Inch and Taller
Forty-seven inches is the working height for goats. We add a barbed or electric strand on top where you have climbers, which most herds eventually produce.

### A Bottom Tight to the Ground
Goats go under before they go over. We follow the contour with extra posts through the dips rather than leaving a gap at every low spot, and we run a bottom strand where the ground is uneven.

### Offset Hot Wire
A single hot wire at nose height on the inside stops leaners and climbers before they start. It costs very little and it is the cheapest fix for a herd that has already learned bad habits.

### Predator Exclusion
Coyotes and loose dogs are the real threat to sheep around here. A tight bottom, a hot wire low on the outside, and no gaps at gates and water crossings is what actually keeps them out.

### Cedar Clearing Included
Goat country in Bosque County is cedar country. We clear the line before we build so the fence goes in straight and you can walk it later. Clearing is quoted as its own line item.

## What Goat and Sheep Fence Costs Around Waco
Most goat and sheep fencing runs $3.50 to $8 per linear foot installed. Fixed-knot 47-inch wire with 4-inch spacing is at the top of that range, and it is what we recommend for a perimeter you do not want to think about again. Hinge-joint field fence with wider stays is cheaper and is a reasonable choice for interior cross fence.

The two costs people do not budget for on goat ground are clearing and corners. In the cedar country around Clifton, Meridian, and Valley Mills, clearing the line can run $1 to $3 per foot (roughly $5,300 to $15,800 a mile) on its own before a post goes in. And rough ground means more direction changes, and every change of direction is a braced corner.

Add a hot wire and an energizer if you have any history of climbers, which is most herds after the first year. The materials are cheap and it protects the rest of the investment. Our ranch fence cost guide puts these numbers next to the other fence types if you are budgeting a whole place.

## Why Four-Inch Mesh, Specifically
This is the single most important decision on a goat fence and the one that gets made wrong most often, usually by buying whatever field fence the farm store had on the trailer.

Standard field fence has 6-inch openings. A horned goat puts its head through a 6-inch opening easily, turns its head, and then cannot get the horns back out. Now you have a goat standing in a fence line in August, and if you do not find it, a predator will. It is the most common non-predator loss we hear about from goat producers, and it is entirely a fencing decision.

Four-inch mesh solves it by not letting the head through in the first place. It costs more per roll because it is more steel, and the difference across a mile of fence is real money. It is still less than losing animals, and far less than the labor of walking the fence twice a day looking for a stuck goat. If your herd is disbudded or polled the pressure is lower, but a mixed herd or one you plan to buy into over time will end up with horns eventually.

## Keeping Coyotes Out, Which Is the Sheep Problem
Sheep are relatively easy to contain and relatively hard to protect. Most sheep producers we work with are not worried about the flock leaving, they are worried about what comes in overnight.

A coyote does not climb a 47-inch fence if there is any alternative, and there almost always is: a washed-out low spot, a gap where a gate meets a post, a water crossing left open, or a place where the ground has settled under the bottom wire. Closing those is more effective than building the fence taller. We walk the line for exactly those spots.

Where pressure is heavy, a hot wire six inches off the ground and six inches outside the fence is the standard addition. It hits a coyote in the nose right where it starts to dig, and it takes one lesson. A second hot wire at the top handles anything that decides to climb. None of this replaces guardian animals, and most of the producers around here run both.

## Building Fence in Bosque County Cedar and Rock
West of the Bosque River the blackland gives out and you are into limestone, cedar, and steep little draws. That is goat country for a reason: goats do well on browse that will not carry a cow. It is also the hardest ground in our service area to fence.

Post holes get drilled rather than augered, and a rock bit turns a fast day into a slow one. We price rock honestly rather than hiding it in the per-foot number, and our note on setting posts in rocky ground west of Waco explains what actually holds in shallow soil over rock.

The cedar is the other half. Ashe juniper along an old fence line has to come out before you can stretch new wire, and it does not resprout from the stump the way mesquite does, which makes clearing here a one-time job rather than an annual one. We handle it as part of the fence bid or as standalone clearing.

We build across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, with most of our small-ruminant work in the western half of that range. Estimates are free and written, and they spell out mesh size, wire class, and height, because those three numbers are the whole fence and a bid that leaves them out is not comparable to anything.

If you already have fence and it is not holding, call before you replace it. Sometimes the answer is a hot wire and a hundred feet of repair rather than a new perimeter, and we would rather tell you that than sell you a mile of wire you did not need.

FAQ

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the best fence for goats in Central Texas?
Forty-seven-inch woven wire with 4-inch mesh openings, stretched tight with the bottom close to the ground, plus an offset hot wire at nose height on the inside. The 4-inch mesh is the part that matters most, because 6-inch field fence lets a horned goat get its head through and stick.

### How much does goat fence cost per foot around Waco?
Most goat and sheep fencing runs $3.50 to $8 per linear foot installed. Fixed-knot 47-inch wire with 4-inch spacing sits at the top of that range. In the cedar country west of the river, clearing the fence line is a separate cost of roughly $1 to $3 per foot (roughly $5,300 to $15,800 a mile).

### Do I need a different fence for sheep than for goats?
The fence itself can be the same, but the priorities differ. Goats test the fence constantly, so mesh size, height, and a hot wire matter most. Sheep mostly stay put, so the job shifts to keeping predators out, which means a tight bottom, no gaps at gates and water crossings, and often a hot wire low on the outside.

### Will electric fence alone hold goats?
Sometimes, and rarely for long. Multi-strand electric is cheaper to put up and works well on trained animals in a rotational setup, but a goat with a thick winter coat may not feel it, and one power outage or shorted-out weed can undo the training. We build electric as an addition to woven wire rather than a replacement for a perimeter.

### Can you clear cedar off the fence line before building?
Yes, and on most Bosque County jobs we have to. It is quoted as its own line item, usually $1 to $3 per foot (roughly $5,300 to $15,800 a mile) depending on how heavy the cedar is. Ashe juniper does not resprout from the stump, so clearing a line here is largely a one-time job.

## Cattle Corrals and Working Pens Built in Waco, TX (https://brazosridgefence.com/corrals-working-pens-waco/)

Our Services

# Cattle Corrals and Working Pens Built in Waco, TX
Pens, alleys, and chute setups laid out so one person and a dog can work the whole herd. Welded pipe, built to the ground you actually have.

Call Now — (254) 870-8898 Get a Free Estimate

A fence keeps cattle in. A corral lets you do something with them. Brazos Ridge Fence Co. builds working pens, sorting corrals, crowding setups, and loading chutes across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties. As a general market range, a complete working facility usually lands between $6,000 and $30,000, driven by head count, layout, and how much of the equipment you already own.

Most of the corral calls we get come from the same place: somebody has been catching cattle in a corner of the pasture with panels and a lot of shouting, and has finally had enough. A pen laid out correctly changes that job from a four-person Saturday into something one person can do on a Tuesday morning. That is what we are actually selling here, and it is worth more than the pipe.

What We Handle

## What's Included in Every Job

### Holding and Sorting Pens
Sized at roughly 20 square feet per head for cows, more for pairs. Enough pens to sort into, because a facility with one pen only lets you gather, not sort.

### Crowding Tub or Bud Box
Both work. A tub uses continuous motion, a bud box uses the cattle turning back past you. We build either and will tell you which fits your ground, your herd, and how you like to work.

### Alleys Sized to the Animal
Twenty-six to thirty inches wide for mature cows, adjustable or sheeted sides for calves. Too wide and they turn around; too narrow and they jam. This is the measurement that makes or breaks a facility.

### Chute and Headgate Mounting
A squeeze chute anchored to concrete or to a pipe frame that does not move when a cow hits it. We set yours if you have one and build the approach if you do not.

### Loading Chute for a Gooseneck
Built to trailer deck height with a solid ramp and sheeted sides, positioned so you can back a gooseneck to it without a spotter and without unhitching.

### Gates You Can Work Alone
Sorting gates hung to swing both ways and latch from either side, with man-passes at the corners. Every gate you can work from where you already are is a trip you do not make.

## What a Working Pen Costs Around Waco
As general market ranges, a small setup for 20 to 30 head, meaning a holding pen, one sorting pen, a short alley, and a headgate, generally runs $6,000 to $12,000. A full facility for 100-plus head with a crowding tub, multiple sorting pens, a loading chute, and a mounted squeeze chute runs $18,000 to $30,000 and up.

The variables, roughly in order of how much they move the number:

- Head count and pen count. More cattle means more square footage, and more sorting means more gates, which are the expensive part per foot.
- Pipe versus continuous panel. Welded drill-stem pipe is stronger and permanent. Bolted continuous panels cost less and can be moved. Most of what we build is pipe, because a corral takes abuse a fence never sees.
- Your equipment or ours. If you already own a squeeze chute, we build around it. If not, the chute itself is a significant line item and you buy it, not us.
- Ground and drainage. A pen that holds water is a pen you cannot work in February. Sometimes there is dirt work before there is pipe.

We quote the pens, the alley, the chute mount, and the loading chute as separate items so you can build in stages. Plenty of operations start with a solid holding pen and alley and add the tub two years later.

## Laying It Out So One Person Can Work Cattle
Layout is the whole job. The pipe is just pipe.

Cattle move well when they are going where they can see, moving toward other cattle, and turning the way they came from. They move badly toward a dark shed, into a dead end, or against a crowd. A good facility uses those tendencies instead of fighting them, which is why the same herd will flow through one setup and wreck another.

Practical things that matter more than people expect: solid sides on the alley and the tub, so cattle look forward instead of at you. A man-pass at every corner, so you never have to climb. Gates that latch from both sides. And enough curve or angle that an animal in the alley cannot see the chute until it is committed.

We lay the pen out on the ground with you before we weld anything, walking through a working day out loud. Where do the cattle come from, where do they go after, where is the trailer parked, which way does the wind blow the dust. That conversation costs nothing and it is the difference between a pen you like and a pen you tolerate.

## Crowding Tub or Bud Box?
This is the one people argue about, and both camps are right about their own operation.

A crowding tub is a curved pen with a sweep gate that funnels cattle into the alley. It handles larger groups with less thinking, works well when several people are helping, and is what most commercial facilities use. It costs more to build and takes more room.

A bud box is a simple rectangular pen where cattle walk in, then turn back past the handler into the alley. It is cheaper, smaller, and works beautifully when it is built to the right dimensions and the handler knows how to position. It is unforgiving when either of those is off.

Our honest read: if you work cattle mostly alone and you are willing to learn the positioning, a bud box gives you more facility per dollar. If several different people will be using it, including neighbors and hired help who have never seen it before, a tub is more forgiving of whoever is standing in the wrong place.

## Pipe, Panels, and What Survives a Corral
A corral takes punishment a fence line never does. Cattle push against it under stress, they hit it, and they do it in the same three places every time. That is why almost everything we build for working facilities is welded drill-stem pipe rather than wire or wood.

Pipe corners in a pen get set deeper than fence corners and are usually filled or sleeved where the abuse concentrates. The rails go on the inside face of the posts so there is nothing protruding into the pen, and joints get ground smooth. Same principle as an arena: nothing that can hook a hip or a hide.

Continuous panel is the reasonable alternative when you want the option to move things later, and it is genuinely cheaper. We build with it when that is what you want, and we say so on the bid rather than quietly substituting. Either way, the setup ties into your existing pipe fence and ranch entrance if we built those too, so the heights match and the braces work together.

FAQ

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does a cattle working pen cost to build?
As general market ranges, a small setup for 20 to 30 head, meaning a holding pen, a sorting pen, a short alley, and a headgate, runs about $6,000 to $12,000. A full facility for 100-plus head with a crowding tub, multiple pens, a loading chute, and a mounted squeeze chute runs $18,000 to $30,000 and up. We quote each piece separately so you can build it in stages.

### How wide should a cattle alley be?
Twenty-six to thirty inches for mature cows. Narrower and animals jam; wider and they turn around, which is how people get hurt. If you run calves through the same alley, we build adjustable or sloped sides so one alley handles both without a compromise that works badly for each.

### Is a bud box or a crowding tub better?
A bud box is cheaper, smaller, and excellent when the handler knows how to position and works mostly alone. A crowding tub costs more and takes more room but is more forgiving of whoever happens to be helping that day. If several different people will use the facility, we usually recommend the tub.

### How much space do cattle need in a holding pen?
Figure roughly 20 square feet per head for mature cows in a holding pen, and more for pairs, since a calf needs somewhere to be that is not under a cow. Crowding pens are deliberately tighter than that, but nothing should hold cattle at crowding density for longer than the few minutes it takes to work them.

### Can you build a corral that ties into my existing fence?
Yes, and it is usually the right way to do it, because the pen wants to sit where the cattle already come to. We tie into existing pipe or wire, match heights, and add braces where a fence corner is suddenly carrying corral loads it was never built for.

## 5-Strand Barbed Wire Built for Central Texas Cattle
Five strands is the standard for cattle in this part of Texas, and there's a reason for it. Four strands leave gaps that calves slip through, and six is usually money you don't need to spend on gentle stock. We space strands so the bottom wire discourages calves from rooting under and the top wire sits high enough that a cow won't lean over it.

Installed prices run $2.50 to $5.50 per linear foot. Flat, clean ground with T-posts lands at the low end. Rocky ground, heavy brush clearing, old fence teardown, or pipe line posts push you toward the top. A quarter mile is 1,320 feet, so figure roughly $3,300 to $7,300 for a quarter mile depending on those factors.

Every build includes braced corner and gate assemblies, because a barbed wire fence is only as good as its corners. If a corner leans, the whole stretch goes slack. For the full math on longer runs, see our ranch fence cost page.

## When Barbed Wire Is the Wrong Fence
Barbed wire holds cattle. It does not hold much else, and on a place running mixed stock it is worth being honest about where it stops working. A combination build, five strands on the cattle perimeter and woven wire on the traps that need it, is what most places around Waco end up with.

- Goats and sheep treat a five-strand fence like a suggestion. See goat and sheep fencing.
- Horses are the safety case, not the containment case. Barbs and a spooked horse in a small trap are a vet bill waiting to happen. See horse fencing.
- Calves and small stock go under the bottom wire. That is a net wire and field fence job, at $3.50 to $8 per foot.
- Deer and exotics need 8 feet, which is game fence rather than anything on this page.

We build all of it, and we would rather tell you which sections genuinely need woven wire than sell you woven wire around the whole place.

## T-Posts or Pipe Posts: Spacing That Actually Holds
Most of the fence we build uses steel T-posts on the line and pipe at the stress points. On typical Central Texas ground we drive T-posts every 8 to 10 feet. On flat, open ground with good wire tension you can stretch that to 12 feet, and on hills or creek crossings we tighten it up. Post spacing is where cheap fence jobs cut corners, and it's why they sag in three years.

Pipe belongs at corners, gates, and pull points. We set pipe corner and H-brace assemblies in concrete, because those posts carry the tension of the entire stretch. On some ranches we run pipe line posts too, every 20 to 30 feet with wire, for a fence that shrugs off leaning cattle and falling limbs.

Want the heavier build? Our pipe fence page covers all-pipe fencing, and if you're dressing up the front of the place, we build ranch entrance gates to match.

## Ag Exemptions and Storm-Damage Repair
A lot of our calls start with an ag valuation. To qualify land for agricultural appraisal in McLennan, Bosque, or Falls county, the appraisal district wants to see the land actually used for agriculture, and for most folks around here that means grazing. You can't graze cattle without a stock-tight perimeter, so a sound 5-strand fence is usually the first real investment in qualifying a property. We're fence builders, not tax advisors, so confirm requirements with your county appraisal district, but we'll build the perimeter that makes a grazing lease possible.

Storms are the other half of this business. Central Texas wind and flood water take out fence every year, and a gap in the wire at midnight means cattle on the road by morning. That's a liability problem, not just a fence problem.

Our emergency line at (254) 870-8898 answers 24/7 for storm damage and cattle-out calls. We'll patch the gap fast to contain your stock, then come back for the permanent repair on a written estimate. These do come back from the stump and the root. We cut low and treat the stump so you are not looking at the same brush in three years.

### Mulching or Piling
Mulched in place is cheapest and leaves the material on the ground as cover. Piled and burned or hauled costs more and leaves the lane clean. Both get quoted so you can choose.

### Clearing Overgrown Existing Fence
Regrowth pulled off a fence that is still sound, so you can see the wire, find the breaks, and get to it. Often the cheapest thing you can do for an old fence.

### Priced as Its Own Line Item
Never buried in the per-foot fence price. Clearing varies more than any other part of a fence job, and hiding it in the bid is how surprise change orders happen.

## What Fence Line Clearing Costs Around Waco
Clearing runs $1 to $3 per foot (roughly $5,300 to $15,800 a mile) for a typical fence lane, and the spread is enormous because the brush is. Light regrowth on a maintained line is a fast day with a skid steer. A quarter mile of mature cedar brake on a Bosque County hillside is a different job entirely, and it can run past the top of that range.

What drives the number:

- Density and species. Scattered mesquite in a pasture is cheap. Solid cedar where the canopy has closed is not.
- Stem size. Anything a mulcher can take in one pass is fast. Trunks that need a saw or a dozer are slow.
- Terrain. Steep, rocky sidehills west of Valley Mills slow equipment down and limit which machine can go where.
- What happens to the material. Mulching in place is the cheapest. Piling and burning costs more. Hauling off costs the most.

When clearing is part of a fence job, it appears on the estimate as its own line rather than folded into the per-foot number. That is deliberate. It is the single most variable cost on a fence bid, and a contractor who averages it across the whole job is either overcharging the easy sections or is going to come back asking for more money on the hard ones.

## Why the Lane Width Matters More Than People Think
Ten to fifteen feet is what we clear for a new build, and it is not arbitrary. The crew needs room to run a stretcher, work a post driver, and get a trailer of wire alongside the line. Cut it narrower and the build slows down, which costs more than the clearing saved.

The bigger argument is what happens afterward. A fence you can drive is a fence you check. A fence buried in regrowth is a fence you find out about when the cattle are on the road. Six to eight feet of maintained lane is enough for a side-by-side, and keeping it open is dramatically cheaper than clearing it again in fifteen years.

There is also the fence itself. Limbs over a line drop on it in every ice storm and every wind event, and a tree growing against a wire will eventually swallow it. Our post on storm damaged fence repair covers what that looks like when it goes wrong. Most of the trees we cut out of fences were saplings somebody decided to leave.

## Cedar, Mesquite, and What Comes Back
The two brush problems in our service area behave completely differently, and knowing which one you have changes what the job is worth.

Ashe juniper, what everyone here calls cedar, does not resprout from a cut stump. Cut it below the lowest green limb and that tree is finished. This is genuinely good news: clearing a cedar line is close to permanent, and what returns comes from seed over many years rather than from the stumps you left. It is why cedar clearing on the limestone country around Clifton and Meridian is worth doing properly once.

Mesquite and huisache resprout aggressively from the stump and from the root crown, and cutting alone will give you a denser thicket than you started with. Those get cut low and the stump treated, or they come back multi-stemmed and worse. Anyone who quotes you mesquite clearing without mentioning the stumps has not thought about year three.

One thing worth checking before you clear mature cedar in Bosque County: stands of older Ashe juniper mixed with oak can be golden-cheeked warbler habitat, and that bird is federally listed. The nesting season runs roughly March through July. If you are clearing a substantial amount of mature juniper woodland rather than a fence lane through regrowth, it is worth a call to a wildlife biologist or the local Fish and Wildlife office first. Clearing outside nesting season, and keeping a fence lane narrow, generally keeps you well clear of the issue.

## Clearing Without a Fence Attached
Not every clearing job has a fence at the end of it, and we take those calls too.

The most common one is an old fence line that is still sound under twenty years of brush. Nobody has walked it in a decade, the cattle have been getting out somewhere, and you cannot even see where. Clearing that line so you can inspect it is frequently the cheapest useful thing you can do, and about half the time the fence turns out to need a few hundred feet of work rather than replacement.

The others are pasture and pen access, opening a road to a water trough or a back gate, and clearing around a working pen so you can get a trailer to it. We quote all of it by the job after walking it, because brush is impossible to price from a photograph.

## Clearing Crews Across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls Counties
We clear within about an hour of Waco. Most of the heavy cedar work is out west toward Valley Mills, Clifton, and Meridian. Mesquite and bottomland brush runs more toward Marlin and the Brazos bottoms south of town.

Winter is the better season for it: the brush is dormant, the ground is firmer than you would think, and it is out of nesting season. But we clear year round, and if you are building fence in the spring, the clearing has to happen when it happens.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does fence line clearing cost per mile?
Most fence lanes run $1 to $3 per foot (roughly $5,300 to $15,800 a mile). Light regrowth on a maintained line is at the bottom of that; mature cedar brake on a rocky hillside can run past the top. We walk it before quoting, because brush genuinely cannot be priced from a satellite photo.

### How wide should a cleared fence line be?
Ten to fifteen feet for a new build, which gives the crew room to stretch wire and get equipment alongside. After that, keeping six to eight feet open is enough to drive a side-by-side down, and a fence you can drive is a fence you actually check.

### Will the cedar grow back after you clear it?
Not from the stump. Ashe juniper does not resprout once it is cut below the lowest green limb, so clearing a cedar line is close to a one-time job. What comes back comes from seed over many years. Mesquite and huisache are the opposite and will resprout aggressively unless the stumps are treated, which we do.

### Do you clear fence lines without building the fence?
Yes. A good share of our clearing work is on lines that already have sound wire on them and just cannot be reached or inspected. We also open access to troughs, back gates, and working pens. It is quoted by the job after we walk it.

### Is there a best time of year to clear?
Winter, generally. The brush is dormant, the ground carries equipment better than the summer cracks suggest, and it falls outside the spring nesting season, which matters if you are clearing mature juniper woodland in Bosque County. That said, we clear year round, and fence schedules do not always wait for January.

# Fence Repair in Waco, TX
Storm damage, downed wire, leaning posts, and cattle out on the road. We answer the emergency line around the clock and patch the break before it costs you a wreck.

Call Now — (254) 870-8898 Get a Free Estimate

Fence repair around Waco is rarely something you planned for. A live oak comes down across the north line, a bull decides the neighbor's grass looks better, or a spring flood takes out a water gap and forty feet of wire with it. Brazos Ridge Fence Co. repairs farm and ranch fence across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and we answer the phone at 2 a.m. because that is usually when the call comes.

Most repair calls run $400 to $2,500 depending on how much fence is down and how hard it is to reach. We quote it in writing before we start, the same way we do a new build. If the line is far enough gone that repair stops making sense, we will tell you that too, and price a rebuild against our ranch fence cost guide so you can see both numbers side by side.

What We Fix

## Repairs We Run Every Week

### Storm and Tree Damage
We cut and clear the timber off the line, replace the crushed posts, and restretch the wire. Where a tree took out a corner, the brace gets rebuilt properly rather than propped back up.

### Cattle-Out Emergencies
Loose stock on a highway is a liability problem before it is a fence problem. We patch the break first so the herd holds, then schedule the permanent fix once everything is back inside.

### Sagging and Slack Wire
Slack wire usually means a brace has moved, not that the wire stretched. We find the assembly that gave, reset it, and retension the run so it stays tight instead of sagging again by fall.

### Leaning and Rotten Posts
Blackland clay heaves posts and ground-line rot eats wood from the inside. We pull the failures, set replacements deep in concrete, and leave the sound posts alone so you are not paying for a full rebuild.

### Washed-Out Water Gaps
Creek crossings take the worst of a flash flood. We rebuild them as breakaway gaps so the next high water carries off a panel you can rehang in an hour, not a whole stretch of fence.

### Hog Damage at Ground Line
Feral hogs work the bottom wire until there is a gap. We close the breach and add a barbed bottom strand so the same spot does not reopen the following month.

### Dragging and Sticking Gates
A gate that will not latch is almost always a leaning hinge post. We reset the post, rehang the gate square, and add a brace or wheel where the span calls for it.

### Corner and H-Brace Failures
When a corner pulls, every run tied to it goes slack. We rebuild the H-brace assembly to spec so the repair holds the next twenty years of tension.

## What Fence Repair Costs Around Waco
Repair pricing depends on three things: how much fence is down, what it takes to reach it, and whether the posts and wire that are still standing are worth saving. Here is roughly where our calls land.

- Splice and retension a run — $400 to $900. Broken wire, a few clips, and a stretch to pull it back tight.
- Reset or replace posts — $45 to $120 per post installed, more in shallow limestone where we bring a rock bit.
- Rebuild a corner or H-brace — $600 to $1,400 depending on post size and whether it is set in concrete.
- Storm and tree clearing plus repair — $900 to $2,500 for a typical downed-timber stretch, including cutting the tree off the line.
- Rebuild a washed-out water gap — $700 to $1,800 depending on the width of the crossing.
- After-hours emergency trip fee — $150 to $250 on top of the repair, based on distance.

Those are real ranges from real calls, not a teaser number. We still walk the damage before quoting, because a hundred feet of downed wire in an open pasture and a hundred feet in a cedar-choked bottom are not the same job.

## Repair or Replace? How We Tell the Difference
Plenty of the fence we look at is worth repairing, and we will say so even though a rebuild is the bigger invoice. The call comes down to what is left.

Repair makes sense when the corners and braces are sound, the wire still has galvanizing on it, and the damage is confined to one stretch. A fence with good bones and one bad section is a cheap fix that buys you another decade.

Replacement makes sense when you are resetting more than about a third of the posts, when the wire is rusting through in several places along the line, or when the original build used Class 1 wire that has simply reached the end of its life. At that point repairs stack up faster than the payments on a new fence.

If a fence has been patched three times in five years, the patches are not the problem. Something structural is moving, and we would rather find it than sell you a fourth patch.

## What to Do Before We Get There
If cattle are out, call the sheriff's non-emergency line before you call us, especially if stock is anywhere near a highway. Under Texas law a loose animal on a road is your liability, and getting a deputy out to slow traffic matters more than the fence in that first hour. Our guide on cattle on road liability in Texas covers where you actually stand.

After that, a few things make our first trip faster. Photograph the damage before anything gets moved, both wide and close up, because that is what an insurance adjuster will want. Note roughly how many feet are down and whether a vehicle can reach the spot. If you can safely close a gate to hold stock in a smaller trap, do it.

Do not try to restretch a broken high-tensile wire by hand. Wire under tension carries real energy and a snapped strand recoils hard enough to cause serious injury. Stabilize the gap with panels if you have them and leave the tension work to a crew with the right tools.

## What Drives Your Price Per Foot
Two ranches a mile apart can get very different bids for the same fence, and it usually comes down to what's in the ground and what's on it. Here are the factors that move the number most:

- Terrain and rock. Limestone and caliche are everywhere around Waco and the Bosque County hills. When we have to rock-drill post holes instead of augering them, labor goes up fast.
- Brush clearing. A clean fence line is a cheap fence line. Heavy cedar or mesquite along the route can add $1 to $3 per foot before the first post goes in.
- Corners, gates, and braces. Every corner and gate needs an H-brace or pipe corner. A square 10-acre tract has more corners per foot than a mile of straight perimeter, so short jobs cost more per foot.
- Materials. Steel t-posts versus pipe line posts, standard barbed wire versus high-tensile game wire, drill stem versus new pipe. Material choice alone can double a bid.
- Access and distance. Fence lines we can drive a truck along cost less than lines we have to carry material into by hand or side-by-side.

This is why we don't quote firm numbers over the phone. We walk the line first, then hand you a written estimate that won't grow on you later.

## Cost by Fence Type: Which One Fits Your Operation
Barbed wire at $2.50 to $5.50 per foot is still the best value for cattle on larger acreage. If you're running goats or sheep, step up to net wire at $3.50 to $8 per foot so small stock stays put and coyotes stay out. Read more on our barbed wire fence page.

Pipe fence at $12 to $28 per foot costs more up front but it's the last fence you'll build on that line. Most of our customers use pipe fencing for road frontage, corrals, and working pens where cattle push hard, then run barbed wire on the back sections.

High game fence at $4.50 to $10 per foot is the standard for deer operations and exotics. On a per-mile basis figure $25,000 to $50,000 depending on clearing and terrain. Our game fence installation page covers heights, wire specs, and water gaps in detail.

Entrances and cattle guards finish the job. A custom ranch entrance runs $5,000 for a clean pipe entrance up to $25,000 and beyond for stone columns and overhead signage. An installed cattle guard runs $3,500 to $8,000 and pays for itself the first year you stop opening gates in the rain.

## Budgeting a Big Job: Per-Mile Math That Actually Works
On tracts over 100 acres, think in miles, not feet. A mile is 5,280 feet, so barbed wire at $2.50 to $5.50 per foot pencils out to roughly $13,200 to $29,000 per mile, and 8-ft game fence lands between $25,000 and $50,000 per mile. Those ranges assume normal Central Texas conditions, some rock, some brush, a few water gaps.

Don't forget the extras that per-foot pricing leaves out: corner braces, gates, cattle guards, and clearing. On a typical perimeter job those items add 10 to 20 percent on top of the wire-and-post number. A good written estimate breaks all of it out line by line so there are no surprises, which is exactly how we quote every job from McGregor to West.

One more tip: fencing whole tracts at once almost always beats doing it in pieces. Mobilization, equipment hauling, and material delivery get spread over more feet, which drops your per-foot cost.

## Fencing for Small-Acreage and Horse Properties
A big share of our China Spring work is small-acreage tracts, places in the 5 to 25 acre range where the old barbed wire came with the land and won't hold a horse. Barbed wire and horses are a bad mix. A spooked horse hits barbed wire and you're looking at a vet bill that costs more than the whole fence, so on horse places we recommend 2x4 non-climb net wire, often with a pipe top rail.

Small tracts also mean close neighbors, so we talk through property lines before we build. We'll help you figure out where the line actually runs, set the fence on your side of it, and build cross fencing to split grazing from the house yard, the barn lot, and the hay patch. Good cross fencing lets small acreage carry more animals without beating the grass to death.

If you're pricing options, our ranch fence cost guide breaks down per-foot numbers for every fence type we build. On a typical China Spring horse place, net wire runs roughly $3.50 to $8 per foot installed, and pipe fence runs $12 to $28 per foot depending on rail count and gates.

## Building Fence Along the Bosque River
Properties along the Bosque River and the creeks that feed Lake Waco come with their own fencing problems. River bottom ground floods, and a standard fence strung tight across a draw becomes a trash dam the first time the water comes up. It catches brush, the wire loads up, and the flood rips out fifty feet of fence along with your corner braces.

The fix is a proper water gap, a breakaway section built across the low spot that lets floodwater and debris pass through, then swings or clips back into place when the water drops. We build water gaps on most river-bottom jobs in the China Spring area, and we set the permanent corner posts up on high ground where the flood can't reach them.

Soil matters out here too. Ground near the river digs easy, but plenty of China Spring sits on shallow limestone where a post hole means rock drilling. We bring the right augers and rock bits so a rocky stretch doesn't turn into a change order surprise. Your written estimate covers it up front.

A quarter mile of barbed wire cross fence usually lands somewhere between $3,300 and $7,300. Rock, brush clearing, terrain, and gate count move those numbers, which is why we walk every line before we quote it.

Every estimate is free, written, and itemized by the foot, so you can compare it line by line against anybody else's bid. No deposit games and no vague allowances. If we hit something unexpected in the ground, we talk to you before we spend your money.

We also build for neighbors down the road in Crawford, Valley Mills, and McGregor, so our crews are in the northwest part of the county most weeks. That usually means shorter waits to get on the schedule.

FAQ

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do you fence across a creek in the Brazos bottoms?
With a breakaway water gap, not a fixed fence. We hang a panel from a cable or a swing arm so high water lifts it out of the way or carries it off a short tether instead of tearing out the anchored fence on both banks. Rehanging a gap takes about an hour; rebuilding a washed-out stretch takes days.

### Does fence in the river bottom cost more than on the prairie?
Yes, typically 20 to 40 percent more for the same footage. Brush clearing, heavier brace material, and water gap construction are the three drivers. We list them separately in the estimate so you can decide what to do now and what to phase.

### How often will bottomland fence need work?
Plan on walking it after every significant rise and clearing brush off the line every three or four years. A bottom fence that gets that attention lasts nearly as long as one on high ground. One that gets ignored is usually a rebuild inside a decade.

### Can you build working pens as part of a fencing job?
Yes, and doing it in the same trip saves a mobilization. We build welded pipe pens, crowd tubs, and alleys sized to your herd and your trailer. Most sets we build in the Robinson area run $8,000 to $25,000 depending on size and whether you want a squeeze chute framed in.

What We Do in Clifton

## Services for Clifton Properties

### Net Wire for Sheep and Goats
Goats are the hardest animal in Texas to keep behind a fence. Fixed knot net wire with tight spacing at the bottom is the answer, not more strands of barbed wire. Our goat and sheep fencing guide covers spacing and cost.

### High Game Fence
A growing share of Bosque County acreage is managed for whitetail and exotics. We build 8 foot fixed knot game fence over rolling limestone, including the grade changes and draws that make it tricky.

### Pipe Fence and Corrals
Welded pipe for pens and corrals plus road frontage. On shallow rock, pipe set in concrete often outperforms wood posts that cannot get depth.

## Building Fence on Bosque County Limestone
The fencing problem around Clifton is depth. In a lot of places you have twelve to twenty inches of soil sitting on solid limestone, and a post that wants to go three and a half feet down simply is not going to.

We drill. A hydraulic auger with a carbide rock bit gets through most of what is out here, and where it will not, we set shorter posts in concrete and change the brace geometry to make up for the lost depth. What we do not do is set a shallow post in dirt and call it good, because that is the corner that pulls in year two.

Grade compounds it. A fence dropping off a ridge into a draw pulls hard downhill, so corners at the top of a grade need bracing sized for the pull rather than the standard assembly. Our H-brace guide explains the geometry.

## What Fencing Costs Around Clifton
Net wire for sheep and goats runs $3.50 to $8 per foot depending on wire class and how much clearing the line needs. Barbed wire runs $2.50 to $5.50, and game fence $4.50 to $10.

Rock drilling is the Bosque County variable. Depending on how much limestone we hit, expect $15 to $40 per hole over a normal set, which on a mile of fence with posts every twelve feet is real money. We walk the line and probe before quoting so the number in the estimate is the number on the invoice. See the ranch fence cost guide for the full picture.

We work Clifton along with Meridian, Valley Mills, and the ranch country along SH 6 and FM 219. Bosque County is a normal run for us out of Waco.

### What fence actually holds goats around Clifton?
Fixed knot net wire, 47 inches or taller, with vertical stays no more than 6 inches apart at the bottom. Barbed wire does not hold goats no matter how many strands you run, and hinge joint wire lets them push through the bottom squares. Expect $3.50 to $8 per foot installed.

### How do you set posts where there is only a foot of soil?
We drill into the limestone with a carbide rock bit and set the post in the rock itself, which actually holds better than deep soil once it is grouted or concreted in. Where the rock is too hard or too shallow, we shorten the post, widen the brace, and adjust the assembly so the geometry still carries the load.

Regularly. Eight foot fixed knot game fence runs $4.50 to $10 per foot here, with the rolling ground and cedar clearing pushing toward the upper half of that range. We handle the clearing, the grade changes, and the water gaps across the draws.

On a heavily cedared line, clearing typically runs $1.50 to $4 per foot on top of the fence itself, depending on stem size and whether you want the material burned, mulched, or windrowed. A cleared line builds straighter and needs far less maintenance, so it is rarely worth skipping.
