# Blog Posts

## 12 Questions to Ask a Fence Contractor Before You Sign (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/questions-to-ask-fence-contractor/)

> Hiring a fence builder in Waco? Here are 12 smart questions to ask a fence contractor about price, posts, wire, and warranties before you sign the contract.

Hiring a Contractor

# 12 Questions to Ask a Fence Contractor Before You Sign
Published August 20, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A bad fence contract doesn't just cost you money. In Central Texas, it can cost you cattle, and if a cow ends up on FM 185 at 2 a.m., it can cost you a whole lot more than that.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A bad fence contract doesn’t just cost you money. In Central Texas, it can cost you cattle, and if a cow ends up on FM 185 at 2 a.m., it can cost you a whole lot more than that.

Most ranchers around Waco get two or three bids, pick one, shake hands, and hope. The smarter move is to walk into that conversation with a list of questions to ask a fence contractor before you sign anything. The right questions take about twenty minutes and can save you thousands of dollars, months of frustration, and at least one rebuilt corner.

We’ve been on the other side of this conversation more times than we can count, and we’ll tell you exactly what a straight-shooting contractor should say to each one. If a bidder dodges more than a couple of these, keep your checkbook in your pocket.

## Why the Cheapest Fence Bid Usually Costs More

Here’s the pattern we see over and over in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties. Three bids come in. One is noticeably cheaper, sometimes 25 or 30 percent under the others. The landowner takes it, because a fence is a fence, right?

It isn’t. Two bids that both say “5-strand barbed wire, 2,600 feet” can describe two very different fences. One might use 12.5 gauge Class 3 galvanized wire on treated posts with welded pipe H-braces at every corner. The other might use thin-gauge Class 1 wire on undersized posts with a single leaning cedar corner post that will pull over by the second summer.

Dale, a cow-calf operator just outside Crawford, learned this the expensive way before he called us. He took a $7,300 bid on 2,600 feet of barbed wire over a $10,400 bid. The cheap crew skipped braced corners entirely. Within eighteen months every corner had leaned, the wire sagged, and his heifers were walking through it. He paid another $2,100 just to rebuild four corners with proper H-braces. The “cheap” fence ended up costing $9,400 and still wasn’t as good as the bid he passed on.

Questions are how you catch that gap before you sign, not after your cattle find it. If you’d rather just talk it through with somebody local, call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk your fence line with you. Written estimates are free and we’ll put every spec on paper.

## Questions to Ask a Fence Contractor About Price and Materials

The first four questions are about what you’re actually buying. Get specific answers, in writing, every time.

1. What exactly does the price per foot include?

“Three dollars a foot” means nothing by itself. Does that include tearing out the old fence? Clearing brush off the line? Corner braces, gates, water gaps? Ask for an itemized bid that separates materials, labor, tear-out, and extras. When the bid is itemized, you can compare it against other bids line by line instead of guessing.

2. What class and gauge of wire are you using?

For barbed wire, the answer you want is 12.5 gauge, Class 3 galvanized. Class 1 wire can start rusting in a handful of years in our humidity, while Class 3 zinc coating commonly lasts decades. The price difference is small per roll and huge over the life of the fence. If the bidder can’t tell you the class of the wire, that tells you plenty. We break this down in detail in our guide to Class 3 galvanized wire.

3. What are the posts, and how far apart?

Ask for species, treatment, diameter, and depth. Around here, a common solid answer is treated pine or cedar line posts set 2.5 to 3 feet deep, or T-posts with wood pulls, on 10 to 12 foot spacing for barbed wire. Wider spacing saves the contractor money and costs you tension. Our fence post spacing guide covers what’s normal for each fence type.

4. How will you brace the corners and gate openings?

This is the single most important structural question on the list. Corners carry the entire pull of the fence, and a fence with weak corners fails no matter how good the wire is. The right answer involves H-braces, either wood with a diagonal brace wire or welded pipe. “We set a big corner post deep” is not an answer. It’s a warning.

Here’s what honest, itemized pricing typically looks like in the Waco area right now:

Fence type Typical installed price What the bid should itemize

5-strand barbed wire $2.50 to $4.50 per ft Wire class, post type and spacing, H-braces

Net wire (field fence) $3.50 to $6.00 per ft Knot style, top barbed strand, brace count

Pipe fence $10 to $20+ per ft Pipe size and schedule, new vs used pipe

High game fence $6.50 to $10+ per ft Wire height, fixed knot spec, clearing

Tear-out of old fence $0.50 to $2.00 per ft Haul-off and disposal included or not

If a bid lands way under these ranges, something on that list is getting skipped. Our ranch fence cost page has fuller numbers by fence type and acreage.

## Questions to Ask Your Fence Builder About the Crew and the Job

Materials are half the fence. The people building it are the other half.

5. Who actually builds the fence, your crew or a sub?

Plenty of good contractors use subcontractors. The problem is when the guy who bid the job never sets foot on it again. Ask who runs the crew day to day, and who you call when there’s a question at 7 a.m. on a Tuesday.

6. Can you show me proof of liability insurance?

Not “yes, we’re insured.” An actual certificate of insurance, sent from the insurance company. If an uninsured crew hits your water line, breaks a septic lateral, or hurts somebody on your land, that bill can land on you.

Marcy runs goats on 30 acres near Valley Mills, and she skipped this question once. The crew she hired trenched through a buried water line to her stock tank, shrugged, and left. No insurance, no recourse, and an $1,800 repair bill she paid out of her own pocket. The certificate takes the contractor five minutes to send. Ask for it every time.

7. How long will the job take, and what about my cattle in the meantime?

A contractor who builds ranch fence for a living has an answer ready: how many feet per day the crew averages, how they’ll sequence tear-out and rebuild so pastures stay closed, and what happens if rain shuts the job down. If you’re running cattle on the place, staging matters as much as speed. See our post on how long fence installation takes for realistic timelines by fence type.

8. What happens when you hit rock, or the creek crossing?

Between the blackland clay east of I-35 and the limestone shelves out toward China Spring and Crawford, surprises underground are normal here. Ask how rock is handled and priced before it happens. Same for water gaps at creeks and draws, which need their own hardware and design. A contractor who says “we’ll figure it out” is telling you the change orders will be figured out on your dime.

## Contract, Warranty, and Cleanup Questions Before You Sign

The last four questions protect you after the handshake.

9. What’s the payment schedule?

A reasonable structure is a modest deposit to hold your spot on the schedule and cover materials, with the balance due when the work is done and you’ve walked the line. Be very careful with anyone wanting half or more up front.

Tommy, west of West up Highway 77, paid a $4,500 deposit, 60 percent of the job, to a crew that then went quiet for two months. He eventually got part of it back, but only after a lot of phone calls and a demand letter. The Texas Attorney General’s office publishes solid guidance on hiring contractors and avoiding home improvement scams at texasattorneygeneral.gov. It’s worth ten minutes of your time before any big job.

10. What’s the warranty, and is it in writing?

Ask two separate questions: what does the manufacturer warranty on materials, and what does the contractor warranty on workmanship? A leaning post or a slipped brace six months in should be the contractor’s problem, not yours. If the warranty isn’t written into the contract, it doesn’t exist.

11. Who hauls off the old fence and cleans up the line?

Old wire, rotten posts, brush piles, and concrete chunks don’t disappear on their own. Tear-out and haul-off should be a line item with a price, not an assumption. Rolled-up old barbed wire left in a pasture is a vet bill waiting to happen.

12. Can you give me addresses of fences you built three or more years ago?

Anybody can show you a fence they finished last month. New fence always looks good. What you want is a fence that’s been through a few Central Texas summers, a couple of ice storms, and a thousand head-rubs. Then drive by and look at the corners. Corners tell the truth.

Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension also publishes good independent material on fence construction and livestock fencing standards at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu if you want to study up before taking bids.

## Red Flags That Should End the Conversation

Some answers should stop the deal on the spot, no matter how good the price looks:

- No written estimate. A verbal quote for a five-figure fence job is not a quote. It’s a setup for a dispute.

- Big cash deposit, right now. Pressure plus prepayment is the oldest bad combination in contracting.

- “Trust me” instead of specs. Wire class, post depth, brace design, and spacing all fit on one page. A pro will happily write them down.

- No local jobs to show. If nobody within an hour of Waco will vouch for the work, there’s usually a reason.

- Vague answers on insurance. “We’ve never had a problem” is not a certificate.

- A bid far below everyone else. Not always a scam, but always a question. Something is different, and you need to know what.

One more thing worth saying plainly. If you’re comparing bids and can’t tell why they’re different, don’t guess. Read our walkthrough on how to compare fence quotes, or bring us the other bids. We’ll tell you honestly what’s in them, even if you don’t hire us. Request a free written estimate and we’ll put our own numbers next to theirs, spec for spec.

## What a Good Answer Sounds Like

You don’t need to become a fencing expert to hire well. You just need to notice how the contractor handles the questions.

A pro answers in specifics. Gauge numbers, post depths, feet per day, brace designs, dollar amounts. They put it in writing without being asked twice. They’d rather lose a job than promise something they can’t build, and they’re comfortable with you checking references and insurance because they’ve got both.

A problem contractor answers in generalities and gets a little irritated that you’re asking at all. The irritation is the answer.

Whether you need a quarter mile of barbed wire fence around a hay trap or two miles of pipe fence along a county road, the questions above work the same. Ask all twelve. Write down the answers. Sign with the outfit whose answers you’d be happy to read back in three years.

If that outfit turns out to be us, good. Call (254) 870-8898 or send us a note and we’ll come walk the line, measure it, and hand you a written bid that answers all twelve questions before you even ask. And if a storm or a downed tree just put your cattle on the wrong side of the wire, our emergency line runs 24/7.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How many bids should I get before hiring a fence contractor?

Three is the sweet spot for most ranch fence jobs around Waco. Fewer than that and you have no baseline for price or specs. More than four or five and you’re mostly burning weeks for small differences. Make sure every bidder quotes the same footage, wire, and brace count so you’re comparing like to like.

### Is a big deposit normal for ranch fencing work?

A modest deposit to cover materials and hold your place on the schedule is normal, especially on pipe fence where the steel order is a real cost. What’s not normal is 50 percent or more up front, in cash, before a post is set. Keep the bulk of the payment tied to finished, inspected work.

### Do fence contractors need a license in Texas?

Texas doesn’t issue a state license specifically for fence contractors, which is exactly why your questions matter so much. Since the state isn’t screening anyone, the screening is on you. Insurance certificates, written contracts, local references, and aged fences you can drive past are how you vet a fence builder here.

### What should be in a fence contract before I sign?

At minimum: total footage, wire type and class, post type, spacing and depth, brace design and count, gates and water gaps, tear-out and haul-off, total price with payment schedule, a start window, and the workmanship warranty in plain words. If it’s not written in the contract, treat it as not included. A one-page handshake deal protects the contractor, not you.

## Fencing and Your Texas Ag Exemption: What Counts and What Doesn't (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/ag-exemption-fencing-texas/)

> Wondering if your fence counts toward a Texas ag exemption? Here's what appraisal districts look for, the sales tax break on materials, and real Waco costs.

Texas Law

# Fencing and Your Texas Ag Exemption: What Counts and What Doesn't
Published July 25, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

The same 25 acres outside Waco can carry a property tax bill of $4,500 a year, or right around $200. Same dirt, same view of the Brazos, same county.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

The same 25 acres outside Waco can carry a property tax bill of $4,500 a year, or right around $200. Same dirt, same view of the Brazos, same county. The difference is agricultural appraisal, what everybody around here calls the ag exemption, and whether you keep it often comes down to something as simple as your fence.

We build fence for a living, not tax law, but the ag exemption fence Texas question comes up on almost every estimate we run in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties. New landowners want to know if building a fence gets them the exemption. Folks who already have it want to know if a sagging fence can lose it. And nearly everybody wants to know if their fencing materials can be bought tax free.

So let’s walk through what counts, what doesn’t, and what it actually costs to get your place fenced to a standard the appraisal district takes seriously. And if you’d rather just talk it through with somebody who builds this stuff every day, call us at (254) 870-8898. The conversation’s free.

## What the Texas Ag Exemption Actually Is (and Isn’t)

First, a quick correction that matters. There’s no such thing as a true ag “exemption” on property taxes in Texas. What you’re really after is open-space agricultural appraisal, usually called 1-d-1 appraisal, under the Texas Property Tax Code.

Here’s the plain-English version. Instead of taxing your land on market value, the county appraisal district taxes it on productivity value, meaning what the land earns as grazing or crop land. Market value on small acreage near Waco might run $12,000 to $20,000 an acre. Productivity value on native pasture might be $100 to $200 an acre. That’s why the tax savings are so dramatic.

To qualify, your land generally has to be used for agriculture to the degree of intensity typical for your area, and it has to have that history. In most cases the land needs ag use in five of the past seven years. Your county appraisal district sets the local standards, so McLennan CAD’s expectations can differ from Bosque or Falls.

The full rules live with the Texas Comptroller, and their agricultural and timber page is worth a read before you make any big decisions. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension also publishes solid, free guidance on stocking rates and land management at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu.

Where does fencing fit? That’s the part most people get wrong, in both directions.

## Does Your Fence Count Toward a Texas Ag Exemption?

Here’s the honest answer: a fence by itself does not qualify land for ag appraisal. You can build the prettiest pipe fence in Central Texas around 20 acres of mowed grass, and if there’s no livestock, no hay operation, no bona fide ag use, the appraisal district owes you nothing.

But flip it around and fencing becomes critical. If your ag use is grazing cattle, sheep, or goats, you cannot demonstrate a real livestock operation without a fence that actually holds livestock. Appraisal districts look at what they call degree of intensity, and for grazing operations that checklist almost always includes:

- Perimeter fencing adequate to contain the class of livestock you run

- Stocking at a rate typical for the county, often in the range of one animal unit per 5 to 15 acres depending on the land

- Working water, and some evidence of management like shredding, feeding, or rotation

So the fence isn’t the qualification. The fence is the proof. A field inspector who finds three strands of rusted wire laying in the weeds, no cattle in sight, has an easy call to make. A tight five-strand barbed wire perimeter with cows behind it tells the whole story in one glance.

If you’re starting from bare land, get your grazing plan and your fence plan moving together. We give free written estimates, and we can usually tell you within a day what a perimeter will cost. Call us at (254) 870-8898 or request an estimate here and we’ll walk the line with you.

One more wrinkle worth knowing. If you’re headed toward a wildlife management exemption, the land must already have ag appraisal first, and high fencing often enters the picture. Our game fence installation crews handle that conversion regularly, and the rules on height and design are stricter than most folks expect.

## The Sales Tax Side: Buying Ag Exempt Fencing Materials in Texas

Here’s where fence and taxes connect in a way that puts real money back in your pocket. Texas charges up to 8.25 percent sales tax. But if you hold an Ag/Timber Number from the Texas Comptroller, fencing materials used exclusively on a farm or ranch to produce agricultural products for sale are exempt from sales tax.

That covers the stuff a working fence is made of. Wire, T-posts, wood posts, pipe, gates, stays, clips, corner brace materials. On a big job, the savings are not pocket change.

A few things trip people up:

- You need the number first. The Ag/Timber Number is free from the Comptroller, and you can apply online. Without it, you pay tax like anybody else.

- The use has to be agricultural production. Fencing your yard, your driveway, or a weekend place with no ag operation doesn’t qualify, even if the land has ag appraisal.

- How your contractor writes the contract matters. Tax treatment can differ between lump-sum and separated contracts. Tell your fence contractor up front that you have an Ag/Timber Number so the paperwork gets done right from day one.

The property tax appraisal and the sales tax exemption are two separate programs. Plenty of landowners have one and not the other. If you run livestock for sale, there’s rarely a good reason not to have both.

Talk is cheap, fence isn’t. Here’s what we’re actually seeing on jobs across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties in 2026, priced per foot and per mile so you can run your own math. A mile is 5,280 feet, and a square 10 acres needs about 2,640 feet of perimeter.

## Mistakes That Cost Landowners Their Ag Valuation

We’ve seen each of these happen to real people in our service area. Learn from them for free.

Building the fence and stopping there. A fence with no livestock and no ag activity behind it is just an expensive property line. The appraisal district needs to see actual use, year after year.

Letting the fence fail while the cattle stay. If the herd spends more time on the county road than your pasture, you’ve got trouble stacked on trouble. Escaped cattle are a wreck risk, and a chronically open perimeter undercuts your claim of a managed operation. If your cows are already testing weak spots, fix the fence before the appraisal district or a passing driver finds the gap for you.

Losing the history when buying land. Ag appraisal doesn’t automatically ride along with a sale. If you buy a place and let the use lapse, requalifying takes years. Walk the fences before you close, and keep stock on the place from day one if you can.

Ignoring rollback taxes. Take land out of ag use, maybe to subdivide or build, and the county can claw back the tax difference for the previous three years plus interest. On land near town, that bill can land in five figures per acre. Know the number before you change the use.

Cheaping out on corners. A CAD inspector may never look at your braces, but your cattle will. Corners and braces are where fence integrity lives, and rebuilding them later costs more than doing them right the first time.

Here’s a good rule for when to stop patching and call a professional: if more than a quarter of a line needs work, if braces are leaning, or if you’re fencing along a road where an escape could hurt somebody, get a pro involved. Wire under tension can hurt you badly, and a fence that fails at the wrong time can cost far more than the repair ever would.

Then build a perimeter that holds your livestock in dry years and wet ones.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does building a fence qualify my land for an ag exemption in Texas?

No. A fence alone doesn’t qualify anything. Ag appraisal is based on actual agricultural use, like grazing or hay production, at the intensity typical for your county, usually for five of the past seven years. The fence is evidence that supports a grazing operation, not a substitute for one.

### Are fencing materials really tax free with an ag exemption?

They can be, but it’s a separate program from your property tax appraisal. You need an Ag/Timber Number from the Texas Comptroller, and the fence has to be used on a farm or ranch producing agricultural products for sale. With the number, wire, posts, pipe, gates, and brace materials can be purchased free of sales tax.

### Will replacing my old fence trigger a rollback or reappraisal?

Replacing or upgrading a fence doesn’t trigger rollback taxes. Rollbacks happen when land changes from ag use to non-ag use, like development, and they reach back three years plus interest. A better fence that keeps livestock where they belong actually strengthens your position with the appraisal district.

### How good does my fence have to be for the appraisal district?

Good enough to genuinely contain the livestock you claim to be raising. For cattle in Central Texas, that usually means a sound 4 or 5-strand barbed wire perimeter or equivalent, with solid corners and gates that close. Districts don’t grade on looks, but a fence that obviously can’t hold stock invites hard questions during a field review.

## The Annual Ranch Fence Maintenance Checklist Every Central Texas Rancher Needs (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/ranch-fence-maintenance-checklist/)

> A season-by-season ranch fence maintenance checklist for Central Texas. Catch sagging wire, rotting posts, and washed-out water gaps before cattle get out.

Ranch Fencing

# The Annual Ranch Fence Maintenance Checklist Every Central Texas Rancher Needs
Published August 20, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A $65 splice today or a $2,300 corner rebuild next spring. That's the real choice most ranchers are making every time they drive past a sagging stretch of wire and tell themselves they'll get to it later.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A $65 splice today or a $2,300 corner rebuild next spring. That’s the real choice most ranchers are making every time they drive past a sagging stretch of wire and tell themselves they’ll get to it later.

We build and repair fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and the pattern never changes. The ranches that spend a few weekends a year on ranch fence maintenance almost never call us in a panic. The ones that don’t are the folks calling our emergency line at 10 pm because a bull is standing in the middle of a farm-to-market road.

This checklist is the same routine we recommend to every customer after we finish a job. Print it, stick it in the truck, and work through it season by season. Most of it takes a pair of fence pliers, a bucket of staples, and a good pair of gloves.

## Why Ranch Fence Maintenance Beats Emergency Repairs Every Time

Fence problems are cheap when they’re small and expensive when they’re not. A loose staple costs nothing to fix. A leaning corner post that’s been pulling for two years takes a full H-brace rebuild, and that’s real money.

Dale Hutchins runs about 120 momma cows on a place near Crawford. Two summers ago he noticed a corner post on his east line starting to lean and figured it would hold through fall. It didn’t. The corner gave way after a wet October, four spans of wire went slack, and his cows found the gap within a week. By the time we rebuilt the corner, restretched 600 feet of wire, and he’d paid a neighbor for a flattened food plot, Dale was out about $2,300. The fix in July would’ve been a $65 brace wire and an afternoon.

That’s the math behind every line on this checklist. Fence doesn’t fail all at once. It fails slowly, then suddenly. Your job is to catch it in the slow phase.

Twice-a-year inspections are the backbone. In Central Texas the natural rhythm is early spring, before things green up and hide problems, and late fall, before winter weather and hungry cattle start testing your wire. If you’d rather have a professional set of eyes on it, we do fence-line inspections with a free written estimate for any work we find. Call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk your lines with you.

## The Spring Ranch Fence Inspection: Walk or Ride Every Foot

Spring is your big one. Winter freezes, saturated clay, and storm season all do their damage between November and March, and you want it found before summer bakes the ground hard.

Ride your entire perimeter, not just the stretches you can see from the county road. Take fence pliers, a hammer, staples, wire clips, and a can of spray paint to mark anything you can’t fix on the spot.

Here’s what to check:

- Every corner and gate post. Push on them hard. Any movement at all means the brace assembly is failing or the ground has let go. Corners carry the tension for the whole line, so a weak corner is a weak fence. If your braces look rough, our guide to H-brace fence corners shows what a proper assembly looks like.

- Wire tension on every stretch. Grab the top strand mid-span. More than an inch or two of easy deflection means it needs a splice-and-stretch. Sagging wire is the number one thing cattle learn to push through, and our post on fixing sagging barbed wire fence walks through the repair step by step.

- Line posts. Look for leaners, snapped T-posts, and wood posts that wiggle at the ground line. Probe wood posts with a screwdriver right at the soil. If the tip sinks in, rot has started. Catch it early and you replace one post, not twenty. More on that in our fence post rot article.

- Staples and clips. Loose staples let wire slide and sag. Reset them as you go. On T-posts, replace any missing wire clips.

- Water gaps. Every creek and draw crossing needs a hard look after spring rains. A washed-out water gap fence is an open door, and cattle find open doors fast.

- Gates and latches. Swing every gate. Tighten hinge bolts, oil latches, and check that gate posts haven’t heaved.

- Grounding and chargers on electric fence. Test voltage at the far end of every hot line, not just at the charger.

Marcy Templin, who runs stockers on leased ground outside China Spring, learned the water gap lesson the hard way. A spring flood took out a gap on Hog Creek and she didn’t check it for three weeks. Fourteen head crossed onto the neighbor’s wheat. Between gathering costs, a hired day of labor, and paying for grazed-out wheat, she figured it cost her about $1,900. The gap itself was a $450 rebuild. Now she checks every crossing within 48 hours of any hard rain.

## Summer Upkeep: Heat, Drought, and Brush on the Line

Summer maintenance is less about the fence and more about what’s happening around it.

Drought is hard on fence in ways people don’t expect. When our blackland clay dries out, it shrinks and cracks, and posts that were tight in April can be loose by August. Walk your corners again in mid-summer and check for movement. If you’re on heavy clay, our post on fence posts in clay soil explains why this happens and what depth and concrete work actually fix it.

Brush is the other summer job. Cedar, mesquite, and greenbriar growing into your fence line do three things: they hide damage, they hold moisture against your wire and speed up rust, and they give feral hogs cover to root right along your fence. Clearing a strip on both sides of the wire is some of the highest-value ranch fence maintenance you can do. It also makes every future inspection twice as fast because you can actually see the fence.

Summer is also when hog damage shows up, since dry conditions push hogs toward creek bottoms and stock tanks. Look for rooted-up soil under your bottom strand and stretched or popped net wire. Patch small breaches immediately, because hogs return to a working hole every night until it’s fixed.

Two more quick summer items:

- Check any stretch of fence near a stock tank or pond. Cattle crowd there in the heat and lean on wire while they wait their turn.

- Look at your shade lines. Wherever cattle bunch up under oaks in July, the fence behind them takes a beating.

## Fall and Winter Prep: The Second Annual Fence Inspection

Your fall inspection mirrors the spring one, but the priorities shift. Now you’re getting ready for winter weather and for the season when grass runs short and cattle start reaching through fences for whatever’s green on the other side.

Work through this list in October or November:

- Restretch anything marginal. Wire that’s borderline in October will be on the ground by February once ice storms and cattle pressure hit it.

- Replace questionable posts now. Setting posts is miserable work in a January cold snap. Do it in decent weather.

- Walk every foot of fence between your herd and a road. This is the stretch that matters most. Texas courts look hard at whether a rancher maintained his fences when cattle end up on a roadway, and our article on cattle on road liability in Texas covers why that fence deserves your best wire and your closest attention.

- Service gates before mud season. A gate that drags in November will be dug into a mudhole by January.

- Test electric fence weekly through winter. Dry winter soil weakens grounding, and a charger that reads fine at the barn can be dead two pastures away.

- Stockpile repair material. Keep a roll of wire, a bag of staples, splice sleeves, and two spare posts in the barn. Storm repairs happen on the storm’s schedule, not yours.

Roy Kubacak, who backgrounds calves on a place east of West, puts it simply: he spends two Saturdays every November on fence and hasn’t had calves out in six years. His neighbor skipped fall prep last year, lost a stretch of rusted wire in a February ice storm, and spent $3,100 on an emergency rebuild plus a long cold night gathering calves off Highway 77 right-of-way. Same weather, same county, very different winter.

If your fall walk-through turns up more problems than you can handle before winter, don’t sit on it. Request a free written estimate and we’ll tell you straight what needs fixing now and what can wait until spring.

## What Maintenance Costs vs. What Neglect Costs

Here’s the comparison we show customers who ask whether maintenance is really worth the time. These are typical Central Texas numbers we see on real jobs.

Problem Caught Early Early Fix Cost Ignored For a Year or Two Typical Cost Later

Loose staples, minor sag $0 to $50 DIY Cattle push through, wire on ground $400 to $900 restretch

One rotting line post $25 to $60 per post Rot spreads, section collapses $1,500 to $4,000 section rebuild

Leaning corner post $50 to $150 brace repair Corner fails, whole line goes slack $1,800 to $3,000 corner and restretch

Small water gap damage $150 to $500 repair Full washout, cattle out $2,000 plus gathering and crop damage

Surface rust on old wire Monitor, spot-splice Brittle wire snaps under load $2 to $4 per foot full replacement

Brush on fence line Weekend of clearing Hidden damage, hog highways, rust Varies, often thousands

Notice the pattern. Almost every line item gets ten times more expensive when it’s ignored. A full picture of replacement pricing is in our ranch fence cost guide, and if your barbed wire is at the end of its life, our barbed wire fence installation page covers what new construction runs per foot.

Good maintenance also stretches the life of the fence itself. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid guidance on livestock fencing construction and materials at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu, and the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service at nrcs.usda.gov offers fencing practice standards and, in some cases, cost-share programs for qualifying landowners. Both are worth a look before your next big fence decision.

## When to Stop Patching and Call a Professional

Most of this checklist is honest DIY work, and we’d never tell a rancher to pay for something he can do with pliers and an afternoon. But there’s a line where patching stops making sense, and knowing where it is will save you money.

Call a professional when:

- Corners or H-braces have failed. Brace assemblies carry serious tension. Built wrong, they fail again within a year, and a snapped brace wire under load can hurt you.

- You’re splicing the same stretch every month. Wire that’s rusted brittle can’t be saved a splice at a time. At some point you’re spending replacement money on repairs.

- More than about a third of your posts in a section are bad. Past that point, section replacement is cheaper per year of fence life than post-by-post patching.

- Storm damage is widespread. Trees on wire, multiple broken posts, and downed spans across a whole pasture need equipment and crew, not a weekend.

- The fence holds cattle next to a road. This is not the place for a marginal repair. The liability risk is too high to gamble on old wire.

One safety note we mean sincerely: never cut a wire that’s under heavy tension without knowing where it will go, and stay clear of any fence tangled with downed power lines. Call the utility first, every time.

If your inspection turned up problems bigger than a bucket of staples can solve, call (254) 870-8898. Estimates are free and in writing, and our emergency line answers 24/7 when cattle are out or a storm has your fence on the ground.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How often should I inspect my ranch fence?

Walk or ride the full perimeter twice a year, once in early spring and once in late fall. Add a quick check after every major storm, flood, or hard freeze, paying special attention to water gaps and any fence along a road. Most serious fence failures give weeks or months of warning to anyone who’s looking.

### How long should a well-maintained barbed wire fence last?

With good posts, quality galvanized wire, and regular upkeep, 30 to 40 years is realistic in Central Texas, and some fences go longer. Neglected fence often needs major work in half that time. The biggest life-extenders are keeping brush off the wire, fixing sags before cattle exploit them, and replacing rotting posts one at a time instead of letting rot spread.

### What’s the most important part of the fence to maintain?

Corners and gate ends, without question. They carry the tension for every strand on the line, so one failed corner can put a quarter mile of fence on the ground. After corners, prioritize water gaps and any stretch separating your cattle from a public road, since those failures cost the most when they happen.

### Is it worth paying someone to do fence maintenance?

Routine work like stapling, clipping, and minor splices is well within most ranchers’ reach. Paying a professional makes sense for brace rebuilds, large restretches, storm damage, and any job where more than a third of the posts or wire in a section is failing. A good contractor will give you a written estimate and tell you honestly which repairs can wait.

# Barbed Wire Fence Cost Per Foot and Per Mile in Central Texas

A mile of 5 strand barbed wire fence around Waco runs about $17,000 to $25,000 installed right now. That number surprises folks in both directions. Some landowners expect double that, and some are still working off prices their dad paid in the 90s.

Here’s the short answer on barbed wire fence cost per foot in Central Texas in 2026: most jobs land between $2.50 and $5.50 per foot installed, depending on strand count, post type, terrain, and how far your corners are apart. Barbed wire is still the cheapest way to hold cattle, and that’s why it covers most of the pasture line in Central Texas. Here’s what installed prices look like around Waco right now.

Fence Type Cost Per Foot (Installed) Cost Per Mile (Installed)

## Barbed Wire Fence Cost Per Mile: Budgeting a Big Stretch

Per-foot pricing makes sense for a 600 foot lot line. Once you’re fencing a quarter section, you need to think per mile.

A mile is 5,280 feet. At $3.25 per foot, that’s $17,160. At $4.25, it’s $22,440. Most full-mile jobs we build in Central Texas land between those two numbers for 5 strand fence.

Longer runs usually cost a little less per foot than short ones. The crew mobilizes once, the corners are farther apart, and we can stretch wire in long pulls. A 300 foot job might price at $4.75 per foot because the fixed costs get spread over almost nothing. A mile of clean, straight line might price at $3.35.

Corners and braces are the hidden line item on big jobs. Every corner, gate, and major grade change needs an H-brace, and a properly built H-brace runs $150 to $300 each in materials and labor. A square 160 acre tract has 4 corners minimum, plus braces at every gate. Skimp here and the whole fence sags inside five years. We covered why in our post on H-brace fence corners.

If you’re fencing smaller acreage, the math shifts again. Small tracts cost more per foot than big ones, because the corners and gates stay the same while the footage shrinks.

## What Pushes Your Price Up or Down

Two neighbors on the same road can get quotes a dollar per foot apart and both quotes can be honest. Here’s what moves the number.

Strand count and wire quality. Each added strand costs roughly $0.25 to $0.40 per foot. Most cow-calf operations around here run 5 strands. Cheap 15.5 gauge high-tensile wire costs less up front than 12.5 gauge Class 3 galvanized, but it won’t last near as long in our weather. If you’re not sure how many strands you need, our guide on how many strands of barbed wire sorts it out by livestock type.

Post type and spacing. T-posts are cheapest. Wood line posts cost more but handle cattle pressure better. Most of our fences run wood posts every 50 to 100 feet with T-posts between, on 10 to 12 foot spacing.

Terrain and soil. Sandy loam east of Waco digs easy. The limestone ridges out toward Crawford and Valley Mills eat auger bits. Rock drilling can add $0.50 to $1.00 per foot on bad stretches. Creek crossings need water gaps, which are their own little project.

Brush and old fence. Clearing a grown-up fence line runs $1.00 to $3.00 per foot depending on how thick it is. Tearing out and hauling off old wire and posts usually adds $0.50 to $1.00 per foot.

Gates and entrances. Every opening adds hardware, bracing, and labor. A plain tube gate is a few hundred dollars. A cattle guard is a few thousand. Decide what each entrance actually needs before the crew shows up, because adding a gate mid-job costs more than planning it in.

Access and distance. A line the truck can drive builds fast. A line we have to pack materials into by hand or ATV builds slow, and slow is what you pay for. Fence lines along a bluff, through a bottom, or behind a locked neighbor gate all add hours that show up on the quote.

One more thing worth saying: wire and steel prices have bounced around a lot since 2020. A quote from two years ago is stale, and so is a price your neighbor got in 2019. If your budget is built on old numbers, get a fresh quote before you commit to a plan.

The USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service publishes cost data and specs for livestock fencing through its conservation practice standards, and it’s worth a look if you want a second reference point. You’ll find it at nrcs.usda.gov. Just remember national averages don’t price your rocky hillside.

## DIY or Hire a Crew? Where the Math Breaks

Plenty of ranchers around here can build fence, and we’ll never pretend otherwise. If you’ve got a tractor with an auger, a helper, and time, you can build barbed wire fence for materials cost plus your weekends.

Here’s the honest math though. Materials run $0.90 to $1.60 per foot. A quarter mile is 1,320 feet, so call it $1,300 to $2,100 in materials. Hiring it out at $3.00 per foot costs about $3,960. You’re saving roughly $2,000 to $2,600 for what’s realistically 4 to 6 full days of hard labor for two people, assuming nothing goes wrong.

Where DIY goes sideways is corners, stretching, and rock. A wire stretcher under tension stores serious energy, and a snapped strand of barbed wire will cut you before you see it move. Post holes in limestone will burn up a rented auger in an afternoon. And a fence with weak corners fails no matter how good the wire work is.

Our rule of thumb: DIY short repairs and small paddocks if you know what you’re doing. Hire out long runs, road frontage, rocky ground, and anything where a failure puts cattle on pavement. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension has solid livestock fencing guidance if you do go the DIY route, at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu.

And know when to stop. If a stretch fails and cattle are out near a road, that’s not a weekend project anymore. That’s a liability problem at 2 a.m. Our 24/7 emergency line exists for exactly that: (254) 870-8898.

Per-foot price with scope spelled out. Strand count, wire gauge and class, post type and spacing, number of braced corners, and gates listed separately. If a quote just says “fence, $2.75/ft,” you don’t know what you’re buying.

Get two or three written numbers, compare what’s actually in them line by line, and pick the crew that walked your ground and answered your questions straight.

## Barbed Wire Gauge: 12.5 vs 15.5 and Why It Matters (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/barbed-wire-gauge/)

> 12.5 or 15.5 gauge barbed wire? See breaking strength, cost per mile, and which gauge holds Central Texas cattle. Waco fence pros explain the difference.

Materials

# Barbed Wire Gauge: 12.5 vs 15.5 and Why It Matters
Published July 26, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Pick up two rolls of barbed wire at the farm store outside Waco and you'll notice something strange. One roll weighs about 80 pounds. The other weighs closer to 47.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Pick up two rolls of barbed wire at the farm store outside Waco and you’ll notice something strange. One roll weighs about 80 pounds. The other weighs closer to 47. Both stretch 1,320 feet, both carry sharp four-point barbs, and both claim they’ll hold your cattle. The difference is barbed wire gauge, and picking the wrong one can cost you a snapped fence, a herd on the county road, or an extra $1,000 a mile you didn’t need to spend.

We build and repair barbed wire fence across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and gauge confusion causes more callbacks than almost anything else. A rancher buys the lighter roll because it’s cheaper, installs it the way his granddad installed the heavy stuff, and wonders why it broke the first winter. Another pays a premium for heavy wire on a long, flat run where the lighter wire would have done the same job for less.

This guide covers what those gauge numbers actually mean, how 12.5 and 15.5 compare on strength and cost, and which one belongs on your place.

## What Barbed Wire Gauge Actually Means

Gauge is a measure of wire diameter, and here’s the part that trips almost everybody up: the bigger the number, the thinner the wire.

- 12.5 gauge wire measures about 0.099 inches across

- 15.5 gauge wire measures about 0.067 inches across

So 15.5 gauge is the skinny wire and 12.5 gauge is the thick wire, even though 15.5 is the bigger number. Blame the old steel mills for that system. It’s been confusing ranchers for a hundred years and it’s not changing now.

Barbed wire is two strands twisted together with barbs wrapped in at set spacing, usually every 4 or 5 inches. So when you compare gauges, you’re comparing the thickness of each of those two strands. Thicker strands mean more steel, more weight per roll, and more resistance to nicks, rust, and abrasion over the years.

But thickness alone doesn’t tell you how strong the wire is. That depends on the steel itself, which is where most buying mistakes happen. We’ll get to that in a minute.

If you’re staring at a fence line right now and don’t know what’s strung on it, we can tell you in about two minutes. Call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk you through checking it, or come out and look for free.

## 12.5 vs 15.5 Gauge: Side by Side

Here’s how the two most common barbed wire gauges stack up. The 12.5 numbers assume standard low-carbon wire, and the 15.5 numbers assume high-tensile wire, because that’s how each gauge is almost always sold.

Spec 12.5 Gauge (Low-Carbon) 15.5 Gauge (High-Tensile)

Strand diameter ~0.099 in ~0.067 in

Typical breaking strength ~950 lbs ~850 to 950 lbs

Roll weight (1,320 ft) 75 to 80 lbs 45 to 50 lbs

Stretch behavior Stretches and stays stretched Barely stretches, springs back

Typical post spacing 10 to 12 ft 15 to 20 ft with stays

Typical roll price $85 to $110 $70 to $90

Ease of hand splicing Easy Harder, wire fights you

Best fit Repairs, heavy stock pressure, brushy or flood-prone lines Long new runs with strong corners

Read that breaking strength row twice, because it surprises people. The skinny 15.5 gauge high-tensile wire breaks at nearly the same load as the thick 12.5 gauge wire. That’s the whole point of high-tensile steel. You get similar strength from about half the weight of material.

Where they really differ is in how they behave before they break, how they handle abuse, and what they demand from your posts and corners.

## Low-Carbon vs High-Tensile: What the Gauge Number Doesn’t Tell You

The gauge number tells you thickness. It doesn’t tell you what kind of steel you’re holding, and that matters just as much.

Low-carbon wire, the traditional 12.5 gauge stuff, is soft and forgiving. It stretches like taffy when you tension it, and it stays where you put it. You can splice it with pliers, tie it off by hand, and wrap it around a staple without a fight. When a cow hits it, the wire gives a little and absorbs the blow. The tradeoff is that it sags over time and needs periodic re-tensioning.

High-tensile wire, which is almost always 15.5 gauge in barbed wire, is a harder steel with roughly double the tensile strength per unit of area. It holds tension for years without sagging, resists elongation, and springs back when livestock hit it instead of stretching out. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension and other land-grant programs have pushed high-tensile fencing for decades because it delivers more fence per dollar on long runs. The University of Georgia’s fencing guide, Fences for the Farm, is a solid free reference on how the two steel types behave.

The catch is that high-tensile wire is unforgiving. It’s springy and hard to hand-splice, it demands properly built corners because it transfers full tension to them, and it can recoil hard when it’s cut under load. If your corner posts are marginal, high-tensile wire will find out. Our guide on H-brace fence corners explains what a corner has to look like before high-tensile wire goes anywhere near it.

One more thing the gauge number hides: coating. Wire in either gauge comes in Class 1 or Class 3 galvanizing, and in Central Texas heat and humidity, Class 1 can start rusting in 8 to 10 years while Class 3 goes 25 or more. We break that down in our post on Class 3 galvanized wire. Never judge a roll by gauge alone. Check the coating class printed on the tag.

## Which Barbed Wire Gauge Fits Central Texas Ranches

There’s no single right answer, but after years of building fence around Waco, China Spring, Crawford, and down through Lorena, the pattern is pretty clear.

Go 12.5 gauge low-carbon when: you’re repairing or extending an existing low-carbon fence, you’ve got heavy cattle pressure on a small pasture, your fence line runs through brush or timber where limbs fall on it, or the line crosses creek bottoms that catch flood debris. Soft wire takes that kind of abuse better and it’s far easier to splice back together after a hit. It’s also the safer choice for anyone doing their own repairs.

Go 15.5 gauge high-tensile when: you’re building a long new perimeter run on open ground, your corners and braces are built right, and you want wider post spacing to cut material costs. On a mile of straight fence, the savings are real.

Two jobs from this past year show both sides of it.

Dale Kubacek runs about 60 cows on 300 acres near West. Last fall he bought eight rolls of 15.5 gauge high-tensile because it was $18 a roll cheaper, then stretched it with a come-along the way he’d always stretched soft wire. Over-tensioned high-tensile has no give left in it, and when a February cold snap contracted the wire, three strands snapped along a quarter mile stretch. Fourteen cows ended up on an FM road at daybreak. Between our emergency call-out, rebuilding two brace corners, and restringing that section correctly, Dale spent about $2,400 fixing a fence that was three months old. The wire wasn’t the problem. The installation was.

The Hoffman place in Crawford went the other way. They had us build a half mile of new five-strand perimeter on open coastal pasture with fresh cedar corner posts. We ran 15.5 gauge high-tensile with Class 3 coating, stretched posts to 16 feet with twist stays between, and the wider spacing plus lighter wire saved them right at $900 compared to the 12.5 gauge quote. Three years on, that fence is still banjo-tight and they haven’t touched it.

Same two gauges. Opposite outcomes. The difference was matching the wire to the site and installing it the way that wire demands.

If you’d rather skip the guesswork, request a free written estimate and we’ll spec the right gauge for your ground, your stock, and your budget.

## What Each Barbed Wire Gauge Costs Per Foot and Per Mile

Here’s the money side, using current Central Texas pricing for a five-strand cattle fence.

Materials only. A mile of five-strand fence needs 20 rolls of wire. At roughly $95 a roll for 12.5 gauge and $80 for 15.5 gauge, that’s $1,900 versus $1,600 in wire, a $300 difference. The bigger savings comes from posts. Stretching T-post spacing from 12 feet to 16 feet with stays drops your post count by about a third, which can trim another $800 to $1,200 per mile.

Installed. Professionally built five-strand barbed wire fence in our area generally runs $1.50 to $2.50 per foot, or roughly $8,000 to $13,000 per mile depending on terrain, brush clearing, corner count, and gates. High-tensile on clean, open ground lands at the low end. Rocky ground, creek crossings, and heavy brush push either gauge toward the high end. You can see full pricing breakdowns on our ranch fence cost page.

Kathy Rivers bought 42 acres outside Valley Mills in 2024 with an old fence strung in bargain 14 gauge low-carbon wire, the thin economy stuff some stores sell to hit a price point. It had rusted through in under ten years. We pulled it and rebuilt with 12.5 gauge Class 3 wire at $1.85 a foot, about $6,100 for her road frontage and one cross fence. The lesson she’d tell you herself: the cheap thin wire wasn’t 15.5 high-tensile, it was just thin, and it cost her a whole second fence.

That’s the trap with gauge. Thin high-tensile wire is an engineered product. Thin low-carbon wire is just less steel. Know which one is on the shelf before you save $15 a roll.

## Installation Mistakes That Break Either Gauge

Most “bad wire” complaints we get are really installation problems. These are the big four.

Over-tensioning high-tensile wire. Soft 12.5 wire forgives a heavy hand on the stretcher. High-tensile 15.5 doesn’t. Tension it to spec, usually around 200 to 250 pounds, and let its springiness do the work.

Weak corners. Every pound of tension in the wire pulls on your corner assemblies. A single leaning corner post will let a whole run go slack no matter what gauge you strung. If your fence is loose everywhere, check the corners first, then read our fix for a sagging barbed wire fence.

Wrong strand count. Gauge won’t save a three-strand fence that needed five. For cow-calf pairs in our area, five strands is the standard. Our post on how many strands of barbed wire you need covers the tradeoffs by stock type.

Cutting wire under tension. This is the safety one, so hear us plainly. A tensioned strand of high-tensile wire stores serious energy, and when it’s cut it can whip fast enough to cut skin and worse. Wear eye protection, relieve tension before cutting, and never cut a loaded strand at face height. If a tree is down across a tight fence or storm damage has strands loaded in ways you can’t read, stop and call a professional. That’s exactly what our 24/7 emergency line is for: (254) 870-8898. Loose cattle and stored wire tension are both problems that get worse by the hour.

For everything else, from a single water gap to a full perimeter, our crews handle barbed wire fence installation in Waco and the surrounding counties with written quotes and no surprises.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is 15.5 gauge barbed wire as strong as 12.5 gauge?

In breaking strength, very close. High-tensile 15.5 gauge wire breaks at roughly 850 to 950 pounds, about the same as standard 12.5 gauge low-carbon wire at 950 pounds. The difference shows up in behavior, not strength. The 12.5 wire stretches and absorbs abuse, while the 15.5 wire holds tension longer but demands better corners and careful installation.

### Which barbed wire gauge lasts longer in Central Texas?

Coating matters more than gauge for lifespan. Class 3 galvanized wire in either gauge typically lasts 25 to 30 years here, while Class 1 coating can show rust in 8 to 10. That said, once rust starts, the thicker 12.5 gauge wire has more steel to lose, so it usually limps along a few years longer than thin wire in the same condition.

### Can I mix 12.5 and 15.5 gauge wire on the same fence?

You can, and repairs often end up that way, but avoid splicing the two directly in the same strand when possible. They tension differently, so a mixed strand tends to develop slack at the splice. If you’re patching a low-carbon fence, patch with low-carbon wire. Save the high-tensile for full runs between braced corners.

### Do I need different posts or spacing for each gauge?

Yes. Standard 12.5 gauge fence typically gets posts every 10 to 12 feet. High-tensile 15.5 gauge fence can stretch that to 15 to 20 feet with twist stays between posts, which is where most of its cost savings come from. Both need properly built H-brace corners, but high-tensile is far less forgiving if a corner starts to lean.

## Barbed Wire vs Net Wire Fence: Which One Fits Your Livestock? (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/barbed-wire-vs-net-wire/)

> Barbed wire vs net wire fence compared for Central Texas ranchers: real per-foot costs, which livestock each one holds, and when to mix both on one place.

Materials

# Barbed Wire vs Net Wire Fence: Which One Fits Your Livestock?
Published July 27, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

One fence runs about $2 a foot installed and holds cattle just fine. The other runs closer to $4 a foot and holds almost anything with four legs.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

One fence runs about $2 a foot installed and holds cattle just fine. The other runs closer to $4 a foot and holds almost anything with four legs. On a mile of fence, that gap is more than $10,000, so picking wrong hurts twice: once in your wallet, and again when your animals end up on the county road.

The barbed wire vs net wire fence question comes up on nearly every estimate we run in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties. And the honest answer isn’t “one is better.” It’s “one is better for your animals, your land, and your budget.” Cattle, goats, sheep, horses, and hogs all treat a fence differently, and the right choice on a Crawford goat place is usually the wrong choice on a West cow-calf operation.

Here’s how we walk landowners through it, with real numbers.

## What’s the Real Difference Between Barbed Wire and Net Wire?

Barbed wire is a psychological fence. Four to six horizontal strands of twisted, barbed steel wire teach cattle to respect the line because leaning on it stings. There’s nothing below the bottom strand but air, and nothing between strands but more air. That’s fine for a 1,200 pound cow. It’s a revolving door for a 60 pound goat.

Net wire, also called field fence or woven wire, is a physical barrier. Vertical stay wires are woven or knotted to horizontal line wires, forming a mesh from the ground up to 39, 48, or 60 inches. Small animals can’t slip through, and predators have a much harder time getting in. Most net wire fences in our area also get one or two strands of barbed wire run across the top to keep cattle from mashing it down.

Both fences hang on the same bones: solid corner and gate braces, line posts every 10 to 12 feet, and wire stretched tight. The wire is the difference, and the wire is what drives the cost.

If you’re staring at a pasture right now trying to decide, skip the guesswork. Call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk the line with you and put real numbers on both options in a free written estimate.

## Barbed Wire vs Net Wire Fence Cost in Central Texas

Here’s what these fences actually cost installed around Waco in 2026, assuming decent ground and a fence line that’s already clear:

Factor Barbed Wire (5 strand) Net Wire (with top barbed strand)

Installed cost per foot $1.75 to $3.25 $3.50 to $5.50

Cost per mile $9,200 to $17,200 $18,500 to $29,000

Cost for 10 acres (about 2,640 ft) $4,600 to $8,600 $9,200 to $14,500

Holds cattle Yes Yes

Holds goats and sheep No Yes

Holds horses safely Not recommended Yes (2x4 mesh)

Predator resistance Poor Good

Typical lifespan 25 to 40 years 20 to 30 years

Repair difficulty Easy, splice one strand Harder, patch or re-stretch a section

Materials explain most of the gap. A mile of net wire is simply a lot more steel than a mile of five-strand barbed, and it takes more labor to stretch flat and tight without bagging. Rocky ground, brush clearing, and long runs without corners all move these numbers, which is why we put everything in writing before work starts. You can see how we break down pricing on our ranch fence cost page.

One more cost note: wire quality matters more than wire type. Cheap Class 1 galvanized wire of either kind can start rusting in under a decade in our humidity. Class 3 galvanized costs maybe 15 percent more up front and roughly doubles the coating life. On a $20,000 fence, that’s the best $3,000 you’ll ever spend.

## Which Livestock Each Fence Actually Holds

This is where most fence decisions should start, because the animal picks the fence more than the budget does.

Cattle. Five strands of barbed wire on good braces holds cows and most bulls. It’s the standard for a reason: it’s the cheapest fence per foot that reliably does the job. If you run only cattle, net wire is usually money you don’t need to spend. Our barbed wire fence crews in Waco build more of this than everything else combined.

Goats and sheep. Barbed wire flat does not hold them. Goats walk through strand fences like they’re not there, and coyotes walk in the same way. You need net wire, and the knot style matters. We cover the details in our guide to fencing for goats and sheep, but the short version is: 48 inch net wire, small mesh at the bottom, and tight to the ground.

Horses. Barbed wire and horses are a bad mix. A spooked horse that hits barbed wire can tear itself up badly enough for a vet bill that costs more than the fence. Net wire with 2x4 inch mesh, often called horse wire, is the safe budget option.

Feral hogs. Neither fence truly stops a determined boar, but fixed-knot net wire slows hogs way down compared to barbed wire, which they walk under without noticing. If hogs are already tearing up your place, read our post on feral hog fence damage before you spend a dime on wire.

Dale Hutchins runs Spanish goats on 60 acres outside Crawford. He bought the place with a tired five-strand barbed fence and figured he’d make it work. In the first year he lost goats to the road and to coyotes, about $1,800 worth by his own count, plus the Saturday mornings spent hauling escapees home. We replaced 1,400 feet along his road frontage with 48 inch fixed-knot net wire for right at $5,900. He told us it paid for itself in three seasons just in goats that stayed home.

## Terrain, Brush, and the Bosque County Factor

Wire type isn’t only about animals. The land votes too.

Net wire hates rough ground. Every dip and rise in the fence line either leaves a gap under the mesh or forces extra posts and dips in the wire. On the broken limestone country west of Valley Mills and Clifton, that adds real labor cost. Barbed wire handles rolling terrain much more gracefully because each strand can follow the ground on its own.

Creek crossings are another dividing line. A water gap built from barbed wire or swinging panels can wash out in a flood and be rebuilt in an afternoon. A net wire fence run through a draw catches every stick and leaf the creek sends down, and a spring rise can take out 100 feet of mesh at once.

Brush pressure matters too. Net wire catches falling limbs and holds them, and a limb lying on mesh stretches it out of shape permanently. Barbed strands shed most limbs or can be re-stretched in minutes.

The knot style is the piece most folks miss. Old-style hinge joint net wire is cheaper but crushes and bags when cattle lean on it or hogs hit it. Fixed-knot wire holds its shape under abuse and spans rougher ground with fewer posts. We break down the difference in fixed knot vs hinge joint if you want the full picture.

Marcy Villarreal learned the knot lesson the hard way on her place south of Valley Mills. Hogs coming up from the creek bottom tore through her older hinge-joint field fence in four places in one winter, and the patch quotes she gathered totaled about $2,200. Instead of patching, we rebuilt the 900 foot creek-side stretch in fixed-knot wire with a barbed bottom strand for $4,300. Two years later that stretch is still tight, and the hogs moved on to easier ground.

## When Mixing Both Fences Makes the Most Sense

Here’s what a lot of first-time land buyers don’t hear: most working ranches around here don’t choose one wire. They use both, in different places.

The common pattern looks like this. Barbed wire on the long perimeter runs where only cattle push it. Net wire on the road frontage, around the house and pens, and on any trap or pasture that holds goats, sheep, weaned calves, or horses. You put the expensive wire only where the expensive problems are.

Roy Kubacak runs cows on about 300 acres west of West. When he priced fencing the whole perimeter in net wire, the number came back near $68,000. Five-strand barbed for the same perimeter priced at about $34,000. He went with barbed on the perimeter and had us build a 12 acre weaning trap in net wire near the pens for another $6,100. Total spend landed around $40,000 instead of $68,000, and every foot of wire is doing exactly the job it’s built for.

One legal note worth knowing: much of rural Texas is still open range under Texas Agriculture Code Chapter 143, but counties and highways carry stock law exceptions, and a fence that doesn’t hold your animals can still put liability on you when they reach a roadway. Good road frontage fence isn’t just about keeping livestock in. It’s about keeping you out of court.

If you’re pricing a mixed setup like Roy’s, request a free written estimate and we’ll price each stretch separately so you can see exactly where net wire earns its keep and where barbed wire saves you thousands.

## How to Decide: Five Questions Before You Buy Wire

Run your place through these five questions and the answer usually falls out on its own.

- What animals will this fence hold in the next ten years? Fence for the livestock you’ll own, not just the livestock you own today. Plenty of folks add goats or a horse two years after building a cattle-only fence.

- What’s trying to get in? Coyote and dog pressure pushes you toward net wire for anything smaller than a cow. Hog pressure pushes you toward fixed-knot.

- What does the ground look like? Smooth, open ground suits net wire. Rocky, brushy, creek-cut country favors barbed.

- Which stretches carry the most risk? Road frontage and pens justify better wire. Back pasture lines usually don’t.

- What’s your real budget per foot? Get both numbers in writing before deciding. Land grant universities publish fence cost worksheets, like the University of Georgia Extension’s Fences for the Farm guide, and they all show the same thing: the spread between fence types is bigger than most owners expect.

A word on doing it yourself. Stringing a few strands of barbed wire between existing braces is honest weekend work. But stretching net wire flat and tight over any distance, and building the H-braces that keep 3,000 pounds of wire tension from pulling your corners over, is where DIY projects go sideways. If a corner post leans or the mesh bags in the first year, the fence fails early no matter how good the wire was. When the job involves new braces, long runs, creek crossings, or rocky ground, that’s the point to put the come-along down and call a professional.

That’s what we do all day, every day, from China Spring to Lorena. Call (254) 870-8898 for a free written estimate, and if a storm or a cow wreck has your fence open right now, that same number reaches our 24/7 emergency line.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I put barbed wire on top of a net wire fence?

Yes, and around here you usually should. One or two barbed strands above the mesh keep cattle from leaning over and mashing the net wire down, and they add a few inches of effective height. It’s the standard build for combination cattle and goat fences in Central Texas.

### Will net wire hold cattle by itself?

It will hold them, but cattle are hard on bare net wire because they lean over it to graze and rub on it. Without a barbed top strand, expect the top of the mesh to bow and bag within a few years. If cattle are the only stock, five-strand barbed is cheaper and takes the abuse better.

### How long does each fence type last in Central Texas?

A well-built barbed wire fence on good posts commonly runs 25 to 40 years, and net wire typically runs 20 to 30. Wire coating matters as much as wire type, since Class 3 galvanized lasts roughly twice as long as Class 1 in our climate. Posts usually fail before good wire does, so post choice sets the real lifespan.

### Is net wire worth the extra cost for a small acreage?

On small places it often is, because the total footage is low and the flexibility is high. Fencing 10 acres in net wire instead of barbed might add $4,000 to $6,000, and in exchange you can run goats, sheep, calves, or a horse without touching the fence again. On a small tract, one fence that holds everything usually beats a cheap fence that holds one species.
