## The Best Fence for Goats and Sheep on Central Texas Land (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/fence-for-goats-and-sheep/)

> What's the best fence for goats and sheep on Central Texas land? Real costs per foot, wire types that hold, and predator-proof tips from Waco fence pros.

Livestock

# The Best Fence for Goats and Sheep on Central Texas Land
Published August 9, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

There's an old saying around here: if a fence won't hold water, it won't hold a goat. That's an exaggeration, but not by a lot.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

There’s an old saying around here: if a fence won’t hold water, it won’t hold a goat. That’s an exaggeration, but not by a lot. We’ve walked hundreds of fence lines in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and the calls that start with “my goats are in the neighbor’s garden again” outnumber almost every other kind.

So what’s the best fence for goats and sheep on Central Texas land? Short answer: 48-inch fixed knot net wire with 4-inch mesh, wood posts on the corners, and a hot wire along the top if your goats are climbers. That setup runs about $6.50 to $9.00 per foot installed around Waco, and it’ll hold goats, hold sheep, and keep most coyotes on the wrong side of it.

The long answer matters more, because the wrong fence for small ruminants is one of the most expensive mistakes a landowner can make. You’ll pay for it twice: once to build it, and again to replace it after your herd proves it doesn’t work.

## Why goats test a fence harder than cattle ever will

A cow mostly respects a fence. She leans on it, she reaches through it for grass, and if a tree knocks it flat she’ll wander. But she’s not out there looking for a way through.

A goat is looking. All day, every day. Goats climb, they jump, they squeeze, and they push their heads through anything wide enough to fit their horns. Sheep are calmer, but they’re escape followers. One goat finds the gap, and your whole flock of ewes is on the county road by supper.

That’s why the 5-strand barbed wire that’s held cattle on Central Texas ranches for a hundred years is close to useless for goats. A mature Boer goat walks between strands two and three without slowing down. Kids go under the bottom wire. We’ve seen folks add strands until they had eight or nine wires, and the goats still got out. You can’t build a barbed wire fence tight enough for goats at any price that makes sense.

Sheep have a second problem barbed wire can’t solve: predators. Barbed wire doesn’t even slow down a coyote, and Central Texas has plenty of them. If you’re running sheep or goats, your fence has two jobs. Keep the animals in, and keep the killers out.

If you’re staring at a pasture right now trying to figure out what that means for your place, call us at (254) 870-8898. We’ll walk the line with you and give you a free written estimate, no pressure and no guessing games.

## The best goat fence for most Central Texas places: net wire done right

For probably 8 out of 10 properties we fence for goats or sheep, the answer is net wire, sometimes called field fence or woven wire. But the details decide whether it works or fails.

Mesh size: 4 inches, not 6. Standard cattle field fence has 6-inch vertical stays. A horned goat pushes his head through a 6-inch opening, can’t pull it back out, and now you’ve got a trapped animal in the July sun. Sheep and goat wire uses 4-inch by 4-inch mesh. Heads stay out, kids stay in, and coyotes can’t slip through.

Knot type: fixed knot beats hinge joint. Hinge joint wire is cheaper, and for goats that’s a trap. Goats stand on fences. Hinge joint mesh folds down under that weight, and after a season you’ve got a ramp instead of a fence. Fixed knot wire holds its shape when a 150-pound buck puts his front hooves on it. We wrote up the full comparison in fixed knot vs hinge joint if you want the details.

Height: 48 inches minimum. Most goats won’t clear 48 inches. If you’re running athletic breeds like Spanish goats or you’ve got a known jumper, go 60 inches or add an offset hot wire at the top.

The bottom matters most. Goats and predators both work the bottom of a fence. We run the wire tight to the ground and, on uneven terrain, add a barbed strand at ground level so nothing digs or shimmies under.

Dale Whitaker out in Crawford learned most of this the hard way before he called us. His Boers had been walking through an old cattle fence for two years, and his neighbor was done being patient about it. We pulled the old wire and built 1,800 feet of 48-inch fixed knot with treated wood corners and a barbed ground wire. The job came to $13,050, right at $7.25 a foot. He told us later the fence paid for itself the first year just in hay he stopped losing and peace he made with the neighbor.

## Sheep fencing and the predator problem

Sheep will test your fence less than goats, but they’ll pay a higher price when it fails. A coyote that gets into a goat pen might kill one animal. A coyote in a sheep pen, especially during lambing, can kill several in one night and come back the next.

The same 4-inch fixed knot net wire is the backbone of good sheep fencing, but for predator country we add layers:

- A barbed wire strand at ground level to stop digging

- One or two barbed strands above the net wire, taking total height to 52 to 56 inches

- An offset electric wire, about 8 inches off the ground on the outside, aimed at the nose of anything trying to dig

Marissa Cantu runs about 30 hair sheep on 12 acres just outside Lorena. She lost four lambs in one spring before she called us. Her net wire was decent, but it was hinge joint with a loose bottom, and the coyotes had found two dig spots along a creek-side low run. We tightened the whole line, added a ground-level barbed strand and an outside hot wire, and rebuilt her water gap. The retrofit cost her $3,400. She hasn’t lost a lamb to a coyote since, and that’s two lambing seasons now.

Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension has good research on predator behavior and non-lethal control if you want to go deeper. Their small ruminant resources at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu are worth an evening of reading before you spend fence money.

## What goat and sheep fencing costs around Waco

Here’s what we’re seeing for installed prices in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties in 2026. Materials, labor, and normal terrain. Rocky ground, heavy brush, and lots of corners push these numbers up.

Fence type Installed cost per foot Holds goats? Stops coyotes? Typical lifespan

5-strand barbed wire $2.00 - $4.00 No No 20-30 yrs

Hinge joint field fence (6” mesh) $4.50 - $6.50 Poorly Somewhat 15-20 yrs

Fixed knot sheep &#x26; goat wire (4” mesh) $6.50 - $9.00 Yes Yes 25-30 yrs

Cattle panels (16 ft, 4” grid) $8.00 - $12.00 Yes Yes 25+ yrs

Electric netting (temporary) $1.50 - $2.50 materials Rotational only Mostly 5-10 yrs

A few notes on that table. Cattle panels make excellent small pens, working corrals, and buck pens, but the per-foot price gets painful fast on a long perimeter. Electric netting is a rotational grazing tool, not a perimeter fence. And that cheap hinge joint line looks tempting until you price the repairs.

The Hendersons outside Valley Mills went with hinge joint on a 2,400-foot perimeter to save money, about $900 less than the fixed knot quote they’d gotten. Within 18 months their goats had mashed down three long sections, and they’d spent roughly $2,600 on repairs and patch panels before they had us replace the worst runs with fixed knot. Cheap wire for goats isn’t cheap.

One more cost note: if you’re improving grazing land, the USDA’s EQIP program sometimes cost-shares fencing for rotational grazing systems. It’s worth a call to your county NRCS office before you build.

Want a real number for your property instead of a range? Request a free written estimate and we’ll measure it, walk it, and price it line by line.

## Electric fence for goats: a good helper, a bad boss

We get asked all the time whether a few strands of hot wire can replace net wire for goats. Our honest answer: not as a perimeter fence in this country.

Electric works on animals that learn and remember. Goats do learn, but a goat with a full winter coat, a scared goat with a dog behind it, or a buck in rut who smells does across the road will take the hit and go. And when a storm knocks your charger out or a grass load drains the line, an all-electric fence is just string.

Where electric earns its keep:

- A top offset wire that stops climbers and leaners cold

- A low outside wire that teaches coyotes and dogs to stay back

- Interior cross-fencing for rotational grazing inside a solid perimeter

If you already have hot wire that’s not doing its job, check the charger, the grounding rods, and the vegetation load before you blame the goats. And know your limits on the DIY side. Fence energizers are safe when installed right, but tying electric into existing wire, grounding in our dry summer soils, and crossing gates and water gaps are places where a mistake bites you. If you’re not sure, have a pro set it up.

## Mistakes that let goats out and coyotes in

After years of fixing goat fences other people built, the same handful of problems keeps showing up:

Loose wire. Net wire has to be stretched properly against solid braced corners. Loose mesh sags, goats climb it, and predators push under it. This is the number one failure we see, and it usually traces back to weak corner assemblies.

Gates that don’t match the fence. A $9-a-foot fence with a sagging tube gate hung 8 inches off the ground is a goat door. Gates need the same mesh, hung tight and low. For heavy-use entrances, a pipe fence corner and gate section takes the abuse goats and equipment dish out.

Ignoring water gaps and washes. Every creek crossing and low spot is an exit. Goats find them in days, coyotes in weeks.

Wrong wire for the animal. If you’re still weighing wire types for mixed herds, our barbed wire vs net wire breakdown covers which animals each one actually holds.

Too few posts. Goat fence wants closer post spacing than cattle fence, especially on hills and curves, because goats load the wire between posts.

And a word on small places: if you’re fencing 2 to 10 acres for a handful of goats or sheep, the math and the layout work differently than a ranch perimeter. We covered that in our guide to small acreage fencing around Waco.

If your current fence is losing the fight, don’t wait for the phone call from the neighbor. Reach out through our contact page or call (254) 870-8898. Free written estimates, licensed and insured, and if animals are out on a road right now, our emergency line runs 24/7.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How tall should a fence be for goats?

Go 48 inches minimum for most breeds. Athletic goats like Spanish or Kiko lines, or a herd with a known jumper, may need 60 inches or a hot offset wire at the top. Height alone isn’t enough, though. A loose 60-inch fence fails faster than a tight 48-inch one, because goats climb slack wire instead of jumping it.

### Will barbed wire hold goats or sheep?

No. Goats walk between the strands and kids crawl under the bottom wire, no matter how many strands you add. Sheep hold a little better but their wool protects them from the barbs, and barbed wire does nothing to stop coyotes. Barbed wire is a cattle fence. For goats and sheep you need 4-inch mesh net wire.

### What does goat fencing cost per foot near Waco?

Installed 48-inch fixed knot sheep and goat wire runs about $6.50 to $9.00 per foot in our area in 2026, depending on terrain, brush, corners, and gate count. A quarter mile (1,320 feet) lands between $8,600 and $11,900 in most cases. Rocky ground west of the Bosque River and heavy cedar push jobs toward the top of that range.

### Can I keep goats behind electric fence alone?

We don’t recommend it for a perimeter. Trained goats respect hot wire most of the time, but chargers fail, grass loads drain lines, and a spooked or motivated goat will take the shock and keep going. Use electric as a top or offset wire on net fence, or for interior cross-fencing inside a solid physical perimeter.

## The Best Fence for Horses (and Why It's Not Barbed Wire) (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/best-fence-for-horses/)

> Barbed wire and horses don't mix. Compare the best fence for horses in Central Texas, real costs per foot, and what we install on ranches around Waco.

Livestock

# The Best Fence for Horses (and Why It's Not Barbed Wire)
Published July 24, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A horse can hit a barbed wire fence at 2 a.m. and hand you a $4,000 vet bill by sunrise. We've seen it happen more times than we'd like around Waco, and almost every time the fence was built for...

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A horse can hit a barbed wire fence at 2 a.m. and hand you a $4,000 vet bill by sunrise. We’ve seen it happen more times than we’d like around Waco, and almost every time the fence was built for cattle, not horses.

Here’s the short version: the best fence for horses is one a horse can see, can’t get a hoof through, and won’t cut when the horse panics. Barbed wire fails all three tests. It’s a fine cattle fence, and we install miles of it every year, but a horse is a different animal with a different brain and much thinner skin.

In this guide we’ll walk through why barbed wire and horses don’t mix, which fences actually work for horses in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and what each one costs per foot installed. Real numbers, no fluff.

If you’ve already got horses standing behind old barbed wire and you’re worried about it, don’t wait on an article. Call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll come look at it. Estimates are free and in writing.

## Why Barbed Wire Hurts Horses (When It Works Fine for Cattle)

Cattle are thick-hided and slow to panic. When a cow leans into barbed wire, the barbs poke, the cow backs off, and everybody goes on with their day. That’s the whole design.

Horses are prey animals with a hair trigger. When something spooks a horse, it doesn’t back up. It runs, and it doesn’t always look where it’s going. A horse that hits barbed wire at speed doesn’t bounce off. The wire wraps, the horse fights it, and the barbs do exactly what barbs do.

There’s a second problem: visibility. Four or five strands of thin wire are nearly invisible to a horse at dusk or in a storm. Horses run through barbed wire fences they simply never saw. University extension programs have said this plainly for decades. Penn State Extension lists barbed wire as unacceptable for horses in its fence planning guide for horses, and the University of Minnesota Extension says the same.

The third problem is legs. Horses paw at fences and reach through them for grass. Barbed wire and loose hinge-joint field fence both let a hoof slip through, and a trapped leg plus a panicking horse is how you get a career-ending injury on an animal you paid five figures for.

One call sticks with us. A gentleman named Doyle out toward Crawford had a nice roping gelding get a front leg through a sagging 1950s barbed wire fence during a thunderstorm. The vet saved the leg, but the bill came to $3,800 and the horse was out of work for eight months. We tore out that quarter mile of old wire and replaced it with no-climb net wire and a top rail for about $9,600. He’ll tell you himself the new fence was cheaper than the wreck.

## What the Best Horse Fence Has to Get Right

Before we rank fence types, here’s the checklist we use when we design a horse fence anywhere in Central Texas. A good horse fence needs five things.

Visibility. The horse has to see the barrier from a dead run. That’s why a top rail, a wide tape, or a solid pipe rail matters so much. Thin smooth wire alone is almost as invisible as barbed wire.

No gaps a hoof fits through. Mesh openings should be 2 inches by 4 inches or smaller. That’s the whole point of no-climb woven wire. A hoof physically can’t pass through it.

Smooth surfaces. No barbs, no sharp wire ends, no protruding bolt heads, no T-post tops without caps. Anything that can cut, will cut, because horses find trouble like it’s their job.

Height and strength. For most horses, 54 to 60 inches at the top. The fence has to take a 1,100 pound animal leaning, scratching, or hitting it without folding.

Honest corners and gates. Horses test gates and corners more than any stretch of line fence. That means real H-brace corners and gates hung on posts set in concrete, not a panel wired to a T-post.

If your current fence fails two or more of those, it’s worth a conversation. You can request a free written estimate here and we’ll walk the line with you.

## The Best Fence for Horses, Ranked for Central Texas

Here’s how the main horse fencing options stack up on our jobs around Waco, from our top pick down.

### 1. No-climb net wire with a top rail (best value)

This is what we recommend for most horse owners: 2x4 inch woven “no-climb” horse mesh, 48 to 60 inches tall, with a wood or pipe top rail so the fence is visible and the mesh can’t get mashed down. Hooves can’t get through it, there’s nothing sharp on it, and good class 3 galvanized mesh lasts 20 to 25 years in our climate.

Installed on wood posts with a top rail, you’re usually looking at $9 to $14 per foot depending on terrain and brush. It’s not cheap, but it’s the best safety per dollar in horse fencing. If you’re weighing mesh types, our barbed wire vs net wire breakdown covers the details.

### 2. Pipe fence (safest and toughest)

Welded steel pipe fence is the gold standard for pens, arenas, stallion runs, and anywhere horses get crowded or worked. It’s highly visible, it doesn’t give, and a horse that hits it slides off instead of tangling in it. With decent paint or bare weathering steel, a pipe fence will outlast the person who built it.

The tradeoff is price. Figure $28 to $45 per foot installed depending on pipe size and rail count, which is why most folks run pipe around pens and the horse trap, then no-climb on the pasture perimeter. Full numbers are in our pipe fence cost guide.

One note for open pasture: some owners add a single electric strand inside a pipe fence, because a spooked horse can still hit rigid steel hard. Pipe won’t cut, but it doesn’t flex either.

### 3. Wood board fence (classic looks, real upkeep)

Three or four rail wood board fence is beautiful and very visible. It’s a fine horse fence when it’s maintained. The problem in Central Texas is sun, moisture swings, and horses that chew. Boards crack, nails back out, and a broken board turns into a spear.

Expect $12 to $20 per foot installed, plus paint or stain every few years and board replacement forever. Most of our clients who want the look run board fence along the road frontage and entrance, then switch to no-climb out back.

### 4. Electric tape or braid (good helper, thin main fence)

Wide electric tape is visible, cheap at $3 to $6 per foot, and horses respect a hot fence once they’ve met it. It’s great for cross-fencing, rotating pasture, and as a standoff strand that keeps horses off a permanent fence.

As the only barrier on a perimeter, we don’t love it. Power fails, chargers die, and a truly panicked horse will blow through tape. A lady named Marisol near China Spring fenced a 3-acre paddock with tape alone for about $2,100. It worked for a year, right up until a neighbor’s dogs ran her mare through it and out onto the county road. Nobody got hurt, and we replaced it with no-climb and a top rail. If you run hot fence anywhere, test it weekly, because a dead charger turns it into string.

### What to avoid entirely

Barbed wire, loose hinge-joint field fence with big openings, and anything built on uncapped T-posts. If you’re stuck with T-posts for now, cap every one of them today. It costs pennies per post and it has saved more than one horse’s chest.

## Horse Fence Cost Comparison for the Waco Area

Here’s what these fences typically run installed on our jobs in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties. Rocky ground, heavy brush, and long material hauls move these numbers, so treat them as honest ranges, not quotes.

Fence type Installed cost per foot Horse safety Typical lifespan

Barbed wire (cattle only) $2.50 to $5.50 Poor, not recommended for horses 25 to 30 years

Total project came in near $52,000, and their insurance agent liked it almost as much as their horses do.

## Height, Post Spacing, and the Details That Keep Horses In

A few build details matter more with horses than with cattle, and this is where a lot of DIY horse fences go wrong.

Height. Run the top of the fence 54 to 60 inches for riding horses, and taller for stallions or known jumpers. A 48-inch cattle fence invites a tall horse to lean over it until it sags.

Post spacing. We set wood posts 8 to 10 feet apart on horse mesh, tighter than a typical cattle fence, because horses lean and rub hard. Rocky or rolling ground can tighten that spacing further.

Bottom gap. Leave a few inches at the bottom so a pawing horse doesn’t wedge a hoof under the mesh, but not so much that a foal can roll under it.

Gates. Use smooth-sided horse gates, not stock panels with exposed cut ends. Hang them on 3 to 4 inch pipe posts set in concrete, and latch them with hardware a clever horse can’t flip open. You’d be amazed what a bored gelding can do with his lips.

Corners. Every fence pull needs a real brace. Skimp on corners and the whole fence loosens in two summers of Texas heat, and a loose horse fence is halfway to being a dangerous one.

## When to DIY and When to Call a Pro

Plenty of horse owners can stretch a run of tape fence, cap their T-posts, or swap a broken board. That’s normal ranch upkeep, and we’ll cheer you on.

Stop and call a professional when the job involves tearing out old barbed wire, stretching woven mesh, welding pipe, or setting gate and corner posts. Old barbed wire under tension can snap back and cut you badly, and rolled-up wire left in the grass will find a horse’s leg years later. Stretching net wire without the right equipment gives you a baggy fence that fails the one night it matters. And nobody should be learning to weld on the fence that holds their horses.

The other time to call is right now, tonight, if a horse is already out or tangled. We run a 24/7 emergency line for exactly that.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the safest fence for horses?

Steel pipe fence is the safest all-around horse fence, which is why it’s standard for pens and arenas. For pasture perimeters, no-climb woven wire with a visible top rail delivers nearly the same safety at a fraction of the price. Both keep hooves out of the fence and have nothing sharp for a horse to hit.

### Can horses ever be kept behind barbed wire?

Some ranch horses live behind barbed wire without incident, but it only takes one spook to end that streak. If replacing it all at once isn’t in the budget, add a visible hot tape offset inside the wire and replace the worst stretches first. We’d rather help you phase it out than treat it as acceptable.

### How tall should a horse fence be?

Plan on 54 to 60 inches at the top rail for most riding horses. Go 60 inches or more for stallions, tall warmbloods, or any horse with a jumping habit. Ponies and minis need shorter mesh openings more than they need extra height.

Around Waco, no-climb net wire with a top rail typically runs $12 to $16 per foot installed, wood board runs $12 to $20, and pipe fence runs $18 to $28. Electric tape cross-fencing runs $3 to $6 per foot. Rock, brush, and gate count move every one of those numbers, so get a written per-foot quote before you commit.

## Cattle Guard Cost and Installation: Sizing, Ratings, and Setting It Right (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/cattle-guard-cost-installation/)

> Installed cattle guard cost runs $3,500 to $8,000 in Central Texas. See how span, width, load rating and foundation work drive the number on your own drive.

Cost Guide

# Cattle Guard Cost and Installation: Sizing, Ratings, and Setting It Right
Published September 13, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A cattle guard that was set wrong does not fail all at once. One end settles an inch, the rails go out of level, silt packs the pit until it is only six inches deep, and then a loaded gooseneck...

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A cattle guard that was set wrong does not fail all at once. One end settles an inch, the rails go out of level, silt packs the pit until it is only six inches deep, and then a loaded gooseneck crosses it on a wet morning and a rail folds. Now you have a truck sitting on a broken guard, an open gate to the county road, and a bill nobody budgeted for.

Installed cattle guard cost in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties runs $3,500 to $8,000. Most of that spread has very little to do with the steel. It comes from how wide the opening is, what rating the guard has to carry, how much rock is under the pit, and whether water has anywhere to go once the hole is open.

Below are the parts of the job that actually move the price, plus the sizing and rating decisions worth getting right the first time.

## What Drives Cattle Guard Cost

The guard itself is usually the smaller half of the number. Excavation, concrete, wing walls, and tying the whole thing back into the fence line are the rest, and those are the parts that change from one entrance to the next.

Here is what moves a bid up or down on a cattle guard:

- Width across the road. A 10-foot interior crossing and a 20-foot main entrance are different jobs, not the same job at two prices.

- Load rating. A heavier rating means heavier rails, more of them, and a foundation designed to carry the load into undisturbed soil.

- What is under the pit. Blackland clay digs fast. Limestone and caliche mean a hydraulic hammer on the excavator, and that is hours, not minutes.

- Drainage. If the entrance sits low, the pit becomes a stock tank, and a culvert or raised approach adds work before the guard is ever set.

- Foundation type. Poured footings on site versus a precast concrete box changes the equipment, the cure time, and the schedule.

- Wings and fence tie-in. Every guard needs deflector wings and a braced connection to the fence, or stock simply walks around the end of it.

If you want a real figure for your own entrance instead of a range, call (254) 870-8898 and we will come walk it with you. On-site estimates are free, and we would rather look at the ground than guess.

Width across the road Where it usually goes Span driven over Rating we would set Where it lands in the $3,500 to $8,000 installed range

10 ft Interior pasture crossing, ranch pickup and side-by-side only 8 ft H-15 Lower end

12 ft Standard private drive off a county road 8 ft H-20 Lower to middle

14 ft Drive that takes goosenecks and feed trucks 8 ft H-20 Middle

16 ft Main entrance, fire apparatus access, hay equipment 8 to 10 ft H-20 or HS-20 Middle to upper

20 ft and wider Highway frontage, wide equipment, split-lane entry 8 to 10 ft HS-20 Upper end

Those bands come off our published ranch fence cost page, which carries the same numbers we quote from the tailgate.

## Sizing a Cattle Guard: Span, Width, and the Trucks That Actually Cross It

Two dimensions matter and people mix them up constantly. The span is the distance you drive across, almost always 8 feet on a standard guard and sometimes 10 feet on a heavy one. The width is the dimension across the road, and that is the one you choose: 10, 12, 14, 16, 20, and 24 feet are the common sizes.

Pick the width off the widest thing that will ever cross it, not off your pickup. A dually with a 8-foot-wide gooseneck needs room to swing when it comes off a county road at an angle. A 12-foot guard on a drive that regularly takes a hay truck turns into a place where somebody eventually drops a trailer tire off the wing.

Rail spacing is the other sizing decision, and it is a stock safety issue rather than a cost issue. Around 4 to 5 inches of clear gap between rails is the working range. Wider than that and a calf or a colt can put a foot through and break a leg. Much narrower and cattle figure out they can walk it.

Round pipe rails are part of why a guard works, because a hoof set on a round rail rolls and cattle learn fast that the footing is wrong. Flat-top rails are quieter under a truck but give an animal a flat place to stand, so the spacing has to be right.

Keep a bypass gate beside the guard for moving stock on foot, for a wide implement, and for the day the pit is being cleaned out. It also gives you somewhere to hang the entrance itself, which is covered on our ranch entrance gates page and in our breakdown of ranch entrance gate cost.

Field scenario. A 40-acre cattle place off a county road near Lorena had a 12-foot guard on a drive that took a 30-foot gooseneck twice a week. The wings were bare wire panels, so the cattle had learned to walk the edge of the pit and step around. We pulled it, went to a 14-foot H-20 guard, poured proper footings, and set welded pipe wings tied into an H-brace on each side. That job came to roughly $5,200, which sits in the middle of our $3,500 to $8,000 installed range.

## Load Ratings: H-15, H-20, and Why the Sticker Matters

Cattle guard ratings borrow the AASHTO highway loading notation, and the shorthand is simpler than it looks. H-15 describes a design truck around 15 tons. H-20 describes one around 20 tons, which works out to roughly a 16,000-pound wheel load. HS-20 and HS-25 add a trailer axle group to the same design truck, which is what you want under anything that hauls loaded.

Here is the practical version. An interior crossing that never sees more than a ranch pickup and a side-by-side can live at H-15. Anything on a drive that a feed truck, a fuel truck, a concrete truck, a loaded cattle pot, or a fire engine will use should be H-20 at a minimum, and HS-20 if the entrance is your only way in.

Ask your rural fire district what they need before you buy. Some districts will not run apparatus across a guard below a stated rating, and finding that out during a grass fire is the wrong time.

One honest caution. A rating assumes the guard is sitting level on a sound foundation with the load carried into undisturbed bearing soil. Set the same guard on soft backfill or a settled footing and it is no longer performing at its rating, whatever the plate says. If the guard is going into a public road rather than a private drive, expect the county to want a licensed engineer to sign off on the design.

## Cattle Guard Installation Cost: What Setting One Really Involves

The install is a dirt-and-concrete job with a steel delivery in the middle, usually two days plus the cure.

Excavate the pit. You want 12 to 18 inches of open air under the rails once the guard is set. Deeper deters stock better and holds more silt before it needs cleaning, but it means more spoil, more concrete, and a harder clean-out later. In the limestone west of the Brazos this is the step that decides your price.

Form and pour the footings. Two continuous footings run under the ends of the guard, sized so the bearing surface reaches undisturbed ground rather than backfill. Precast boxes skip the forming, but they need a machine that can set them and an approach a truck can reach.

Set the guard and tie in the wings. The guard goes on the cured footings, level in both directions and flush with the finished drive. Wings, either pipe panels or poured wing walls, flare from each end back to the fence so stock cannot step around the pit, and they get braced into the fence line the same way any corner does.

Backfill, grade, and wait. Compacted backfill on both approaches keeps the guard from becoming a step. Concrete should have about 7 days before heavy traffic and reaches full design strength near 28 days, so plan another way in for the first week.

Field scenario. A limestone hill section near Valley Mills needed a 16-foot guard at the top of the drive where the caliche starts about eight inches down. Every bit of that pit came out with a hydraulic hammer, and the spoil had to be hauled off instead of spread. Same guard, same concrete, but the excavation ran nearly a full extra day and the job landed around $7,400, near the top of the installed range. That is what rock does, and it is why we do not quote a guard over the phone.

As a general materials-only estimate, a bare 8-by-12-foot H-20 steel guard runs somewhere around $1,600 to $2,800 and weighs enough that you are not setting it with a tractor loader. That is not our quote. It moves with steel pricing and freight, and it does not include a shovel of the work above.

Ready for a number on your own entrance? Call (254) 870-8898 or ask for a free on-site estimate and we will walk the drive, check the drainage, and put it in writing.

## What a Cattle Guard Will Not Hold

A cattle guard is a cattle tool. It is good at cattle and roughly nothing else.

Sheep and goats cross guards. Their feet are small enough to find purchase and they are patient enough to work it out, so if you run small stock you need a gate, not a guard. Our post on fencing for goats and sheep covers what does hold them.

Horses are unpredictable. Most respect a guard, some walk them once they have watched a horse do it, and a spooked horse crossing a guard is how you get a shattered cannon bone. On a horse place we would rather hang a good gate than trust a pit.

Deer step over or jump one entirely, so a guard does nothing for a high-fenced operation. Hogs go under the wings if the wings are not tight to the ground, and a loose wing is exactly the sort of gap feral hogs work on until it is a hole.

Painted guards, meaning stripes on concrete with no pit, are not a substitute. They work on some cattle for some period of time, and then one animal tests it and the whole herd learns. If the consequence of a failure is stock on a county road, do not build the version that depends on cattle staying fooled.

Field scenario. A 300-acre cattle lease west of Crawford wanted three interior crossings so the hand could run the loop without opening gates. All three were pickup-and-side-by-side traffic only, on dirt, with no drainage problem and easy digging. Those went in as 12-foot H-15 guards on poured footings and each landed near the bottom of the range, around $3,900. The main entrance off the county road on that same place was a different animal and got a 16-foot H-20.

## County Roads, Right-of-Way, and Texas Stock Law

If the guard sits entirely on your own drive, past the right-of-way line, it is your business. If any part of it sits in a county road right-of-way, or you are proposing to put a guard across the county road itself, that is the commissioners court’s call. County authority over roads and bridges sits in Texas Transportation Code Chapter 251, and every county handles requests a little differently. Call the precinct commissioner’s office before you dig.

An entrance off a state highway is a TxDOT access matter and needs a permit for the driveway itself, not just the guard. That process takes longer than the install does, so start it early.

Worth knowing the background too. Whether your stock is required to be fenced in, and what happens when they get out, comes from local stock law rather than a single statewide rule. The fence and range provisions live in Texas Agriculture Code Chapter 143, and the practical county-by-county picture is in our guide to Texas stock law by county. A guard that stops working turns into a liability question.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does a cattle guard cost installed in Central Texas?

Installed cattle guard cost in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties runs $3,500 to $8,000. Width, load rating, digging conditions, and drainage decide where in that band your entrance lands. Rock is the biggest variable, which is why we look at the site rather than price over the phone.

### What size cattle guard do I need?

Standard widths are 10, 12, 14, 16, 20, and 24 feet across the road, with an 8-foot span in the direction of travel. Size it off the widest vehicle that will ever use the drive, not your pickup, and give yourself room for a trailer swinging in off a county road. Twelve feet handles most private drives, and 14 to 16 feet is the safer choice if goosenecks, hay equipment, or fire apparatus come through.

### Will a cattle guard hold horses, goats, or sheep?

Not reliably. Goats and sheep cross guards routinely, and horses vary from animal to animal with real injury risk if one tries to cross and slips. Guards are a cattle tool, and for anything else you want a gate.

### How often does a cattle guard need cleaning out?

Every two to five years for most places, sooner on a drive that washes silt into the pit. Once the open depth under the rails drops below about a foot, the guard stops reading as a hazard and cattle will start walking it. Cleaning is a backhoe and an hour, which beats replacing a guard that has been carrying loads on packed fill.

## Cattle Keep Getting Out of Fence? 7 Problems to Check First (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/cattle-getting-out-of-fence/)

> Cattle keep getting out of your fence? Check these 7 common failure points, see real repair costs, and learn when to call a Waco fence pro. Free estimates.

Fence Repair

# Cattle Keep Getting Out of Fence? 7 Problems to Check First
Published July 24, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

It's 6 a.m., your phone's buzzing, and it's your neighbor telling you your cows are standing in the middle of the FM road again.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

It’s 6 a.m., your phone’s buzzing, and it’s your neighbor telling you your cows are standing in the middle of the FM road again. If your cattle keep getting out of fence lines you swore were fine last month, you’re not dealing with bad luck. You’re dealing with a fence that’s telling you exactly where it’s failing, and it usually gives you the answer in one of seven places.

We build and repair ranch fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and when a rancher calls about escaping cattle, the problem is almost always on this list. Walk your fence line with these seven checks and you’ll find the weak spot before your herd finds it again.

And if you’d rather have a second set of eyes on it, call us at (254) 870-8898. We do free written estimates, and we run a 24/7 emergency line for cattle-out situations, because a cow on the highway at midnight can’t wait until Monday.

## 1. Loose, Sagging Wire: The Top Reason Cattle Keep Getting Out of Fence

Barbed wire only works when it’s tight. A properly stretched strand has enough tension that a 1,200 pound cow leaning on it feels resistance and backs off. Once that wire loses tension, it stops being a barrier and starts being a suggestion.

Here’s the test. Grab a strand mid-span and push it down with moderate pressure. If it deflects more than 3 or 4 inches, it’s loose enough for a motivated cow to push through or step over. Cattle learn fast. One cow reaches through a slack spot for green grass, stretches it further, and within a couple weeks the whole herd knows where the door is.

Wire goes slack for a few reasons: heat expansion in our Texas summers, tree limbs falling across the line, cattle rubbing on it, and staples pulling out of dry posts. Small sections can be re-tensioned with a fence stretcher and inline crimps, and we cover the full process in our guide to fixing sagging barbed wire fence.

If more than a quarter of the fence line is slack, though, re-tensioning strand by strand becomes a losing game. That usually means the bracing has failed, which brings us to the next two problems.

## 2. Rotten, Broken, or Leaning Posts

Posts are the skeleton of your fence. When they fail, everything attached to them fails with them.

Walk the line and push on each wood post at chest height. A solid post won’t move. A post that wobbles, leans, or flexes at the ground line is done, even if it looks fine above grade. Wood posts almost always rot right at the soil line where moisture and oxygen meet, so a post can look healthy at eye level and be mush six inches down. Kick the base or probe it with a screwdriver. If the blade sinks in easy, that post isn’t holding anything.

T-posts fail differently. They bend when cattle or equipment hit them, and they heave out of the ground in our Central Texas clay, which swells when wet and shrinks hard in a drought. A t-post that’s lifted 4 inches has lost most of its grip.

Danny Kolar runs about 40 head just outside West, and he’d been patching the same stretch of fence for two years, one post at a time, maybe $30 or $40 in materials each trip. His heifers kept finding the next weak post anyway. When we finally walked the whole line with him, 22 of 60 posts failed the push test. We replaced the bad posts and re-stretched a quarter mile of wire for about $1,850, and he told us later it was cheaper than the diesel and Saturdays he’d burned chasing cattle.

Replacing scattered posts is a fair DIY job. If a third or more of your posts are failing, get a professional opinion before you spend another weekend on it, because the fence may be at the end of its life.

## 3. Failed Corner Braces and H-Braces

Here’s the one most folks miss. If your wire keeps going slack no matter how many times you tighten it, the problem usually isn’t the wire. It’s the corners.

Every strand of tensioned wire pulls on the corner and end assemblies. A proper H-brace, two posts with a horizontal rail and a diagonal tension wire, spreads that load so the corner post can’t lean. When the brace rots, the diagonal wire snaps, or the assembly was never built right to begin with, the corner post slowly tips inward. Every inch it leans, every strand on that pull loses tension at once. You can re-stretch wire all day and it’ll be slack again in a month.

Check each corner: is the post vertical, is the rail solid, is the diagonal wire tight? A leaning corner post with tight wire attached is a corner that’s actively failing.

Rebuilding an H-brace properly means new posts set deep in concrete or well-tamped, a solid rail, and correctly wrapped tension wire. It’s precise work, and it’s the foundation of the whole fence. This is a spot where hiring it out pays for itself, because a brace built wrong fails again in a year. On a barbed wire fence, we figure a new H-brace assembly runs $250 to $450 depending on access and soil.

## 4. Gates That Sag, Drag, and Get Left Unlatched

Ask any rancher where cattle get out and half will admit it: the gate. Gates fail three ways.

First, they sag. A 16 foot tube gate on a rotting wood post drops at the far end, drags the ground, and stops latching clean. Folks start chaining it loosely instead, and a smart cow noses a loose chain until the gate swings.

Second, the latch itself. Cattle work latches with their noses more than people believe. If your latch can be opened with a push and a wiggle, a bored cow will eventually open it. Use a latch that requires a lift and a pull, or add a chain with a clip.

Third, plain human error. Feed deliveries, hunters, utility crews. If a gate keeps ending up open, a spring-loaded latch or a posted “close the gate” sign costs almost nothing compared to a loose herd.

If your entrance gate is the weak point, a properly hung gate on a concrete-set steel post is a permanent fix. We build and repair ranch entrance gates around Waco and can usually re-hang a sagging gate in a morning. Want us to look at yours? Request a free estimate and we’ll put a number on it in writing.

## 5. Electric Fence That Isn’t Actually Hot

Electric fence is a psychological barrier. The wire itself won’t stop a cow. The memory of the shock does. Which means the moment your fence drops below about 3,000 volts, you effectively have no fence, and it can look perfect the whole time.

Carla Simmons runs cows on 60 acres near Crawford, and hers started walking through a two-strand electric cross fence like it wasn’t there. She was quoted $12,000 by an out-of-town outfit to rebuild the whole interior fence system. When we tested it, the charger was putting out fine at the box but the fence read under 800 volts. The culprit was two bad ground rods in dry soil and a stretch of grass loading down the bottom wire. Roughly $400 in ground rods, insulators, and labor brought it back over 6,000 volts, and her cows quit testing it within a week.

Check these in order: charger output at the terminals, ground rod system (three rods, 6 to 8 feet, is the standard for most chargers), vegetation touching the wire, cracked insulators, and broken splices. A $40 fence tester will save you hours of guessing. Our full troubleshooting walkthrough is here: why your electric fence isn’t working.

One safety note. Never troubleshoot charger wiring on the supply side while it’s plugged in, and if your setup involves anything on the 120 volt side beyond plugging in the charger, that’s electrician territory, not fence territory.

## 6. Water Gaps, Washouts, and Hog Damage

Creeks and draws are the back doors of every Central Texas ranch. A water gap, the flexible fence section that crosses a drainage, is designed to swing or break away in a flood so the whole fence doesn’t go with it. That also means it’s the first thing to fail after every big rain, and cattle find the opening within days.

After heavy rain, check every creek crossing before you check anything else. Look for washed-out gaps, debris piled on wire, and banks that have eroded away from your end posts. Marcus Villarreal, who runs stockers near Lorena, learned this one the expensive way. A May storm took out a water gap on Bull Hide Creek, and before he found it, his steers had spent two days in the neighbor’s coastal patch. He paid the neighbor $600 for hay damage, and we rebuilt the gap with a swinging panel design for about $650. Now it’s the first spot he checks after every rain.

Feral hogs cause a similar problem from below. Hogs root under the bottom wire and leave a torn-up gap that calves slip through first, then cows follow. If you’re finding rooted-up dirt and lifted bottom wire, you’ve got a hog problem and a fence problem, and we wrote up the fixes in our guide to feral hog fence damage.

## 7. When Cows Keep Getting Out Through a Decent Fence

Sometimes you walk the whole line and the fence honestly checks out. If cows keep getting out anyway, look at the herd and the setup.

Every rancher eventually owns a fence crawler, one cow that’s learned to work through anything. One crawler will train your whole herd, and the honest answer is usually a trailer ride to the sale barn. It’s a hard call, but she’s cheaper to replace than a mile of fence upgrades.

Hungry cattle test fences and content cattle don’t. If your pasture is grazed down and the other side of the wire is green, no reasonable fence stops that pressure forever. Same story with a bull who can smell cycling cows on the neighbor’s place. Four strands of aging barbed wire won’t hold a determined bull, and that’s a situation where five or six tight strands, an offset hot wire, or a stout pipe fence around the pens is the real fix.

Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension has solid guidance on stocking rates and forage management for our part of the state if grazing pressure is the root cause: agrilifeextension.tamu.edu.

Here’s what we typically see for repair costs in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties. Your numbers will move with access, soil, and materials, which is why we always put estimates in writing.

One rule of thumb we give every caller: if you’ve repaired the same stretch three times in a year, stop patching and price a rebuild. Repair money spent on a fence that’s structurally done is money you’ll spend again.

There’s a legal reason to stay ahead of this too. In much of Texas, and especially along highways and in counties with stock laws, a livestock owner can face real liability when cattle end up on a roadway. The state’s fence and stock law framework is laid out in Texas Agriculture Code Chapter 143, and it’s worth knowing where your county stands.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why do my cattle keep getting out even after I fix the fence?

Usually because the visible break wasn’t the real problem. Slack wire almost always traces back to a failed corner brace or leaning posts, so patching the wire alone means it goes loose again within weeks. Walk the corners and push-test the posts before you blame the wire, and check whether one specific cow is leading the escapes.

### How many strands of barbed wire does it take to hold cattle?

Five strands of tight, properly spaced barbed wire is the standard for cattle in Central Texas, and four can work for calm cows on good grazing. Bulls, weaned calves, and cattle under grazing pressure justify five or six strands or an added offset hot wire. Strand count matters less than tension, though. Five loose strands hold less than four tight ones.

### Am I liable if my cattle get out on the road in Texas?

It depends on your county and the road. Texas is historically open range, but most populated counties, including much of our area, have adopted stock laws, and state law separately requires keeping livestock off U.S. and state highways. If your cattle cause a wreck where a stock law applies, you can be on the hook, so a sound fence is cheap insurance. Check your county’s stock law status to know where you stand.

### When should I stop repairing and replace the whole fence?

If more than a third of the posts fail a push test, the wire is rusted through in multiple spots, or you’ve repaired the same section three or more times in a year, replacement is usually the better spend. A full 5-strand barbed wire rebuild typically runs $2.50 to $5.50 per foot here. We’re glad to walk the line and tell you honestly which side of that call your fence is on.

## Cattle on Road Liability in Texas: Who Pays When Your Herd Gets Out? (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/cattle-on-road-liability-texas/)

> A driver hits your cow on a Central Texas road. Are you liable? Plain answers on open range law, county stock laws, and the fence fixes that protect you.

Texas Law

# Cattle on Road Liability in Texas: Who Pays When Your Herd Gets Out?
Published July 28, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A driver hits your cow on a dark stretch of FM 185 at 10 p.m. The car is totaled, the cow is dead, and his lawyer calls your house Monday morning.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A driver hits your cow on a dark stretch of FM 185 at 10 p.m. The car is totaled, the cow is dead, and his lawyer calls your house Monday morning. Do you owe him a dime?

The honest answer is: it depends on which road, which county, and what shape your fence was in. Cattle on road liability in Texas confuses even lifelong ranchers because the state runs on a patchwork of old open range law, county-by-county stock laws, and one big highway statute that overrides both. We build and repair ranch fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and we’ve watched good neighbors learn these rules the hard way. Here’s how it actually works.

## Texas Is Still Open Range by Default

Most states make livestock owners fence their animals in. Texas flipped that script back in the trail-drive days. Under Texas common law, the default rule is “fence out.” Your neighbor has to fence cattle out of his property if he doesn’t want them there. You have no general duty to fence them in.

The Texas Supreme Court backed this up as recently as 1999 in a case called Gibbs v. Jackson, where a horse wandered onto a farm-to-market road and caused a wreck. The court refused to invent a new duty for the owner. No stock law, no highway statute, no liability.

But hold on before you relax. That default rule has two huge exceptions, and one or both of them cover most of the roads around Waco:

- The state highway statute. On U.S. and state highways, a separate law applies everywhere in Texas.

- Local stock laws. Counties and precincts voted decades ago to flip themselves from open range to closed range, and most of the settled parts of Central Texas did exactly that.

So “Texas is open range” is true the way “Texas is dry” is true. It depends entirely on where you’re standing.

If you already know your fence is the weak link in this whole conversation, don’t wait for a lawyer’s letter to find out how the rules apply to you. Request a free written estimate or call Brazos Ridge Fence at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk your road frontage with you.

## Cattle on Road Liability in Texas Comes Down to Three Questions

When a wreck happens, every lawyer, adjuster, and judge involved works through the same three questions.

1. What kind of road was it? A U.S. highway or state highway (think I-35, US 84, TX 6, TX 317) triggers the statewide highway statute. A numbered farm-to-market road, a county road, or a gravel lane does not. This distinction alone decides a surprising number of cases.

2. Does a stock law cover that spot? If the county or precinct passed a stock law, the area is closed range and you have a legal duty not to let cattle run at large. If it didn’t, the old open range rule still applies on local roads.

3. Was the owner negligent, or did he knowingly let stock roam? This is the big one. Texas does not make cattle owners automatically liable just because a cow was in the road. Even in closed range country, the driver has to prove you were negligent. On highways, he has to show you knowingly permitted the animal to roam. A cow on the pavement is not proof by itself. A cow on the pavement for the third time this month, through the same broken wire your neighbor texted you about, is a different story.

Keep those three questions in mind and the rest of this article will snap into place.

## The Highway Rule: U.S. and State Highways Play by Statewide Law

Texas Agriculture Code Section 143.102 says a person who owns or controls cattle, horses, or other listed livestock “may not knowingly permit the animal to traverse or roam at large, unattended, on the right-of-way of a highway.” You can read the full chapter yourself on the Texas Legislature’s statutes site.

Three things matter here.

It applies everywhere in Texas. Open range county, closed range county, doesn’t matter. If your bull is standing on US 84, this statute is in play.

“Highway” has a narrow definition. The statute defines highway as a U.S. highway or a state highway, and it specifically excludes numbered farm-to-market roads. That’s why the FM road question comes up so often in these cases, and why demand letters over FM road wrecks sometimes fall apart.

“Knowingly” is the fight. Violating the statute is a misdemeanor, and it opens the door to civil liability. But the driver’s side has to show you knew. Evidence that wins these cases for drivers looks like this: prior escapes you didn’t fix, a fence that’s been visibly down for weeks, calls from the sheriff’s office you ignored, or gates you knew didn’t latch. Evidence that wins for ranchers looks like a tight five-strand fence, dated repair receipts, and a cut wire or storm-downed limb nobody could have predicted.

If storm damage is what put your fence down along a highway, that’s exactly why we run a 24/7 emergency line. A tree through your right-of-way fence at midnight is a tonight problem, not a Monday problem.

## Stock Laws in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls Counties

Stock laws are local option elections, most of them held between the early 1900s and the 1930s. Voters in a county or a single precinct could adopt a law making it illegal to let cattle, horses, hogs, sheep, or goats run at large. Where a stock law passed, that area became closed range, and it still is today.

Here’s the frustrating part: there’s no clean statewide map. The election results live in dusty commissioners court minutes at each county clerk’s office. Most of the populated parts of Central Texas, including the areas around Waco, adopted stock laws for cattle generations ago, but coverage can vary by precinct and by species. Before you bet your ranch on being open range, verify it with the county clerk in Waco, Meridian, or Marlin. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension also publishes solid plain-language material on fence law and stock laws at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu.

Here’s how liability tends to shake out by road type:

Where the wreck happens Open range area Closed range (stock law) area

U.S. or state highway (I-35, US 84, TX 6) Liable only if you knowingly let stock roam Same highway rule, plus your local duty

Farm-to-market road (FM 185, FM 933) Generally no duty to fence cattle in Liable if the driver proves negligence

County road or gravel road Generally no duty Liable if the driver proves negligence

Private lane or easement Rarely a liability issue Rarely a liability issue

One more time, because it matters: even in a closed range precinct, Texas courts do not apply strict liability. The driver must prove you failed to act as a reasonably prudent rancher. Your fence, and your paper trail on that fence, is what that fight is about.

## Who Ends Up Liable for Cattle on the Road: Three Central Texas Stories

Rules are abstract. Here’s what they look like on real ground around here.

The 2 a.m. call outside West. Danny runs about 40 pairs on leased ground northeast of West. Last spring a rusted-out water gap let six heifers onto a county road, and a deputy had him out of bed at 2 a.m. pushing cattle in his boots and shorts. No wreck, thank God, so no lawsuit. But the scare cost him real money anyway: about $3,800 to rebuild the water gap and re-stretch a quarter mile of wire, plus a formal warning that the county considered him on notice. If those heifers get out again and someone gets hurt, that warning becomes Exhibit A on the “knowingly” question.

The bull on Highway 6 near Valley Mills. Rachel keeps a small commercial herd along TX 6. Her old netwire had been sagging for two seasons, and her bull had already walked through it twice. The third time, a pickup clipped him at dusk. The driver’s claim came in at $11,000 in truck damage plus medical bills. Because a neighbor had texted her photos of the down fence weeks earlier, “knowingly” was very much on the table under the highway statute. Her farm liability carrier settled for $18,500, her premium jumped, and she finally replaced 1,900 feet of fence at roughly $8 a foot. The fence would have cost about $15,000. The escape cost more, and she still had to build the fence.

The demand letter in Crawford. Tommy’s cows got onto an FM road west of Crawford after a feral hog rooted under his wire. A driver swerved, hit a culvert, and his attorney sent Tommy a $14,000 demand. Tommy’s lawyer answered with two points: the FM road isn’t a “highway” under Section 143.102, and the driver would have to prove negligence under the local stock law, which he couldn’t, because Tommy had receipts showing the fence was checked and repaired that same month. The claim died. Winning still cost Tommy about $2,500 in legal fees. His maintenance records are what kept it from costing ten times that.

Three different roads, three different outcomes, one common thread: the condition of the fence, and the proof of it, decided everything.

## Your Fence Is Your Best Legal Defense

You can’t control juries, drivers, or county stock law records from 1922. You can control your fence. In practice, cattle owner liability in Texas rises and falls on whether you can show you kept a reasonable fence in reasonable repair.

Here’s what “reasonable” looks like along road frontage in our country:

- Five strands of barbed wire, stretched tight, on posts spaced right for the terrain. A saggy three-strand relic won’t impress an adjuster. If your wire is drooping, start with our guide to fixing sagging barbed wire fence, or have us rebuild the barbed wire fence properly.

- Solid corners and braces. Most fence failures start where the tension lives. Along highways, a lot of our customers step up to pipe fence for road frontage because it shrugs off vehicle strikes and never rots.

- Working gates and water gaps. Gates left unlatched and washed-out water gaps are the two most common escape routes we see. Check them after every rain.

- A paper trail. Photos, receipts, and dated notes every time you walk or fix the fence. Tommy’s $2,500 outcome instead of a $14,000 one came down to receipts.

- Fast response when cattle get out. Get animals off the road safely, call the sheriff’s non-emergency line, and put flashers on if it’s dark. Never try to haze cattle off a highway alone at night in dark clothes. Your life is worth more than the cow.

If your cattle are getting out and you can’t figure out where, our article on why cattle get out of fences covers the usual suspects. And if you want the deeper history on fence-in versus fence-out, we broke down the Texas open range law in plain English.

Know your limits on the DIY side, too. Patching a stretch of wire on an interior cross fence is a Saturday job. Rebuilding storm-flattened fence along a state highway right-of-way, with traffic flying by at 75 and liability hanging over your head, is not. That’s when you stop and call a professional crew with the equipment to do it fast and do it right.

That’s what we’re here for. Brazos Ridge Fence builds and repairs cattle-tight fence across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, we’re licensed and insured, and estimates are free and in writing. Call (254) 870-8898, day or night on the emergency line if you’ve got cattle out or storm damage on a road, or reach us here to get on the schedule.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Am I automatically liable if a driver hits my cow in Texas?

No. Texas has no strict liability rule for livestock on roads. On U.S. and state highways, the driver must show you knowingly let the animal roam at large. On other roads in closed range areas, the driver must prove ordinary negligence, and in true open range areas there’s generally no duty at all on local roads.

### Does open range law still apply in McLennan County?

Mostly no in practice. Like most settled Central Texas counties, McLennan County adopted stock laws for cattle generations ago, though coverage can vary by precinct and species. The election records sit with the county clerk, so verify your specific precinct before you rely on open range status. And remember the highway statute applies everywhere regardless.

### What should I do first if my cattle get out on the road?

Get there fast, but work safe. Call the sheriff’s non-emergency line so deputies can slow traffic, use your truck’s flashers, and move cattle off the pavement toward the nearest gate. Once they’re contained, photograph the escape point before you fix it, then repair it and keep the receipt. That documentation protects you if a claim shows up later.

### Will my insurance cover a cattle-vehicle accident?

A standard farm and ranch liability policy usually covers damage your livestock cause to third parties, including vehicle wrecks, and it pays for your legal defense. Homeowners policies often exclude livestock operations, so don’t assume. Talk to your agent about your herd, your road frontage, and your policy limits before you need them.

## Cattle Panel Fence vs Net Wire: Strength, Cost, and Best Uses (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/cattle-panels-vs-net-wire/)

> Comparing cattle panels and net wire for your Central Texas ranch? See real costs per foot, strength differences, and which fence fits your stock and budget.

Materials

# Cattle Panel Fence vs Net Wire: Strength, Cost, and Best Uses
Published July 29, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A 1,400 pound bull does not care what your fence cost. He cares whether it moves when he leans on it. That one fact settles most of the cattle panel versus net wire debate before we ever pull a tape...

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A 1,400 pound bull does not care what your fence cost. He cares whether it moves when he leans on it. That one fact settles most of the cattle panel versus net wire debate before we ever pull a tape measure.

We build both all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and we get this question weekly. Should I run net wire down the whole property line, or should I spend more and put up a cattle panel fence? The honest answer is that they are different tools. Panels are rigid steel built for pressure and close quarters. Net wire is a stretched mesh built to cover distance for less money. Put each one where it belongs and you will spend less over ten years than the neighbor who picked one and used it everywhere.

Here is how we walk customers through it, with the numbers we actually quote in Waco.

## What a cattle panel fence actually is

A cattle panel is a welded steel grid, usually 16 feet long and around 50 to 52 inches tall. The rods are welded at every crossing, so the panel holds its shape on its own. You do not stretch it. You stand it up against posts and clip or weld it in place.

Panels come in different rod thicknesses, and the gauge matters more than most folks realize. A light 6 gauge utility panel from the farm store runs $28 to $40 and will bend if a cow hits it hard. A true bull panel with 4 gauge rods runs $70 to $110 per panel and will take a real beating. When we build working pens, we use the heavy stuff, because a bent panel in an alley is worse than no panel at all.

Because each panel is rigid, a cattle panel fence shrugs off point pressure. An animal pushing on one spot loads the whole grid, and the grid pushes back. That is why panels dominate in corrals, sorting pens, bull traps, and anywhere animals get crowded and cranky.

The tradeoff is cost and labor. Every 16 feet needs solid post support, and the material price per foot is several times what net wire costs. Nobody fences a quarter section with panels. Nobody should.

If you are pricing a full property and want a gut check on your budget, look at our ranch fence cost guide or call us at (254) 870-8898 and we will talk through it. Written estimates are free and we do not play games with the numbers.

## Net wire in plain terms

Net wire, also called field fence or woven wire, is a mesh of horizontal and vertical wires stretched between braced corners. Instead of welds, the wires are joined with knots. The two knot styles you will see are hinge joint and fixed knot, and the difference is bigger than the price gap suggests. We broke that down in detail in our fixed knot vs hinge joint post, but the short version is this: hinge joint is cheaper and folds under heavy impact, while fixed knot holds its grid and springs back.

A standard 330 foot roll of 12.5 gauge hinge joint field fence runs $180 to $260 around Waco right now. Fixed knot runs $280 to $420 for the same length, depending on height and wire class. Stretched properly on good posts with solid H braces at the corners, net wire makes a clean, tight fence that holds cattle, and it is the default choice for goats and sheep because the mesh stops the escape artists that walk right through barbed wire.

The catch is in that phrase “stretched properly.” Net wire is only as strong as its bracing. A beautiful stretch on weak corners will sag inside two years. If you have ever wondered why one neighbor’s field fence looks like a hammock and another’s still sings when you pluck it, the answer is almost always in the corner posts, not the wire.

## Strength: cattle panels vs net wire when animals hit them

Strength is where these two products stop being comparable and start being different animals.

A heavy cattle panel resists bending because every joint is welded and every rod carries load. Hang a gate wrong, back a trailer into it, let a bull fight through it, and a 4 gauge panel usually survives with a scuff. Panels also hold their height forever. There is no stretch to lose, so there is no sag to fight.

Net wire works on tension. It is strong against steady pushing but weaker against sharp, concentrated impact. A hinge joint fence hit hard by a spooked cow will often kink and stay kinked. Fixed knot handles impact much better, which is why game fence builders use it, but even fixed knot will not match welded steel rod in a squeeze pen.

Then there are hogs. Feral hogs root under net wire and tear through the bottom courses, and Central Texas has no shortage of them. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension (agrilifeextension.tamu.edu) has good material on hog behavior and exclusion if you want the research side. From the fence side, we covered what hog damage looks like and how to fight it in our feral hog fence damage post. Panels resist hogs better at ground level, but hogs will still dig under anything if the bottom is not addressed.

Here is a real one. Dale Kubacak runs about 40 pairs outside Crawford. His working pens were 20 year old hinge joint net wire on cedar posts, and in March a bull went through the sorting pen side like it was a screen door. That wreck cost him a morning, a gate, and $340 in vet work on a heifer that got caught in the tangle. We rebuilt his pens with 4 gauge bull panels welded to pipe posts, about 280 feet of pen for $6,800. His words when we finished: “Should have done this ten years ago.” The perimeter of his place is still net wire, because out there it is doing exactly what net wire does well.

## Cattle panel fence cost vs net wire cost

Numbers first, talk after. These are typical installed ranges we quote in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties as of mid 2026. Materials alone will run roughly a third to half of these figures.

Fence type Materials per foot Installed per foot Best lifespan on good posts

Hinge joint net wire (12.5 ga) $0.90 - $1.60 $3.25 - $5.50 15 - 20 years

Fixed knot net wire $1.40 - $2.30 $4.50 - $7.00 25 - 30 years

Utility cattle panels (6 ga) $2.00 - $3.00 $6.00 - $9.00 15 - 20 years

Bull panels (4 ga) on T-posts $4.50 - $7.00 $9.00 - $14.00 25 - 30 years

Bull panels welded to pipe posts $6.00 - $9.00 $16.00 - $28.00 30 - 40 years

Read that table with acreage in mind. A mile of perimeter is 5,280 feet. At $4.50 a foot, net wire runs about $23,800 installed. The same mile in bull panels on pipe would top $90,000, which is why nobody does it. Flip it around for a set of pens: 300 feet of pen fence in panels might cost $4,000 to $7,000, and that is 300 feet that takes the hardest abuse on the whole ranch. Spending panel money there is not a splurge. It is insurance.

Post choice moves these numbers too. Panels on T-posts are fine for garden and horse paddock duty, but working pens want pipe. If you are already thinking about pipe, our pipe fence page covers what we build and why used oilfield pipe is the workhorse around here.

Marcy Villareal in Lorena had us quote both options for a 2 acre goat paddock last fall. Net wire came in at $4,100. Panels came in at $7,900. She went with fixed knot net wire and put the $3,800 difference into a better ranch entrance gate and a hog apron along the creek side. A year in, zero escapes. Right tool, right spot.

Want a number for your own place instead of a table? Request a free written estimate and we will walk the line with you.

## Best uses: where each one earns its keep

After a few hundred fence jobs in Central Texas, the pattern is pretty clear.

Use cattle panels for working pens, corrals, alleys, and loading areas. Use them for bull pens and anywhere you crowd animals. Use them for round pens, hog traps, small horse paddocks with hot wire on top, and garden fence where deer pressure is moderate. Panels also shine for odd shaped small enclosures because you are not fighting a stretch around corners.

Use net wire for perimeter and cross fencing on acreage. Use it for goat and sheep pastures, for keeping dogs in and coyotes honest, and for any run longer than a few hundred feet where panel pricing stops making sense. On pure cattle perimeter, plenty of ranchers still choose 5 strand barbed wire over both, and that is a fair fight we covered in barbed wire vs net wire. Our barbed wire fence crew builds more miles of it than anything else we do.

The combination approach usually wins. A typical 50 acre place near us ends up with barbed or net wire on the perimeter, net wire cross fences, and a panel built pen complex near the barn. Each product sits where its strengths matter and its price makes sense.

One more note on rules and cost share. If you are fencing along a road, remember most of Texas is still legally open range at the county level with big exceptions, so your liability picture depends on local stock laws. And if you are improving grazing land, the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (nrcs.usda.gov) runs cost share programs through EQIP that sometimes help pay for livestock fencing. Worth a phone call to the Waco field office before you build.

## Where DIY ends and a pro should take over

Plenty of our customers hang their own utility panels, and we will cheer you on. Setting a dozen panels around a garden with T-posts is a good Saturday project. Keep the bottom rod close to the ground, tie every panel at top, middle, and bottom, and do not skimp on post depth.

Stop and call somebody when the job involves stretching net wire past a couple hundred feet, building H braces, welding panels to pipe, or any fence that will hold bulls or sit along a public road. Corner bracing is the whole ballgame with net wire, and a failed brace lets the entire stretch go slack at once. Welding on pipe near dry grass in a Central Texas summer is its own hazard, and a pen that fails with cattle and people inside it is a genuinely dangerous failure, not just an expensive one.

Frank Novosad out in West learned that the hard way before he called us. He stretched 600 feet of field fence himself off corners set 18 inches deep in sand. It looked great in October. By June the corners had walked, the fence was on the ground in two spots, and his calves were grazing the county right of way. Redoing the corners and restretching cost him $1,150, most of which he would have avoided with proper braces the first time. If your fence is heading the same direction, our post on leaning fence posts explains what is happening underground.

We are licensed and insured, and we answer a 24/7 emergency line for cattle out and storm damage calls. If something just went through your fence tonight, call (254) 870-8898 and we will get you contained.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Will cattle panels hold a bull?

Heavy 4 gauge bull panels on well set posts will hold most bulls, and panels welded to pipe posts will hold about anything that walks in Texas. Light 6 gauge utility panels will not, and a determined bull will fold them. If bulls are part of the plan, buy the heavy panel and put pipe behind it.

### Is a cattle panel fence cheaper than net wire?

No, not per foot. Installed net wire typically runs $3.25 to $7.00 per foot in our area, while panel fencing runs $6.00 to $28.00 depending on panel gauge and post type. Panels win on cost only when you count the years, because a pen that never needs restretching or wreck repair costs less over a couple of decades of hard use.

### How tall are cattle panels, and are they tall enough for horses?

Standard cattle panels are 50 to 52 inches tall, which is short for horses. For horse pens we recommend 60 inch panels or a top rail that brings the fence to at least 5 feet, since horses will reach over and lean on shorter panels. Smooth welded panels are safer for horses than barbed alternatives, but check for sharp clipped ends at eye height.

### Can I combine cattle panels and net wire on the same place?

Yes, and most well fenced ranches around Waco do exactly that. Panels go on the pens, alleys, and high pressure spots near the barn, and net wire or barbed wire covers the perimeter and cross fences. You get panel strength where animals fight the fence and net wire economics across the long runs.
