## Cedar vs Treated Pine Fence Posts: What Holds Up in Texas (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/cedar-vs-treated-pine-posts/)

> Cedar vs treated pine fence posts compared for Central Texas ranches: true costs per post, lifespan in Waco clay, and which posts we set on our own jobs.

Materials

# Cedar vs Treated Pine Fence Posts: What Holds Up in Texas
Published July 30, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Most of the fence repair calls we run in McLennan County trace back to a failed post, not failed wire. The wire gets the blame, but the post did the quitting.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Most of the fence repair calls we run in McLennan County trace back to a failed post, not failed wire. The wire gets the blame, but the post did the quitting. That’s why the cedar vs treated pine fence posts question deserves a straight answer, because picking the wrong post is the most expensive small decision you’ll make on a ranch fence.

Get it right and your fence stands 25 to 40 years. Get it wrong and you’re pulling rotten stubs out of black clay in year six, paying twice for the same quarter mile.

We build fence every week across Waco, China Spring, Crawford, McGregor, Valley Mills, Lorena, and West. We’ve set thousands of both kinds of posts and dug out thousands more that failed. Here’s what we’ve learned, with real numbers.

## Why the Post Decision Matters More Than the Wire

A five strand barbed wire fence is only as good as what’s holding it up. Wire almost never wears out first. Posts do.

Here’s the math that stings. Line posts run 10 to 20 feet apart on most ranch fences. On a quarter mile of fence, that’s 65 to 130 posts. If your posts fail at year 8 instead of year 30, you don’t just buy new posts. You pay for pulling the old ones, hauling them off, re-drilling holes, resetting, and restretching wire. Replacement almost always costs more than the original build.

Dale, who runs cows northwest of Crawford, learned that the hard way before he called us. A previous crew set his line posts with cheap untreated pine timbers in 2019. By 2023 he could push them over by hand. Redoing a quarter mile of line posts and restretching the wire ran him about $3,800. The right posts up front would’ve added maybe $400 to the original job.

So before you compare wire types or strand counts, get the post question settled. If you’d rather talk it through with somebody who sets posts for a living, request a free written estimate or call us at (254) 870-8898. We’ll shoot you straight on what your soil and stock actually need.

## Cedar Fence Posts: What the Old Timers Got Right and Wrong

Drive any county road in Bosque County and you’ll see cedar posts that have stood since before most of us were born. That’s not a myth. It’s also not the whole story.

The cedar on those old fences is heartwood, the dense reddish center of a mature tree. Heartwood is loaded with natural oils that resist rot and insects. A true heartwood cedar post, the kind with almost no white wood on it, can last 20 to 25 years in Central Texas ground, sometimes longer in dry, well drained spots.

The problem is what’s sold as “cedar posts” today. A lot of it is young, fast cut Ashe juniper with a thin core of heartwood wrapped in two inches of white sapwood. Sapwood has none of that natural protection. It can rot off at the ground line in 5 to 7 years, and the skinny heartwood core left behind won’t hold a fence tight.

Marcy runs goats and a few horses outside Valley Mills, and her granddad’s cedar corner posts from the 1990s are still solid. When she added new cross fencing in 2021, she bought a trailer load of bargain cedar at $9 a post. By last spring, 14 of them had rotted through at the dirt. Replacing them, plus fixing the sagging wire they let loose, cost her right at $1,100.

Cedar’s other weak spot is brittleness. Old dry cedar snaps under impact. A 1,300 pound bull leaning on a cedar line post is one thing. That same bull hitting it at a run is another, and cedar loses that fight more often than treated pine does.

What cedar still does well:

- Looks right. That silver gray weathered post is the classic Texas ranch look, and nothing else matches it.

- No chemicals. Some folks want untreated wood near gardens, wells, or organic operations.

- Corner and gate posts in big diameters. A fat 8 inch heartwood cedar corner is a genuinely good post.

## Treated Pine Fence Posts: What That Green Tint Actually Buys You

Treated pine posts are plantation grown southern yellow pine, pressure treated with preservative that’s forced deep into the wood. Pine takes treatment better than almost any other species because its sapwood is thick and absorbent. That’s the whole trick. The part of the tree that rots fastest in cedar is the part that carries the protection in pine.

Done right, a treated pine post is the most rot resistant wood post you can buy. The USDA Forest Products Laboratory has run ground contact stake tests for decades, and properly treated pine routinely outlasts naturally durable species in ground contact. You can dig into their wood durability research at the Forest Products Laboratory.

The catch is those two words: done right. Treatment quality varies a lot, and this is where most treated post horror stories come from.

Look for these three things:

- Retention level. For fence posts, you want CCA treated posts rated for ground contact, generally 0.40 pcf retention or better. Landscape timbers and “ground contact” deck lumber at 0.15 to 0.23 are not fence posts, no matter what the pallet sign says.

- A quality stamp or tag. Reputable posts carry a tag showing the preservative, retention, and inspection agency.

- Full penetration. Cut ends and dry centers on poorly treated posts rot from the inside out.

A fellow named Kurt near West found this out in 2022. He bought a bargain pallet of untagged “treated” posts at an estate sale for a new hay trap. Within three years the ground line on most of them had gone punky, and he paid us about $2,100 to pull and replace 60 of them with properly rated posts. The tagged posts would’ve cost him roughly $250 more the first time.

If you’re wondering about the chemicals, CCA is restricted for most residential lumber but still approved for agricultural fence posts. The EPA keeps a plain language rundown of wood preservatives and where each is allowed at epa.gov.

## Cedar vs Treated Pine Fence Posts: Cost and Lifespan Side by Side

Here’s how the two stack up on the jobs we build around Waco. Prices are typical retail ranges as of this year and will swing with diameter and supplier.

Factor Cedar (true heartwood) Treated pine (CCA 0.40+)

Line post, 4 in x 6.5 ft $12 to $22 $8 to $14

Corner or brace post, 6 to 8 in $30 to $60 $22 to $40

Expected life in Central Texas soil 15 to 25 years, less if sapwood heavy 25 to 35 years

Ground line rot risk Low for heartwood, high for sapwood Low when properly treated

Impact strength Fair, brittle when old and dry Good, flexes before it breaks

Holds staples Fair, can split Good

Insect resistance Natural, heartwood only Chemical, full post

Consistency post to post Varies a lot Very consistent

Looks Classic silver gray ranch look Green fading to gray brown

On a full quarter mile with around 90 line posts, the post material difference between good cedar and good treated pine usually lands between $300 and $700. That’s real money, but it’s small next to the cost of rebuilding early. Lifespan and treatment quality matter far more than the sticker price per post.

For the full picture of what a complete fence runs, our ranch fence cost guide breaks down materials and labor per foot.

## What Central Texas Clay, Heat, and Drought Do to Both

Soil is the referee in this fight, and around here the referee plays rough.

Most of McLennan and Falls County sits on blackland clay. That clay swells when it rains and shrinks hard in drought, opening cracks along every post. Those cracks funnel water straight down the post face, then seal up and hold that moisture against the wood for weeks. It’s a near perfect rot chamber, and it’s why the ground line, not the buried tip, is where posts fail. We cover the mechanics in our post on setting fence posts in clay soil.

Treated pine handles this cycle better because the protection goes where the rot happens. Sapwood heavy cedar fails fastest in exactly these conditions.

West of the Bosque River, around Crawford, Valley Mills, and parts of McGregor, you run into shallower, rockier, better drained ground. Cedar performs noticeably better there. Less standing moisture at the ground line means heartwood cedar can genuinely reach that 25 year mark.

Heat and drought punish cedar in one more way. Extended dry spells check and split dry cedar, and checked posts shed staples and snap easier. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid fencing guidance for exactly our conditions, and it’s worth a read before any big build.

One thing no post choice fixes: bad bracing. A 35 year post won’t save a corner that wasn’t built right. If your corners lean, the post species was never the problem. See our guide on H-brace fence corners for how a corner should actually be built.

## What We Actually Set on Jobs Around Waco

After all the back and forth, here’s the honest answer we give customers at the kitchen table.

For most working barbed wire fences in our area, we set properly treated pine for corners, braces, and wood line posts, usually mixed with steel T-posts between them. It’s the most predictable post you can buy. Every post on the trailer has the same protection, which isn’t something you can say about a load of cedar. If you’re weighing wood against steel for your line posts, our T-post vs wood post comparison walks through that call.

We reach for cedar when it fits: entrance fences and yard fences where looks matter, well drained rocky ground, and customers who want no treated wood on the place. When we do, we’re picky. Big diameter, heavy heartwood, minimal white wood. We’ll reject half a supplier’s stack to get it.

And for corners and gates that take serious abuse, or anywhere horses and heavy cattle crowd a fence line, welded pipe fence beats both woods and never rots at all.

A word on DIY. Swapping a handful of line posts is a fine weekend job if you can match the set depth and get the tamping right. But if you’re seeing rot across a whole stretch, if corners or gate posts are moving, or if cattle are already testing weak spots, stop and get help before a small problem becomes a loose herd on FM 185. Bracing and stretching under tension can hurt you, and a poorly rebuilt corner fails the whole fence.

Want a straight recommendation for your soil and your stock? Ask for a free written estimate or call (254) 870-8898. We’re licensed and insured, and if a storm or a cattle-out emergency can’t wait, that line answers 24/7.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How long do cedar fence posts last in Texas?

True heartwood cedar posts typically last 15 to 25 years in Central Texas, and longer in dry, rocky, well drained ground. Sapwood heavy cedar can rot off at the ground line in as little as 5 to 7 years, especially in blackland clay. The quality of the individual post matters more than the species name on the invoice.

### What treatment rating should treated pine fence posts have?

For fence posts, look for CCA treated posts with a retention of 0.40 pcf or higher, tagged for ground contact by an inspection agency. Landscape timbers and light duty treated lumber around 0.15 to 0.23 retention will rot in a few years when buried. If a post has no tag and no stamp, treat it as untested and price it accordingly.

### Is treated pine safe to use around livestock?

Yes, properly treated and dried posts are widely used on cattle, horse, and goat operations, and CCA remains approved for agricultural fence posts. The preservative is bonded into the wood, so normal contact and occasional chewing aren’t considered a meaningful risk. Don’t burn old treated posts, and keep sawdust from cutting them out of feed areas.

### Can I mix cedar and treated pine posts in the same fence?

You can, and plenty of ranches do. A common setup is treated pine or pipe at the corners and gates, where strength and lifespan matter most, with cedar or T-posts on the line. Just remember the fence ages at the speed of its weakest posts, so keep the quality consistent within each stretch.

## Cheapest Horse Fencing That Is Still Safe: Real Costs Per Foot (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/cheapest-horse-fencing/)

> The cheapest horse fencing that will not cut a horse, priced per foot for Central Texas. No-climb mesh, electric and pipe compared on real Waco-area numbers.

Cost Guide

# Cheapest Horse Fencing That Is Still Safe: Real Costs Per Foot
Published September 11, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A horse hits a fence at a dead run and the fence either turns him or cuts him. That is the whole question, and it's why the cheapest horse fencing on most price lists is not fencing you can put a...

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A horse hits a fence at a dead run and the fence either turns him or cuts him. That is the whole question, and it’s why the cheapest horse fencing on most price lists is not fencing you can put a horse behind.

Barbed wire runs $2.50 to $5.50 a foot installed around Waco. It’s the least expensive livestock fence anybody builds here, and it’s the right call for cattle. Put a horse behind it and you have financed a vet bill instead of a fence.

There is a real answer to the cheap question, though. On most small places around McLennan, Bosque and Falls counties, the cheapest fence you can safely keep horses in lands in the $3.50 to $8 per foot range, and the smart moves are about layout and material choice, not about buying the thinnest wire on the rack.

What follows is what each option runs per foot around here, and where the cheap version holds up.

## What Cheap Has to Mean When a Horse Is Behind It

Cattle are thick hided and slow to spook. Horses are prey animals with thin skin and a panic reflex, and they run before they look.

A horse fence has three jobs a cattle fence does not. The horse has to see it from a run. A hoof must not fit through it. And nothing on it can cut when 1,100 pounds leans, paws or rolls into it.

Extension programs have been saying this in print for decades. Penn State Extension lists barbed wire as unacceptable for horse fencing in its fence planning guide for horses, and the University of Georgia Extension fences-for-horses bulletin says the same about visibility and hoof-sized openings.

So when we talk about the cheapest option, we mean the cheapest fence that clears those three tests. Go under that line and the money shows up later, usually at the vet.

If you already have horses standing behind old wire and you are trying to work out what it takes to fix it, call (254) 870-8898. Walking the line is free and takes about an hour, and you’ll get a number before anybody talks you into a fence you don’t need.

## The Cheapest Horse Fencing Options, Priced Per Foot

Here is the honest spread for Central Texas in 2026. The installed prices are our range for McLennan, Bosque and Falls counties. The electric line is a materials-only general estimate, not a quote, because what it costs to install depends entirely on how much of the old fence stays.

Fence type Installed cost per foot Safe behind horses Where it fits

5-strand barbed wire $2.50 - $5.50 No Cattle perimeter only, never a horse pen

Plain hinge-joint net wire $3.50 - $8 Only with a sight rail on top Mixed stock, back pastures, low-traffic runs

No-climb 2x4 horse mesh Upper end of the $3.50 - $8 net wire band Yes The value pick for horse pasture

Electric tape or coated rope Materials-only estimate, roughly $0.60 to $1.50 per foot of material As an interior divider, yes; as a sole perimeter, no Cross-fencing, rotation, temporary paddocks

Welded pipe $12 - $28 Yes Road frontage, corrals, high-traffic pens

Read the table as a spread, not a menu. Almost every horse place we price ends up mixing two of these, and the mix is where the savings live. Full per-foot and per-mile pricing for every fence type sits on the ranch fence cost page.

One thing the table cannot show you is corners. A square 5-acre paddock has far more corners and braces per foot of fence than a long straight run, so short jobs always price higher per foot than big ones. That is not a markup, it is bracing, and it is the main reason a small horse place costs more per foot than a cattle lease.

## No-Climb Mesh Is the Cheapest Horse Fence We Will Stand Behind

Two-by-four woven mesh, the stuff most people call no-climb, is the value answer for horses on small acreage in this part of Texas. The openings are too small for a hoof, the wire is smooth, and there isn’t a barb anywhere on it.

It sits at the upper end of our net wire and field fence band, so budget toward the $8 side rather than the $3.50 side. Worth saying plainly: horse-grade mesh isn’t the cheap end of net wire, it’s the expensive end. What you’re paying for is tighter knots, heavier wire and a fence that stays tight when a horse leans on it for ten years.

Two decisions move that number more than anything else. Fixed-knot mesh costs more than hinge joint and holds its shape far better under pressure. And a top rail or a top sight line, whether that is a pipe rail, a wood cap or a strand of coated electric, is what makes the fence visible at dusk.

If the budget is tight, mesh without a top rail is still a safe fence. It’s just a less visible one, and we’d rather add a hot strand on standoffs for pennies a foot than skip the sight line entirely. The material choices are laid out in our no-climb horse fence guide.

## Electric Is the Cheapest Horse Fencing on the Board, With Conditions

Coated electric rope or 1.5-inch tape on fiberglass or capped steel posts is the least expensive horse-safe barrier you can put up, and the materials-only estimate above holds for most jobs. It’s visible, it doesn’t cut, and horses learn it fast.

Here is the condition. Electric is a psychological fence, not a physical one. It works because the horse respects it. It quits working the moment the charger fails, the ground rods dry out in an August drought, or a limb shorts the line.

That makes it excellent for cross-fencing and rotation inside a secure perimeter, and a poor choice as the only thing between your horses and a farm-to-market road. If your place fronts a paved road, spend the money on a physical perimeter and use electric inside it.

Grounding is the part most people get wrong here. Blackland clay holds moisture and grounds well most of the year, but the same ground goes to concrete in a dry summer and your fence goes quiet without telling you. Our post on electric fence for horses covers charger sizing, ground rods and the order to troubleshoot in.

## Three Central Texas Jobs and What They Run

Numbers land better than adjectives, so here are three situations we price regularly. Treat the totals as worked examples for planning, not as quotes, because the ground under your fence line is the variable nobody can price over the phone.

A 12-acre horse place outside Lorena. Two mares, flat blackland, about 2,900 feet of perimeter with an old four-strand barbed wire fence on it. Pull the wire, keep the good corner posts, run no-climb mesh at 60 inches with a hot strand on standoffs for a sight line. At the upper end of the net wire band that job prices in the low twenty thousands, and the interior cross-fence that splits it into two turnout pastures adds electric rope at materials cost plus a day of labor.

A limestone hill section near Valley Mills. Around 900 feet where every post has to be rock-drilled instead of augered. Same mesh, same wire, same crew, and the price runs to the top of the $3.50 to $8 band because drilling caliche and limestone is slow work with a hydraulic drill. Rock doesn’t change the material list, it changes the hours, and anybody who quotes that line at flat-country prices has not walked it.

A 5-acre place with 300 feet of road frontage near West. Welded pipe across the front at $12 to $28 per foot depending on whether it’s new pipe or used drill stem, then no-climb mesh on the three sides nobody sees from the road. Splitting the job that way costs a fraction of piping the whole perimeter and puts the strongest fence where a loose horse would do the most damage. If pipe is on your list, the pipe fence page has the sizing and the per-foot detail.

Want your own line priced instead of somebody else’s? Call (254) 870-8898 or ask for an on-site estimate and we will walk it with you before any number gets quoted.

## Where to Spend First When the Budget Is Tight

If you can’t fence everything this year, fence in this order.

Start with the road side. A horse loose on a county road is the failure that costs the most, and it’s the one section where pipe or heavy mesh pays for itself the first time it holds.

Second, fence the turnout the horses actually live in. A tight, safe 3-acre paddock beats 12 acres of half-good fence every time, and it lets you take the rest of the perimeter in stages next season.

Third, fix the corners and braces before you buy more wire. A fence is only as tight as its H-braces, and mesh stretched against a weak corner will sag inside two summers no matter what you paid per foot.

Last, phase the pretty parts. Entrances, gates and rail fence along the drive can wait. Nothing about them keeps a horse home.

One more piece of arithmetic worth knowing. Fencing the whole perimeter in one go almost always beats doing it in pieces, because mobilization, equipment hauling and material delivery get spread across more feet. If you can wait one season and do it all at once, the per-foot number usually drops. Our page on horse fence in Waco covers how we phase these jobs, and what it costs to fence 10 acres runs the perimeter math for a small tract.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the cheapest fence that is genuinely safe for horses?

For a permanent perimeter, no-climb 2x4 woven mesh with a visible top line is the cheapest fence that clears all three horse-safety tests. Expect it at the upper end of our $3.50 to $8 per foot net wire range. Electric tape is cheaper per foot on materials, but it belongs inside a physical perimeter rather than replacing one.

### Can I just use net wire instead of no-climb mesh to save money?

Sometimes, and it depends on the mesh spacing and the horses. Standard hinge-joint field fence has larger openings toward the top and can trap a hoof or a shoe, and it loosens faster when horses lean on it. If the budget forces plain field fence, add a sight rail or a hot strand at the top and check the fence often.

### Does barbed wire ever belong on a horse property?

On the outside of a cattle pasture that horses never enter, yes. Along any fence line a horse can touch, no. Plenty of Central Texas places run barbed wire on the far perimeter and horse-safe mesh around the traps and turnouts, which is a reasonable way to spend a limited budget.

### Why did two contractors quote such different prices for the same fence?

Usually rock, brush and bracing. A line that has to be rock-drilled, cleared of cedar, or braced at eight corners costs far more in labor than a clean straight run, and different bids often assume different mesh grades and post spacing. Ask each bidder what wire, what post spacing and how many braces, then compare like for like. A bid that comes in $2 a foot under everybody else is usually missing bracing, not saving you money.

## Class 1 vs Class 3 Galvanized Fence Wire: Which One Outlasts the Other? (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/class-3-galvanized-wire/)

> Class 3 galvanized fence wire lasts 2 to 3 times longer than Class 1 in Central Texas. See real costs, lifespan numbers, and when the upgrade pays off.

Materials

# Class 1 vs Class 3 Galvanized Fence Wire: Which One Outlasts the Other?
Published July 31, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Two rolls of barbed wire sit side by side on the shelf at the farm store. Same gauge, same twist, same shine, and one costs about thirty bucks more.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Two rolls of barbed wire sit side by side on the shelf at the farm store. Same gauge, same twist, same shine, and one costs about thirty bucks more. Here’s the part the price tag doesn’t tell you: the cheaper roll may start rusting in 8 years, while the other one can still be holding cattle 30 years from now.

The difference is the zinc coating, and it’s the single most ignored spec in ranch fencing. Class 3 galvanized fence wire carries roughly three times the zinc of Class 1, and that coating is the only thing standing between the steel and the rust. We build fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and when we tear out a fence that failed early, thin galvanizing is the reason more often than not.

This article breaks down what the classes actually mean, how long each one lasts in Central Texas conditions, what the upgrade really costs per foot, and when Class 1 is honestly good enough. Real numbers, no fluff.

## What the Zinc Coating Actually Does for Your Fence Wire

Bare steel wire rusts fast. Out in a Central Texas pasture with humidity rolling up from the Gulf, morning dew, and the occasional wet winter, unprotected steel can show surface rust in months and lose real strength within a few years.

Galvanizing fixes that by bonding a layer of zinc to the steel. Zinc does two jobs. First, it’s a physical barrier that keeps water and oxygen off the steel. Second, it’s a sacrificial metal. Even when the coating gets scratched, the zinc around the scratch corrodes first and protects the exposed steel underneath.

Here’s the key point: zinc wears away at a fairly steady rate for a given climate. That means the life of your wire is almost directly tied to how much zinc is on it. Double the zinc, roughly double the years before rust shows up. Triple it, and you’re talking about a fence that outlives the posts holding it.

That’s the whole argument between the classes. It’s not about stronger steel or a better barb. It’s about how thick the zinc is.

If you’re pricing a new perimeter fence and want somebody local to walk the line and talk wire specs with you, give us a call at (254) 870-8898. Estimates are free and in writing.

## Class 1 vs Class 3 Galvanized Wire: The Real Difference

The classes come from ASTM standards that spell out the minimum ounces of zinc per square foot of wire surface. For common 12.5 gauge fence wire, the numbers look like this:

- Class 1: about 0.28 ounces of zinc per square foot

- Class 3: about 0.80 ounces of zinc per square foot

So Class 3 galvanized fence wire carries close to three times the zinc coating of Class 1 on the same wire. Same steel, same gauge, same breaking strength on day one. The difference only shows up over time, which is exactly why the cheap roll sells so well. Both look identical on the shelf.

Land grant universities have tested this for decades. Oklahoma State University Extension reports that Class 1 coatings can show rust in as little as 8 to 10 years in humid climates, while Class 3 coatings commonly go 20 to 30 years before rust appears. You can read their fencing materials fact sheet here: Oklahoma State University Extension, Selecting Wire Fencing Materials. The University of Georgia’s Fences for the Farm bulletin backs up the same pattern.

Central Texas isn’t the Gulf Coast, but it’s not West Texas desert either. Waco averages around 36 inches of rain a year, and low spots, creek bottoms, and shaded lines hold moisture. Our real-world experience lands close to those university numbers.

There’s also a Class 2 in some product lines, but you’ll rarely see it on a farm store shelf around here. The practical choice is almost always Class 1 or Class 3.

### What About “Commercial” or Unlabeled Wire?

Some bargain import wire doesn’t state a coating class at all. Treat unlabeled wire as worse than Class 1, because it often is. If the tag or the manufacturer’s spec sheet won’t tell you the zinc weight, that’s your answer.

## How Long Each Class Lasts in Central Texas Conditions

Rust doesn’t hit a whole fence evenly. It starts where moisture lingers: creek crossings, water gaps, shaded tree lines, and anywhere the wire touches vegetation. Once the zinc is gone in those spots, the steel underneath starts losing diameter, and a 12.5 gauge wire that’s rusted down loses breaking strength fast. That’s when a cow leaning on the fence turns into a cow on the county road.

Here’s what we tell customers to expect around Waco, assuming decent construction and normal maintenance:

Spec Zinc coating (12.5 ga) First visible rust Useful life in Central Texas Typical cost per 1,320 ft roll

Unlabeled import wire Often under 0.25 oz/sq ft 3 to 6 years 8 to 12 years $75 to $95

Class 1 galvanized 0.28 oz/sq ft 8 to 10 years 12 to 18 years $85 to $110

Class 3 galvanized 0.80 oz/sq ft 15 to 25 years 25 to 35 years $110 to $145

Notice the cost column. On a quarter mile of 5-strand barbed wire fence, upgrading every strand from Class 1 to Class 3 usually adds $125 to $175 in materials. The labor, posts, braces, and gates are identical either way. You’re paying a few cents more per foot to roughly double the life of the whole fence.

Dale Prescott, who runs cows on a place along the Middle Bosque near Crawford, learned that math the hard way. His previous fence went in with bargain Class 1 wire, and the strands through his creek bottom were rusted through in under 10 years. We rebuilt about 2,600 feet of it for him at roughly $5,900, and the Class 3 wire on that job added only about $260 to the total. He’d have paid that upgrade ten times over to skip the rebuild.

Rust creeping in on an older fence? Before you decide anything, read our guide on whether rusted barbed wire is worth repairing or needs replacing.

## What Class 3 Galvanized Fence Wire Costs, and When It Pays Off

Let’s put the numbers on a whole project, because per-roll prices hide the real story.

Say you’re fencing a quarter mile, 1,320 feet, with 5 strands of 12.5 gauge barbed wire, T-posts on 10-foot centers, and wood corner braces. Installed by a crew like ours, that job typically runs $2.50 to $4.00 per foot, call it $3,300 to $5,300 total depending on terrain and clearing.

The wire itself is only about 10 to 15 percent of that cost. Everything else is posts, braces, hardware, and labor. So look at what the coating choice does to your cost per year of fence life:

- Class 1 fence at $4,000 lasting 15 years: about $267 per year

- Class 3 fence at $4,150 lasting 28 years: about $148 per year

The Class 3 fence costs 4 percent more up front and roughly half as much per year of service. That’s the whole case in two lines.

Marcy Kolar, outside West, called us in 2024 to fence a new 10-acre horse trap. The Class 3 upgrade on her job came to $340 over the Class 1 quote of $8,200. She took it, and her reasoning was simple: she never wants to build that fence twice. That’s the right way to think about it, because the most expensive part of any fence is doing the work again.

When Class 1 still makes sense:

- Temporary cross fencing you plan to move or remove within 10 years

- Interior division fences where a failure means cattle in the wrong pasture, not on the highway

- Land you plan to sell soon, though a buyer walking the fence line will notice rust

For perimeter fence, highway frontage, or anything holding bulls, we spec Class 3 galvanized barbed wire as our standard on barbed wire fence installs in the Waco area. Same logic applies to net wire and to the woven wire we hang on game fence projects, where the fence is taller, costs more per foot, and is even more painful to rebuild.

Want a side-by-side quote with both wire classes priced out for your place? Request a free written estimate and we’ll break the numbers down foot by foot.

## How to Tell What Class of Wire You’re Buying

The frustrating part is that Class 1 and Class 3 look identical new. Both come off the spool bright and shiny. Here’s how to protect yourself:

- Read the tag. Reputable American mills print the class right on the roll tag, along with the gauge and ASTM standard. If the tag says “12.5 ga Class 3,” you’re good.

- Check the weight. More zinc means a slightly heavier roll, but the difference is small enough that you can’t judge by feel. Trust the printed spec, not your hands.

- Be suspicious of prices that seem too good. A 1,320-foot roll of true Class 3 barbed wire under $100 in 2026 deserves a hard look at the label.

- Ask your contractor what they’re installing. A good fence builder will tell you the brand, gauge, and coating class without hesitating. If the answer is vague, that’s a red flag. Our list of questions to ask a fence contractor covers this and nine other things worth asking before you sign anything.

One more spec worth knowing: high-tensile wire is usually sold with Class 3 coating by default, which is part of why it lasts so long. Standard low-carbon barbed wire is where you have to watch the label, because both classes sit on the same shelf.

Gauge matters too. A heavier 12.5 gauge wire with Class 3 coating is the sweet spot for cattle in our area. If you’re weighing thickness options, our barbed wire gauge guide walks through it.

## Make the Coating Match the Rest of the Fence

Here’s a mistake we see on DIY builds: premium Class 3 wire stretched between corner braces that won’t last 10 years, or hung on thin-wall T-posts that bend the first time a bull tests them. The fence is a system. The wire, the posts, the braces, and the stays all need similar lifespans, or the weakest piece sets the schedule for the whole rebuild.

If you’re going with 25-year wire, pair it with:

- Proper H-braces at corners and pulls. A fence is only as tight as its braces.

- Posts that will still be solid in 25 years. That means good treated pine, cedar, or pipe, not landscape timbers.

- Class 3 or better on the accessories too. Staples, clips, and stays rust just like wire does.

And know when to stop DIYing. Stretching 5 strands over flat, clean ground is a reasonable weekend project for a handy landowner. Creek crossings, big elevation changes, rocky ground, long pulls over a quarter mile, or any fence along a public road is where mistakes get expensive or dangerous. Wire under tension can whip hard enough to cut you when a stretch goes wrong, and a badly built water gap will take out a whole corner in one flood. That’s the point to bring in a crew that does this every day.

Ray Villarreal, south of Lorena, called us last spring to bid on replacing what he assumed was a worn-out fence from the previous owner. We walked the line and found 28-year-old Class 3 wire that was still bright under a little surface dust, with maybe 40 rusted feet at one water gap. Instead of the $11,000 replacement he expected, he spent about $850 fixing the water gap and resetting two braces. Good wire earns its keep in ways you don’t see until decades later.

Fence emergencies don’t wait, either. If storm damage or a blown-out water gap has cattle out right now, our emergency line answers 24/7 at (254) 870-8898.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is Class 3 galvanized fence wire worth the extra cost?

For any permanent perimeter fence, yes. The upgrade usually adds 3 to 5 percent to the total installed cost of a barbed wire fence and roughly doubles its useful life. Per year of service, Class 3 galvanized fence wire is about half the cost of Class 1. Skip it only on temporary fencing you plan to remove within a decade.

### How long does Class 3 galvanized wire last in Central Texas?

Expect 25 to 35 years of useful life around Waco with normal maintenance, and often longer on dry, open ground. Class 1 wire in the same conditions typically gives 12 to 18 years, with rust showing up around year 8 to 10. Creek bottoms, shade lines, and spots where wire touches brush will always rust first regardless of class.

### Can I mix Class 1 and Class 3 wire on the same fence?

You can, and sometimes it makes sense, like running Class 3 on the wet stretch through a creek bottom and Class 1 on high, dry ground. But most folks are better off keeping the whole fence one spec, because a fence built to two lifespans still has to be worked on when the cheaper wire fails. The labor to splice in new wire later costs more than the coating upgrade would have.

### How do I know if my existing fence wire is Class 1 or Class 3?

On an existing fence you mostly judge by age and condition, since the tags are long gone. Wire that’s 15-plus years old and still mostly bright is almost certainly Class 3, while wire showing heavy rust at 8 to 10 years was likely Class 1 or unlabeled import. If you’re deciding whether that fence has life left, we’ll walk it with you as part of a free estimate.

## Clearing a Fence Line: Brush, Trees, and Right-of-Way Basics (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/clearing-fence-line-brush/)

> What clearing a fence line costs in Central Texas, which brush to cut, when to bring in a dozer, and how right-of-way rules work on Waco area ranches.

Ranch Fencing

# Clearing a Fence Line: Brush, Trees, and Right-of-Way Basics
Published August 1, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Here's a number that surprises most landowners: on a brushy Central Texas place, clearing a fence line can run 30 to 50 percent of the whole fence budget. The wire and posts are the easy part.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Here’s a number that surprises most landowners: on a brushy Central Texas place, clearing a fence line can run 30 to 50 percent of the whole fence budget. The wire and posts are the easy part. It’s the cedar, mesquite, and yaupon standing in the way that eat the money.

We build fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and clearing a fence line the right way is where every good job starts. Do it wrong and you’ll fight regrowth, snapped wire, and neighbor disputes for the next twenty years. Do it right and your fence goes in faster, costs less per foot, and lasts a decade longer.

This guide covers what clearing actually costs around Waco, which trees to cut and which to leave, how wide to clear, and where your right-of-way ends and your neighbor’s land begins.

## Why a Clean Fence Line Matters More Than the Wire

A fence is only as good as the ground it sits on. Brush against a fence does four things, and all of them cost you money.

First, limbs and trunks fall on wire. One dead cedar dropping across five strands of barbed wire can flatten 40 feet of fence in a single storm. Second, brush holds moisture against posts and wire, which speeds up rot and rust. Third, cattle use brush lines as scratching posts and shade, so they pressure the fence in exactly the spots you can’t see. Fourth, you can’t inspect or fix what you can’t reach.

There’s also the build itself. A fence crew working a clean, cleared line can stretch wire in long, straight pulls. A crew dodging trees has to short-pull, add extra braces, and hand-dig around roots. That labor shows up on your invoice whether you see the line item or not.

If your existing fence is already buried in brush and sagging, it might be past saving. A walk-through will help you decide, and if you want a second opinion, call us at (254) 870-8898. We’ll walk the line with you and give you a free written estimate, no pressure.

## What It Costs to Clear a Fence Line in Central Texas

Cost depends on three things: how thick the brush is, how big the trees are, and what kind of equipment can reach the line. A smooth pasture edge with scattered mesquite is one price. A creek bottom choked with 20 years of cedar is another animal entirely.

Here’s what we see landowners paying around Waco in 2026:

Brush condition Typical method Cost per foot Cost per mile

Light grass and weeds, few saplings Tractor and shredder $0.25 to $0.75 $1,300 to $4,000

Moderate brush, mesquite under 4 inches Skid steer with mulcher $1 to $2.50 $5,300 to $13,200

Heavy cedar or mesquite, trunks 4 to 10 inches Forestry mulcher or dozer $2.50 to $5 $13,200 to $26,400

Old fence tangled in heavy brush Dozer plus fence tear-out $4 to $8 $21,100 to $42,200

Two notes on that table. Stump grubbing costs more than mulching because you’re pulling roots, but mesquite will come right back if you only cut it at ground level. And if there’s an old fence buried in the brush, budget for tear-out too. Our fence removal cost guide breaks down what that part runs.

Roy Kolar, who runs cows on about 180 acres outside Crawford, learned the hard way. He had 2,600 feet of old net wire completely swallowed by cedar. He spent two weekends on it with a chainsaw and a 35 horsepower tractor, got maybe 400 feet done, and wore out a set of chains. He ended up paying a dozer operator $4,900 to clear and grub the full line in a day and a half. His words: “I should’ve written the check on day one.”

## Brush and Trees: What to Cut and What to Leave

Not everything on the line needs to go. Here’s how we think about it, species by species, because Central Texas brush isn’t all the same.

Cut it all: Ashe juniper (cedar). Cedar is the number one fence killer in Bosque and western McLennan counties. It grows fast, it burns hot, and it drinks water your grass needs. Cut it flush and it won’t resprout from the stump, which makes it one of the easier species to kill. Don’t leave “just a few” along the line. They’ll seed the whole corridor.

Grub it, don’t just cut it: mesquite. Mesquite resprouts from buds below the soil line. Shred it or chainsaw it and you’ll have a thicker stand in three years. It needs to be grubbed out below the bud zone, or cut and treated with an approved herbicide on the fresh stump. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid guidance on mechanical and chemical brush control for exactly these species.

Same story: yaupon and huisache. Both resprout aggressively. Mulching knocks them down but doesn’t kill them, so plan on follow-up spraying for two or three seasons.

Think twice: live oaks and pecans. A healthy mature oak 15 or 20 feet off the line isn’t hurting anything, and it’s worth real money in shade and land value. We’ll trim limbs back off the fence corridor and leave the tree. Never top a live oak in spring or summer without sealing the cuts, because oak wilt spreads through fresh wounds.

One more thing while the brush is coming out: look at what it was hiding. Around here that’s usually feral hog rooting along the low spots. If you find torn-up ground, read our piece on feral hog fence damage before you pick your wire, because hogs will dictate the fence design more than the cattle will.

## Right-of-Way, Property Lines, and Your Neighbor

This is where clearing a fence line gets legal, and where a Saturday project can turn into a lawsuit. Three rules keep you out of trouble.

Rule one: know exactly where the line is before anything gets cut. Old fences in Texas wander. A fence built in 1962 might sit 8 or 10 feet inside your deeded line, or 8 feet onto your neighbor’s. If you clear a strip on land you don’t own, you can be liable for the value of every tree you took, and mature hardwoods appraise higher than most people expect. On any boundary fence where the line is in doubt, spend the $500 to $1,500 on a survey first. We cover the ownership side in fence on the property line in Texas.

Rule two: talk to your neighbor early, in person if you can. Most boundary fences in Texas are shared by handshake, and most neighbors will happily split clearing costs since a clean line benefits both sides. Get the agreement in writing, even if it’s two sentences in a text message. Who pays what, who keeps which trees, and where the new fence sits.

Rule three: call 811 before any grubbing or dozer work. Buried gas, water, and fiber lines cross rural fence lines more often than you’d think, especially near county roads. The call is free, the locate is free, and hitting a pipeline is neither. Along public roads, remember the county or TxDOT controls the road right-of-way, so don’t clear, push brush into, or burn inside that strip without checking first.

The Kubacek place north of West is the cautionary tale we tell. They cleared 1,400 feet of shared line and took out a row of cedar elms their neighbor considered his windbreak. No survey, no conversation first. The trees turned out to straddle the line. It took a surveyor, a lawyer letter, and about $3,200 in settled damages to smooth it over, more than the clearing itself cost. A 20 minute conversation would have prevented all of it.

## Fence Line Clearing: DIY or Hire It Out?

Plenty of this work is landowner-friendly. Some of it isn’t. Here’s an honest split.

Good DIY work: shredding grass and light saplings with a tractor, chainsawing scattered cedar under 6 inches, hauling and stacking brush, spot-spraying regrowth, and trimming limbs you can reach from the ground. A rented walk-behind brush cutter runs about $250 a day around Waco and handles a lot of light clearing.

Hire it out: anything needing a dozer, excavator, or forestry mulcher, trees leaning over structures or existing fence, stump grubbing, and any tree work that puts a chainsaw above your shoulders. Chainsaw injuries send around 36,000 Americans to the emergency room every year, and storm-bent or fence-grown trees are the most unpredictable cuts there are. Wire that’s grown into a trunk can grab a chain and kick the bar back before you can react. The U.S. Forest Service and OSHA both publish chainsaw safety guidance worth reading before you ever pull a cord.

Dale Prosser in Valley Mills split it smart. He and his son shredded and chainsawed about half a mile of light stuff themselves over a few weekends, then paid $2,800 for a mulcher to eat the heavy cedar in the creek bottom they couldn’t safely touch. Total out of pocket was less than half what full-service clearing would have run, and nobody got hurt doing it.

The honest tiebreaker is time. If the brush is heavy enough that you’re measuring progress in feet per hour instead of feet per minute, machine work will beat your labor on cost alone. Tell us what you’re up against through our contact form and we’ll tell you straight which parts are worth doing yourself.

## How Wide Should You Clear, and What Comes Next

For a standard barbed wire or net wire fence, we want a corridor 12 to 16 feet wide, centered on the fence line where possible. That gives equipment room to work on both sides, lets a truck drive the line for inspections, and keeps limbs off the wire for years instead of months. For a game fence, go wider, 16 to 20 feet, because you’re working 8 feet up and exotics will exploit any limb that overhangs the top.

Once it’s clear, don’t let it grow back. A cleared line you shred once a year stays cleared for almost nothing. A cleared line you ignore is a thicket again in five to seven years, and you’ll pay full clearing price twice in one fence’s lifetime. Put fence line shredding on the same calendar as your other upkeep, right alongside checking braces and tightening wire.

And think hard about timing. The best window for clearing in Central Texas is late summer through winter, when the ground is firm, snakes are slower, and you’re ahead of spring sap rise for stump treatments. Clearing in February and fencing in March is about the smoothest sequence there is.

That’s also the moment to price the whole project as one job. We quote clearing and fence construction together on most builds, which usually saves money because the equipment is already mobilized. Whether it’s barbed wire on a pasture line or pipe and cable at the headquarters, call (254) 870-8898 for a free written estimate that covers the clearing and the fence in one number. And if a storm drops timber on an existing fence and cattle are testing the gap, that same number is our 24/7 emergency line.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does clearing a fence line cost per foot?

Around Waco, figure $0.25 to $0.75 per foot for light shredding, $1 to $2.50 for moderate brush with a mulcher, and $2.50 to $5 or more for heavy cedar and mesquite that needs a dozer. Old fence tangled in the brush adds tear-out cost on top. Get the clearing quoted with the fence build, since one mobilization usually beats two.

### How wide should I clear for a new fence?

Clear 12 to 16 feet for a standard barbed wire or net wire fence, and 16 to 20 feet for a high game fence. That width gives equipment room during the build and lets you drive the line for inspections afterward. Narrower corridors work, but you’ll be back with a chainsaw sooner.

### Can I clear brush right up to my neighbor’s side of the fence?

Not without permission. Your right to clear stops at the property line, and trees on or over the line are usually shared property under Texas law. Confirm the line with a survey if there’s any doubt, get your neighbor’s agreement in writing, and never cut a boundary tree without talking first.

### Will mesquite and yaupon grow back after clearing?

Yes, unless you kill the root. Both species resprout from below ground, so shredding or mulching alone buys you two or three years at best. Grub the stumps out or treat fresh-cut stumps with an approved herbicide, then spot-spray regrowth for a couple of seasons. Cedar is the exception, since it dies when cut flush.

## Cost to Fence 10 Acres in Central Texas (Plus 25 and 100 Acre Numbers) (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/cost-to-fence-10-acres/)

> What it costs to fence 10, 25, and 100 acres in Central Texas. Real per-foot prices for barbed wire, net wire, and pipe fence from a Waco ranch fence crew.

Cost Guide

# Cost to Fence 10 Acres in Central Texas (Plus 25 and 100 Acre Numbers)
Published August 3, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Two landowners in McLennan County can fence the same 10 acres and one pays $7,000 while the other pays $70,000. Same dirt, same property line, wildly different bill. The difference isn't a scam.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Two landowners in McLennan County can fence the same 10 acres and one pays $7,000 while the other pays $70,000. Same dirt, same property line, wildly different bill.

The difference isn’t a scam. It’s fence type, terrain, and how much clearing the line needs. The real cost to fence 10 acres in Central Texas runs anywhere from about $6,600 for basic barbed wire to well past $30,000 for pipe fence, and 25 or 100 acres doesn’t scale the way most folks expect.

We build ranch fence every week around Waco, China Spring, Crawford, and down through Lorena, so we’ll walk you through the actual numbers we quote. If you’d rather skip the math and get a firm figure for your place, request a free written estimate or call us at (254) 870-8898.

## Why Acreage Math Fools Almost Everybody

Here’s the thing nobody tells you at the feed store: you don’t pay for acres. You pay for feet of fence line. And perimeter doesn’t grow at the same rate as acreage.

A square 10 acre tract has about 2,640 feet of perimeter, exactly half a mile. Quadruple the land to 40 acres and the perimeter only doubles. That’s why fencing cost per acre drops fast as tracts get bigger.

Rough perimeter numbers for square tracts:

- 10 acres: about 2,640 linear feet (0.5 mile)

- 25 acres: about 4,180 linear feet (0.8 mile)

- 100 acres: about 8,350 linear feet (1.6 miles)

Real tracts are rarely square. A long skinny 10 acres along a county road can carry 3,500 feet of line or more, and that’s 30 percent more fence for the same acreage. Creek crossings, rock, and brush move the number too, which is why we always measure before we quote.

The other thing that moves your bill is corners and gates. Every corner needs a braced assembly, and H-braces are where good fences earn their keep. A tract with eight corners and three gates costs real money beyond the straight-line footage.

## The Real Cost to Fence 10 Acres

For a typical square 10 acres with decent access and light clearing, here’s what we see quoted around Waco in 2026:

- 5-strand barbed wire: $2.50 to $4.50 per foot installed, so $6,600 to $11,900 for the tract

- Net wire (field fence) with a top barbed strand: $3.50 to $6.00 per foot, so $9,250 to $15,850

- High game fence: $4.50 to $8.00 per foot, so $11,900 to $21,100

- Pipe fence: $12 to $28 per foot, so $31,700 and up

Barbed wire is still the workhorse for cattle on small acreage. Net wire earns its premium if you run goats, sheep, or you want to keep dogs in and coyotes out. Pipe is the forever option for perimeters along roads and around headquarters.

Last spring we fenced 10 acres off Old Lorena Road for Travis Kubacek, a young family that bought their first piece of land outside Lorena. He’d budgeted $5,000 off a national cost website. His tract was long and narrow with 3,100 feet of line, heavy cedar on the back side, and blackland clay that had swallowed the old posts. The real number for 5-strand barbed wire with two 16-foot gates came to $9,850, and the clearing was almost $1,800 of that.

That’s the pattern we see over and over. The wire is the cheap part. Clearing, corners, gates, and terrain are what separate the internet estimate from the written quote.

One more line item people forget: tearing out the old fence. If there’s a rusted, grown-in fence on the line already, removal and haul-off typically adds $1 to $2 per foot.

## Cost to Fence 25 Acres: The Per-Foot Sweet Spot

Twenty five acres is where the per-acre math starts working in your favor. You’ve got 2.5 times the land of a 10 acre tract but only about 60 percent more fence line.

Typical 2026 ranges for a square 25 acres (about 4,180 feet):

- 5-strand barbed wire: $10,500 to $18,800

- Net wire: $14,600 to $25,100

- High game fence: $18,800 to $33,400

Per-foot pricing usually improves a little on jobs this size too. Once a crew can mobilize for a week instead of two days, the setup costs spread out and most contractors sharpen the pencil.

Doyle Pritchett runs about 15 cow-calf pairs on 25 acres between Crawford and Valley Mills. His granddad’s net wire had rusted through and the cows had started walking through it to visit the neighbor’s winter oats. We replaced the full perimeter with 5-strand barbed wire on t-posts with cedar corners, plus one new 14-foot gate, for $14,300. The rocky stretch along the county road took a hydraulic breaker for about 40 post holes, which added around $1,100.

Doyle’s job shows why we quote after walking the line, not before. On paper his tract priced at $12,000. Rock and a washed-out water gap moved it $2,300, and he knew that before we drove the first post because it was in the written estimate.

If you’re pricing a job this size, get two or three bids and make sure they specify wire class, post spacing, and brace count so you’re comparing the same fence. We wrote a whole guide on comparing fence quotes line by line.

## Fencing 100 Acres: Mile and a Half of Wire

At 100 acres you’re a real ranch operation, and you’re buying fence by the mile. A square 100 acres carries about 8,350 feet of perimeter, roughly 1.6 miles.

Typical 2026 ranges:

- 5-strand barbed wire: $20,900 to $37,600

- Net wire: $29,300 to $50,100

- High game fence: $37,600 to $66,800

Cross-fencing changes the total fast. Most cattle operations this size want at least two or three pastures for rotation, and every cross fence is more footage. A single cross fence through the middle of a square 100 adds about 2,090 feet, call it $5,200 to $9,400 in barbed wire.

Two years back we fenced a full 100 acre perimeter for the Machalek place north of West, a family that had leased the land for hay and finally bought it. They went with 5-strand barbed wire using Class 3 galvanized wire on the long runs, a short stretch of net wire around the pens, and a 20-foot pipe entrance off the FM road. All in, the project ran just under $34,000, and the ranch entrance gate was about $6,500 of it.

At this scale, wire quality matters more than anywhere else. Cheap Class 1 wire can start rusting in under a decade in our humidity, while Class 3 galvanized commonly lasts 25 to 30 years or more. On a mile and a half of fence, you do not want to do this twice.

One planning note for bigger tracts: if you’re running livestock, fencing is generally an eligible practice under USDA cost-share programs like EQIP in some situations, and it factors into your ag valuation. Check the USDA NRCS Texas office and the Texas Comptroller’s ag exemption rules before you build, because paperwork done early can save real money.

## Side by Side: 10, 25, and 100 Acres by Fence Type

Here’s the whole picture in one table. These are installed ranges for square tracts with normal access and light clearing, based on what jobs are actually running around McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties in 2026.

Fence type Cost per foot 10 acres (~2,640 ft) 25 acres (~4,180 ft) 100 acres (~8,350 ft)

## How to Keep the Bill Down (and When to Stop DIYing)

You can trim a fencing budget without building a fence you’ll regret. A few honest ways to do it:

Fence in phases. Do the road frontage and the hot side where cattle pressure is worst this year, and finish the back line next year. Wire prices move, but a planned phase two beats a maxed-out credit card.

Share the line cost with your neighbor. Texas has its own rules on boundary fences, and a neighbor who splits a half-mile of line fence cuts your bill by thousands. Get the agreement in writing before anybody buys wire.

Don’t cheap out where it counts. Corners, braces, and wire class are the fence. Stretching post spacing from 12 feet to 20 feet to save money is how you end up with a saggy fence and cattle on the county road. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid guidance on fence construction and livestock management if you want a second opinion from the university folks: agrilifeextension.tamu.edu.

Know your DIY limit. Plenty of landowners can string a repair stretch or hang a gate. But building corner braces that hold a quarter mile of stretched wire, drilling post holes in rock, and stretching net wire on a slope are jobs where mistakes get expensive or dangerous. High-tensile wire under tension can cut you badly when it snaps, and a bad brace fails in year two, not day two. If the job involves tensioned wire over long runs, road frontage, or anything near power lines or buried utilities, call a professional and always call 811 before you dig.

We’re happy to be the second or third bid on your project. Our estimates are written, itemized, and free, and we’re licensed and insured. Tell us your acreage and what you’re running on it at our contact page or call (254) 870-8898. If a storm just dropped your fence and cattle are out tonight, that same number is our 24/7 emergency line.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does it cost to fence 10 acres with barbed wire?

For a typical square 10 acres around Waco, plan on $6,600 to $11,900 installed for a 5-strand barbed wire fence, which covers about 2,640 feet of line. Odd-shaped tracts, heavy brush, rock, and extra gates push it higher. Get a walked-the-line written quote before you set a budget.

### Is it cheaper per acre to fence more land?

Yes, and by a lot. Perimeter grows much slower than acreage, so 100 acres has only about three times the fence line of 10 acres. Barbed wire that costs roughly $660 to $1,190 per acre on a 10 acre tract drops to roughly $210 to $375 per acre on a square 100.

### What’s the cheapest fence that will actually hold cattle?

A properly built 5-strand barbed wire fence on t-posts with wood or pipe corner braces is the most cost-effective cattle fence in Central Texas. The key word is properly built, meaning good braces, correct post spacing, and Class 3 galvanized wire. A cheap fence that lets cattle out onto a road can cost you far more than the savings.

### How long does it take to fence 25 or 100 acres?

A good crew can typically build a 25 acre perimeter in barbed wire in about one to two weeks, depending on clearing and rock. A 100 acre perimeter usually runs three to five weeks. Weather, terrain, and gate and entrance work are the usual variables, and we put a schedule in every written estimate.

# DIY Fence vs Professional: An Honest Ranch Fencing Breakdown
Published August 4, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Can you really save half the money building your own fence? Sometimes, yes. And sometimes you spend $4,000 on materials, burn three weekends, and end up calling us anyway to rebuild your corners.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Can you really save half the money building your own fence? Sometimes, yes. And sometimes you spend $4,000 on materials, burn three weekends, and end up calling us anyway to rebuild your corners.

We install fence for a living, so you’d expect us to tell you to hire a pro every time. We won’t. The honest answer on diy fence vs professional is that it depends on the job, your ground, your tools, and how much your Saturdays are worth. Plenty of Central Texas ranchers are perfectly capable of stretching wire, and we’ll tell you which jobs make sense to tackle yourself.

But we’ve also rebuilt enough failed DIY fence between China Spring and Lorena to know where the wheels come off. This article lays out the real numbers for both routes so you can decide with your eyes open.

Want a number to compare against before you commit either way? Call (254) 870-8898 or request a free written estimate. It costs nothing, and it gives your DIY budget an honest benchmark.

## The real math on a DIY barbed wire fence

Let’s price a quarter mile, 1,320 feet, of 5-strand barbed wire. That’s a common stretch for a cross fence or a road frontage on small acreage around here.

Materials first. Figure t-posts on 10 to 12 foot spacing, wood or pipe corner posts, five rolls of wire, clips, staples, and concrete for the braces. At 2026 prices in the Waco area, you’re looking at roughly $1.30 to $1.90 per foot in materials for decent quality. Call it $1,700 to $2,500 for the quarter mile. If you cheap out on wire, buy Class 3 galvanized or better, because bargain wire rusts years sooner.

Now the part DIY budgets always skip: tools and equipment. A powered post driver or auger rental runs $100 to $350 a day. A decent wire stretcher, fence pliers, a spinning jenny for the wire rolls, and post levels add another $200 to $400 if you don’t own them. Hit rock, and you may need a skid steer with a hydraulic auger at $300 to $500 a day. Lots of ground west of the Bosque River is exactly that kind of rocky.

Then there’s time. A two-person crew that’s never built fence will spend 4 to 6 full days on a quarter mile if the ground cooperates. Clearing brush, setting and bracing corners, driving 110 to 130 posts, then stretching and tying five strands. If you’re doing it on weekends, that’s a month of Saturdays.

So the true DIY cost on our quarter mile is roughly $2,100 to $3,300 in cash, plus 80 to 100 man-hours. That’s the honest number to compare against a quote, not the materials receipt alone.

## What professional fence installation actually costs

A professional crew in McLennan, Bosque, or Falls County will typically run $2.50 to $4.50 per foot for 5-strand barbed wire, installed, depending on terrain, brush, and corner count. Our quarter mile comes out around $3,300 to $5,900. Pipe corners, heavy brush, or rock push you toward the top of that range. The full picture by fence type is on our ranch fence cost guide.

What do you get for the difference? Mostly three things.

Speed is the obvious one. A crew with a skid steer, a hydraulic driver, and a pre-loaded wire trailer will knock out that quarter mile in a day and a half, maybe two. Your cattle are behind wire this week, not next month.

Corners are the second. Corner and brace assemblies carry the entire load of the fence. When we see a failed DIY fence, it’s almost never the wire. It’s an H-brace that was built wrong or skipped entirely, and the whole stretch went slack within a year. We build braces the same way every time because we’ve watched what happens when you don’t. If you do go DIY, our H-brace corner guide is the one article you should not skip.

The third is accountability. A licensed and insured contractor stands behind the work. If a stretch goes slack in six months, you make a phone call instead of losing another weekend.

If you’d rather see a real quote than guess from ranges, get a free written estimate here. We break out materials and labor so you can compare it line by line against your DIY math.

## DIY fencing stories from around Waco: where it goes wrong

Names and numbers below are real jobs from the last couple of years, shared with permission.

Danny runs about 30 acres outside Crawford. He built 1,800 feet of barbed wire himself in the fall of 2024 and did most of it right. He spent $2,900 on materials and about five weekends. But he set his corner posts only two feet deep in soft ground with no concrete, and he didn’t brace them. By the next summer, the corners had pulled, and every strand on the place was sagging. We rebuilt six corner assemblies and re-stretched the wire for $2,140. His fence is fine now, but his total came within a few hundred dollars of our original bid, plus five weekends he’ll never get back.

Marcus, down in Lorena, had the opposite experience, and it’s worth telling. He fenced a 400 foot garden and orchard perimeter with t-posts and net wire for about $1,100 in materials over two weekends. Small job, no heavy corners under load, flat ground. He did it well and saved real money. That’s exactly the kind of project we’ll tell you to do yourself.

Then there’s Kathy near Valley Mills. She rented an auger for $280 a day to set posts along her west line and hit solid limestone 18 inches down on the first hole. Two rental days and eleven holes later, she’d spent $560 and had a tenth of her posts set. Rock work is its own trade. We put her remaining posts in with a hydraulic breaker in one day. If your ground sounds like hers, read fence posts in rocky ground before you rent anything.

## Jobs worth doing yourself, and jobs that aren’t

After twenty-plus rebuilds of failed DIY fence, here’s how we’d sort it.

Good DIY projects: short runs of t-post and barbed or net wire on flat, soft ground. Garden and yard perimeters. Replacing broken strands or splicing wire. Swapping a bent t-post. Small goat or chicken pens. Repairs and maintenance in general, honestly. A rancher who can splice wire and reset a t-post will save thousands over the life of a fence.

Think hard before you DIY: quarter mile or longer runs, anything with more than four corner assemblies, ground you already know is rocky, and fence lines that need serious brush clearing first.

Leave it to a crew: pipe fence, full stop. Cutting and welding pipe corners and top rail is fabrication work, and a bad weld on a corner post fails under the first real load. High-tensile game fence is the same story, because 8 foot fixed-knot wire under proper tension will hurt somebody who doesn’t have the right stretching equipment. Entrance gates with long heavy leaves need to be hung dead level on properly set posts or they’ll sag inside a year.

One more that people underestimate: barbed wire along a road frontage or a shared property line. Under Texas law, a fence that fails and lets cattle onto a highway can put real liability on you. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes good plain-language material on fence law and livestock liability at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu, and the statutes themselves live in Texas Agriculture Code Chapter 143. A fence that’s holding cattle off FM 185 is not the place to learn bracing by trial and error.

And a safety line we mean sincerely: wire under tension stores a lot of energy. Wear eye protection, never stretch wire with a vehicle, and if a job involves welding, big rock, or an old fence tangled in brush, stop and call somebody who does it every day.

## How to make the call for your place

Ask yourself four questions.

How long is the run? Under 500 feet, DIY is on the table. Over a quarter mile, the time cost usually kills the savings.

What’s your ground like? Dig one test hole before you buy anything. If you hit rock or heavy clay at 18 inches, price professional installation before you price rentals.

What’s the fence holding? A garden fence that fails costs you tomatoes. A perimeter fence that fails puts cattle on the road at 2 a.m. Match the stakes to the builder.

What’s your realistic schedule? If the fence needs to be up before you turn cattle out in 30 days, a crew is the only honest answer. Weekends have a way of filling up.

If you land on hiring it out, get your quote in writing and make sure it specifies wire class, post type and spacing, and brace construction. If you land on DIY, spend your money on good corners and good wire, and start with our cost to fence 10 acres breakdown so your budget survives contact with reality.

Either way, we’re glad to look at your project. Call (254) 870-8898 or send us the details online and we’ll get you a free written estimate. If it’s a job you should do yourself, we’ll tell you that too. We’d rather earn the pipe fence job next year than talk you out of a garden fence you can handle this weekend.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does DIY fencing actually save?

On a typical barbed wire job, DIY saves roughly 35 to 50 percent of the installed price in cash, before you count your time. On a quarter mile, that’s usually $1,200 to $2,600. The savings shrink fast if you have to rent equipment more than a day or two, and they can disappear entirely if corners fail and have to be rebuilt.

### What’s the most common DIY fence mistake you see?

Weak or missing corner braces, by a wide margin. The corners carry all the tension in a stretched wire fence, and a corner post set shallow without an H-brace will lean within a year and let the whole fence go slack. Posts set too shallow in general and bargain-grade wire are the next two on the list.

### Is it cheaper to repair my old fence or build new?

If the posts are sound and the wire isn’t badly rusted, repair is almost always cheaper, and it’s the kind of work most owners can do themselves. Once you’re replacing more than about a third of the posts or the wire has lost its galvanizing, new construction usually wins on cost per year of life. We’ll give you a straight answer either way on a free estimate.

### How long does professional fence installation take?

For barbed wire, a good crew covers a quarter to a half mile a day once corners are set, so most small-acreage jobs finish in one to three days. Pipe fence and game fence run slower because of welding and heavier bracing. Weather and rock are the usual wild cards, which is one more reason to get the timeline in writing with your quote.

## Drought Fence Problems: Why Dry Summers Shift Your Posts and Gates (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/drought-fence-problems/)

> Drought fence problems hit Central Texas ranches hard. See why dry clay shifts posts and gates, what repairs really cost, and when to call a Waco fence pro.

Fence Repair

# Drought Fence Problems: Why Dry Summers Shift Your Posts and Gates
Published August 5, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

By late July around here, the cracks in a Blackland clay pasture get wide enough to swallow a fence pliers.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

By late July around here, the cracks in a Blackland clay pasture get wide enough to swallow a fence pliers. If your gate quit latching in June and your corner posts look like they’re leaning into the wind, you’re not imagining it.

Drought fence problems are one of the most common calls we take at Brazos Ridge Fence Co. between June and September. Ranchers in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties watch straight fences go wavy, gates drop an inch or two, and brace posts heave right out of ground that was rock solid in April. The wire didn’t fail. The soil under it did.

This article walks through why dry summers move fence posts, which parts of your fence take the worst beating, what repairs actually cost, and what you can do now to limit the damage before the next dry stretch.

## What Drought Does to the Clay Under Your Fence Line

Most of the ground between Waco and Valley Mills is expansive clay. Blackland Prairie soil is famous for it. When that clay is wet, it swells. When it dries out, it shrinks, and it doesn’t shrink a little. It shrinks enough to open surface cracks two or three inches wide and several feet deep.

Your fence posts are set in that clay. When the soil shrinks away from a post, the post loses the friction grip that holds it plumb. Then the wire tension takes over. A barbed wire fence pulling 150 to 250 pounds of tension per strand will lean any post that’s lost its grip, and it always pulls toward the corners and low spots.

The Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension Service has documented how expansive clays in Central Texas move structures, foundations, and yes, fence posts, through repeated shrink and swell cycles. Foundation repair companies stay busy here for the same reason fence companies do.

Here’s the part most folks miss. The damage isn’t done during the drought. It’s done in the cycle. Clay shrinks in August, the post shifts, then October rains swell the clay back around the post in its new leaned position. Now the lean is locked in. Three or four summers of that and a fence that was dead straight in 2020 looks like a snake track.

If you’re seeing that pattern on your place, get eyes on it before the next rain locks things in tighter. Call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk your line and give you a free written estimate on what’s worth fixing now versus what can wait.

## The 5 Drought Fence Problems We See Most in Central Texas

After enough dry summers in this county, the failure list gets predictable. Here’s what shows up on our work orders every August, roughly in order.

1. Leaning line posts. Wood posts set 24 to 30 inches deep lose soil grip first. T-posts actually handle drought a little better because they’re driven, not set in a dug hole, but they’ll still lean where the cracking is bad. We cover the full diagnosis in our guide to leaning fence posts.

2. Sagging gates. A gate is a lever hanging off one post. When drought loosens that hinge post, a 12 foot gate multiplies the problem. The latch end drops an inch for every small tip of the post. If you’re lifting your gate to latch it, the post moved, not the gate.

3. Failed corner and brace assemblies. Corners carry the tension of the whole stretch. When clay shrinks off a corner post, hundreds of feet of wire tension start pulling it over. Once a corner goes, every span it anchors goes slack behind it.

4. Slack wire and dropped stays. Wire that was tight in spring goes loose by August because the posts holding it moved inward. Loose barbed wire is how calves learn to push through. Loose net wire is how feral hogs get a snout under the bottom.

5. Heaved posts. Less common but real. Repeated shrink and swell can jack a shallow post upward over several seasons, an inch or two a year, until it’s barely holding.

Any one of these is annoying. Two or three together is how cattle end up on the county road at 2 a.m. If that’s already happened, our line on cattle getting out of fence covers your liability exposure, and our 24/7 emergency line covers the immediate problem.

## Real Numbers: What Drought Fence Damage Cost 3 Local Ranchers

Talk is cheap, so here’s what this actually looked like on three jobs from recent dry summers.

Crawford, hinge post failure. Dale runs about 60 cow-calf pairs west of Crawford. His main entrance gate, a 16 footer on a wood hinge post, dropped until it was dragging dirt. He’d been chaining it shut for a month. The hinge post had leaned 6 inches out of plumb in cracked clay. We pulled it, set a 4 inch pipe post in concrete with a proper deadman, rehung and adjusted the gate. Total: $1,150. He waited a season longer than he should have, and the dragging gate had also tweaked the hinges, which added to the bill.

China Spring, corner blowout. Marcy has 45 acres off Wortham Bend Road. During the 2024 drought her southeast corner post leaned enough to slack about 900 feet of 5 strand barbed wire on two sides. A neighbor’s bull found the slack section and her heifers found the neighbor’s oat patch. Rebuilding the corner with a pipe H-brace, restretching both runs, and splicing two damaged sections came to $2,340. The vet bill and the apology to the neighbor were extra.

Lorena, the cheap fix that wasn’t. Jim, south of Lorena, tried the classic DIY move on a leaned line post: dig it out, straighten it, tamp it back. It worked until the first good rain, then the post leaned again because the disturbed clay never regained its grip. He called us after round two. Resetting 11 line posts properly, with compacted base material instead of loose native clay, ran him $880. His first two weekends of labor ran him free but bought nothing.

The pattern in all three: waiting made it more expensive. A $100 problem in June is a $1,000 problem by October.
