## How to Protect Your Fence Before the Next Dry Spell

You can’t stop the clay from shrinking. You can make your fence a lot less sensitive to it. Here’s what actually works, in rough order of bang for buck.

Walk your line in early summer, not late summer. Catch a corner at a 2 degree lean and it’s a brace repair. Catch it at 10 degrees and it’s a rebuild. June beats September every time.

Fix small leans before the fall rains. Remember the lock-in cycle. A post straightened and properly tamped before the rain returns to plumb. A post left leaning gets cemented into its lean by swelling clay.

Upgrade corners and gate posts to pipe set in concrete. Concrete spreads the load and pipe doesn’t rot, so the assembly rides out shrink and swell cycles that wreck shallow wood corners. Deeper is better in clay. We set gate and corner posts 36 to 48 inches deep here for exactly this reason.

Don’t overtighten wire in August. Wire stretched drum-tight in dry heat gets even tighter in a cold snap and pulls harder on drought-weakened posts. Snug is enough. You can take up slack again in spring.

Watch your water gaps and low crossings. Drought drops creek levels and exposes fence that’s about to take the full force of the first flood. Drought and flood damage are two halves of the same Texas year.

Keep an eye on official drought conditions. The U.S. Drought Monitor at drought.gov updates weekly and shows exactly how deep the dry spell is in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties. When your area slides into D2 or worse, that’s your cue to walk the fence line.

For the full seasonal routine, our ranch fence maintenance checklist lays out what to check every quarter, drought or not.

## When to Stop DIY and Call a Fence Professional

Plenty of drought fixes are honest weekend work. Restapling wire, driving a replacement T-post, tightening a gate’s adjustment bolts. Have at it.

But know where the line is. Call a pro when:

- A corner or H-brace is leaning. Corners hold the stored tension of hundreds of feet of wire. Cut or release that tension wrong and it can whip. This is the single most dangerous fence repair there is.

- Wire needs a full restretch. Barbed wire under stretcher tension will find your forearms if a splice or tool slips. Gloves and eye protection are minimum, and experience is the real safety gear.

- A gate post needs replacing. Getting the depth, concrete, and hinge alignment right the first time is the difference between a 15 year fix and a 15 month one.

- You’ve straightened the same post twice. The soil grip is gone. It needs a proper reset with compacted base material or an upgrade to pipe, not a third tamping.

- Cattle are already getting out. That’s not a project anymore, it’s a liability clock ticking. In most of this county you’re under stock law, and a cow on the highway is your problem in every sense.

Brazos Ridge Fence Co. is licensed and insured, we work these three counties every day, and we run a 24/7 emergency line for cattle-out and storm-damage calls. Whether it’s one sagging gate in West or two miles of drought-slacked barbed wire outside McGregor, call (254) 870-8898 or request your free written estimate and we’ll get you a straight answer with real numbers on it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why do fence posts lean during a drought?

Central Texas clay shrinks as it dries, and it pulls away from the posts set in it. Once the soil loses its grip, wire tension and gate weight tip the post out of plumb. When fall rain swells the clay back, it locks the post into its new leaned position, which is why leans get worse every cycle instead of fixing themselves.

### Should I water the ground around my fence posts in a drought?

Around a high-value gate or corner post, slow soaking the soil once or twice a month can reduce cracking and help the post keep its grip, the same trick homeowners use on slab foundations. It’s not practical for a mile of line fence, and it’s no substitute for well-set posts. Spend the effort on the handful of posts that carry the most load.

### Will my drought-damaged fence fix itself when the rain comes back?

Mostly no. Swelling clay can firm up around a post, but it firms up around the post wherever it sits, lean and all. Slack wire stays slack and sagged gates stay sagged. The best window to straighten and reset posts is after a dry spell but before the ground fully re-swells, so the repair gets locked in instead of the damage.

### How much does it cost to fix a fence after a drought?

Small stuff is cheap: resetting line posts usually runs $60 to $110 each and restretching wire runs about $0.50 to $1.25 per foot. Corners and gate posts are the big tickets, from $350 to around $900 depending on materials. We give free written estimates, so you’ll know the full number before any work starts.

## Electric Fence Not Working? A Simple Troubleshooting Guide (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/electric-fence-not-working/)

> Electric fence not working? Walk the line with this simple troubleshooting guide from a Waco fence pro. Find shorts, dead chargers, and bad grounds fast.

Fence Repair

# Electric Fence Not Working? A Simple Troubleshooting Guide
Published August 7, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Your fence tester reads 900 volts on a wire that should be pushing 7,000. Or worse, the cows are standing in the neighbor's coastal field and the hot wire didn't so much as tickle them on the way...

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Your fence tester reads 900 volts on a wire that should be pushing 7,000. Or worse, the cows are standing in the neighbor’s coastal field and the hot wire didn’t so much as tickle them on the way through.

An electric fence not working is one of the most common calls we get at Brazos Ridge Fence Co., and here’s the good news: about 8 out of 10 of these problems come down to three things. A dead or weak charger, a bad ground system, or a short somewhere along the line. All three are things you can check yourself in an afternoon with a $30 fence tester and a little patience.

This guide walks the whole troubleshooting process in the order a pro would, charger outward. We chase electric fence problems every week across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, so this advice is built for Central Texas: dry summers, cracked clay, hog damage, and grass that eats voltage alive by June.

If you get to the end and the fence still won’t hold voltage, or you’d rather skip the walking and hand it to somebody who does this daily, call us at (254) 870-8898. Estimates are free and written, and we answer the emergency line 24/7 when cattle are out.

## Start at the Charger: Is Your Electric Fence Energizer Working?

Never start by walking the fence line. Start at the box. If the charger isn’t putting out power, you can walk five miles of wire and learn nothing.

Here’s the test. Disconnect the fence lead wire and the ground wire from the charger completely. Now touch your fence tester across the two terminals on the charger itself, fence terminal to ground terminal. You should read the charger’s rated open-circuit voltage, usually somewhere between 6,000 and 10,000 volts depending on the unit.

Two outcomes, two very different paths:

The charger reads strong with the fence disconnected. Good. The charger is fine, and your problem lives out on the fence or in the ground system. Skip ahead to the next sections.

The charger reads weak or dead with the fence disconnected. The problem is the charger or its power supply. Before you buy a new unit, check the cheap stuff first:

- Is the outlet live? Plug a drill or a lamp into it. GFCI outlets in barns trip all the time, especially after rain.

- On battery units, load-test the battery. A 12-volt battery that reads 12.6 volts sitting idle can still collapse under load. Batteries in Central Texas heat rarely last past 3 or 4 years.

- On solar units, clean the panel and make sure a tree or a shed shadow hasn’t crept over it since spring. A dirty panel can cut charging by a third.

- Check the fuse if your model has one, and look for scorch marks near the terminals. Lightning kills more chargers around here than old age does.

Dale, who runs about 40 pairs east of Crawford, called us last August convinced his whole perimeter fence had shorted out because nothing was hot. We tested the charger first thing: dead as a hammer, cooked by a lightning strike two pastures over. A new 6-joule charger ran him $289, and the fence itself needed nothing. Ten-minute diagnosis. He’d been budgeting $2,000 for a rewire he didn’t need.

A surge protector and a lightning diverter cost about $60 combined and would have saved Dale the charger. Cheap insurance in storm country.

## Check the Ground System, Because Most Weak Fences Fail Here

If the charger tests strong but the fence is weak, check grounding before you go hunting shorts. Poor grounding is the single most common cause of a weak electric fence, and it’s especially bad in Central Texas because our clay soil dries out and pulls away from the ground rods every summer.

An electric fence is a loop. The pulse leaves the charger, travels down the wire, passes through the animal, goes into the soil, and returns to the charger through the ground rods. If the soil connection is poor, the loop can’t complete, and the animal feels a weak tap instead of a real correction. The fence looks fine. The wire even reads decent voltage. But nothing respects it.

Here’s the field test for grounding:

- Walk out at least 300 feet from the charger.

- Short the fence out on purpose by leaning a few steel T-posts against the hot wire so current is forced to flow.

- Go back and put your tester between the last ground rod and the soil a foot away from it.

- If you read more than about 400 volts on the ground rod, your grounding is inadequate.

The fix is usually more rods, deeper rods, or wetter rods. The standard that works here: at least three galvanized ground rods, 6 feet deep, spaced 10 feet apart, connected with one continuous insulated wire and good clamps. Don’t mix copper rods with galvanized wire; the joint corrodes and quietly chokes the system.

Marcy keeps horses on 12 acres outside China Spring, and her fence went from hot to useless every July like clockwork. Her single 3-foot ground rod was sitting in powder-dry clay by midsummer. We drove two more 6-foot rods, tied all three together, and told her to dump a bucket of water on the rod bed during long dry spells. Total fix was $85 in materials and an hour of labor. That fence has held 6,000-plus volts through two droughts since.

Drought does more damage to fences than most folks realize, and grounding is only part of it. We covered the rest in our post on drought fence problems.

## Walk the Line: Finding the Short When Your Electric Fence Isn’t Working

Charger’s good, ground’s good, but the voltage is still low? Now you walk. Somewhere out there, your fence is leaking power to the ground, and your job is to find the leak.

Before you take a step, know what you’re looking for:

- Vegetation load. Grass, weeds, and brush touching the hot wire bleed voltage constantly. One wet sunflower won’t kill a fence, but a quarter mile of johnsongrass laying on the bottom wire will drag a 7,000-volt fence under 2,000. If your fence line looks like a hay crop, start there. Our guide to clearing fence line brush covers the fastest ways to knock it down.

- Cracked or missing insulators. Sun-rotted plastic insulators let the hot wire touch the post. On a steel T-post, that’s a dead short. Look for black scorch marks and listen for a snapping tick.

- Broken or sagging wire. A hot wire lying on the ground, wrapped in a fallen limb, or touching a barbed strand below it will short. Hogs are a common culprit here, and if you’re seeing rooted-up dirt along the line, read our post on feral hog fence damage before you patch and repeat.

- Bad splices and rusted wire. Every hand-twisted splice is a resistor. Rusty wire carries pulse poorly. Proper splice sleeves or figure-8 knots fix it.

- Underground lead-out wire. The insulated cable that carries power under a gate is a classic hidden failure. Nicked insulation lets the pulse leak straight into the soil where you’ll never see it. If the fence is hot on the charger side of a gate and dead past it, you’ve found your section.

- Gate handles and jumpers. Spring gate handles corrode, and jumper wires get knocked loose by cattle and equipment.

The fast way to walk a line is the half-split method. Most electric fences have cut-out switches or places you can disconnect a section. Kill power to half the fence. If voltage jumps back up, the short is in the half you disconnected. Split that half again. Three or four splits will corner a fault on a mile of fence in under an hour, instead of walking the whole thing staring at every insulator.

Better still, spend $70 to $130 on a digital fault finder. It reads voltage and current together and literally points an arrow toward the short. It pays for itself the first Saturday it saves.

At night, shorts show themselves. Walk the line after dark and look for the blue-white arc, or tune your truck radio to a dead AM station and drive the line. The tick gets louder as you close in on the fault.

## What the Voltage Numbers Mean

A fence tester is only useful if you know what reading you’re aiming for. Here’s the cheat sheet we work from, along with typical fix costs when a reading comes up short.

Reading on the fence What it means Typical fix DIY cost range

5,000 to 9,000 volts Healthy fence for cattle and horses Nothing, keep mowing the line $0

3,000 to 5,000 volts Working but marginal; small stock and bulls may test it Clear vegetation, tighten splices $0 to $50

1,000 to 3,000 volts Serious leak: dead short, brush load, or weak ground Half-split the line, fix insulators, add ground rods $20 to $150

Under 1,000 volts Dead short or charger failure Test charger direct; replace insulators, splice, or charger $5 to $400

Hot at charger, dead past a gate Failed underground lead-out cable Replace with double-insulated 12.5-gauge cable $40 to $120

Two notes on targets. Goats and sheep need more voltage than cattle because wool and hair insulate, so aim for 4,500 volts minimum on small stock. And a bull that has learned a fence is weak will keep testing it even after you fix it, which is why we tell folks to fix voltage problems fast, before the livestock get an education. If your animals have already picked up bad habits, our post on cattle getting out of the fence walks through breaking the cycle.

For deeper reading on energizer sizing and fence design, Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid, research-based fencing guidance for our exact soil and climate at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu, and the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service covers grazing fence standards at nrcs.usda.gov.

Found your problem and just need parts? Great, that’s the outcome we hope for. Still stumped, or staring at a half-mile of fence that needs more than a patch? Request a free written estimate and we’ll put real numbers on it.

## When to Stop Troubleshooting and Call a Pro

Most electric fence problems are honest DIY territory. Some aren’t, and knowing the difference saves money and occasionally a trip to the ER.

Stop and call somebody when:

- The fence crosses water or a creek bottom. Water gaps short constantly and rebuilding them right is its own skill. Never troubleshoot a hot wire while standing in water.

- The charger has internal damage. If a charger is buzzing, smells hot, or has visible scorching, unplug it and leave it unplugged. Don’t open the case. These units store real energy.

- There’s any chance the fence contacts utility power. A hot wire tangled with a downed power line is a killer, not a fence problem. Stay back and call the utility.

- The whole system is undersized or aged out. If you’re fighting the same fence every month, the math changes. Sometimes the right answer is retiring a tired hot wire and building permanent fence. A properly built barbed wire fence needs no charger, no battery, and no Saturday walks with a tester, and for working pens and high-pressure areas, pipe fence ends the conversation entirely.

Tom, who runs stockers on leased ground near Lorena, spent most of last spring chasing shorts on 30-year-old hot wire strung on rotten cedar posts. He’d already sunk about $350 in chargers, insulators, and weekends. We rebuilt the worst 900 feet as 5-strand barbed wire for $2,700, left the hot wire on the sections still worth keeping, and his cattle calls stopped. Sometimes troubleshooting is the wrong tool, and the honest move is to say so.

If you’re weighing that same decision, our comparison of electric fence vs barbed wire lays out costs and lifespan side by side.

Cattle out right now and the fence is dead? Don’t wait on business hours. Our emergency line runs 24/7 for exactly this: (254) 870-8898.

## A 10-Minute Monthly Check That Prevents Most of This

The cheapest troubleshooting is the kind you never have to do. Once a month, do this:

- Read voltage at the charger terminals, then at the far end of the fence. Write both numbers down. A slow decline over months is a warning you can act on before the fence fails.

- Eyeball the ground rods and clamps. Tug the wire connections.

- Drive or walk the line looking for sag, limbs, and hog rooting.

- Knock down vegetation before it touches wire, not after.

- After any big storm, test before you trust.

Keep a log taped inside the barn door. When a fence that reads 6,800 volts every month suddenly reads 4,100, your search shrinks from “the whole fence” to “whatever happened recently.” That habit alone cuts most troubleshooting jobs from hours to minutes.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why is my electric fence clicking but not shocking?

The click is the charger firing its pulse, so the unit is alive. No shock means the pulse isn’t completing the loop, which points to a bad ground system, a break in the line, or a dead short draining the voltage before it reaches the animal. Test voltage at the charger terminals first, then check your ground rods before walking the fence.

### How many volts should my electric fence have?

For cattle and horses, aim for 5,000 to 9,000 volts on the wire. Goats, sheep, and thick-hided bulls need the higher end of that range because hair and wool insulate against the pulse. Anything under 3,000 volts is a fence most livestock will eventually walk through.

### Can wet grass or weeds really short out an electric fence?

Yes, and vegetation is one of the top causes of a weak fence in Central Texas by early summer. Each grass stem touching the wire bleeds a little current to ground, and a few hundred feet of heavy contact can drop a fence from 7,000 volts to under 2,000. Mowing or spraying the fence line is voltage maintenance, not just cosmetics.

### How much does it cost to fix an electric fence?

Most DIY fixes are cheap: insulators run under a dollar each, ground rods about $15 to $25 apiece, and splice sleeves pennies. A replacement charger runs $120 to $400 depending on the miles of fence it has to push. If you hire it out, most single-fault repair calls in the Waco area land between $150 and $450, and we’ll always give you a written number before work starts.

## Electric Fence vs Barbed Wire: Cost, Upkeep, and Cattle Control (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/electric-fence-vs-barbed-wire/)

> Electric fence vs barbed wire for Central Texas cattle: real costs per foot, upkeep needs, and which one holds stock. Waco ranch fence pros break it down.

Cost Guide

# Electric Fence vs Barbed Wire: Cost, Upkeep, and Cattle Control
Published August 8, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A mile of five strand barbed wire around Waco runs $15,000 to $24,000 installed. A mile of two strand electric fence can go in for less than half that.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A mile of five strand barbed wire around Waco runs $15,000 to $24,000 installed. A mile of two strand electric fence can go in for less than half that. So why does barbed wire still line almost every county road in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties?

Because cheap up front isn’t the whole story. The electric fence vs barbed wire question comes down to three things: what it costs to build, what it costs to keep working, and whether it actually holds your cattle when a storm rolls through or a bull decides the neighbor’s grass looks better. We build both kinds all over Central Texas, and the honest answer is that each one wins in different spots on the same ranch.

Here’s how they stack up, with real numbers from real jobs.

## Electric Fence vs Barbed Wire Cost: The Real Numbers

Let’s start where everybody starts, the price per foot. These are typical installed ranges we see around Waco in 2026, materials and labor together, on ground that isn’t solid rock.

Electric (1-2 strand hot wire) Barbed Wire (5 strand)

Installed cost per foot $1.25 to $2.50 $2.50 to $4.50

Cost per mile $6,500 to $13,000 $15,000 to $24,000

Energizer and grounding $300 to $900 one time None

Typical lifespan 15 to 25 years (wire), 5 to 10 (energizer) 25 to 40 years with upkeep

Works during power or battery failure No Yes

Annual upkeep Check charge weekly, mow or spray fence line Restretch, restaple, replace the odd post

Best use Cross fencing, leases, rotational grazing Perimeter and road frontage

Two things jump out. Electric is the clear winner on upfront cost, mostly because you’re driving fewer posts. Hot wire carries almost no physical load, so posts can sit 30 to 50 feet apart instead of the 10 to 12 foot spacing barbed wire needs. Fewer posts, fewer holes, less labor.

But barbed wire is a physical barrier that works 24 hours a day whether or not a battery is charged. That difference matters more than any number on this table, and we’ll get to why.

Danny Vaculin, who runs stockers on leased coastal ground outside West, is a good example of electric done right. He picked up an 80 acre lease last spring and needed about a mile and a half of cross fence fast. A five strand barbed job would’ve run him around $22,000, which makes no sense on a three year lease. We built him two strand high tensile electric with a solar energizer for about $9,600. His steers respected it within a week, and when the lease ends he can pull most of it and take it with him.

If you’re trying to figure out which side of that table your project lands on, call us at (254) 870-8898 or request a free written estimate. We’ll walk the line with you and give you numbers for both options, in writing.

## How Each One Controls Cattle

Barbed wire is a physical barrier. Electric is a psychological one. That’s the whole comparison in two sentences, and everything else follows from it.

A properly built five strand barbed fence stops cattle because they physically can’t get through it without pain and effort. Even a hungry cow testing a fence line hits the barbs and backs off. It doesn’t need electricity, doesn’t care about weeds, and works exactly the same at 3 a.m. in a thunderstorm as it does on a clear afternoon. If you want the details on strand counts, our post on how many strands of barbed wire you need breaks it down by livestock type.

Electric fence stops cattle because they’ve been trained to fear it. A cow touches a hot wire once, gets a sharp 5,000 to 8,000 volt reminder, and gives that wire a wide berth from then on. Trained cattle will respect a single strand of hot wire that a calf could walk through if it wanted to.

The key word is trained. Cattle new to electric fence need to learn it, ideally in a small trap where they can test the wire without ending up on a farm to market road. And here’s the catch nobody likes to talk about: when the fence goes dead, cattle figure it out faster than you’d think. Some cows will start testing a fence within a day or two of the charge dropping. A dead electric fence is barely a fence at all.

Then there’s pressure. A hot wire handles casual pressure fine, a cow reaching for grass or scratching an itch. It does not handle panic. A deer strike, a pack of dogs, or a Fourth of July fireworks show can send cattle straight through electric fence like it’s not there. Barbed wire usually turns that same panicked cow, or at least slows her down and leaves you evidence of where she went through.

## Upkeep: What Each Fence Asks of You Every Year

No fence is maintenance free, but the two types ask for very different kinds of attention.

Electric fence needs regular, frequent, small attention. You need to check voltage at least weekly with a fence tester, because the fence only works when it’s carrying a charge. Grass and weeds growing into the wire bleed voltage into the ground, so you’re mowing or spraying the fence line two or three times a year in a wet spring. Solar panels need cleaning, batteries die every few years, and lightning loves energizers. If your charger is clicking but the fence reads low, our guide on why your electric fence isn’t working covers the usual suspects, bad grounding being the big one. Around here, dry summer soil is a terrible conductor, and a fence that snapped hard in April can feel like a static tickle by August.

Barbed wire needs occasional, heavier attention. You’re walking the line a couple times a year, restretching slack wire, replacing a rotted post here and there, and fixing whatever the last storm dropped on it. The work is more physical but far less frequent, and the fence keeps doing its job between visits. Budget roughly $100 to $300 per mile per year for materials on a barbed fence in decent shape, more as it ages past 25 or 30 years.

Gene Pruitt’s place in Valley Mills shows how the two can cover each other’s weaknesses. His barbed perimeter was 30 years old and his bulls had learned to lean through it to reach the neighbor’s oats. Rebuilding the whole line would’ve cost him north of $20,000. Instead we ran a single offset hot wire down 2,600 feet of the worst stretch, about $1,800 all in. The bulls quit leaning, the old wire quit stretching, and he bought himself years before a full rebuild.

Oklahoma State University’s extension service publishes a solid economic comparison of livestock fencing options if you want to see lifetime cost math laid out per foot per year. Their numbers line up with what we see in the field: electric wins on total cost, barbed wins on reliability, and the gap narrows the longer you own the land.

## Hot Wire vs Barbed Wire in Central Texas Conditions

Fence charts made for Missouri pasture don’t always survive contact with Central Texas. A few local realities push the hot wire vs barbed wire decision one way or the other.

Drought and dry soil. Electric fence needs moist soil to complete the circuit through the cow’s hooves. In a Central Texas July, blackland clay bakes hard and cracks, and fence voltage that reads fine at the energizer delivers a weak shock at the animal. Extra ground rods and a pos-neg wire setup help, but this is a real weakness here that it doesn’t have in wetter country.

Storms and lightning. One good spring storm can kill an energizer and drop limbs on any fence. The difference is what happens next. A barbed fence with a limb on it usually still turns cattle. An electric fence with a dead charger turns nothing.

Feral hogs. Hogs go under fences, not through them, and they’ll root out the bottom of either type. A low hot wire at snout height is actually one of the better hog deterrents going, which is a point for electric or for adding a hot strand to barbed.

Liability on roads. Texas is technically open range, but stock laws in McLennan and most surrounding counties, plus Chapter 143 of the Texas Agriculture Code on highways, mean cattle on the pavement can become your problem fast. That’s why we almost never recommend electric alone on road frontage. One dead battery between you and a wreck on Highway 6 is a bad bet.

Marcy Holt learned that one the hard way near Crawford. She’d fenced her whole 120 acres in electric to save money, and it worked fine for two years. Then a May lightning strike cooked her energizer while she was out of town, and by the next evening eight steers were grazing the right of way on a farm to market road. A neighbor got them penned before anything worse happened. She called us that week, and we rebuilt her mile and a quarter of road frontage in five strand barbed for about $21,000. She kept the electric for interior cross fencing, where a failure means cows in the wrong paddock instead of cows on the road. If your cattle have been finding their way out, our post on why cattle get out of fences is worth ten minutes.

## The Setup That Wins on Most Ranches

After enough of these jobs, a pattern shows up. The ranches with the fewest escapes and the lowest lifetime fence bills almost never pick one or the other. They use both, each where it’s strongest.

Barbed wire on the perimeter. Especially road frontage and property lines. It’s the fence that works when nothing else does, it satisfies the “sufficient fence” standard your county stock law expects, and a well built one is a 30 year asset. Our barbed wire fence crews in Waco build these to a spec that includes h-braced corners and Class 3 galvanized wire, because the cheap version costs more in the long run.

Electric for cross fencing. Interior paddocks, rotational grazing, temporary leases, and protecting hay ground. It’s cheap, fast, and easy to move. A failure inside the perimeter is an inconvenience, not an emergency.

A hot offset wire to protect aging barbed fence. Often the highest return fencing dollar you can spend. One strand on offset insulators stops the rubbing and leaning that destroys older fence.

Budget-wise, that combo means spending the real money once, on the perimeter, then covering the interior for a fraction of the cost. For the full picture on what perimeter fence runs, see our ranch fence cost guide or the deeper dive on barbed wire fence cost.

One safety note before you run wire yourself: never power any fence with a homemade or plug-in charger that isn’t a listed, low-impedance fence energizer. People have been killed by improvised fence chargers. And if a storm drops a tree across your fence and cattle are already out, that’s not a DIY afternoon. Our emergency line at (254) 870-8898 answers 24/7 for exactly that situation, and we’re licensed and insured for the work.

If you’re weighing electric against barbed for a specific pasture, the cheapest mistake to avoid is building the wrong fence in the wrong spot. Reach out for a free written estimate and we’ll price both options side by side for your ground, your cattle, and your budget.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is electric fence cheaper than barbed wire?

Yes, usually by half or more up front. Around Waco, a two strand electric fence runs $1.25 to $2.50 per foot installed, while five strand barbed wire runs $2.50 to $4.50 per foot. Electric also carries ongoing costs barbed doesn’t, like energizers, batteries, and weed control on the fence line, so the lifetime gap is smaller than the upfront gap.

### Will a single hot wire really hold cattle?

Trained cattle, yes, most of the time. Cattle that have learned to respect electric fence will honor a single strand at about nose height. It won’t hold untrained cattle, panicked cattle, or cattle standing at a dead fence, which is why we don’t recommend hot wire alone along roads or property lines.

### Can I add electric to my existing barbed wire fence?

Yes, and it’s often the best money you can spend on an older fence. A single hot wire on offset insulators keeps cattle from leaning, rubbing, and reaching through, which is what wears out barbed fence early. Expect roughly $0.60 to $1.00 per foot for an offset hot wire added to sound existing fence.

### How long does each type of fence last in Central Texas?

A well built five strand barbed fence with quality galvanized wire and good bracing lasts 25 to 40 years here. High tensile electric wire lasts 15 to 25 years, but energizers typically need replacement every 5 to 10 years, sooner if lightning finds them. Heat, drought cracked clay, and feral hogs shorten both, so an annual walk of the line pays for itself.

## Electric Horse Fence: Wire, Tape, Chargers and What Goes Wrong (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/electric-fence-for-horses/)

> How an electric horse fence really performs in Central Texas: wire vs tape, charger sizing, grounding in cracked clay, cost ranges, and the ways it quits.

Well Care

# Electric Horse Fence: Wire, Tape, Chargers and What Goes Wrong
Published September 9, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A horse walked through a single strand of poly tape at eleven at night in August, and the owner spent the next two hours walking a county road ditch with a flashlight.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A horse walked through a single strand of poly tape at eleven at night in August, and the owner spent the next two hours walking a county road ditch with a flashlight. The fence had tested fine in June. What changed was not the tape and not the horse. It was the ground under the ground rods, which had opened up into cracks you could drop a pen into, and a fence that cannot find dirt cannot shock anything.

That is the whole story of an electric horse fence in Central Texas. The hardware is cheap and the theory is simple, and almost every failure traces back to soil, vegetation, or a charger that was undersized the day it was bought. Done right, hot wire is one of the most useful tools on a horse place. Treated as a substitute for a real perimeter, it is how horses end up on the highway.

Below is what electric fence does well for horses, how to choose between wire, tape, rope and coated rail, how to size a charger and a ground field for clay and limestone, and what actually goes wrong out here.

## What an Electric Horse Fence Actually Does, and What It Doesn’t

An electric fence is a psychological barrier. It teaches an animal to respect a line. It does not physically stop anything, and a horse that is genuinely panicked, or that has learned the fence is dead, will go through it and barely notice.

That matters more for horses than for cattle. A cow tests a fence with her nose at walking speed. A horse spooks and leaves at a dead run, sometimes in the dark, sometimes toward a road.

Here is the split we recommend on almost every horse place we walk. Physical fence on the perimeter, especially anything fronting a public road. Electric on the inside, for cross fencing, rotational grazing, temporary paddocks, keeping horses off a new wire fence, and keeping them out of the round bale.

For the perimeter itself, no-climb woven mesh with a visible top rail is the common answer here, and horse-grade 2x4 mesh sits at the upper end of our net wire and field fence band of $3.50 to $8 per foot. Welded pipe runs $12 to $28 per foot and is what most folks put around pens and road frontage. Our horse fence page covers both, and the no-climb horse fence writeup gets into mesh specs.

If you are trying to decide how much of a place needs physical fence and how much can be hot wire, that is a fence line conversation, not a phone conversation. Call (254) 870-8898 and we will walk it with you. On-site estimates are free.

## Wire, Tape, Rope or Braid: Picking the Conductor

The single biggest safety factor in an electric horse fence is whether the horse can see it. A horse that sees the line slows down. A horse that does not see the line learns about it at speed.

Smooth high-tensile wire is the best conductor and the cheapest to run, and it is close to invisible at dusk. If you use it, give the horse something to look at: a wide tape on the top strand, a top rail, or sighter markers.

Poly tape is the opposite. The conductive filaments woven through it are thin, so it carries current poorly over distance and breaks down under Texas UV. Wide tape also acts like a sail, and on an exposed line 2 inch tape will loosen posts and stretch out of shape faster than most people expect.

Poly rope and braid sit in the middle. They are visible enough for most horses, they shed wind better than wide tape, and the better ones carry mixed metal filaments that hold conductivity longer than cheap tape. For interior division fences on a small place, rope is usually the practical answer.

One rule with no exceptions on horses: never electrify barbed wire. A shocked horse that jumps into barbs is the wreck the electric fence was supposed to prevent. If you have existing barbed wire and you want it hot, the answer is an offset smooth wire on standoff insulators, sitting 6 to 10 inches in front of the barbs.

Conductor Visibility Typical service life Materials-only estimate, per foot Where it fits

12.5 ga high-tensile smooth wire Poor on its own 20+ years $0.05 - $0.12 Long cross fences, offset wires on existing fence

Poly rope or braid, about 1/4 in Good 5 - 10 years $0.10 - $0.25 Interior division fences, temporary paddocks

Poly tape, 1.5 in Very good 4 - 8 years $0.15 - $0.35 Short runs, sheltered lines, foal paddocks

Poly tape, 2 in and wider Best 3 - 7 years $0.25 - $0.60 Sighter strand on a top line, arena wings

Coated polymer electric rail Very good 15 - 20 years $1.50 - $3.50 Barns, show places, high-traffic frontage

Those figures are general materials-only estimates for the strand itself, not a quote from us. Posts, insulators, the energizer, gate handles and labor sit on top of them, and our installed pricing is on the ranch fence cost page.

## Sizing the Charger and Getting the Ground Right

Chargers are rated in joules and in miles. Ignore the miles number. It assumes clean wire with nothing touching it, which describes no fence in McLennan County in April.

Size on output joules instead. A rough working rule out here is one joule of output per mile of conductor, then double it if the line runs through grass, brush, or anything you are not going to spray and mow. Vegetation load, not acreage, is what decides the size.

Mains power beats solar every time you can reach it. Solar units are sized to their battery and panel, they lose ground on short December days, and a dusty panel under a cedar is a slow fade nobody notices until the horses find it.

Grounding is where most of these fences fail. The circuit runs charger to wire to horse to soil and back through the ground rods, so dry soil is a broken circuit. Plan on a minimum of three galvanized ground rods, 6 to 8 feet long, spaced at least 10 feet apart, tied together with continuous galvanized wire and galvanized clamps.

Keep the metals matched. Copper clamps on galvanized rod corrode at the joint and quietly cost you a thousand volts a year later. Put the ground field somewhere that stays damp, usually the shaded side of a barn or near a tank overflow rather than out in the open.

Then there is our particular problem. Blackland clay shrinks in a dry summer and pulls away from the rod, and limestone and caliche will not let you drive a rod at all. On rocky ground the options are a drilled and backfilled ground bed, a horizontal ground trench, or a hot and ground return design, where alternate strands are wired to the ground system so the horse completes the circuit through two wires instead of through dry dirt.

Test with a digital fence tester, not by grabbing it or laying a grass stem across it. For horses we want to see roughly 3,000 volts or better at the far end of the fence, and anything under about 2,000 is a fence horses will start to test. Penn State Extension’s fence planning guide for horses and University of Georgia Extension both cover the safety side in more detail.

## What Goes Wrong With an Electric Horse Fence

Almost every dead fence we get called about is one of these six things, roughly in order of how often we find it.

The ground field. Too few rods, rods too short, rods in rock, corroded clamps, or soil that has dried out since the fence was installed. A fence can read fine at the charger and near zero at the horse when the ground is the problem.

Vegetation. Spring grass on the bottom strand will pull a fence down to nothing in a week. The bottom wire should either sit high enough to stay clear or be left dead.

Insulators and staples. Cracked plastic, UV-brittle insulators, or a staple driven tight over a wire on a wood post. Any of them will leak to the post, worse when the wood is wet.

Tape connections. Poly tape does not conduct through a knot. Every splice and corner needs a buckle or crimp connector, and a tape fence with four knotted repairs has four dead sections behind them.

Lightning. A strike on a long line will take out an energizer, and this is a summer thunderstorm region. A lightning arrestor on its own ground is the difference between a $40 part and a new charger.

Gates and undergrounds. The lead-out from the charger and any wire crossing under a gate has to be double-insulated underground cable. Bare wire in poly pipe is not insulation.

If your fence has quit and you want to run the checks yourself, we walked through the diagnostic order in electric fence not working. If you would rather someone else find it, book a free estimate and we will bring a tester and a fault finder.

## Three Places Around Waco Where This Plays Out

A 12-acre horse place outside Lorena. Two mares, road frontage on one side, and one strand of tape around the whole thing from the previous owner. We put horse-grade no-climb mesh with a top rail on the road side and the two neighbor lines, priced at the upper end of the $3.50 to $8 per foot net wire band because of the 2x4 mesh and the rail. The interior stayed electric, about 900 feet of poly rope on two strands with a mains energizer, which let the owner run three paddocks and rest the grass. Electric where a loose horse ends up in the next paddock, physical fence where a loose horse ends up on pavement.

A 300-acre lease west of Crawford. Cattle and a few using horses, two miles of tired barbed wire the owner did not want to replace yet. We ran an offset hot wire on standoff insulators along the worst mile and a half, which stopped the leaning that was flattening the wire in the first place. That took a 6 joule mains energizer and a proper three-rod ground field, and the offset conductor itself was a materials-only cost in the low hundreds. It bought that fence several more years, but it did not make it a horse fence.

A limestone hill section near Valley Mills. Every post hole on that ridge is a rock drill hole, and the ground rods would not go in past 18 inches. The fix was a hot and ground return layout on the hot wire sections so the circuit did not depend on that dry shelf rock, plus a drilled ground bed down at the bottom of the slope where there was actual soil. That is a case where the site decides the design, and no amount of charger will substitute for a ground field that cannot work.

## Where Electric Fits in a Real Horse Fence Budget

Electric fence looks cheap on paper because people price the wire and forget the rest. A charger, ground rods, insulators, gate handles, a cutout switch and a tester add up before the first strand goes on, and none of it holds a horse without posts.

The way we think about it is simple. Spend the money on the perimeter, particularly the part that touches a road, and use hot wire to make that perimeter last longer and to divide the interior. An offset wire that keeps horses from rubbing and leaning is the cheapest fence-life extender there is.

If the current fence is old barbed wire and horses are already behind it, hot wire is a stopgap and not a fix. Compare the options in best fence for horses and electric fence vs barbed wire, then decide which sections need real wire and which can wait.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Will an electric fence hold a horse by itself?

Sometimes, and not reliably. Electric fence is a training barrier, so it works on a horse that has learned to respect it and does nothing for a horse that is running scared or that has figured out the power is off. For interior paddocks that is an acceptable risk, but we do not recommend electric alone as the perimeter on any place with road frontage.

### How many strands does an electric horse fence need?

Most horse paddocks here run three strands, with the top around 48 to 54 inches, a middle strand at chest height, and a third low enough to discourage reaching under. Small acreage with foals or minis often needs a fourth. Leave the bottom strand dead or set it high enough to stay out of the grass, otherwise vegetation will short the fence every spring.

### What voltage should an electric horse fence read?

Check it with a digital fence tester at the far end of the fence, not at the charger. Aim for about 3,000 volts or better for horses. Below roughly 2,000 volts, horses start testing the fence, and the cause is almost always the ground field, vegetation on the wire, or a failed insulator rather than the energizer itself.

### Can I electrify my existing barbed wire fence for horses?

No. Electrified barbed wire is the one setup we will not build on a horse property, because a shocked horse that jumps into barbs is exactly the injury you are trying to avoid. If you want to hot up an existing barbed wire line, run a smooth offset wire on standoff insulators 6 to 10 inches in front of the barbs so the horse meets the hot wire first.

## Building a Fence on the Property Line in Texas: Get a Survey First (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/fence-on-property-line-texas/)

> Building a fence on the property line in Texas? Get a survey first. A Waco ranch fence pro covers Texas fence law, neighbor cost splits, and setback options.

Texas Law

# Building a Fence on the Property Line in Texas: Get a Survey First
Published August 10, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A fence built three feet over the line can end up costing more than the fence itself. We've seen it happen more than once around Waco, and it always starts the same way: a landowner points at an old...

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A fence built three feet over the line can end up costing more than the fence itself. We’ve seen it happen more than once around Waco, and it always starts the same way: a landowner points at an old cedar post or a rusted wire and says, “that’s the line, it’s always been the line.”

Sometimes it is. Plenty of times it isn’t. If you’re planning a fence on the property line in Texas, the smartest $400 to $700 you’ll ever spend is a boundary survey before the first post goes in the ground. This article walks through why that survey matters, what Texas law actually says about line fences, how to handle the neighbor conversation, and where the real dollar risks hide.

## Why Every Fence on the Property Line in Texas Starts With a Survey

Here’s the uncomfortable truth about rural land in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties: a lot of the old fences out here were never on the line to begin with. Crews in the 1950s and 60s built where the ground was easiest, not where the deed said. They dodged rock, skipped creek crossings, and followed tree lines. Then sixty years passed and everybody just assumed the fence was the boundary.

When you replace one of those fences, you inherit the mistake. And unlike a sagging wire, a boundary mistake doesn’t get cheaper with time.

A rancher we’ll call Dale, out near Crawford, learned that the hard way in 2024. He replaced 1,400 feet of old net wire with new 5-strand barbed wire along what he figured was his east line. Total job ran about $9,200. Eight months later his neighbor sold, the buyer ordered a survey, and the new fence turned out to sit 15 feet inside the neighbor’s tract for most of its run. Dale ended up pulling posts, re-drilling holes, and rebuilding on the true line. The do-over added roughly $4,100 to a fence that was already paid for. A survey up front would’ve cost him about $600.

That’s the math in one story. The survey is a rounding error next to the fence. The mistake is not.

If you’re pricing a line fence right now and want real numbers before you commit, call us at (254) 870-8898. Estimates are free and in writing, and we’re happy to walk the line with you before anybody digs.

## What Texas Property Line Fence Laws Actually Say

Texas fence law surprises people, mostly because of what it doesn’t say.

First, Texas has no statewide statute that forces your neighbor to split the cost of a boundary fence. If you build it, you pay for it, unless the two of you agree otherwise. That’s different from a lot of other states, and it’s the number one thing landowners get wrong. We covered the cost-sharing question in detail in our post on who pays for a fence between neighbors in Texas.

Second, most of rural Texas is still legally open range, meaning livestock owners aren’t automatically required to fence animals in. Counties and voters can flip that with local stock laws, and most Central Texas counties have. Where a stock law applies, you’re fencing cattle in, not fencing them out. Our breakdown of the Texas open range law explains which rules apply where, and why it matters if a cow ends up on FM 185.

Third, the state’s main fence statute, Texas Agriculture Code Chapter 143, deals mostly with what counts as a “sufficient fence” and with stock laws, not with who owns a boundary fence or where it must sit. That question comes down to your deed, your survey, and any written agreement with the neighbor.

One more wrinkle worth knowing: if a fence sits off the true line long enough and both sides treat it as the boundary, doctrines like adverse possession and acquiescence can come into play. That’s lawyer territory, not fence-builder territory, and it’s exactly the kind of mess a survey prevents.

## Survey Cost vs. Mistake Cost: The Real Numbers

People balk at survey quotes until they see what the alternative runs. Here’s how the numbers typically stack up in our area. Survey prices vary with tract size, terrain, and how findable the original corner markers are.

Item Typical Cost in Central Texas Notes

Boundary survey, 10 to 25 acres $400 to $900 More if corners are lost or brush is heavy

Boundary survey, 50 to 200 acres $900 to $2,500 Often priced per corner or per acre

New 5-strand barbed wire fence $2.50 to $4.50 per foot See our barbed wire fence cost guide

Tearing out and rebuilding a misplaced fence $4 to $7 per foot Removal plus rebuild, often in worse ground

Attorney fees in a boundary dispute $3,000 to $15,000+ Before anyone touches a fence

Losing a strip of land to adverse possession Whatever that acreage is worth Plus the neighbor relationship

Read that table bottom to top and the survey starts looking like the cheapest line item on the whole project. On a mile of fence, even a small angle error compounds. Two degrees off at the starting corner puts you about 180 feet off the mark by the far end of a mile run.

Find a licensed surveyor through the Texas Board of Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, which keeps a public license lookup. Ask for a boundary survey with corners marked and flagged, and tell them a fence crew will be building to those stakes.

## Talk to Your Neighbor Before You Set the First Post

The legal side matters, but out here the neighbor side matters just as much. You’re going to share that line for decades. A ten-minute phone call before you build saves years of cold shoulders at the co-op.

Marcus, who runs cattle on about 60 acres outside China Spring, did this the right way in early 2025. His shared west line fence was shot: rotten posts, rusted wire, cattle testing it weekly. Instead of just building, he took our written estimate to his neighbor, and they agreed in writing to split a $7,800 rebuild straight down the middle. Each side paid $3,900, both herds stayed put, and both tracts got more valuable. No statute made that happen. A conversation did.

When you talk to your neighbor, cover four things and put them on paper:

- Where the fence will sit, referenced to the survey, on the line or inside it

- Who pays what, including future repairs

- What kind of fence it’ll be, since a shared fence should hold both owners’ livestock

- Who maintains which stretch going forward

Even a one-page signed agreement beats a handshake when one of the properties sells. And they all sell eventually.

If you’d like a written estimate you can hand your neighbor, request one here. It costs nothing and it turns a vague conversation into a real number.

## On the Line or Inside It: Where Should the Fence Actually Go?

Once the survey stakes are in, you’ve got a genuine decision to make. There are three ways to place a boundary fence, and each has trade-offs.

Centered on the line. The classic shared fence. Posts straddle the boundary, both owners typically treat it as joint property. Best when both neighbors agree in writing on cost and upkeep. Risky when they don’t, because now you co-own a fence with someone who may not maintain their end.

Fully inside your line. You set the fence six inches to a couple feet inside your boundary. It’s 100 percent yours: your fence, your rules, your maintenance schedule, and nobody can touch it. The cost is a sliver of grazing you give up along the run, and you’ll still want to keep the strip on the far side from growing up in brush.

Well inside your line. On rough country, some owners pull the fence back 10 or 20 feet to dodge a creek bank, a rock ledge, or a stand of cedar. Practical, but mark the true corners anyway so the fence doesn’t get mistaken for the boundary by the next owner.

Consider this couple’s experience near Valley Mills. The Hendersons bought 25 acres in 2023 and assumed the old south fence was their line. Their $650 closing survey showed the fence sat almost 30 feet inside their deeded boundary for a quarter mile. That strip worked out to nearly three quarters of an acre they were about to fence themselves out of. They built the new fence on the surveyed line, with corners set as proper H-braces, and picked up land they’d already paid for.

Whatever placement you choose, build it once and build it stout. On property lines we usually recommend either a heavy 5 or 6 strand barbed wire fence for cattle country or a pipe fence where the line fronts a road or a headquarters area and you want something that shrugs off vehicles and time.

## When to Stop Guessing and Call a Pro

There’s plenty of fence work a handy landowner can do. Stretching wire on a short, flat, surveyed run with a helper and a good stretcher is a fair weekend project.

But some situations call for stopping and picking up the phone:

- You can’t find your corner markers, or the deed calls don’t match what’s on the ground. That’s a surveyor first, then a fence crew.

- The neighbor disputes the line. Do not build anything until that’s settled. A fence built into a live dispute becomes evidence, and sometimes a demolition bill.

- The line crosses a creek, a county road right of way, or a utility easement. Water gaps and easement rules trip up even experienced hands.

- The run is long. At a half mile or more, small layout errors compound, and corner bracing has to be dead right or the whole fence sags inside five years.

- There’s any question about stock law status and your liability if cattle get out onto a road.

We build property line fences across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and we build to survey stakes, not to guesses. We’re licensed and insured, every estimate is free and in writing, and if a storm drops a tree across your line fence at 2 a.m. and the cattle are walking, our emergency line answers around the clock.

Get the survey. Have the neighbor conversation. Then let’s build a fence that’ll still be on the right line thirty years from now. Call (254) 870-8898 or request your free written estimate today.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I build a fence directly on the property line in Texas?

Yes, if it’s truly on the line and your neighbor doesn’t object, though the smart move is a written agreement first. A fence centered on the boundary is generally treated as shared, which means shared decisions about repairs and replacement. If you want full control of the fence, build it a short distance inside your own line so it’s entirely on your property.

### Does my neighbor have to pay for half the fence in Texas?

No. Texas has no statute requiring a neighbor to share the cost of a boundary fence, so whoever builds it pays for it unless both parties agree otherwise. Many neighbors do split costs voluntarily since both sides benefit. Get any split in writing, including who handles future repairs.

### How much does a property line survey cost before building a fence?

For typical small acreage around Waco, expect roughly $400 to $900, with larger or brushier tracts running $900 to $2,500 or more. Price depends on tract size, terrain, and whether the original corner markers can be found. Compared to tearing out and rebuilding a misplaced fence at $4 to $7 per foot, the survey is cheap insurance.

### What happens if my fence is over the property line?

Best case, the neighbor doesn’t mind and you sign an agreement acknowledging the fence isn’t the boundary. Worst case, you’re required to remove and rebuild it, and if the encroachment stands long enough, boundary doctrines like adverse possession can even shift ownership of the strip. If you discover an encroachment, talk to the neighbor early and get a real estate attorney involved before anyone pulls a post.

## Fence Post Rot at the Ground Line: Why Wood Posts Fail and How to Fix Them (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/fence-post-rot/)

> Wood fence posts rotting at the ground line? Learn what causes fence post rot, how to fix or replace bad posts, and real costs from a Waco ranch fence crew.

Fence Repair

# Fence Post Rot at the Ground Line: Why Wood Posts Fail and How to Fix Them
Published August 11, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Grab a ten-year-old wood post on your place and give it a hard shove. If it wobbles, creaks, or snaps clean off at the dirt, you just found the most common fence failure in Central Texas.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Grab a ten-year-old wood post on your place and give it a hard shove. If it wobbles, creaks, or snaps clean off at the dirt, you just found the most common fence failure in Central Texas.

Here’s the strange part. Pull that broken post and the buried bottom two feet often look fine. So does the top. The damage sits in a six-inch band right at the soil line, and that’s no accident. Fence post rot almost always starts at the ground line because that narrow zone gives wood-eating fungi everything they need at once.

We’ve pulled thousands of rotten posts out of pastures across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties. Here’s why posts rot where they do, how to catch it early, which fixes are worth your money, and how to set new posts so you’re not back at it in eight years.

## What Causes Fence Post Rot Right at the Ground Line

Rot isn’t the wood “going bad” on its own. It’s a living fungus eating the post, and fungi need four things: moisture, oxygen, mild temperatures, and food. The food is your post.

Deep underground there’s moisture but very little oxygen, so fungi struggle. Above ground there’s oxygen but the post dries out fast after rain. The ground line is the overlap zone. Soil holds moisture against the wood, air is still available, and Texas soil temperatures sit in the fungal comfort range most of the year.

That’s why a post can be solid at the top, solid at the bottom, and completely hollowed out in the middle. The USDA Forest Products Laboratory has studied wood decay for over a century, and their findings back up what every fence builder sees in the field: decay concentrates where moisture and oxygen meet.

Two other culprits speed things up around here:

- Grass and brush against the post. Vegetation traps humidity at the ground line and keeps the wood from drying between rains.

- Soil that holds water. Our blackland clay swells up tight around posts and holds moisture for weeks. If you’re fencing in that gumbo east of I-35, read our guide on setting fence posts in clay soil before you dig.

If you’d rather have a professional eye look over a fence that’s starting to lean, request a free written estimate and we’ll walk the line with you. No charge, no pressure.

### What Makes Rot Worse in Central Texas Pastures

The ground-line science is the same everywhere, but a few local factors make fence post rot move faster in our part of the state.

Untreated or poorly treated posts. A bare pine post set in Central Texas soil can rot through in 2 to 5 years. Properly pressure-treated pine rated for ground contact should give you 20 to 30. The problem is that a lot of bargain posts are treated to a retention level meant for above-ground use, not burial. If the treatment only penetrated a quarter inch, the fungus just eats its way in behind it.

The wrong species. Native cedar heartwood resists rot naturally, but cedar sold today often includes sapwood, which rots about as fast as untreated pine. We break down the real differences in cedar vs. treated pine posts.

Concrete collars done wrong. Concrete poured level with or below grade forms a cup that catches water and holds it against the post. We dig up “concreted” posts all the time that rotted faster than posts set in plain dirt.

Our wet-dry cycle. Central Texas swings between soaking spring rains and baked-hard summers. Each cycle opens checks and cracks in the wood at the soil line, and every crack is a new doorway for fungus and moisture.

Robert Mynar, who runs cattle on about 90 acres outside West, called us in March after a wind storm laid over 40 feet of his perimeter fence. The wire was fine. The posts had snapped at the dirt like pencils. They were untreated pine a previous owner set around 2012. We replaced 22 posts and re-stretched the wire for $1,890, and he told us the worst part was that the fence looked fine from the truck the week before.

That’s the trap with rot. It hides until something pushes on it, and that something is usually a storm or a bull.

## How to Spot Rotten Fence Posts Before They Drop Your Wire

You don’t need special tools to check for fence post rot. You need a screwdriver, a hammer, and an hour walking your fence line. Here’s the routine we use:

- Push hard on every wood post. A sound post barely moves. A post that flexes at the ground line while the top swings is telling on itself.

- Do the tap test. Knock on the post with a hammer just above the soil. Solid wood rings sharp. Rotten wood answers with a dull thud, like knocking on a watermelon.

- Probe at the ground line. Push a flathead screwdriver into the wood right at the dirt. If it sinks in more than a quarter inch with hand pressure, decay has started.

- Scrape back the soil. Pull dirt and grass away from the post an inch or two down. Soft, dark, stringy, or spongy wood below grade means the rot is ahead of what you can see.

- Look for mushrooms and staining. Fungal growth at the base, or a dark wet-looking band that never dries, both point to active decay.

Check corners and gate posts first. They carry the load of the whole stretch, and a rotten corner takes hundreds of feet of wire down with it. If your corners are failing, our article on H-brace fence corners explains how to rebuild them so the fence stays tight.

Also pay attention to posts that lean before they wobble. A slow lean can be rot, but it can also be soil movement, and the fix is different. We cover how to tell them apart in why fence posts lean and how to fix them.

## Fixing Fence Post Rot: What Works and What’s a Waste of Money

Once rot is established at the ground line, you can’t reverse it. Fungus has consumed wood fiber, and no spray or filler puts that strength back. So every “fix” is really one of three moves: reinforce the post, sister a new support next to it, or replace it. Here’s how the options stack up for a working ranch fence:

Repair option Cost per post (typical) How long it lasts Best for

Steel post repair spike or E-Z Mender $15 to $35 DIY 3 to 8 years Line posts with light rot, low load

Sister a new post beside the old one $25 to $60 DIY 10 to 20 years Line posts where wire can’t be dropped

Full post replacement, treated pine $45 to $95 installed 20 to 30 years Any post, the default fix

Full replacement, steel pipe post $90 to $180 installed 40+ years Corners, gates, high-load spots

Concrete or epoxy patch at ground line $10 to $20 DIY 1 to 2 years Nothing. Skip it.

A few honest notes on that table.

Repair spikes are a bandage, not a cure. They drive into the ground alongside the post and clamp onto the sound wood above the rot. On a light-duty line post they’ll buy you years. On a corner post under thousands of pounds of wire tension, they will fail, usually at the worst time.

Patching rot with concrete or filler is throwing money in a hole. The fungus keeps eating behind the patch and you’ve just hidden the evidence.

Replacement is almost always the right call for corners and gates. When a corner post shows rot, we recommend rebuilding the whole brace assembly, because the diagonal and the brace post are usually the same age and the same condition.

Linda Vasek near Valley Mills learned that one the expensive way. She paid a handyman $260 to drive repair spikes on two rotten corner posts on her horse trap. Fourteen months later a spring storm hit, both corners folded, and her mare ended up on FM 56 at dusk. Nobody was hurt, thank God. We rebuilt both corners with pipe and re-stretched about 600 feet of wire for $1,450. Steel corners cost more up front, but she won’t touch them again in her lifetime. If you’re weighing that trade, our pipe fence page covers why we set pipe at every corner we build now.

If cattle are already testing a weak stretch, don’t wait on it. Call us at (254) 870-8898. We run a 24/7 line for cattle-out and storm-damage emergencies, because a rotten post never fails on a convenient day.

## Replacing a Rotten Post the Right Way

Swapping one line post is a fair DIY job if you do it in the right order. Here’s the short version:

- Support the wire first. Loosen staples and rest the strands on temporary T-posts so tension doesn’t whip loose wire at you. Wear gloves and eye protection around barbed wire.

- Pull the old post, stub and all. A rotten stump left in the hole rots the new post faster. A farm jack and a chain wrapped low will pull most stubs.

- Dig deep. Line posts want 24 to 30 inches in the ground, corners 36 to 42. Shallow posts heave and lean long before they rot.

- Use ground-contact treated posts. Look for a treatment tag rated for ground contact. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid guidance on fence construction and post selection at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu.

- Tamp in lifts and crown the top. Add dirt or crushed base a few inches at a time and tamp each layer hard. Mound the surface so water sheds away from the post.

- Re-stretch and re-staple. Angle the staples slightly and leave a hair of play so the wire can move without cutting in.

Know when to stop. If the rotten post is a corner, a gate post, or part of a long run gone slack, it’s no longer a post swap. It’s a tension system rebuild, and getting it wrong means doing the job twice. That’s where calling a crew saves money instead of costing it.

## How to Keep New Fence Posts From Rotting

You can’t make a wood post immortal in Texas dirt, but you can stack the odds hard in your favor.

- Buy ground-contact treatment, not the cheap stuff. The tag matters more than the color of the wood.

- Coat the ground-line zone. Brushing copper naphthenate preservative from 6 inches above grade to 18 below adds real years, especially on cut ends.

- Never cut the buried end. Factory treatment is deepest at the original surface. Trim the top and put the untouched end in the ground.

- Crown the soil at every post. A small mound sheds water. A dished collar collects it.

- If you pour concrete, dome it above grade so water runs off instead of pooling around the wood.

- Keep grass and brush off the fence line. A clean line dries faster and lets you spot trouble early.

- Mix in steel where it counts. Pipe corners and gates with wood or T-post line posts is the workhorse setup around Waco, and it puts rot-proof material exactly where failure hurts most.

Jim Kolar out in Crawford went that route in 2023 on a 60-acre perimeter. Pipe corners, treated pine line posts on crowned tamped bases, and a mowed fence line. We checked that fence this spring, and every post still rings sharp under a hammer. His neighbor’s fence, built the same year with bargain posts in dished concrete, already has three you can wiggle by hand. Same soil, same rain, different habits.

## What Fence Post Rot Repairs Cost Around Waco

For budgeting, here’s what we see on real jobs in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties. Single-post replacements run $45 to $95 for treated wood and $90 to $180 for pipe, installed. Corner rebuilds with an H-brace typically land between $350 and $700 per corner depending on materials. Larger rot jobs, where a whole stretch of posts from the same era fails together, usually price out between $8 and $15 per foot to re-post and re-stretch existing wire.

At some point, replacement beats repair. If more than a quarter to a third of the posts in a run are soft, you’ll spend less per year of fence life rebuilding the stretch than chasing failures one post at a time. Our ranch fence cost guide breaks down full rebuild pricing per foot and per mile so you can compare honestly.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How long do wood fence posts last before rotting in Texas?

Untreated pine can rot through in 2 to 5 years in Central Texas soil. Ground-contact pressure-treated pine typically lasts 20 to 30 years, and good cedar heartwood often runs 15 to 25. Actual life depends heavily on drainage, soil type, and whether the ground line was kept clear of grass and pooled water.

### Can you treat fence post rot without replacing the post?

You can slow rot with a copper naphthenate preservative and reinforce a lightly damaged line post with a steel repair spike or a sistered post. You cannot restore strength the fungus has already eaten. For corner posts, gate posts, or any post that flexes at the ground line, replacement is the only fix that holds.

### Does setting posts in concrete stop rot?

No, and done wrong it makes rot worse. Concrete that sits level with or below the soil forms a cup that traps water against the wood. If you use concrete, dome it a few inches above grade so water sheds off. Many ranch fences do better with well-tamped native soil or crushed base and a crowned surface.

### When should I call a pro instead of fixing rotten posts myself?

Swapping one or two line posts is a reasonable DIY job. Call a professional when the rot involves corner or gate posts, when a long stretch has gone slack, when livestock are actively getting out, or when storm damage has put wire under unpredictable tension. Loaded barbed wire and failing braces can injure you fast, and a crew can rebuild the tension system correctly in one visit.
