## Fence Post Spacing for Barbed Wire, Net Wire, and Pipe Fence (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/fence-post-spacing/)

> Get fence post spacing right for barbed wire, net wire, and pipe fence in Central Texas. Real numbers, costs, and mistakes to avoid from Waco fence pros.

Ranch Fencing

# Fence Post Spacing for Barbed Wire, Net Wire, and Pipe Fence
Published August 12, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Here's a number that surprises most landowners: stretching your post spacing from 12 feet to 20 feet on a mile of barbed wire fence cuts out about 175 posts.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Here’s a number that surprises most landowners: stretching your post spacing from 12 feet to 20 feet on a mile of barbed wire fence cuts out about 175 posts. At $12 to $20 per T-post installed, that’s $2,100 to $3,500 back in your pocket per mile. So why doesn’t everybody run posts at 20 feet and call it a day?

Because fence post spacing isn’t one number. It changes with the wire you’re hanging, the animals you’re holding, the ground you’re driving into, and how hard the pressure hits the fence. Get it right and your fence stands tight for 25 years. Get it wrong and you’re walking the line every spring pushing leaning posts back up and splicing sagging wire.

We build barbed wire, net wire, and pipe fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and post spacing questions come up on almost every estimate. This guide gives you the real numbers we use in the field, what they cost, and where cheap spacing turns expensive.

Not sure what spacing your place needs? Call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk your fence line with you. Written estimates are free.

## Why Fence Post Spacing Matters More Than Most People Think

Posts do two jobs. They hold the wire at the right height, and they take the hit when something pushes on the fence. Wire does the actual stopping. That’s why a well-braced fence with good wire tension can run wider spacing than most folks expect, and why a fence with weak corners fails no matter how many posts you drive.

Wider spacing saves money up front. Tighter spacing spreads out impact, keeps wire heights honest over uneven ground, and gives cattle less room to work a gap. The right answer sits between those two pulls, and it’s different for each fence type.

One more thing before the numbers. Post spacing only works if your corners and ends are built right. A line post at 15 feet on centers means nothing if the H-brace at the corner is leaning. If your corners are suspect, read our guide on H-brace fence corners before you worry about anything between them.

## Barbed Wire Fence Post Spacing: The 12 to 20 Foot Range

For a standard 5-strand barbed wire cattle fence in Central Texas, we set line posts at 12 to 15 feet for most jobs. On flat, open country with light cattle pressure, you can stretch to 16 or even 20 feet if the wire is high-tensile and the braces are stout. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension and most land-grant fencing guides put acceptable barbed wire spacing in that same 12 to 20 foot window, with tighter spacing where pressure is higher.

Here’s how we decide where to land in that range:

- 12 feet: Heavy cattle pressure, bulls, fence lines along roads, pens and traps, rolling ground.

- 15 feet: The workhorse spacing. Standard pasture fence for cow-calf operations on decent ground.

- 16 to 20 feet: Big open pastures, light stocking, straight flat runs, high-tensile wire, budget matters.

Most of our barbed wire jobs run a wood post every fourth or fifth post with T-posts between. The wood posts add stiffness to the line and give you something solid to tie into. On rocky ridges west of the Bosque River we sometimes flip that ratio because driving wood posts in rock gets expensive fast. If that’s your ground, our post on setting fence posts in rocky ground covers your options.

A quick story from Crawford. Dale runs about 60 cow-calf pairs on 300 acres, and the previous owner had built the perimeter with T-posts on 25-foot centers to save money. The wire heights wandered, the stays had slid, and his cows learned to push between strands. He lost two calves through the fence onto a county road before he called us. We added posts to bring the line to 12.5-foot centers and rebuilt six braces for $4,800. That’s real money, but one vet bill and one liability scare made the math easy for him.

Sagging wire between wide-set posts is the most common symptom we see. If your fence already droops, start with our guide on how to fix a sagging barbed wire fence, then decide if the spacing itself is the disease.

## Net Wire Post Spacing for Sheep, Goats, and Horses

Net wire (field fence) needs tighter post spacing than barbed wire. The mesh carries more wind load, catches more weight when animals lean or climb, and shows every dip in the ground. We set net wire posts at 8 to 12 feet on most jobs.

Goats are the deciding factor more often than not. A goat treats a fence like playground equipment. They stand on it, rub it, and climb corners. For goat and sheep fence we hold spacing at 8 to 10 feet, run a barbed strand on top, and keep the bottom wire snug to the dirt. Horses do fine at 10 to 12 feet with fixed-knot net wire, which holds its shape better than hinge-joint when a hoof strikes it.

Terrain moves this number too. Net wire can’t bend over a hump or dip the way individual barbed strands can. Every grade change needs a post to hold the mesh at the right height, so hilly ground pulls your average spacing tighter whether you planned it or not.

The Hendersons in Valley Mills learned this the expensive way. They fenced 12 acres for Boer goats with hinge-joint net wire on 16-foot centers, a spacing the feed store had suggested for cattle. Within a year the mesh had bellied out between posts, the goats were flattening it at the low spots, and three got into a neighbor’s coastal field. We rebuilt 1,900 feet with fixed-knot wire on 10-foot centers for about $6.75 a foot, roughly $12,800 total. Their original fence had cost them close to $9,000 and lasted 14 months.

If you’re planning a small-acreage net wire job and want it done once, reach out for a free written estimate. We’ll spec the wire, the spacing, and the braces in writing so you can compare it against any other bid.

## Pipe Fence Post Spacing and Why It Runs Tighter

Pipe fence flips the logic. With barbed and net wire, the wire does the stopping and posts just hold position. With pipe fence, the posts and rails ARE the fence. That’s why pipe fence posts run tighter, usually 8 to 10 feet on centers.

The spacing is really set by your top rail. Most pipe rail comes in lengths that work out clean at 8 or 10 foot spans, and a 2 3/8 inch top rail spanning much more than 10 feet will flex when a 1,400-pound cow leans on it. For horse pens, working pens, and arena fence we hold 8-foot centers. For pipe-and-cable or pipe top rail over net wire along a driveway, 10 feet is common.

Because pipe posts get set in concrete, each post costs a lot more than a driven T-post, so the temptation to stretch spacing is strong. Resist it. A pipe fence is a 40-year asset when it’s built right. Stretching spans to save four posts per hundred feet is how you end up with a wavy top rail that bugs you every time you drive in the gate.

## Corner Posts, Braces, and Gates: Where Spacing Rules Change

Everything above covers line posts. Corners, ends, and gates play by different rules, and they matter more.

Every corner and every end of a wire fence needs a brace assembly, usually an H-brace with the horizontal rail at least twice the fence height in length. On long runs of barbed wire, we add an inline brace roughly every quarter mile so the wire can be tensioned in manageable pulls. Water gaps, big grade changes, and gate openings all get their own bracing regardless of what the line spacing is.

Gate posts carry the most load on the whole fence. A 16-foot pipe gate hanging on an undersized post will sag no matter how pretty the rest of the fence is. We set gate posts heavy, deep, and in concrete every time. If you’re planning an entrance, our ranch entrance gates page shows what proper gate post construction looks like.

Marcus outside Lorena had us diagnose a fence that kept going slack even though his line posts were fine at 15 feet. The problem was corners. His braces were single posts with a diagonal wire and no horizontal rail, and they’d pulled 6 inches out of plumb. Wire tension bled away every season. We rebuilt eight corner and end assemblies for $2,650 and re-tensioned his existing wire, and the fence has held tight for three years since. He didn’t need more posts. He needed better corners.

## Fence Post Spacing Chart and Cost Comparison

Here’s the quick reference we hand landowners at estimates. Costs are typical installed ranges for our area in 2026 and include posts, labor, and hardware for the line itself.

Fence type Line post spacing Typical post mix Installed cost per foot

5-strand barbed wire, standard 12 to 15 ft 1 wood per 4 to 5 T-posts $2.50 to $4.50

5-strand barbed wire, wide spacing 16 to 20 ft High-tensile wire, stout braces $2.00 to $3.50

Net wire, cattle and horses 10 to 12 ft Wood corners, T-post lines $4.00 to $7.00

Net wire, goats and sheep 8 to 10 ft Fixed-knot wire preferred $4.50 to $7.50

Pipe fence, 4-rail 8 ft All pipe, set in concrete $18 to $30

Pipe top rail with net wire 10 ft Pipe posts, wire infill $9 to $15

Two notes on that table. First, tighter spacing raises cost per foot but usually lowers cost per year of fence life, because the fence lasts longer and needs fewer repairs. Second, rocky or heavy clay ground can push these numbers up 15 to 25 percent because posts take longer to set. The USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service publishes fencing practice standards that follow the same logic if you want a second opinion from a neutral source: https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/.

## Soil, Terrain, and Weather: When to Tighten Up

Central Texas ground doesn’t make fencing easy, and it should factor into your spacing decision.

Blackland clay swells when wet and shrinks hard in drought. That movement works posts loose over time, and loose posts plus wide spacing equals a leaning fence. In heavy clay we favor the tight end of every spacing range and set wood posts deeper. Limestone country west of Waco brings the opposite problem, shallow rock that stops a post driver cold. There we sometimes pin posts to rock or drill, which changes the cost math on every post.

Wind load matters on net wire. A long, exposed run of mesh fence catches gusts like a sail, and our spring storms will test it. Flood-prone creek crossings need water gaps built to break away and be rebuilt cheap, not tighter spacing.

And know when to stop doing this yourself. Driving T-posts on flat ground is honest DIY work. But corner braces, pipe welding, long wire stretches under high tension, and any post setting near buried utilities are where people get hurt and fences fail. Call 811 before you dig, every time. Stretched high-tensile wire stores real energy, and a snapped strand can cut you badly. If any of that gives you pause, that’s the moment to bring in a pro.

We build barbed wire fence, net wire, and pipe fence across Waco, China Spring, Crawford, McGregor, Valley Mills, Lorena, and West. If you’d rather get it right once, call (254) 870-8898 for a free written estimate, and remember we run a 24/7 emergency line for storm damage and cattle-out situations.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How far apart should T-posts be for barbed wire fence?

For a typical 5-strand barbed wire cattle fence, set T-posts 12 to 15 feet apart, with a wood post every fourth or fifth post. You can stretch to 20 feet on flat ground with light cattle pressure and strong braces. Go tighter, around 12 feet, near roads, in pens, or anywhere cattle push hard.

### Does closer fence post spacing make a fence stronger?

Up to a point, yes, because each post shares impact load and keeps wire heights consistent. But past a certain tightness you’re spending money without gaining much, since wire tension and corner bracing do most of the holding. A fence with 15-foot spacing and excellent H-braces will outlast a fence with 8-foot spacing and weak corners.

### What spacing do pipe fence posts need?

Most pipe fence runs 8-foot centers for horse pens, working pens, and arenas, and up to 10 feet for pipe top rail over net wire. The span is limited by how much your top rail flexes under animal pressure. Pipe posts should be set in concrete, typically 2 to 3 feet deep depending on soil.

### Can I just add posts to fix a sagging fence?

Sometimes, but diagnose first. If the wire sags because posts are too far apart, adding posts between the existing ones helps. If the sag comes from failed corner braces, rusted wire, or rotten posts, new line posts won’t cure it. We’re glad to look at it and tell you which problem you have before you spend anything.

## Why Fence Posts Lean and How to Straighten Them for Good (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/leaning-fence-posts/)

> Fence posts leaning on your Central Texas place? Learn why clay soil and rot tip posts over, how to straighten them for good, and when to call Brazos Ridge.

Fence Repair

# Why Fence Posts Lean and How to Straighten Them for Good
Published July 24, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A post that leans 10 degrees in October will be lying in the grass by April. We've watched it happen on hundreds of places around Waco, and it almost never stops on its own.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A post that leans 10 degrees in October will be lying in the grass by April. We’ve watched it happen on hundreds of places around Waco, and it almost never stops on its own. Fence posts leaning is one of those problems that looks small from the truck window and turns expensive the longer you let it ride.

Here’s the part most folks miss. The lean is a symptom, not the disease. Something under the ground failed, and if you just push the post back up and stomp the dirt, it’ll be right back where it was after two good rains. Fixing it for good means figuring out why it moved, and that’s what this article walks you through.

If you’d rather skip the shovel work, call us at (254) 870-8898. We give free written estimates anywhere in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and we’ll tell you straight whether a post needs straightening, resetting, or replacing.

## Why fence posts start leaning in the first place

Every leaning post comes down to one of five causes. Sometimes two of them are working together.

Wire tension. A fence is a constant tug of war. Four or five strands of barbed wire pulling at 150 to 250 pounds each puts real load on every post, and corner posts carry the whole line. If a corner wasn’t braced right on day one, it starts tipping toward the pull within a few years. Our post on H-brace corners covers why a single fat post, no matter how deep, can’t hold a quarter mile of tight wire by itself.

Rot at the ground line. Wood posts don’t rot at the bottom. They rot in the top 6 inches of soil, where there’s enough moisture and enough oxygen for fungus to work. The post looks fine above ground and solid below, but that ring at ground level turns to punk. Wind or a cow leaning on the wire does the rest. If your post wiggles like a loose tooth, read our piece on fence post rot before you spend a dime straightening it.

Shallow setting. The old rule is a third of the post in the ground. A 6.5 foot line post needs about 2 feet of burial, and a corner post needs 3 to 3.5 feet. Plenty of fences around here were built with 18 inch holes because the digging got hard, and those posts never had a chance.

Livestock and wildlife. A 1,300 pound cow scratching on a post is a battering ram on a schedule. Feral hogs rooting along the fence line undermine posts from below. Horses crib on top rails and push posts sideways over time.

Soil movement. This one deserves its own section, because in Central Texas it’s the big one.

## Central Texas clay is the main reason for leaning fence posts

Most of McLennan and Falls counties sit on Blackland Prairie clay. That soil shrinks when it dries and swells when it soaks, and the movement is strong enough to crack house slabs, so a fence post doesn’t stand a chance. In a dry August the clay pulls away from the post and leaves a gap. The first big rain fills that gap with water, the clay swells, and the post gets squeezed and shoved, usually not in the direction you’d like.

Drought years are the worst. The 2022 and 2023 dry spells opened cracks in pastures around Lorena wide enough to drop a fence pliers into. Posts that had stood straight for 15 years leaned that winter, because the soil that held them simply wasn’t in the same place anymore. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension has good background on how these Vertisol clays behave if you want the science.

Kenny Braddock, who runs about 60 pairs outside Crawford, called us in March after a wet winter followed that kind of drought. Both corner assemblies on his south line had heaved and tipped, and 14 line posts between them were leaning past 15 degrees. The wire was still attached, which meant the whole quarter mile was slowly going slack. We rebuilt the two corners as proper H-braces set 3.5 feet deep, reset the 14 line posts, and re-tensioned five strands. The bill was $1,850. His neighbor had quoted him “just pushing them back up” for $400, and that fix would’ve lasted one season.

If your soil turns to concrete in summer and gumbo in winter, our article on setting fence posts in clay soil goes deeper on what actually holds in this ground.

## How to straighten a leaning fence post yourself

Some leaning posts are a fair DIY job. Here’s how we’d tell you to do it, in order.

Step 1: Find the cause first. Grab the post at chest height and push it back and forth. If it pivots at ground level and feels spongy, it’s rotted and straightening is wasted effort. If the whole post moves like it’s in loose sand, the soil failed and you can re-tamp. If it barely moves but leans toward the wire pull, your brace is the problem, not the post.

Step 2: Take the tension off. Never fight a post against tight wire. Un-staple the strands from the leaning post and the two posts on either side, or loosen your inline strainers a few clicks. This alone lets some posts come back near plumb.

Step 3: Excavate the high side. Dig a wedge of soil out of the side the post is leaning away from, down 12 to 18 inches. You’re making room for the post to swing back without compressing soil against it.

Step 4: Pull it plumb. A fence post level that straps onto the post is a $12 tool worth owning. For stubborn posts, a ratchet strap to the truck’s receiver hitch works, but go slow. Pull a rotted post too hard and it snaps at ground level, and now you’ve got a stub to dig out.

Step 5: Tamp in lifts. This is where most DIY fixes fail. Backfill 3 or 4 inches of soil at a time and tamp each lift hard with a digging bar before adding more. Dumping the whole pile in and stepping on it leaves air pockets that turn to mush in the first rain. Done right, tamped native soil holds a line post as well as concrete in most cases. In heavy clay, mixing in crushed limestone or road base gives water somewhere to go and cuts down on future heaving.

Step 6: Re-tension the wire. Bring the strands back up to tension evenly, working from the middle strand out. If the wire itself has gone slack and stretchy, it may need splicing and re-stretching too.

For steel t-posts, the fix is usually simpler. Straighten the post with a t-post jack or pull it entirely, then re-drive it a foot over in undisturbed soil. A bent t-post is a $6 part. Don’t spend an hour saving one.

Know when to stop. If the post is a corner or gate post, if it’s set in a failed concrete footing, or if more than a handful of posts in a row are leaning, put the shovel down. Those jobs involve serious wire tension and heavy pulling, and a snapped brace wire or a post that lets go under load can hurt you. That’s a call, not a project. Reach us anytime through our contact page and we’ll come look at it for free.

## When a leaning fence post can’t be saved

About a third of the leaning posts we look at aren’t worth straightening. Here’s how to tell.

Rot you can see or feel. Poke the post at ground level with a screwdriver. If it sinks in more than half an inch, the post is done. Replace it.

Concrete footing moving as one piece. If the post and its concrete plug rock together, the footing has broken loose from the soil. You’ll need to pull the whole plug, which usually means a tractor, and reset from scratch.

Corner and gate posts. These carry too much load to gamble on. A failed corner takes the whole line slack, and slack wire is how cattle end up on the county road. If that’s already happening on your place, check every corner before you blame the wire.

Rosa Delgado keeps 11 acres with goats and two horses off Highway 317 near Valley Mills. Her gate post had leaned far enough that the gate dragged and wouldn’t latch, and she’d been lifting it into place for a month. The post looked fine, but it was a cedar post set 20 inches deep in sand with no concrete and no brace. We replaced it with a 4 inch drill stem post set 4 feet deep in concrete and hung the gate fresh. Total was $685, and that gate will still swing true when her grandkids own the place. Pipe posts cost more up front, but for gates and corners they end the leaning problem permanently. That’s a big part of why pipe fencing has taken over on working ranches around here.

## What it costs to fix leaning fence posts

Here’s what folks around Waco are actually paying in 2026. These are typical ranges, and your written estimate may land differently based on access, soil, and how many posts we’re fixing in one trip.

Fix Typical cost per post When it makes sense

Straighten and re-tamp (DIY) $0 to $15 in materials Sound post, failed soil, line posts only

Straighten and re-tamp (pro) $35 to $75 Several posts at once, wire re-tensioned

And if the lean traces back to a fence that’s just plain worn out, sometimes repair money is better spent on new construction. ## How to keep posts from leaning again

Straightening a post is maintenance. Keeping it straight is design. A few habits make the difference.

Set posts deep enough the first time. A third of total length in the ground, minimum, and 3.5 to 4 feet for corners and gates. The USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service fencing standards that ag programs use call for braced corner assemblies on any stretched wire fence, and there’s a reason cost-share money won’t pay for a fence without them.

Build real H-braces at every corner, gate, and direction change, and add brace assemblies every quarter mile on long straight runs. Tension belongs on braces, not on line posts.

Walk your fence twice a year, spring and fall, and after every big storm. Catching a 5 degree lean costs you ten minutes with a tamping bar. Catching it at 30 degrees costs a Saturday or a service call. Keep the fence line clear of brush too, since roots and falling limbs start more leans than most people think.

And match the post to the soil. In our clay, that means road base or crushed rock in the backfill, or pipe posts at the pressure points. In sand, it means concrete and extra depth.

If you’ve got a line of leaning posts and you’d rather spend your weekend doing anything else, we’ll handle it. Call (254) 870-8898 or request a free written estimate at brazosridgefence.com. We’re licensed and insured, and our emergency line answers around the clock for storm damage and cattle-out situations.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Should I set a leaning fence post back in concrete?

Usually not for line posts. Well-tamped native soil, or soil mixed with crushed rock, holds a line post fine and drains better than concrete in our clay. Concrete earns its keep on gate posts, corner posts, and posts in loose sandy soil. If you do use concrete, crown it above grade so water sheds away instead of pooling around the post.

### How much lean is too much to ignore?

Anything past about 10 degrees, or any lean on a corner or gate post, needs attention now. A leaning corner is already letting your whole fence line go slack, and slack wire leads to escaped livestock. A slight lean on one line post in the middle of a run can wait for your next fence-walking day, but put it on the list.

### Why do my fence posts lean after every heavy rain?

That’s Central Texas clay doing what it does. The soil shrinks and cracks in dry weather, then swells hard when it soaks, and each cycle shoves posts a little further off plumb. Backfilling with road base or crushed limestone, setting posts deeper, and using pipe at high-load points all help. Shallow-set posts in straight clay will keep leaning no matter how many times you push them back.

### Can I just push a leaning post upright and pack the dirt?

You can, and it’ll look fixed for a few weeks. Without digging out the high side, tamping in shallow lifts, and dealing with whatever caused the lean, the post goes right back over with the next rain or the next cow that scratches on it. Ten extra minutes of doing it right saves redoing the job every season.

## Old Fence Removal Cost and What Tear-Out Actually Involves (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/fence-removal-cost/)

> Real fence removal cost per foot for barbed wire, net wire, and pipe fence in Central Texas, what tear-out actually involves, and when to call in a pro.

Cost Guide

# Old Fence Removal Cost and What Tear-Out Actually Involves
Published August 15, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

That rusted fence line you've been ignoring for ten years? Pulling it out will probably run you $1 to $5 per foot, and on a ranch that adds up faster than most folks expect.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

That rusted fence line you’ve been ignoring for ten years? Pulling it out will probably run you $1 to $5 per foot, and on a ranch that adds up faster than most folks expect. A half mile of old barbed wire tear-out can cost $3,000 or more before a single new post goes in the ground.

Here’s the thing most landowners around Waco don’t realize. Fence removal cost isn’t just about yanking wire off posts. It’s cutting fence loose from twenty years of embedded brush, pulling posts set in concrete or clay, rolling up wire that wants to slice your forearms open, and hauling everything to a place that’ll legally take it. Skip any of those steps and you’ve got a hidden hazard sitting in your pasture waiting to lame a horse or shred a tractor tire.

This guide breaks down what tear-out really costs in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, what the work actually involves, and where you can save money without creating a bigger problem.

## Fence Removal Cost Per Foot in Central Texas

Most fence removal around Waco gets priced per linear foot, and the number depends on what’s coming out of the ground. Here’s what we typically see on ranch and farm jobs in our area.

Fence Type Removal Cost Per Foot Cost Per 1,000 Feet Main Cost Driver

3 to 5 strand barbed wire, T-posts $1.00 to $2.00 $1,000 to $2,000 Wire condition, brush

Barbed wire, wood posts $1.50 to $2.75 $1,500 to $2,750 Post pulling, rot

Net wire (field fence) $1.75 to $3.00 $1,750 to $3,000 Wire weight, grass grown through

Chain link $2.00 to $3.50 $2,000 to $3,500 Concrete footings

Wood privacy or rail $2.50 to $4.50 $2,500 to $4,500 Haul-off volume

Pipe fence (cut and haul) $3.00 to $5.00 $3,000 to $5,000 Torch work, steel weight

A few things to keep in mind about those numbers. Most contractors, us included, charge a minimum trip fee of $300 to $500 for small jobs, so removing 100 feet of fence won’t cost you $150. And if you’re replacing the fence at the same time, tear-out usually gets rolled into the new build at a discount, often $0.50 to $1.50 per foot instead of standalone pricing.

That’s the single biggest money-saving move: bundle removal with replacement. If your old fence is coming down because a new barbed wire fence or pipe fence is going up, get one quote for the whole job.

Want a real number for your place instead of a range? Call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk the line with you and put it in writing. Estimates are free.

## What Tear-Out Actually Involves, Step by Step

Folks picture fence removal as pulling a few staples and rolling up wire. On a fence that’s been standing since the 80s, it’s a different animal. Here’s the real sequence.

1. Walk the line and flag problems. Before anything gets cut, you find the gates, the water gaps, the spots where the neighbor’s fence ties in, and any wire that’s disappeared into tree trunks. Trees grow around wire. Cutting it wrong can send tension snapping back at you.

2. Clear the brush. Most old fence lines in Central Texas are buried in mesquite, cedar, and greenbriar. You can’t safely remove wire you can’t see. On overgrown lines, brush clearing is often a third of the total bill.

3. De-tension and cut the wire. Old barbed wire holds tension even when it looks slack. Pros cut at the posts in sections, never in the middle of a long tight run.

4. Roll or spool the wire. Loose piles of barbed wire are how livestock get cut and tires get ruined. Wire gets rolled tight, tied off, and staged for haul-off.

5. Pull the posts. T-posts come out with a jack or a tractor loop. Wood posts set in clay or concrete are the fight. Rotten ones snap at ground level, and then you’re digging out the stub or grinding it below grade.

6. Sweep for debris. Staples, clips, broken wire ends, and post stubs get picked up. A good crew runs a magnet bar over high-traffic areas. This step is what separates a clean tear-out from a future vet bill.

7. Haul off and dispose. Wire, posts, and concrete go to a metal recycler or an approved disposal site. More on that below, because it’s where a lot of DIY jobs go sideways.

## What Drives Fence Removal Costs Up or Down

Two fences of the same length can cost wildly different amounts to remove. These are the factors that move the number.

Brush and access. A clean fence line a tractor can drive along is cheap. A line swallowed by ten years of mesquite, or one running through a creek bottom no machine can reach, can double or triple the price. If your line is overgrown, clearing it first changes everything, and we covered how in our guide to clearing a fence line of brush.

Post material and how they’re set. T-posts pull in seconds. Wood posts in concrete take real time. Pipe posts set deep in concrete usually get torched off at ground level because pulling the footing costs more than it’s worth.

Post condition. Ironically, badly rotted posts can cost more to remove than solid ones, because they break off instead of pulling clean. If your posts are crumbling at the ground line, that’s rot doing its work, and our post on fence post rot explains why it happens so fast in our soils.

Wire condition. Rusted, brittle wire snaps constantly during removal, which slows the rolling and multiplies the sharp ends on the ground. If you’re on the fence about whether your old wire is worth saving, read our breakdown on rusted barbed wire, repair or replace.

Terrain and soil. Rocky ground around Valley Mills and Crawford makes digging out stubs slow. Blackland clay near Lorena and West grips wood posts like concrete when it’s dry.

Haul-off distance and volume. Steel is heavy and treated wood can’t just go anywhere. Distance to the recycler or landfill is baked into every quote.

## Real Tear-Out Jobs From Around Waco

Numbers on a chart are one thing. Here’s what actual jobs look like.

Danny in West: 1,300 feet of net wire, $2,340. Danny bought 12 acres off Tokio Road with an old field fence that grass and johnsongrass had grown clean through. Pipe tear-out is never cheap, but the steel at least pays you back a little.

If any of those sound like your place, request a free written estimate and we’ll give you both numbers: removal alone, and removal bundled with a new fence.

## Disposal, Haul-Off, and What You Can’t Just Dump

This is the part of fence removal cost that surprises people most. Getting the fence out of the ground is half the job. Getting it off your property legally and safely is the other half.

Steel wire and T-posts go to a metal recycler. Waco has several scrap yards that take fencing steel, and on big pipe jobs the scrap value offsets some of your haul-off cost. Don’t expect to get rich. Rusty barbed wire fetches shredder-grade prices, but it beats paying to landfill it.

Treated wood posts are the tricky one. Most treated posts from older fences contain preservatives like creosote or CCA, and they should never be burned. Burning treated wood releases toxic compounds, and it’s prohibited under Texas outdoor burning rules. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality spells out what you can and can’t burn on your own land at tceq.texas.gov, and treated lumber is firmly on the can’t list. Treated posts go to the landfill.

Concrete footings can go to a construction and demolition landfill, or honestly, a lot of ranchers keep them for filling washouts and erosion cuts. Free riprap.

Old wire left in piles is the worst outcome. Buried or piled wire injures livestock, wrecks hay equipment, and tangles shredders for decades. If a previous owner left wire piles on your place, budget to clean them up. It’s cheaper than one colic surgery or a new baler pickup.

## Should You Tear Out a Fence Yourself?

Plenty of ranchers pull their own fence, and for the right fence it makes sense. A quarter mile of loose 3-strand on T-posts across open pasture? If you’ve got a tractor, a T-post jack, gloves, eye protection, and a free Saturday, have at it. You’ll save $500 to $1,000.

But know where the line is. Call a professional when:

- The wire is under tension you can’t read, especially high-tensile or wire grown into trees

- Posts are set in concrete or the line runs through rock

- The line is heavily overgrown and you’d be cutting wire blind inside brush

- There’s a slope, creek crossing, or water gap involved

- It’s a boundary fence shared with a neighbor, where cutting the wrong wire creates a legal mess and loose cattle

- You’re removing pipe fence, because torch work and multi-ton steel handling aren’t weekend jobs

Old wire under tension can whip back with enough force to take an eye. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid guidance on fence construction and wire handling at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu, and their consistent message applies to tear-out too: respect the stored energy in stretched wire.

There’s also a middle path. Some of our customers clear the brush and pull the T-posts themselves, then hire us for the tensioned wire, the concrete-set corners, and the haul-off. That hybrid approach usually trims 30 to 40 percent off the removal bill.

One more reason to get a pro’s eyes on it before you start: sometimes the fence doesn’t need to come out at all. Solid posts with tired wire can often be re-wired for far less than full replacement. And if you are replacing, knowing your rebuild number first matters, because tear-out pricing changes when it’s bundled. Our barbed wire fence cost guide covers what new fence runs per foot so you can see the whole picture.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does it cost to remove 1,000 feet of barbed wire fence?

Plan on $1,000 to $2,750 for a standalone job, depending on post type, brush, and terrain. T-posts on clear ground land at the low end, wood posts in brushy or rocky country at the high end. If you’re rebuilding the same line, bundled tear-out often drops to $500 to $1,500.

### Is old barbed wire worth anything as scrap?

A little, but not much. Rusty barbed wire sells as shredder-grade scrap, often just a few cents per pound, and a thousand feet of 5-strand only weighs a few hundred pounds. Pipe fence is the exception, since heavy steel pipe can return $100 or more per ton and meaningfully offset haul-off costs.

### Can I burn old treated fence posts on my property?

No. Treated posts contain preservatives like creosote or CCA that release toxic smoke and ash when burned, and Texas outdoor burning rules prohibit burning treated wood. Haul them to a landfill that accepts treated lumber. Untreated cedar posts can usually go in a legal burn pile, but check current TCEQ rules and county burn bans first.

### Does fence removal cost less if I’m installing a new fence?

Almost always, yes. The crew and equipment are already on site, so most contractors fold tear-out into the new build at $0.50 to $1.50 per foot instead of $1 to $5 standalone. Always ask for the quote both ways so you can see exactly what the removal portion costs you.

## Feral Hog Fence Damage: How to Stop Hogs Tearing Up Your Fence (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/feral-hog-fence-damage/)

> Feral hogs tearing up your fence? Learn why hogs wreck ranch fencing in Central Texas, which repairs actually hold, and what hog-proof fencing costs per foot.

Fence Repair

# Feral Hog Fence Damage: How to Stop Hogs Tearing Up Your Fence
Published August 16, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A sounder of feral hogs can undo a quarter mile of fence in one night. Not over a season. One night. If you ranch anywhere in McLennan, Bosque, or Falls County, you already know the drill.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A sounder of feral hogs can undo a quarter mile of fence in one night. Not over a season. One night.

If you ranch anywhere in McLennan, Bosque, or Falls County, you already know the drill. You walk your line on a Saturday morning and find net wire peeled up like a sardine can, a tunnel dug under the bottom strand, and hog tracks headed straight for your coastal field. Feral hog fence damage is one of the most common repair calls we run at Brazos Ridge Fence, and it’s getting worse every year. Texas holds somewhere north of 2.5 million wild pigs, and the Brazos and Bosque river bottoms are prime habitat.

The good news: hogs are predictable. Once you understand how they attack a fence, you can build one they’ll quit testing. This article covers why hogs beat most fences, what the damage really costs, the quick fixes that buy you time, and the fencing that actually holds.

## Why hogs go through your fence instead of around it

A mature boar can weigh 250 pounds or more, and he carries most of that weight low, right at the height of your bottom wire. Hogs don’t jump. They root, they push, and they shove their snouts under the lowest point they can find and lift.

That’s why a fence that holds cattle just fine does almost nothing against pigs. Cattle push at chest height, where your wire is tight and your posts are strongest. Hogs attack the bottom 12 inches, where most fences are weakest.

Three spots fail first on almost every place we look at:

- Water gaps and creek crossings, where flood debris has already loosened the wire

- Low spots and washes, where the bottom strand sits 6 or 8 inches off the dirt

- Old net wire with rusted bottom stays, which tears the moment a hog gets his nose in it

Hogs also follow routine. They travel the same trails between bedding cover and food, night after night. Once a sounder learns your fence has a hole, they’ll use that hole until you close it, and then they’ll test the fence 20 feet on either side of the patch. Texas Parks and Wildlife has a good rundown of feral hog behavior and legal control options on their nuisance wildlife page if you want the biology behind it.

If you’re finding fresh rooting along your line right now and stock is getting out, don’t wait on it. Call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll get eyes on the damage, usually within a day or two. Estimates are free and written.

## What feral hog fence damage looks like, and what it costs you

The fence repair is usually the cheap part. It’s everything that follows the hole that hurts.

Dale Kunkel runs about 60 cow-calf pairs on 300 acres outside Crawford, with a half mile of fence along a Middle Bosque creek bottom. Hogs tunneled under his net wire at a water gap in March. Before he found the breach, his cows had pushed through the widened hole and scattered across a county road. He spent $1,850 with us rebuilding 400 feet of bottom wire and the water gap, but he figures the real cost was closer to $4,000 once he counted a vet bill for a cut-up heifer and two lost days rounding up cattle. Loose cattle on a road are also a liability problem, which we’ve covered before in our post on cattle getting out of the fence.

Out in China Spring, Marisol Vega leases 80 acres for coastal hay. A sounder of about 15 hogs rooted up close to 4 acres of her best field in two weeks, coming in through a gap they’d opened under a sagging corner. Her hay loss alone ran about $3,200 at last summer’s bale prices, on top of $900 to disk and re-sprig the rooted ground. The fence fix that would have kept them out cost less than either number.

USDA puts feral swine damage nationwide at over $2.5 billion a year in agricultural losses, and their feral swine damage program exists because the problem keeps growing. Here in Central Texas, the pattern we see on repair calls is consistent: the landowner patches the hole, the hogs open a new one, and the patching bill quietly passes what a proper hog-resistant stretch of fence would have cost in the first place.

## Quick fixes that slow hog damage to your fence

You can’t hog-proof a whole ranch overnight, and you don’t need to. Most places only get hit along one or two stretches, usually the side facing water or heavy brush. Here’s what buys you time on those stretches.

Drop a barbed strand at ground level. If you’re running 5-strand barbed wire, adding one tight strand at 2 to 3 inches off the dirt makes rooting under a lot less comfortable. It won’t stop a determined boar, but it turns away casual pressure. While you’re at it, fix any slack in the existing strands, because loose wire is an open invitation. Our guide on fixing sagging barbed wire walks through re-tensioning step by step.

Stake down your low spots. Anywhere the bottom wire sits more than 4 inches off the ground, drive a t-post or rebar stake and tie the wire down to it. Cheap, fast, effective.

Add a hot wire at snout height. A single electric offset wire at 8 to 10 inches, run off a good low-impedance charger, is the best dollar-for-dollar hog deterrent there is. Hogs test with their nose, and their nose is wet. One solid hit and most of them remember. Keep it clear of grass, or it’ll short out and train them the wrong way.

Rebuild your water gaps first. Nine times out of ten, the hogs’ front door is a water gap. A properly built swinging water gap closes the hole after every rise instead of leaving it open. We wrote up how these work in our water gap fence guide.

One honest warning. Patching torn net wire by lacing in scrap pieces is fine for a week, not for a year. Every splice is a weak point, and hogs find weak points for a living. If a stretch has more patches than original wire, it’s past saving.

## Fencing that actually stops feral hogs

When you’re ready to stop patching, here’s what holds pigs, roughly in order of how often we build it.

Fixed knot net wire, hog height. This is our workhorse hog fence. A 48-inch fixed knot fence with a barbed strand at ground level and posts on 8-foot spacing will turn nearly all hog traffic. Fixed knot matters because the knot won’t slip when a hog pushes into it, unlike the hinge joint field fence on most older places. We broke down the difference in fixed knot vs hinge joint, and it’s the single biggest upgrade you can make.

Net wire plus hot offset. Same fence, plus an electric wire at snout height on the pasture side or the outside, depending on where the pressure comes from. This combination is what we recommend along river bottoms where hog pressure never really stops.

Hog panels for small, high-value areas. Around pens, gardens, feed storage, and trap sites, 34-inch heavy galvanized hog panels clipped to t-posts are nearly bulletproof. Too expensive per foot for long runs, perfect for the 200 feet that matter most.

Game fence. If you’re already considering high fence for deer management, a properly built game fence with an apron or buried bottom edge handles hogs as part of the deal. See our game fence installation page for how we build those.

Whatever wire you pick, the bottom of the fence decides whether it works. Tight bottom wire, short post spacing on hog trails, and solid H-braces at the corners. A hog fence with a floppy bottom is just a regular fence that cost more.

## What hog-resistant fencing costs in Central Texas

Here’s what we’re quoting in the Waco area as of mid-2026. These are installed prices for typical terrain, and your ground, brush, and old fence removal can move them.

Fence type Installed cost per foot Stops hogs? Best use

5-strand barbed wire $2.50 to $4.00 No, slows them at best Cattle on low hog pressure land

Barbed wire + ground strand + hot wire $3.50 to $5.50 Moderate Upgrading existing barbed lines

Hinge joint net wire $3.00 to $5.00 Poorly, tears under pressure Sheep and goats, light pressure

48” fixed knot + barbed ground strand $4.50 to $6.50 Yes, best all-around Perimeters, creek bottoms

Fixed knot + electric offset $5.25 to $7.50 Yes, highest deterrence Heavy pressure river bottoms

Heavy hog panels on t-posts $7.00 to $9.00 Yes Pens, gardens, short runs

For a quick gut check on a bigger project, a half mile of fixed knot hog fence lands somewhere around $12,000 to $17,000 installed. That sounds like real money until you stack it against a few years of rooted hay fields, patch labor, and cattle on the highway. If you want exact numbers for your place, our barbed wire fence page covers strand options and pricing, and you can request a free written estimate with your acreage and we’ll walk the line with you.

## When to stop patching and call a pro

Plenty of hog fixes are honest DIY work. Staking down low spots, tightening strands, and running a hot wire are all Saturday jobs if you’re handy.

Call in help when you hit any of these:

- The damage runs longer than about 100 feet, or keeps reopening in the same stretch

- Water gaps are involved, since a bad water gap rebuild washes out on the first rise and takes your fence with it

- Corners and H-braces are leaning, because re-tensioning wire on a failing brace makes the lean worse

- You’re splicing old rusted net wire, which usually snaps somewhere new every time you pull tension

- Livestock are actively getting out, and every night the hole stays open costs you more

There’s also a safety piece. Feral hogs can be aggressive, especially sows with piglets, and stretching wire alone in thick river bottom brush where hogs are bedded is a good way to have a bad afternoon. Wear gloves, watch your footing, and don’t work a heavy hog trail alone at dusk.

Marcus Teel, who runs goats on 40 acres near Valley Mills, patched the same creek-side stretch of hinge joint fence six times in one year. He kept receipts: about $640 in wire, clips, and posts, plus most of a weekend each time, and the hogs still opened it back up before Thanksgiving. We rebuilt that 500-foot stretch in fixed knot with a hot offset for $2,900 last December. As of July, it hasn’t been breached once.

If you’re at that point, we’d rather look at it now than after the next breach. Brazos Ridge Fence is licensed and insured, we serve Waco and all of McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and we keep a 24/7 emergency line for cattle-out situations. Call (254) 870-8898 any time, or send us the details and we’ll get you a free written estimate.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Will an electric fence alone stop feral hogs?

A hot wire at snout height turns away most hogs, and it’s the cheapest effective deterrent per foot. But electricity alone has failure modes: grass shorts, charger problems, and storm outages, and hogs test constantly. We recommend hot wire as an addition to a physical hog fence, not a replacement for one, especially along river bottoms with steady pressure.

### How tall does a hog fence need to be?

Height isn’t the issue, the bottom is. Feral hogs rarely jump anything over about 30 inches, so a standard 48-inch net wire fence is plenty tall. What matters is a tight bottom wire within 2 to 3 inches of the ground, fixed knot construction that won’t slip, and staked-down low spots so nothing can root underneath.

### Can I shoot or trap the hogs instead of upgrading my fence?

You can, and in Texas no hunting license is needed to take feral hogs on private land with landowner permission. The catch is that trapping and shooting knock the population back but never to zero, and new sounders move in from the river bottoms within months. Most landowners we work with do both: control the hogs they can, and build fence that handles the ones they can’t.

### How fast can hogs damage a fence?

Fast. A sounder of 10 to 20 hogs can open multiple holes in a single night and root up an acre of pasture in a few days. That’s why we tell folks to walk their creek-side fence lines weekly during spring and fall, when hog movement peaks, and to close any breach within a day or two before the whole sounder learns the route.

## Fixed Knot vs Hinge Joint Fence: Which Net Wire Lasts Longer? (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/fixed-knot-vs-hinge-joint/)

> Comparing fixed knot vs hinge joint fence for your Central Texas ranch? See real costs per foot, lifespan numbers, and which net wire survives cattle and hogs.

Materials

# Fixed Knot vs Hinge Joint Fence: Which Net Wire Lasts Longer?
Published August 18, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Two net wire fences can look identical from the county road, yet one will still be standing tight in 30 years while the other sags out in 12.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Two net wire fences can look identical from the county road, yet one will still be standing tight in 30 years while the other sags out in 12. The difference usually comes down to one small detail you can pinch between two fingers: the knot.

If you’re weighing a fixed knot vs hinge joint fence for your place, the choice matters more here in Central Texas than almost anywhere else. We’ve got cattle that lean, feral hogs that plow, deer that jump, and summer heat that makes wire expand and go slack. Around Waco, McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, we build both types every month, and we’ve torn out plenty of both too. Here’s the honest breakdown, with real numbers.

## What Actually Separates Fixed Knot From Hinge Joint Wire

Both are net wire, sometimes called woven wire or field fence. Both come in rolls, both use vertical stay wires crossing horizontal line wires, and both will turn a cow that’s not motivated. The difference is how those wires connect.

Hinge joint wire wraps each vertical stay around the horizontal wire in a loose loop, like a door hinge. That loop lets the fence flex, which sounds good until you understand what flexing means over 20 years. Every time a calf pushes through it, a hog roots under it, or a buck hits it at speed, that hinge folds. It doesn’t spring back. It stays folded, and the fence slowly develops that swaybacked look you see on old field fence all over Bosque County.

Fixed knot wire uses a separate piece of wire wrapped tight around the joint, locking the vertical and horizontal wires in place. Nothing pivots. When something hits it, the whole panel absorbs the load and the high tensile wire springs back to shape. Fixed knot is almost always built from high tensile wire in the 12.5 gauge range with heavy galvanizing, while most hinge joint rolls are softer low carbon wire.

That knot is why a fixed knot fence can run 15 to 20 feet between posts while hinge joint really wants a post every 8 to 12 feet. Fewer posts per mile is real money, and we’ll get to those numbers below.

One more piece matters as much as the knot: the coating. Look for Class 3 galvanized wire on either style. The short version on coatings: Class 3 carries roughly triple the zinc of Class 1 and can double the rust-free life of the wire. The Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension Service covers wire selection and fence planning for Texas operations if you want the research side of it.

Not sure what’s on your fence line now? Call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk your place, identify what you’ve got, and give you a free written estimate on what it’d take to fix or replace it.

## Where Hinge Joint Fence Still Makes Sense

We’re not here to trash hinge joint wire. It’s been holding livestock in Texas for a hundred years, and for some jobs it’s the right call.

Hinge joint shines when the budget is tight and the pressure is low. A small trap for gentle cows, a boundary line behind a hay field nobody pushes on, a temporary division fence you plan to move in ten years. In those spots, spending extra on fixed knot is money you won’t get back.

It’s also more forgiving to install for a DIY crew. Low carbon wire stretches and ties easier than high tensile, and it doesn’t punish sloppy bracing quite as fast. If you’re fencing a few acres yourself, hinge joint with wood posts on 10-foot centers will do the job. Just build your corners right, because net wire of any kind pulls hard on the ends, and a weak H-brace will let either wire type go slack.

Where hinge joint falls apart, literally, is under animal pressure. Goats climb it and fold the hinges down. Horses paw it. Bulls fight across it. And feral hogs treat it like a screen door. Once hogs find a soft spot in hinge joint wire, they’ll open a hole in one night that your calves find by morning. We covered what that costs ranchers in our feral hog fence damage post, and it’s not pretty.

## A Tale of Two Fences in Crawford and Valley Mills

Last spring we got a call from Dale, who runs about 120 cows on leased ground outside Crawford. His hinge joint perimeter fence was 14 years old and he’d spent, by his own math, around $3,800 over three years patching hog holes and splicing folded sections. Then a section gave out along FM 185 and two heifers ended up on the road. No wreck, thank God, but that was the last straw. We replaced 2,600 feet of his worst line with fixed knot on t-posts and wood line posts for about $11,700. His words at the walkthrough: “Should’ve done this the first time.”

Contrast that with Marcy in Valley Mills, who bought 25 acres in 2024 to run Boer goats. Her land came with decent hinge joint cross fences, and she asked if she had to rip it all out. We told her no. We built her 1,900 feet of new fixed knot goat fence, using a tighter 4-inch mesh at the bottom, on the two sides where her goats and the neighbor’s dogs met, for right at $9,300. The old hinge joint stayed on the quiet sides. She spent money where the pressure was and saved roughly $8,000 by not fencing all four sides in fixed knot. If you’re running goats, our fence for goats and sheep guide digs into mesh sizes and predator issues.

That’s the honest answer on fixed knot vs hinge joint fence: it’s not one or the other for your whole place. It’s matching the wire to the pressure on each line.

## Fixed Knot vs Hinge Joint Fence: Cost and Lifespan Numbers

Here’s what these fences actually run in the Waco area in 2026, installed with good bracing on typical ground. Rocky ground, heavy brush clearing, and long material hauls move these numbers up.

Factor Hinge Joint Fixed Knot

Wire type Low carbon, 12.5 to 14 gauge High tensile, 12.5 gauge typical

Materials only, per foot $0.90 to $1.60 $1.40 to $2.40

Installed, per foot $2.50 to $4.50 $3.50 to $6.00

Post spacing 8 to 12 ft 15 to 20 ft

Typical lifespan here 10 to 20 years 25 to 40 years

Hog and predator resistance Poor to fair Good to excellent

Best use Low-pressure lines, tight budgets Perimeters, goats, hogs, game fence

Read that lifespan row twice. A hinge joint fence at $3.50 a foot that lasts 15 years costs you about 23 cents per foot per year. A fixed knot fence at $4.75 a foot that lasts 32 years costs about 15 cents per foot per year. The cheaper fence is the expensive one, as long as you’re planning to own the land past the first fence’s funeral.

The post spacing line is where fixed knot claws back its higher wire price. On a mile of fence, going from 10-foot to 16-foot spacing cuts out roughly 200 posts. At $8 to $15 per t-post or line post installed, that’s $1,600 to $3,000 saved per mile before you’ve hung any wire.

Every place prices out a little different, which is why we do free written estimates instead of guessing over the phone. Request yours here and we’ll put real numbers on your actual fence lines, usually within a week.

## Which Net Fence Lasts Longer on Central Texas Ground?

On lifespan alone, fixed knot wins and it isn’t close. But it’s worth understanding why, because our conditions do the damage.

First, heat cycling. Wire out here might see 25 degrees in January and 140 degrees of surface temperature in August. Low carbon hinge joint wire stretches with each cycle and doesn’t recover, so it goes slack, and slack wire is what livestock learn to push through. High tensile fixed knot wire holds tension through those swings. You’ll retension a hinge joint fence every couple of years if you want it tight. A well-built fixed knot fence mostly gets left alone.

Second, our clay soils move. Blackland clay swells when it rains and shrinks hard in drought, which heaves posts and changes wire tension along the whole run. A fence that tolerates fewer, better-set posts and holds its own tension handles that movement better. Ask anybody who fenced through the dry years what August did to their old field fence.

Third, animal pressure never stops. Hogs are in every county we serve. Whitetail numbers keep climbing. If your fence sees deer traffic, fixed knot is also what taller game fence is built from. We install a lot of it, and you can see what that involves on our game fence installation page.

One caveat: fixed knot only outlasts hinge joint when the bracing is right. High tensile wire pulls 150 to 250 pounds of tension per strand, and a weak corner will lean over in a season. Corner and end construction is the whole ballgame. The USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service publishes fence standards that spec brace assemblies for exactly this reason, and their drawings look a lot like what we weld and set every week.

## How to Pick for Your Place

Here’s the decision process we walk through with customers from West down to Lorena.

Start with what’s pushing on the fence. Gentle cows on improved pasture, hinge joint can work. Goats, sheep, horses, hogs, deer pressure, or a road frontage where an escape becomes a liability problem, go fixed knot. If it’s a boundary along a highway, that’s not the place to save a dollar a foot.

Then look at your timeline. Selling in five years? The cheaper fence might pencil out, though good perimeter fence does show up in land value. Holding the place for your kids? Fixed knot with Class 3 galvanizing is the last net fence that line will need in your lifetime.

Then be honest about maintenance. Hinge joint isn’t a build-it-and-forget-it fence. It needs walking, splicing, and retensioning, and every hog hole needs patching the week it appears or your stock finds it. If you’d rather check your fence twice a year than twice a month, that’s an argument for fixed knot.

And if net wire isn’t the clear answer at all, it might be that plain barbed wire fits your cattle operation better and cheaper. We compared the two head to head in barbed wire vs net wire, and our barbed wire fence page covers what those builds cost.

A word on DIY: stretching high tensile fixed knot wire is a different animal than rolling out field fence. The wire stores serious energy under tension, and a slipped stretcher bar or a snapped strand can hurt you badly. Pulling a few hundred feet of hinge joint with a truck and a stretcher is a reasonable weekend job. Building fixed knot corners and tensioning a quarter mile of 949 wire is where we’d tell most landowners to stop and call a professional crew with the right stretching equipment.

One last gut check, from a job in China Spring: a landowner named Pete priced his own materials for 1,200 feet of fixed knot, figured $2,100 in wire and posts, and started building. Two pulled-over corners and one trip to urgent care for a wire whip across the forearm later, he called us. We rebuilt the corners, restretched the wire, and finished the run for $4,400 on top of what he’d already spent. He’d have been at roughly $5,900 total if we’d built it from scratch. DIY can save money, but only if the corners and the stretch are done right the first time.

Whatever direction you’re leaning, we’ll give you a straight answer and a written number. Call (254) 870-8898 or request a free estimate. We’re licensed and insured, and if a storm or a cow wreck takes a fence down tonight, our emergency line answers 24/7.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is fixed knot fence worth the extra cost over hinge joint?

For perimeter fence, high-pressure lines, and anything holding goats or facing hog traffic, yes. Fixed knot costs roughly $1 to $1.50 more per installed foot but lasts 10 to 20 years longer and needs wider post spacing, which claws back much of the price difference. On low-pressure interior cross fences, hinge joint can still be the smarter spend.

### How long does a hinge joint fence last in Central Texas?

Plan on 10 to 20 years depending on wire coating, animal pressure, and maintenance. Class 1 galvanized hinge joint under heavy cattle and hog pressure can be sagging badly inside 10 years, while Class 3 wire on a quiet line can push past 20. Heat cycling and our shrink-swell clay soils shorten the low end compared to milder climates.

### Can I use t-posts with fixed knot wire?

Yes, and most of our fixed knot builds mix t-posts with wood or pipe line posts. The critical parts are the corners and ends, which must be braced heavily enough to hold high tensile wire at full tension for decades. T-posts between strong braces work fine at 15 to 20 foot spacing on typical ground.

### What mesh size do I need for goats or exotics?

For goats and sheep, we usually run fixed knot with smaller openings low on the fence, often a 4-inch stay spacing, so kids can’t slip through and predators can’t push in. For whitetail and exotics, fixed knot game fence runs 7.5 to 8 feet tall with graduated mesh. The right spec depends on your animals, so have a contractor look at your operation before ordering wire.

## High Game Fence Cost: Per Foot, Per Acre, and Per Mile (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/game-fence-cost/)

> High game fence cost runs $4.50 to $10 per foot in Central Texas. See real per-acre and per-mile numbers, what drives prices up, and how to budget your ranch.

Cost Guide

# High Game Fence Cost: Per Foot, Per Acre, and Per Mile
Published July 24, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A mile of 8 foot game fence will run you somewhere between $24,000 and $42,000 in Central Texas right now.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A mile of 8 foot game fence will run you somewhere between $24,000 and $42,000 in Central Texas right now. That number stops a lot of landowners cold, and it should, because high fence is the most expensive wire fence you can put on a ranch.

But here’s the thing. Game fence cost only looks scary until you break it down per foot, per acre, and per mile, and then compare it against what you’re protecting. A managed whitetail herd, a handful of axis deer, or just keeping the neighbor’s hogs and dogs off your place can justify the spend fast. We build high fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and in this guide we’ll give you the same numbers we quote from the tailgate of the truck.

## Game Fence Cost Per Foot: What You’ll Actually Pay

In the Waco area, installed game fence cost runs $4.50 to $10 per linear foot for a standard 8 foot fence. That price includes materials, labor, and normal corner bracing on ground that a skid steer or tractor can work.

Here’s how that per foot number breaks apart:

- Materials usually run $2.50 to $4.00 per foot. That covers 96 inch fixed knot wire, line posts, corner and brace posts, clips, and staples.

- Labor and equipment run $2.00 to $6.00 per foot depending on terrain, brush, and how far your place is from town.

Cheap quotes exist. If somebody offers you high fence at $3.00 per foot installed, ask hard questions. That price usually means hinge joint wire instead of fixed knot, light gauge wire, posts set too shallow, or corners without proper bracing. On a fence that’s supposed to hold deer for 25 years, those shortcuts show up in year three.

If you want a real number for your specific place, not an internet range, we’ll walk your fence line and put it in writing for free. Call us at (254) 870-8898 or request a free written estimate. Our game fence installation crew in Waco builds high fence year round, so we quote from current material prices, not last year’s.

## Game Fence Prices Per Acre and Per Mile

Per acre pricing confuses people because fence cost follows the perimeter, not the acreage. A square 40 acre tract has exactly one mile of perimeter, 5,280 feet. Double the acreage and the perimeter only grows by about 40 percent. That’s why big places are cheaper per acre to fence than small ones.

Here’s what full perimeter high fence looks like at $4.50 to $10 per foot, assuming a roughly square tract:

Acreage Perimeter (ft) Total Cost Range Cost Per Acre

10 acres 2,640 $11,900 to $26,400 $1,190 to $2,640

20 acres 3,735 $16,800 to $37,400 $840 to $1,870

40 acres 5,280 $23,800 to $52,800 $595 to $1,320

100 acres 8,350 $37,600 to $83,500 $376 to $835

640 acres 21,120 $95,000 to $211,000 $148 to $330

Per mile, that same math lands at $23,800 to $52,800 for a mile of finished 8 foot fence. Most of the jobs we build around Waco settle in the $28,000 to $40,000 per mile range once you account for gates, a water gap or two, and normal brush clearing.

Long, skinny tracts cost more per acre than square ones because they carry more perimeter for the same ground. River frontage adds cost too, since every draw and creek crossing needs a water gap built to survive a flood.

## What Drives High Game Fence Cost Up or Down

Two ranches a mile apart can get quotes $2.00 per foot different, and both quotes can be honest. These are the factors that move the number.

Terrain and soil. Flat pasture with deep soil is the cheap end. Rock changes everything. When we hit limestone shelf in western McLennan or Bosque County, we’re drilling or driving pilot holes for every post, and that can add $1.00 to $2.00 per foot. Steep grades and creek crossings slow the crew down the same way.

Brush clearing. A clean fence line is a quoted-price fence line. If we have to dozer a 12 to 15 foot lane through cedar and mesquite first, expect $1.50 to $4.00 per foot extra depending on how thick it is.

Fence height and wire. Standard game fence is 8 feet. Some exotic operations go taller or add offset wires. A 20 inch apron of wire pinned at ground level to stop hogs from rooting under adds material and labor, but if you’ve seen what a sounder can do to a fence line, it’s cheap insurance. We wrote about that damage in our post on feral hog fence damage.

Gates and entrances. Every ranch needs at least one 16 foot gate tall enough to match the fence, and most owners want a main entrance that looks like something. Gates run from $850 for a basic tall gate installed to $8,000 and up for a fabricated pipe entrance.

Old fence removal. Tearing out an existing barbed wire fence, rolling the wire, and pulling posts adds $1.00 to $2.50 per foot before the first new post goes in.

Distance and access. A place 45 minutes from the nearest material yard, with one narrow gate for equipment access, costs more than a place on a farm-to-market road. Fuel and drive time are real line items.

## Where the Money Goes: Wire, Posts, and Gates

Knowing where each dollar lands helps you compare quotes like a pro instead of just looking at the bottom line.

Wire is the biggest single item. Quality 96 inch fixed knot wire in Class 3 galvanized runs roughly $350 to $500 per 330 foot roll. Fixed knot holds its shape when a 200 pound buck hits it at speed, and it lets you stretch longer runs between posts. Hinge joint wire is cheaper up front but sags and gaps over time on a tall fence. If you’re weighing the two, read our breakdown of fixed knot vs hinge joint wire before you sign anything.

Posts are second. Most high fence around here uses 4 inch pipe or heavy CCA treated wood posts on corners and pull points, with steel t-posts or smaller pipe on the line. Line posts on game fence typically run 15 to 20 feet apart. Corners take the real load. An 8 foot fence stretched tight puts serious pull on every corner, so braces get built heavier and set deeper than on a 4 strand barbed wire fence.

Gates and entrances finish it out. Budget them early, not as an afterthought. A tall game gate that sags in two years defeats the whole fence. If you want the front of the ranch to match the investment behind it, look at our ranch entrance gates in Waco page for what fabricated pipe entrances cost.

## How to Budget for a Game Fence Without Getting Burned

A few habits will save you real money on a high fence project.

Get the quote itemized. Wire brand and gauge, post size and spacing, corner brace design, gate count, clearing, and removal should each show up as their own line. If a contractor won’t itemize, that tells you something.

Phase the job if you need to. Plenty of owners fence the front half one year and the back half the next. A good contractor will design the phases so nothing gets rebuilt later.

Check the legal side before you build. Texas doesn’t require a permit to high fence your own property, but deer breeding and some exotic operations bring Texas Parks and Wildlife rules into play. Start with the TPWD private lands page at tpwd.texas.gov, and read our plain-English summary of Texas high fence rules. Fencing can also matter for your ag valuation, and the Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension folks publish good material on wildlife management use.

Know when DIY stops making sense. Stretching a few hundred feet of net wire on flat ground is a fair weekend project. An 8 foot fence is different. The wire is heavy, the stretch loads are big, and a corner brace that fails under tension can hurt somebody. If your project involves rock, creek crossings, long pulls, or any fence you expect to hold expensive animals, bring in a crew that builds high fence for a living. The redo costs more than doing it right once.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does game fence cost per foot in Texas?

Installed 8 foot game fence runs $4.50 to $10 per linear foot in Central Texas in 2026. Easy ground with a clear fence line lands near the bottom of that range. Rock, heavy brush, creek crossings, and old fence removal push jobs toward the top.

### How much does it cost to high fence 100 acres?

A roughly square 100 acre tract carries about 8,350 feet of perimeter, so full high fence runs $37,600 to $83,500 installed. Most jobs that size land in the middle once you add gates and a water gap or two. Long, narrow tracts cost more because they carry more fence per acre.

### Is a high fence worth the money?

It depends on what you’re protecting. If you’re managing whitetail genetics, running exotics, or losing real money to hogs and trespassing cattle, the fence usually pays for itself over its 25 to 30 year life. If you just need to turn cows, a 5 strand barbed wire fence at a fraction of the price is the better buy.

### How tall does a game fence need to be for deer?

Eight feet is the standard for whitetail, and it’s what nearly every high fence in Texas uses. A healthy deer can clear 7 feet from a standstill, so shorter fences leak. Some exotics like nilgai or red stag justify going taller or adding offset wires, which raises the cost per foot.

## H Brace Fence Basics: Why Fence Corners Fail Without Them (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/h-brace-fence-corners/)

> Learn why fence corners fail without a proper H brace, what a good h brace fence costs in Central Texas, and when to call a pro. Waco ranch fencing advice.

Ranch Fencing

# H Brace Fence Basics: Why Fence Corners Fail Without Them
Published August 19, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Here's a number that surprises most landowners: a single strand of barbed wire stretched tight to fence tension pulls on your corner post with around 200 to 250 pounds of force.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Here’s a number that surprises most landowners: a single strand of barbed wire stretched tight to fence tension pulls on your corner post with around 200 to 250 pounds of force. Run five strands and you’re asking one post to hold back more than half a ton, all day, every day, in Central Texas clay that swells when it rains and shrinks hard when it doesn’t.

That’s why the h brace fence corner exists. It’s not decoration and it’s not overkill. It’s the anchor that makes the whole fence work. When we get called out to fix a sagging fence in McLennan, Bosque, or Falls County, we can usually tell you what went wrong before we’re out of the truck. Nine times out of ten, the corner wasn’t braced right, or wasn’t braced at all.

This article walks through what an H brace actually does, why corners fail without one, how a proper brace goes together, and what it costs to do it right around Waco.

## What an H Brace Fence Corner Actually Does

Picture your corner post as a lever stuck in the ground. The wire pulls on it near the top, and the dirt holds it near the bottom. Wire tension never sleeps, but soil does. Every wet spring softens the ground, every August drought cracks it open, and the post loses a little grip each cycle.

An H brace turns one post into a team of two. You’ve got the corner post, a second brace post set 8 feet away down the fence line, a horizontal rail pinned between them at the top, and a diagonal brace wire twisted tight from the bottom of the corner post to the top of the brace post. From the side it looks like a capital H, which is where the name comes from.

The magic is in how the parts share the load. The wire tries to tip the corner post over. The horizontal rail pushes that force into the brace post. The diagonal wire pulls it back down toward the base of the corner. Instead of one post fighting a lever battle it can’t win, the whole assembly spreads the pull across two posts, a rail, and about 20 square feet of soil contact.

Done right, a wood H brace fence assembly holds 3,000 pounds of pull or more. That’s enough to keep five strands of barbed wire or a full run of net wire banjo tight for decades.

If your corners are already leaning, get eyes on them before you restretch anything. Request a free written estimate and we’ll tell you straight whether your braces can be saved or need to be rebuilt.

## Why Fence Corners Fail Without a Brace

An unbraced corner post doesn’t fail all at once. It creeps. First season, it leans an inch and the wire drops a little tension. You tighten the wire, which pulls the post harder, and next season it leans two more inches. Within three to five years the post is pointing at the neighbor’s place and the bottom wires are loose enough for calves to walk through.

Central Texas soil makes it worse. Our blackland clay acts like a sponge. When it’s saturated, a post can lean under wire tension alone. When it bakes dry, the clay pulls away from the post and leaves a gap that fills with water at the next rain. If you’ve read our piece on leaning fence posts, you know this wet-dry cycle is the number one killer of fences in our area, and corners take the worst of it because they carry the most load.

Here’s what that failure costs in real life. Dale Hoffman runs cows on 160 acres outside Crawford. His previous fence guy set the corners in concrete but skipped the braces, figuring concrete was enough. It isn’t. Concrete just makes a heavier lever. After the wet spring of 2024, three corners rolled over, a quarter mile of five-strand went slack, and his cows found the county road. Dale paid us $4,100 to rebuild the corners and restretch the wire. Proper H braces on day one would have run him about $1,100. The lean cost him three times what the brace would have.

And that’s the cheap version of the story. A loose fence with cattle on a road is a liability problem, not just a fencing problem. If your fence is slack right now and stock are testing it, that’s a today problem. Call our line at (254) 870-8898, day or night, and we’ll get a crew moving.

## How a Proper H Brace Goes Together

There’s a right way to build an H brace, and there are a dozen wrong ways that look fine for a year. Here’s the spec we build to, and it lines up with what university fencing guides like the University of Missouri Extension’s wire fence construction guide recommend.

Posts. Both posts should be at least 5 to 6 inches in diameter, pressure treated or a durable species. The corner post goes 3.5 to 4 feet in the ground, and depth matters more than concrete. A post set 4 feet deep in tamped native soil will outhold a post set 2 feet deep in a bag of sakrete every single time.

Spacing. Set the brace post 8 feet from the corner post, measured center to center. Short braces are one of the most common mistakes we see. A 4 foot brace makes a steep diagonal that actually helps jack the corner post out of the ground.

The rail. The horizontal rail should be a 4 inch or bigger post, 8 feet long, pinned into both posts with steel brace pins near the top, roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of the way up. Toenailing it with a couple of screws won’t cut it once real tension hits.

The brace wire. Run a double loop of 9 gauge smooth galvanized wire from the bottom of the corner post to the top of the brace post, then twist it tight with a stick or an in-line strainer. Direction is the part people get backwards. The wire runs low on the corner, high on the brace post, so it pulls the corner post down and back against the pull of the fence.

Doubling up. For pulls longer than about 650 feet, for net wire, or for high-tensile game fence, we build a double H brace, which is two H assemblies in a row sharing three posts. On heavy gate corners, a welded pipe fence corner is the no-maintenance option, since steel doesn’t rot and doesn’t care how wet the spring gets.

One more thing worth saying: brace post spacing and line post spacing are different jobs. Your line posts just hold wire up and stock off. Your braces hold the whole fence tight. Our guide on fence post spacing covers how the two work together.

Now compare that to the cost of not bracing. Restretching a quarter mile of slack five-strand runs $600 to $1,200. Rebuilding a failed corner plus restretching is usually $900 to $1,500 per corner.
