## Common H Brace Mistakes We Fix Every Week

Even fences that have braces fail when the braces are built wrong. These are the ones we see most on repair calls:

Brace wire running the wrong direction. High on the corner and low on the brace post looks the same from the truck, but it pulls the corner post over instead of holding it down. We see this on maybe a third of DIY braces.

Brace too short. A 4 or 5 foot rail makes the diagonal too steep, and the assembly lifts the corner post instead of loading it. Eight feet, center to center.

Rail too low. A rail pinned at knee height does almost nothing, because the wire pulls near the top of the post. Two-thirds of post height or better.

Shallow posts. A corner post 2 feet deep will lean no matter how pretty the brace is. In our clay, 3.5 feet is the floor and 4 is better. Rocky ground west of Crawford and Valley Mills takes different technique, and soggy bottomland near the Brazos takes another. Depth is not negotiable in either one.

Skipping the twitch. The diagonal wire has to be twisted tight enough to hum. Loose brace wire is a decoration.

Cedar rails on treated posts. Untreated rails rot at the pin in 5 to 8 years, and then the brace quietly stops working while looking fine.

Tommy Kubacek, who runs stockers on leased ground outside West, called us about a stretch of fence that wouldn’t stay tight no matter how many times he crimped and spliced. The wire was fine. Every brace on the line had the diagonal wire run backwards, built that way 15 years ago and creeping ever since. We rebuilt four braces for $1,350 and restretched the run, and he told us it was the first winter in a decade he didn’t patch that fence. The USDA’s Natural Resources Conservation Service fencing standards make the same point our crews do: the brace assembly, not the wire, decides how long a fence stays tight.

## When to Brace It Yourself and When to Call Us

Plenty of handy landowners can build a solid H brace, and if you’ve got a tractor with an auger, good posts, and a free Saturday, a single brace on flat ground is a fair DIY project. Follow the spec above, take your time on the diagonal wire, and check it after the first hard rain.

Call a professional when any of these are true. You’re anchoring a long pull or high-tensile wire, where a brace failure releases a lot of stored energy fast. You’re in rock and can’t get to depth. You’ve got multiple failed corners, because that usually means the whole fence needs tension work, not just new posts. Or the fence is currently down and stock are loose, because that’s an emergency, not a weekend project. Stretching wire against a fresh brace is also where most DIY injuries happen, so if you’ve never used a fence stretcher under real tension, have someone show you before you learn the hard way.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How far apart should H brace posts be?

Set the brace post 8 feet from the corner post, measured center to center. Shorter spans steepen the diagonal wire and can actually lift the corner post out of the ground under tension. If you can’t get 8 feet, get as close as the site allows and never go under 6.

### Do H brace posts need concrete?

Depth and tamping matter far more than concrete. A 6 inch post set 3.5 to 4 feet deep in well-tamped native soil holds better than a shallow post in concrete, and concrete can trap moisture against wood and speed up rot. We use concrete selectively, mostly on gate posts and in loose or sandy spots.

### How many H braces does a fence need?

You need a brace assembly at every corner, every end, every gate, and roughly every 650 feet on long straight pulls of barbed wire. Net wire and high-tensile fence need double H braces at the same points because they carry more total tension. Big elevation changes may need extra bracing at the top and bottom of steep grades.

### Can I fix a leaning corner post without rebuilding it?

Sometimes, if the post itself is sound and the lean is under a few inches. We can excavate, plumb the post, re-tamp, and add a proper brace assembly to stop the creep. If the post is rotted at the ground line or leaning past about 10 degrees, rebuilding the corner is cheaper than fighting it, and it’s the only fix that lasts.

## Horse Pasture Fencing: Paddock Layout, Acreage and Turnout Planning (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/horse-pasture-fencing-layout/)

# Horse Pasture Fencing: Paddock Layout, Acreage and Turnout Planning
Published September 14, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

The two most expensive mistakes we see in horse pasture fencing around Waco are both layout mistakes, not material mistakes. One is fencing the whole place as a single pasture.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

The two most expensive mistakes we see in horse pasture fencing around Waco are both layout mistakes, not material mistakes. One is fencing the whole place as a single pasture. The other is hanging a 10 foot gate where a 14 foot gate belonged.

Neither one shows up the week the fence goes in. They show up the first dry July, when three horses have grazed twelve acres down to bare dirt and there is nowhere left to move them. Or the first time you try to back a hay trailer through a gate that will not take it.

Material matters, and we will get to cost per foot. But layout is the part you live with for twenty years, and the part almost nobody puts on paper first.

Walk your place with a builder before you buy a single roll of wire. We will come out, walk the line with you, and give you a free on-site estimate. Call now at (254) 870-8898.

## How Many Acres Per Horse Actually Works Around Waco

The number people quote is two acres per horse. That is a reasonable planning figure for Central Texas, but it is not a promise of grazing.

What an acre grows here depends on soil, rainfall and what was done to the ground before you bought it. Blackland clay in a wet spring will carry stock that the same acreage of thin limestone soil west of the river will not. In a drought year, and we get them, no amount of acreage grazes.

So plan for the dry side. If you have twelve acres and three horses, do not build one twelve acre pasture and call it done. Build grazing paddocks you can rest, plus a smaller lot you can hold horses on when the grass is gone or the ground is too wet to walk on.

Extension programs publish pasture management guidance worth reading before you draw a fence line. The University of Georgia Extension’s fences-for-horses bulletin covers the rotation logic well, and it applies here even though our forage species are different.

Here is the plan we lay out most often on a small horse place:

- One sacrifice lot or dry lot near the barn, roughly a half acre to an acre, built tough.

- Two or three grazing paddocks you rotate through.

- A lane connecting them so you can move a horse without leading it across a paddock you are resting.

That is three to five fence runs instead of one, and yes it costs more up front. It is also the difference between pasture and a dirt lot with a fence around it.

## Horse Paddock Layout: Shapes, Lanes and Gate Widths

Horses hurt themselves in corners. Two geldings sort out who is boss, one gets pushed into a corner, and there is nowhere to go.

A few layout rules we build to.

No acute corners. Any corner tighter than 90 degrees is a trap. If the property line forces a sharp angle, we round it off with two or three short runs, or we fence across it and give up the sliver of grass. Losing a tenth of an acre is cheaper than a vet call.

Nothing narrower than 16 feet. Lanes, alleys and the strip between two paddocks all need room for a horse to turn around. Twelve feet works for equipment. Sixteen to twenty feet is better when horses use it.

No dead ends. A lane that stops at a solid corner will eventually have a horse in it that cannot get out and another one coming. Put a gate at both ends.

Keep water out of the corners. A trough set in a corner puts the boss horse in position to hold everybody else off it. Set troughs along a straight run, and if you can, set one in the fence line so it waters two paddocks at once. One water line, one float, half the trips.

Look at where the horses run. Most pastures have a natural run along one line, usually toward the barn or the neighbor’s horses. That run needs the most visible fence you are willing to pay for, because that is where a horse hits at speed.

Get gate width right the first time. It is the cheapest thing to plan and the most annoying thing to fix later. Our rule of thumb:

- 12 feet minimum anywhere a tractor goes.

- 14 to 16 feet where hay equipment, a stock trailer or a truck and trailer has to swing through.

- A 4 foot walk gate near the barn so you are not swinging a big gate twice a day.

Hang gates so they open into the paddock and away from the direction horses crowd. Gate posts take more abuse than any other post on the place, so they get set deeper and in concrete, and on a horse lot we will often set pipe.

Post spacing on horse mesh runs 8 to 12 feet depending on terrain and how hard the fence gets used. Wider than that and the mesh bellies out when a horse leans on it. Spacing is one of the numbers to ask about when you compare quotes, and we cover it in our fence post spacing guide.

Cap every T-post. An uncapped T-post is the most common preventable injury on a horse place, and caps cost a couple of dollars each.

A 2x4 inch no-climb roll with a top rail, built where a horse will lean on it, prices near the $8 end. ## Three Field Examples With Real Numbers

A 12-acre horse place outside Lorena, three horses. The owner wanted the whole thing in horse fence. We laid it out as an 8 acre grazing block split into two 4 acre halves, a 3 acre back paddock, and a 1 acre dry lot off the barn. Perimeter came to about 2,900 feet, cross fencing another 1,400 feet.

We built the perimeter and the cross fences in 2x4 inch no-climb with a treated top rail, posts on 10 foot centers. At the upper end of the net wire band that came to roughly $19,000 to $23,000 for the wire fence, plus a short pipe run around the dry lot where the horses crowd the gate. Three paddocks instead of one means the grass gets a rest, and the dry lot means she is not turning horses onto soaked clay in February.

A limestone hill section near Valley Mills where every post has to be drilled. About 1,400 feet of it. There is four to eight inches of soil over rock, and an auger will not take a post down. Every hole gets drilled and the post gets set in concrete or rock is packed back around it.

That work is slower, it needs a rock drill on site, and it prices at the top of whatever band the fence type falls in. On that job the mesh line ran near the $8 per foot ceiling where the flat ground on the same property ran closer to $6. If a builder quotes you rocky ground at flat-ground prices, ask what happens when the auger stops. Our notes on setting fence posts in rocky ground go through it in more detail.

A 40-acre place north of China Spring with a seasonal creek. Two horses and a hay meadow. The mistake already in the ground was a single perimeter fence with the creek crossing it, so every high-water event took out sixty feet of wire.

We put the horses on 9 acres of fenced paddock away from the creek, left the meadow open for hay, and built a proper water gap at the crossing so the next rise takes out a hanging panel instead of a braced corner. Gates went in at 16 feet so the hay equipment clears them. Fixing the layout cost less than rebuilding the same fence a fourth time.

## Building Horse Pasture Fencing That Survives Blackland Clay

Central Texas clay swells when it is wet and shrinks when it is dry, and it does both hard. Posts move. A fence that was tight in May can be loose by September, then tight again after a wet spell.

That is why bracing matters more here than in most of the country. Every corner and every gate post needs a proper H-brace with the horizontal set at the right height and the brace wire twisted tight. A corner that is not braced right will lean within two seasons, and a leaning corner takes the whole run with it.

Wire choice matters too. Class 3 galvanized mesh holds up far longer than class 1 in our humidity, and on a horse fence you are paying for the fence to last twenty years, not eight.

Electric wire has a place on a horse fence, usually a single hot strand on standoffs to keep horses off the mesh and stop them rubbing the top rail down. It is not a perimeter fence on its own, and it will not stop a spooked horse. If you want to run it, our page on electric fence for horses is worth ten minutes.

For the safety reasoning behind mesh, visibility and smooth wire, Penn State Extension’s fence planning guide for horses is a good independent read.

## Where to Spend and Where to Save

If the budget is tight, spend it in this order.

First, the dry lot and the barn lot. That is where horses spend the most hours and stand closest to each other, so that is where pipe or heavy mesh earns its money. See corrals and working pens for what we build there.

Second, the run. Whatever line the horses gallop toward gets the visible, hoof-proof fence.

Third, the perimeter along a road. A horse loose on a farm-to-market road at night is a problem far bigger than a fence bill.

Last, the back paddock line where horses drift rather than run. That line can be lighter, and honestly it can wait a year if the budget says so. We would rather build half your place right than all of it thin. Details on what we install are on our horse fence page and in our guide to no-climb horse fence.

When you are ready to put it on the ground, call now at (254) 870-8898. We will walk the fence line with you, talk through the paddock layout, and give you a free on-site estimate before any number gets quoted.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How many acres do I need per horse near Waco?

Two acres per horse is a fair planning figure for grazing in Central Texas, but it depends entirely on your soil, your rainfall and the condition of the pasture. Blackland clay ground carries more than thin soil over limestone. Plan for a dry year, and build a dry lot so you have somewhere to hold horses when the grass is gone or the ground is too wet.

### What is the smallest paddock size that is safe for turnout?

For a single horse to move and stretch, most people work from about a quarter acre as a minimum turnout, and a dry lot of a half acre to an acre works well on small acreage. The shape matters as much as the size. A long narrow paddock with no acute corners is safer than a square one with a tight angle a horse can get pinned in.

### Can I use barbed wire on a horse pasture?

We build a lot of barbed wire, and it is a good cattle fence, but it is not a horse fence. Horses do not back off wire the way cattle do, and thin strands are nearly invisible at dusk. If you already have barbed wire and horses, the highest value change is usually mesh on the run line and the road line first.

### How much does it cost to fence a 10 acre horse pasture?

Ten acres squared up is roughly 2,640 feet of perimeter, so at the horse-grade end of our net wire range of $3.50 to $8 per foot you are looking at a wide band depending on terrain, brush and how much of it is rock. Cross fencing, gates and a dry lot are on top of that. The only way to get a real number is to walk the line, which we will do at no charge.

# How Long Does a Barbed Wire Fence Last? (And What Shortens Its Life)
Published August 20, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

There's a fence off FM 185 near Crawford that's been holding cattle since the 1960s, and two pastures over there's one built in 2016 that's already sagging into the grass. Same county, same weather, same cows. So how long does a barbed wire fence last? The honest answer is 20 to 50 years, and the gap between those two numbers comes down to what wire you bought, what posts you set, and how the fence was built in the first place.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

There’s a fence off FM 185 near Crawford that’s been holding cattle since the 1960s, and two pastures over there’s one built in 2016 that’s already sagging into the grass. Same county, same weather, same cows. So how long does a barbed wire fence last? The honest answer is 20 to 50 years, and the gap between those two numbers comes down to what wire you bought, what posts you set, and how the fence was built in the first place.

We build and repair barbed wire fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, so we’ve seen fences at every age from brand new to older than the rancher who owns them. This article walks through the real lifespan numbers, the things that quietly kill a fence early, and how to tell whether yours is worth patching or ready for the dozer pile.

## The Short Answer: 20 to 50 Years, Depending on What’s in the Ground

A barbed wire fence isn’t one thing. It’s wire, posts, braces, and staples, and each part ages on its own clock.

The wire itself is usually the longest-lived part. Good galvanized barbed wire in a dry climate can stay serviceable for 40 to 50 years. The posts are the weak link. Untreated or poorly treated wood posts can rot out in 10 to 15 years, and once posts go, the whole fence goes with them, no matter how good the wire still looks.

Here’s how the pieces typically hold up in Central Texas conditions:

Component Typical Lifespan What Usually Kills It

Class 1 galvanized wire 15-25 years Thin zinc coating rusts through

Class 3 galvanized wire 40-50 years Barb damage, stretching, hog impacts

Untreated wood posts 5-15 years Ground-line rot, termites

Treated pine posts 20-30 years Rot at the ground line, cattle pressure

Cedar heart posts 25-40 years Slow rot, splitting with age

Steel T-posts 25-35 years Rust at the soil line, bending

Pipe corners and H-braces 40+ years Almost nothing if set right

Notice that spread on wire. Class 1 galvanizing carries roughly a third of the zinc that Class 3 does, and in our humidity that difference shows up as rust streaks within a decade. We wrote a whole piece on why Class 3 galvanized wire is worth the extra cost if you want the details.

If your fence is showing its age and you’d rather have a professional eye on it, request a free written estimate or call us at (254) 870-8898. We’ll tell you straight whether it needs a repair crew or a rebuild.

## What Determines How Long a Barbed Wire Fence Lasts

Four things decide whether your fence dies at 20 or cruises past 50. None of them are luck.

Wire quality. As the table shows, the galvanizing class matters more than the brand name on the spool. Class 3 wire costs maybe 15 to 20 percent more per roll and roughly doubles the wire’s life. That’s the cheapest longevity you can buy on a fence.

Post material and setting. Posts fail from the ground down. A treated pine post set in concrete that traps water can rot faster than a bare post in well-drained soil. Cedar heart posts and steel T-posts shrug off most of what our clay throws at them. If you’re weighing options, our cedar vs treated pine comparison breaks down the real-world numbers.

Bracing and tension. A fence is only as strong as its corners. Weak corner assemblies let the wire slacken, slack wire lets cattle lean, and leaning cattle destroy fences years ahead of schedule. Proper H-braces at corners and pulls are what let a fence hold tension for decades.

Soil and drainage. Blackland clay holds moisture against posts through every wet winter. Sandy or rocky ground drains fast and posts last noticeably longer. Same materials, different dirt, different lifespan.

Land-grant universities that study fencing economics figure barbed wire fence depreciation over roughly a 25 year useful life, which lines up with what we see when average materials meet average maintenance. Oklahoma State University’s fence cost fact sheet is a good outside reference if you want to see how the accountants look at it. Build better than average and maintain it, and you’ll beat that number by a wide margin.

## What Shortens a Barbed Wire Fence’s Life in Central Texas

Now for the killers. These are the things we find over and over when a fence dies young around Waco.

Post rot at the ground line. This is cause of death number one. The wood right at the soil surface stays wet, dries, and stays wet again, and that cycle feeds decay fast. By the time a post wiggles by hand, the underground half is usually mush. Our guide on spotting and fixing fence post rot shows you what to look for before it spreads.

Cattle pressure. Cows scratching, leaning, and reaching through for the grass on the other side put hundreds of pounds of sideways force on wire and posts. A fence line next to a heavily stocked pasture ages twice as fast as one along an empty hayfield. Slack strands make it worse, because cattle learn quick that a loose fence is a suggestion.

Feral hogs. Hogs don’t lean on a fence, they hit it. A sounder rooting under the bottom strand will stretch and snap wire, pop staples, and shove posts out of line in one night. Repeated hog traffic can take a decade off a fence’s life along a creek bottom.

Fire, floods, and falling limbs. Grass fires cook the temper out of wire even when it looks fine afterward. Flood debris in water gaps drags whole sections down. And every mesquite or hackberry growing in the fence line is a future limb across your top strand.

Cheap wire and skipped maintenance. Class 1 wire in our humidity, staples driven too tight so the wire can’t move, no tension checks for years at a time. None of these kills a fence overnight. All of them together take 20 years off its life.

Here’s a real example. Doyle Krizan runs about 60 pairs outside Valley Mills, and he called us after hogs tore up the same creek crossing three times in one spring. The fence was 1980s wire on posts that were already soft, so every hog hit snapped strands instead of flexing. Patching it each time was running him around $600 a visit. We rebuilt 900 feet of the creek-bottom stretch with Class 3 wire, steel posts, and a proper water gap for about $4,100, and he hasn’t had a cow out through that bottom since.

## Repair or Replace: How to Read an Aging Fence

Somewhere around year 25 to 30, most barbed wire fences hit a fork in the road. Here’s how we call it.

Repair it when the problems are local. A few broken strands, one leaning corner, a stretch of slack wire after a wet winter. If 80 percent of the posts are solid when you push on them, the fence has years left and repairs are money well spent. Most strand splices and re-tensioning jobs run $2 to $4 per foot on the affected sections.

Replace it when the problems are everywhere. If you can rock every third post, if the wire snaps when you try to re-tension it, or if you’re patching the same line every few months, you’ve crossed into throwing good money after bad. Brittle, rusted-through wire can’t hold a splice, and there’s no fixing that. Our rusted barbed wire repair or replace guide has a simple test you can do with a pair of pliers.

The quick field check takes ten minutes. Walk a 200 foot stretch and push hard on every post. Grab a strand mid-span and pull. Look at the wire where it crosses the staples, because that’s where rust bites first. Count what fails. A few failures means repair. Failures every span means replacement.

One caution on the DIY side: re-tensioning old wire is the job that sends people to the emergency room. Brittle wire under a stretcher can snap and whip, and a loaded strand carries real force. Splicing a single break with gloves and eye protection is fine. Re-stretching whole spans of 30 year old wire, pulling H-braces, or rebuilding corners is work for a crew with the right tools. When a job crosses that line, call a professional rather than gambling with a wire stretcher.

Marcy Halbert learned the repair-versus-replace math the practical way. She and her husband bought 42 acres near West in 2024 with a fence the seller called “solid.” First winter, cattle were out on the county road twice. We walked the line with her and found ground-line rot in about half the posts and Class 1 wire that was down to bare steel. Patching what she’d already spent about $900 on piecemeal was never going to end. A full rebuild of her worst three-quarter mile came to roughly $13,500, and the rest of the perimeter tested good enough to leave alone. That’s the outcome you want: replace the dead sections, keep the living ones.

Not sure which side of the line your fence is on? Call (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk it with you. The written estimate is free, and if repair is the right answer, that’s what we’ll tell you.

## How to Make Your Barbed Wire Fence Last Longer

Getting 40+ years out of a fence isn’t complicated. It’s five habits.

Buy Class 3 wire from day one. On a typical barbed wire fence build, upgrading the wire adds a small fraction to the total cost and doubles the life of the strands. There’s no better trade on the whole invoice.

Overbuild the corners. H-braces with solid diagonal bracing, set below frost depth in concrete where the soil calls for it. Corners hold the tension, and tension is what keeps cattle honest and wire off the ground.

Walk the line twice a year. Spring and fall. Tighten slack strands, re-drive loose staples, and replace the odd bad post before it loads its neighbors. An hour of walking beats a weekend of rebuilding.

Keep the fence line clean. Brush shading the line holds moisture against posts, and trees drop limbs on wire. A clean line also lets you actually see problems before the cows find them.

Fix small problems the week you find them. One broken bottom strand becomes a hog highway. One leaning post becomes five. Fence problems compound, and early fixes are cheap fixes.

Deal with water gaps properly. Creek crossings are where fences die first in our counties. A purpose-built water gap that swings or breaks away in a flood saves the fixed fence on either side of it.

If the fence is past saving, know what you’re budgeting for. New five-strand barbed wire fence in our area typically runs $2.50 to $4.50 per foot depending on terrain, post choice, and gates, which puts a mile between roughly $13,000 and $24,000. Our ranch fence cost page has current numbers for barbed wire, net wire, and pipe so you can compare options before you commit. The USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service also publishes conservation practice standards for fencing through NRCS, and their specs are a good baseline for what a long-lived fence should look like.

One more story, because it shows what the maintenance habit is worth. Ray Stanek’s place outside McGregor has barbed wire his father strung in the late 1980s, and most of it is still working fence. His secret isn’t fancy. He walks it every March and October with a bucket of staples and a fence tool, and he’s replaced posts a handful at a time for decades. When we did work for him last year, the only section we rebuilt was 400 feet a storm-felled oak took out, about $1,700. That’s a 35+ year old fence with a repair bill most folks would envy, and the only difference is he never let small problems get big.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How long does a barbed wire fence last on average?

Plan on 20 to 30 years for a fence built with standard materials and average maintenance, which matches the 25 year useful life most agricultural economists use. A fence built with Class 3 galvanized wire, good posts, and strong braces routinely reaches 40 to 50 years in Central Texas. Cheap wire on untreated posts can fail in 10 to 15.

### Does the wire or the posts fail first?

Usually the posts. Galvanized wire often outlives wood posts by a decade or more, because posts rot right at the ground line where moisture sits. That’s why you’ll see old fences with decent wire flopping between rotten stubs, and why post inspection matters more than wire inspection on a fence under 20 years old.

### Is it worth repairing a 30 year old barbed wire fence?

It depends on the posts and the wire condition, not the birthday. If most posts are solid and the wire still holds a splice without snapping, targeted repairs at $2 to $4 per foot make sense. If posts rock everywhere you push and the wire is brittle, replacement is cheaper than endless patching. Walk it, test it, then decide section by section.

### How often should I inspect my fence?

Walk or ride the full line at least twice a year, spring and fall, plus a quick check after any major storm or flood. You’re looking for slack strands, loose staples, leaning posts, and hog activity under the bottom wire. Catching those early is the single biggest factor in pushing a fence past the 40 year mark.

## How Long Does It Take to Build a Fence? Ranch Timelines Start to Finish (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/how-long-fence-installation-takes/)

> Straight answers on how long it takes to build a fence in Central Texas: real timelines by fence type, what causes delays, and when crews can actually start.

Ranch Fencing

# How Long Does It Take to Build a Fence? Ranch Timelines Start to Finish
Published August 20, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A good crew can roll out a quarter mile of barbed wire in a single day. So why did your neighbor's fence take six weeks from handshake to last staple?

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A good crew can roll out a quarter mile of barbed wire in a single day. So why did your neighbor’s fence take six weeks from handshake to last staple?

If you’re asking how long does it take to build a fence, the honest answer is that the building is the fast part. On most ranch jobs around Waco, the actual construction takes days. The waiting, the scheduling, the material orders, and the weather take weeks. This article walks through real timelines from jobs we’ve run in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, so you can plan calving season, a land closing, or a hunting lease around actual dates instead of guesses.

## How long does it take to build a fence? The short answer

Here’s the rule of thumb we give folks on the phone. A three man crew building 5 strand barbed wire on decent ground covers about 1,000 to 1,500 feet per day once posts are set. Post setting runs slower, roughly 60 to 100 wood posts a day with an auger, faster with T-posts.

Put it all together and typical ranch jobs shake out like this:

- A quarter mile of barbed wire cross fence: 2 to 4 working days.

- Ten acres fully perimeter fenced (about 2,640 feet): 4 to 7 working days.

- A full mile of new perimeter fence: 2 to 3 weeks.

- A mile of 8 foot game fence: 3 to 5 weeks.

Those are construction days. Add 1 to 3 weeks of lead time before a crew shows up, longer in spring when everybody in Central Texas wants a fence at once.

If you’re trying to hit a hard date, a cattle delivery or a closing on land, call us early. We’ll walk the line, give you a free written estimate, and put a real start date on paper. Reach us at (254) 870-8898 or through our contact page.

## What eats up the calendar before the first post goes in

Most of a fence timeline happens before anyone digs a hole. Here’s where the days go.

The estimate and the walk. A contractor should walk your line in person, not quote off an aerial photo. That visit usually happens within a few days of your call. The written quote follows in another day or two.

Property lines. If you’re not sure where your line sits, get a survey before the fence goes up. A survey can take 2 to 4 weeks to schedule in our area, and it’s a lot cheaper than moving a fence later. Texas boundary disputes get ugly fast, and a fence built two feet onto the neighbor’s place is a problem you’ll own for years.

Materials. Standard barbed wire, T-posts, and treated pine posts are usually in stock locally. Specialty items are not. Fixed knot game wire, custom entrance gates, and oilfield pipe in specific sizes can take 1 to 3 weeks to land. Pipe prices also move around, so a quote older than 30 days may need updating.

Brush and old fence. A fence line choked with mesquite and cedar has to be cleared before construction starts. Clearing a heavily grown mile can take 2 to 5 days with a skid steer. Tearing out old wire and rotten posts adds another day or two per mile.

Weather. Rain doesn’t just stop work on the wet day. Black clay ground around Waco stays too soft for trucks and augers for 2 or 3 days after a good soak. A wet spring can push a two week job into a month, and no honest contractor can promise otherwise.

## Fence installation time by fence type

Different fences move at very different speeds. Wire goes up fast. Welded pipe does not. Here’s what we typically see per crew on ground that’s not solid rock:

Fence type Typical production per day Quarter mile (1,320 ft) Full mile (5,280 ft)

5 strand barbed wire, T-posts 1,000 to 1,500 ft 2 to 3 days 7 to 10 days

Barbed wire, wood posts 700 to 1,000 ft 3 to 4 days 10 to 14 days

Net wire (field fence) 500 to 800 ft 3 to 5 days 12 to 16 days

8 ft fixed knot game fence 400 to 600 ft 4 to 6 days 15 to 25 days

Welded pipe fence 150 to 300 ft 5 to 9 days 20 to 35 days

Pipe entrance with gate n/a 2 to 4 days n/a

Those numbers assume the corners are already in. H-braces and corner assemblies are their own line item. A proper H-brace takes an hour or two to build, and concrete set corners need 24 to 48 hours of cure time before you can stretch wire off them. Skipping that cure time is how fences end up leaning in year one. We covered the details in our post on H-brace fence corners.

Rock changes everything. Ground west of the Bosque River around Crawford and Valley Mills hides limestone shelf a foot down. When the auger hits rock, production can drop by half, and sometimes we switch to a rock drill or pound pilot holes. If your place has shallow rock, budget extra days and read our piece on setting fence posts in rocky ground before you panic at the quote.

## A real job, day by day: 4,200 feet near West

Danny Kolar runs cows on 60 acres off Tokio Road outside West. Last fall he called us on a Tuesday because his east line fence was 40 years old and his heifers had figured that out. Here’s how his job actually went.

Day 1 after the call, we walked the line with him and measured 4,200 feet. Two days later he had a written quote: $12,600 for 5 strand barbed wire on T-posts with wood line posts every 100 feet, four new H-brace corners, and one 14 foot gate. He signed that Friday.

Materials were stock items, so we scheduled him 12 days out. Construction went like this:

- Day 1: Tear out old wire, clear brush at the south corner, set corner posts in concrete.

- Day 2: Corners curing, so the crew drove T-posts and set wood line posts.

- Day 3: More posts, hung the gate, hit a rock shelf near the creek and lost half a day.

- Day 4: Stretched and tied all five strands.

- Day 5: Half day of cleanup, clips, and a final walk with Danny.

Call to finished fence: just under three weeks. Actual construction: four and a half days. That ratio is normal, and it’s why the smart move is booking the crew before the old fence fails completely. If your fence is already down and cattle are on the road, that’s a different conversation. We run a 24/7 emergency line for exactly that at (254) 870-8898.

## How long does it take to fence 10 acres or a full mile?

Ten acres is the most common request we get from folks buying small places around Lorena, China Spring, and McGregor. A square 10 acres needs about 2,640 feet of fence. In barbed wire, that’s 4 to 6 working days. In net wire it runs closer to a week, because net wire is slower to stretch and usually gets a barbed strand on top.

Carla Mendez bought 10 acres south of Lorena in March for a goat operation. Goats laugh at barbed wire, so she needed net wire all the way around plus two gates. Her quote came in at $23,400. We ordered wire on a Monday, started the next week, and then it rained four inches. The black clay on her place wouldn’t hold a truck for three days. Total construction time was six working days spread across two and a half weeks. The fence didn’t care about the delay. Her closing date did, which is why we’d quoted the job with weather margin built in.

A full mile is a different animal. The Braun family put a mile of 8 foot game fence on their Bosque County place near Valley Mills ahead of deer season. Game fence uses taller posts, deeper holes, and 20 foot rolls of fixed knot wire that fight you on hills. Their job ran $52,800 and took 19 working days across four calendar weeks, including two days lost to rock and one to rain. They signed in July and were done in early September, with time to spare before the season opener. If they’d called in September, they’d have hunted next to a construction site.

Costs scale with distance and terrain, and the per foot math matters more than the total. Our ranch fence cost guide breaks down current per foot pricing, and the post on what it costs to fence 10 acres runs the numbers for small places specifically.

## What you can do to keep your fence job on schedule

You control more of the timeline than you might think. A few things that save real days:

Mark your line before the estimate. Flag the corners and know where the property pins are. If you can’t find them, start the survey process now, not after you’ve signed a fence contract.

Clear what you can. If you own a tractor with a shredder, knocking down light brush along the line ahead of time can shave a day or two off the job and a few hundred dollars off the bill. Leave the big mesquite and the old wire tangles to the crew.

Decide on gates early. Gate locations, widths, and swing direction sound like small details until the crew is standing there waiting on an answer. A 16 foot gate handles most trucks and trailers. Equipment like combines may need 20 feet.

Ask about crew scheduling honestly. Any contractor juggling jobs will have a queue. What matters is whether they’ll commit to a window in writing and tell you when weather pushes it. The USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service publishes fencing standards that good contractors build to, and you can read their conservation practice specs at nrcs.usda.gov if you want to know what a spec built fence looks like on paper.

Handle the utility check. In Texas, call 811 before any digging. Locates are free and usually done within two business days. A cut phone line or gas service will stop a job cold and cost far more than the wait.

## When to stop doing it yourself and call a crew

Plenty of ranchers can build fence, and a short stretch of repair is a fine weekend project. But the math shifts on bigger jobs. A landowner working weekends might set and stretch 200 to 300 feet a day. At that pace, a mile of fence is 20 or more weekends, most of a year of Saturdays. A crew does it in two to three weeks because they have an auger on a skid steer, hydraulic post drivers, and wire stretchers that cost more than most folks want to spend for one project.

There are also jobs where DIY goes wrong in expensive ways. Corner braces that aren’t built right will let the whole fence sag inside two years. Stretching high tensile game wire without the right equipment can hurt you; that wire stores a lot of energy and does not forgive mistakes. And post holes near buried utilities are not a place to guess. The University of Georgia Extension’s fencing guide, Fences for the Farm, is a solid free read on brace construction and wire handling if you want to see what proper technique involves before deciding.

Our general advice: repairs and short runs, do them yourself and take pride in it. Full perimeters, game fence, pipe fence, and anything on rock or near utilities, hire it out. Your time is worth something, and a professionally built barbed wire fence around here should give you 30 plus years before it needs real attention.

The black clay soil common around Waco stays too soft to support trucks and augers for 2 to 3 days after a heavy rain, and holes augered in saturated clay don’t hold posts well. A contractor who works through that is trading your fence quality for their schedule.

## How Many Strands of Barbed Wire Do You Need for Cattle? (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/how-many-strands-barbed-wire/)

> Most Central Texas cattle need 5 strands of barbed wire, not 3. Get strand counts, wire spacing heights, and real per-foot costs from a Waco fence builder.

Livestock

# How Many Strands of Barbed Wire Do You Need for Cattle?
Published July 24, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Three strands of barbed wire will hold a fat, happy cow on a good day. The trouble is, nobody builds fence for the good days.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Three strands of barbed wire will hold a fat, happy cow on a good day. The trouble is, nobody builds fence for the good days. You build it for the February morning when the herd is hungry, the neighbor’s bull is bellowing across the line, and a cold front has every animal on the place pacing the wire.

So how many strands of barbed wire for cattle is actually enough? For most Central Texas operations, the answer is five. Four will do the job in some interior pastures. Three is asking for a phone call about your cows standing in the middle of a county road.

We build and repair barbed wire fence around Waco every week, across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and strand count is the first question almost every landowner asks. Here’s the straight answer, with real numbers behind it.

## The Short Answer: 5 Strands Holds Most Cattle

A 5-strand barbed wire fence, built 48 to 54 inches tall on good posts with solid corner braces, will hold commercial cow-calf pairs, stockers, and most bulls in typical Central Texas conditions. That’s the standard we recommend for perimeter fence, and it’s what the big ranches around Crawford and Valley Mills have settled on for decades.

Why five? Cattle challenge a fence three ways. They reach over the top for grass, they push through the middle when they’re crowded or spooked, and calves scoot under the bottom. Five strands lets you defend all three zones at once: a stout top wire at 48 inches or better, three wires guarding the belly-height middle, and a bottom wire low enough that a calf thinks twice.

Texas law sets a much lower bar, by the way. The state’s definition of a “sufficient fence” in Texas Agriculture Code Chapter 143 is only three barbed wires on posts no more than 30 feet apart. That’s a legal minimum from another era, not a recommendation. A fence can meet the statute and still let your herd out every other weekend.

Here’s what the legal minimum costs in practice. Danny Kolar runs about 40 pairs outside West, on a place he bought with an old 3-strand perimeter. Last fall his bull went through the west line chasing a neighbor’s heifers, and Danny spent a Saturday getting him home. The tally: $350 to a hauler with a stock trailer, a $290 vet visit for wire cuts, and roughly $480 in patch materials and lost time. Call it $1,100 for one escape, and he got lucky it happened on a pasture road instead of the highway. He had us rebuild that line to five strands the next month.

If you’re staring at a tired 3-strand fence right now and wondering whether it’ll hold through fall, call us at (254) 870-8898. We’ll walk the line with you and give you a free written estimate, no pressure.

## How Many Strands of Barbed Wire for Cattle in Each Situation

The right count depends on what’s leaning on the fence and what’s on the other side of it. Here’s how we spec jobs around Waco:

Perimeter fence along roads: 5 strands, no debate. If cattle get through this fence, they’re on pavement. A wreck involving your cow is a lawsuit risk on top of a dead animal, so this is the last place to save a few cents per foot.

Perimeter fence between neighbors: 5 strands. Especially if the neighbor runs bulls or has cows that cycle. A shared line fence takes pressure from both sides, twice the animals testing the same wire.

Interior cross fence: 4 strands is usually fine. If a cow slips through a cross fence, she’s still on your place. Four strands saves real money on long divisions, and you can always add a fifth wire later if a particular pasture gets tested.

Bulls, or a bull pasture: 5 strands minimum, 6 if he’s proven he’ll push. A 2,000 pound bull that wants through a fence needs more than wire to stop him. For chronic fence-walkers, a lot of our customers add a single offset hot wire instead of a sixth barbed strand. It’s cheaper and it works on the animal’s mind, not just his hide.

Cow-calf pairs: 5 strands with a low bottom wire. Calves go under, not through. A bottom wire at 12 inches or higher is an open door for a month-old calf, and mama will find her own way to follow.

Stockers and weaned calves: 5 strands, tight. Fresh-weaned calves are the hardest animals in the cattle business to fence. They’re light, they’re panicked, and they’ll hit wire at a run. Wire tension matters as much as count here.

If your fence problem is less about strand count and more about cattle already getting out, start with our guide on why cattle get out and how to stop it.

## Strand Spacing: Where Each Wire Should Sit

Five strands hung in the wrong spots hold cattle worse than four strands hung right. Cattle put pressure on a fence between roughly 26 and 42 inches off the ground, which is chest and neck height on a mature cow. That middle zone is where your wires need to be stacked closest together.

Here’s the spacing we use on a standard 5-strand cattle fence, measured from the ground up: 14, 22, 30, 39, and 49 inches. For a 4-strand interior fence: 16, 26, 36, and 46 inches. University fencing guides, like the Fences for the Farm publication from UGA Extension, land in the same neighborhood, tighter spacing through the middle and a top wire at 48 inches or better.

Two spacing mistakes we fix constantly on older Central Texas fences:

Bottom wire too high. Anything over 15 or 16 inches lets calves duck under without touching wire. If you also fight feral hogs, there’s a trade-off, because a low bottom wire takes more hog damage. We cover that in our post on feral hog fence damage.

Even spacing top to bottom. Splitting five wires evenly across 50 inches leaves 10-inch gaps right at pushing height. Cattle find those gaps. Stack the middle tighter and let the gap ride higher, above where they push.

One more thing on height: 48 inches is the working minimum for the top wire. In brushy country around Bosque County where deer traffic is heavy, some folks run the top wire a touch lower, or use a smooth top wire, to cut down on deer-strike damage. That’s a judgment call we’re glad to talk through on site.

## What More Strands of Barbed Wire Cost Per Foot and Per Mile

Adding strands is cheap insurance, because the expensive parts of a fence are the posts, the corner braces, and the labor to set them. Once the framework is in the ground, each extra wire is mostly just wire and clips.

Here’s what full builds typically run in our service area in 2026, using 12.5 gauge Class 3 galvanized wire on T-posts with wood line and corner posts:

Fence Build Cost Per Foot Cost Per Mile Best Use

3-strand barbed $1.60 to $2.00 $8,400 to $10,600 Legal minimum only, not recommended

4-strand barbed $1.85 to $2.40 $9,800 to $12,700 Interior cross fence

5-strand barbed $2.10 to $2.75 $11,100 to $14,500 Perimeter, pairs, most herds

6-strand barbed $2.40 to $3.10 $12,700 to $16,400 Bulls, high-pressure lines

5-strand plus offset hot wire $2.45 to $3.20 $12,900 to $16,900 Chronic pushers, bull pastures

Look at the gap between 4 and 5 strands: roughly 25 to 35 cents a foot. On a quarter mile of fence, that fifth wire costs about $330 to $460. Danny’s one escape in West cost $1,100. The math isn’t close.

Retrofitting is even cheaper if your posts and braces are still sound. The Muellers in China Spring had us add a fourth and fifth strand to 2,600 feet of decent 3-strand cross fence last spring. At 95 cents a foot for two wires, stays, and labor, the job came to about $2,470, a fraction of the $6,000 plus a full rebuild would have run.

Full pricing breakdowns are in our barbed wire fence cost guide, and if you’re budgeting a bigger project, our ranch fence cost page covers every fence type we build. Want a number for your place instead of a range? Request a free written estimate and we’ll measure it off aerials before we ever set foot on the property.

## Why Cattle Still Get Out With Enough Strands

Strand count gets the attention, but most escapes we’re called out on trace back to something else. Before you add wire, check these four things.

Loose wire. A slack strand is a suggestion, not a barrier. Cattle learn to lean into loose wire and walk it down. Barbed wire should be tight enough to sing a low note when you strike it. If yours sags, fixing tension is a half-day job, and our post on fixing sagging barbed wire walks through it.

Failing corners and braces. Every ounce of wire tension loads onto the corner assemblies. When an H-brace rots or racks, the whole stretch goes slack at once, and no strand count saves you. This is the number one structural failure we see on fences over 20 years old.

Post spacing that’s too wide. Posts every 30 feet meets the statute, but the wire between them flexes like a trampoline. We set T-posts at 10 to 12 feet on cattle fence. Tighter spacing stiffens every strand you’ve paid for. More on that in our fence post spacing guide.

Hunger and habit. A fence-crawler that’s learned the trick will teach the herd. Sometimes the honest fix is culling one cow, not rebuilding a mile of fence.

Here’s a real one: Ray Simcik near Crawford called us about heifers getting into his neighbor’s coastal patch. He assumed he needed a sixth wire on a quarter mile of line. When we walked it, the fence had five good strands, but the wire had gone slack against a leaning corner post. We rebuilt one H-brace and re-tensioned the stretch for about $680, instead of the $1,600 he’d budgeted for new wire he didn’t need. An honest walk-through before the work starts saves money more often than it costs.

A word on safety before you tackle any of this yourself. Re-tensioning barbed wire stores serious energy in the strand, and a snapped wire under tension can cut you badly. Wear leather gloves and eye protection, never stretch rusted or brittle wire, and if a stretch involves rebuilding corners or crossing a creek, stop and call a professional. That’s exactly the work we’re built for.

## When Barbed Wire Isn’t the Right Answer at All

Strand count only matters if barbed wire is the right tool, and sometimes it isn’t.

If you’re running calves that slip any barbed fence, net wire with a barbed top wire holds everything from calves to goats. It costs more per foot, but on small acreage the difference is manageable. We compare the two honestly in barbed wire vs net wire.

If bulls are destroying your pens and working areas, wire of any count is the wrong material. Corrals, bull traps, and high-traffic lots need pipe fence, which shrugs off pressure that would flatten a wire fence weekly.

And if horses share the pasture, skip barbed wire entirely. Horses hit wire differently than cattle and the injuries are ugly and expensive.

For a standard cow herd on Central Texas pasture, though, 5-strand barbed wire remains the best value per foot of anything you can build. Get the strand count right, hang the wires at the right heights, and build it on corners that will still be standing when your kids run the place.

We’re licensed and insured, we answer the phone, and we keep a 24/7 emergency line for storm damage and cattle-out calls, because fences never fail at a convenient hour.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Will 3 strands of barbed wire hold cattle?

Sometimes, and that’s the problem. Three strands meets the Texas legal definition of a sufficient fence and may hold settled cows on good grass, but it fails under pressure from bulls, weaned calves, drought, or a neighbor’s herd. Nearly every escape call we run in McLennan County involves a 3-strand fence. Treat three strands as a temporary condition, not a plan.

### Is 4 or 5 strand barbed wire better for cattle?

Five strands is better for any perimeter fence, any fence along a road, and any pasture with pairs or bulls. Four strands is a reasonable saver on interior cross fences where an escape just means a cow in the wrong pasture. The cost difference is usually 25 to 35 cents per foot, so we lean toward five anywhere the consequences of an escape are real.

### How high should a barbed wire fence be for cattle?

Build the top wire at 48 to 54 inches. Shorter fences invite cattle to reach over and eventually lean the top wire down, and taller than 54 inches buys little for cattle alone. Just as important, stack your middle wires between about 22 and 39 inches, because that’s the zone where cattle actually push.

### How many strands of barbed wire do I need for a bull?

Plan on five tight strands as the floor, and six for a bull that’s proven he’ll test fence. Even better than a sixth strand, in our experience, is a single offset electric wire at nose height on the bull’s side. It trains him to stay off the fence entirely, which protects the whole line instead of just adding one more wire for him to stretch.

## How to Compare Fence Quotes and Spot the Red Flags (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/compare-fence-quotes/)

> Learn how to compare fence quotes line by line, spot lowball bids and contract red flags, and hire the right ranch fence contractor in Waco and Central Texas.

Hiring a Contractor

# How to Compare Fence Quotes and Spot the Red Flags
Published August 2, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Three quotes land on your kitchen table for the same mile of pasture fence: $9,800, $14,500, and $21,000. Same land, same cattle, same request.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Three quotes land on your kitchen table for the same mile of pasture fence: $9,800, $14,500, and $21,000. Same land, same cattle, same request. So why is one bid more than double another, and which contractor is telling you the truth?

If you own land around Waco, Crawford, or Valley Mills, you’ll face this exact situation sooner or later. Knowing how to compare fence quotes is the difference between a fence that holds cattle for 30 years and a fence you’re rebuilding in three. The good news is that fence quotes aren’t complicated once you know what to look for. The bad news is that the worst contractors count on you not knowing.

This guide walks you through comparing fence bids line by line, the numbers that actually matter, and the red flags that should send you looking for somebody else.

## Why Quotes for the Same Fence Can Be Thousands Apart

A fence quote isn’t one number. It’s a stack of decisions about posts, wire, spacing, bracing, and labor, and every one of those decisions moves the price.

Take a plain 5-strand barbed wire fence. One contractor bids it with treated wood posts every 12 feet, class 3 galvanized wire, and proper H-braces at every corner. Another bids t-posts every 20 feet, class 1 wire, and a single wood post where the braces should be. Both quotes say “barbed wire fence, one mile.” The first fence will outlive your truck. The second one will sag inside five years, and you’ll be out fixing it every time a cow leans on it.

Terrain matters too. Rocky ground off Highway 6, heavy clay bottoms near the Brazos, creek crossings that need water gaps, brush that needs clearing before a single post goes in. A contractor who’s actually walked your line prices that work. A contractor bidding off a satellite photo doesn’t, and the difference shows up later as a change order.

So a big spread between bids doesn’t automatically mean somebody’s cheating you. It usually means the bids aren’t describing the same fence. Your job is to make them describe the same fence, and that starts with the paperwork. If you’d rather skip straight to a detailed written bid from folks who walk every line, request a free written estimate or call us at (254) 870-8898.

## How to Compare Fence Quotes Line by Line

Never compare bottom-line totals. Compare line items. If a quote doesn’t have line items, that’s your first red flag, and we’ll get to those shortly.

Here’s what every serious ranch fence quote should spell out:

Total footage. Measured on the ground or with a wheel, not eyeballed. If one bid says 5,100 feet and another says 5,400 feet for the same line, somebody didn’t measure. On a $3.50 per foot fence, that 300-foot gap is more than a thousand dollars of confusion.

Price per foot. This is your true comparison number. Divide the total by the footage if the contractor didn’t do it for you. Around Central Texas, barbed wire typically runs about $2 to $4.50 per foot installed, net wire more, and pipe fence considerably more. We break down full numbers in our barbed wire fence cost guide.

Post type, size, and spacing. “Wood posts” means nothing. You want species and treatment (treated pine or cedar), diameter, set depth, and spacing between posts. Tighter spacing costs more and holds better. So does concrete on corners and gates.

Wire specification. Gauge, class of galvanizing, number of strands, and brand if possible. Class 3 galvanized wire costs more up front and lasts roughly twice as long as class 1 in our weather.

Corners and braces. Corner and end bracing is where cheap fences fail first. The quote should count H-brace assemblies and say how they’re built. If braces aren’t mentioned at all, assume they’ll be done wrong. Our post on H-brace fence corners shows what right looks like.

Gates, clearing, tear-out, and haul-off. Are gates included or extra? Who clears the brush on the fence line? Who removes the old fence, and where does it go? Every one of these can be a surprise bill if the quote is silent on it.

Timeline, payment terms, and warranty. When they start, when they finish, what you pay and when, and what happens if a post heaves or wire sags in the first year.

Once every bid answers those questions, you can finally compare apples to apples. You’ll often find the “expensive” bid and the “cheap” bid are pricing two very different fences.

## The Quote Comparison Table: What Good Looks Like

Print this out and set your bids next to it. A solid quote checks every row. A risky quote leaves half of them blank.

Line Item Complete Quote Shows Red-Flag Quote Shows

Footage Measured footage, per section One round number, “approx.”

Price Per-foot price plus total Lump sum only

Posts Species, size, depth, spacing ”Wood posts” or nothing

Wire Gauge, class, strand count ”Barbed wire”

Braces H-brace count and build spec Not mentioned

Gates Each gate priced and sized ”Gates extra,” no numbers

Site prep Clearing and tear-out included or itemized Silent, becomes a change order

Deposit 10% to 33%, balance on completion 50% or more up front, cash only

Timeline Start window and duration ”We’ll fit you in”

Warranty Written workmanship warranty Verbal promise

Paper Written contract, proof of insurance Handshake deal

Keep that middle column in mind when we talk real prices. If you want to sanity-check a bid you’ve already got in hand, our ranch fence cost guide lists current per-foot ranges for every fence type we build.

## Red Flags That Should End the Conversation

Some warning signs mean “ask more questions.” These mean “walk away.”

A big cash deposit up front. A third down is normal on larger jobs so the contractor can buy materials. Half or more up front, especially in cash, is how landowners lose money. Levi Brandt, who runs cattle west of West, learned that in 2024. A door-knocker quoted him $7,200 for a quarter mile of net wire, took a $3,500 cash deposit “for materials,” and never came back. No contract, no address, no recourse. The Federal Trade Commission lists this exact pattern in its guidance on hiring a contractor.

No written contract. If it’s not on paper, it doesn’t exist. Footage, materials, price, timeline, payment schedule, warranty. All of it, signed.

No proof of insurance. Ask for a certificate of general liability insurance, and verify it’s current. If a worker gets hurt on your place or a skid steer takes out your water line, an uninsured contractor’s problem becomes your problem.

A bid that’s dramatically below the others. If two bids are around $14,000 and one is $8,500, the cheap one isn’t a bargain. It’s missing something: post depth, wire class, braces, insurance, or the intention to finish the job.

Pressure to sign today. “This price is only good until I leave your driveway” is a sales tactic, not a business practice. Fence prices don’t expire overnight.

They won’t walk the line. Nobody can price rocky ground, creek crossings, or brush from the road. A contractor who bids without walking your fence line is planning to make up the difference later.

Vague answers about who does the work. Some outfits sell the job and sub it out to whoever’s available. That’s not automatically bad, but you should know who’s showing up and who stands behind the work.

We put together a full list of questions to ask a fence contractor before you sign anything. Ask us the same questions. We’re happy to answer every one at (254) 870-8898.

## Comparing Fence Bids: Two True Stories From Down the Road

The cheap bid that cost double. Dale Hutchins, outside Crawford, needed 2,000 feet of 5-strand barbed wire to split a grazing paddock. Bids came in at $6,200, $7,900, and $8,400. He took the $6,200. The crew used lightweight posts spaced 20 feet apart, skipped concrete on the corners, and strung thin-gauge, class 1 wire. Eighteen months later the corners had pulled, the wire had gone slack, and his heifers were testing it daily. Rebuilding it right cost $9,400. Total spent: $15,600 for a fence that should have cost $7,900 once.

The bid in the middle. Marcy Teel in Valley Mills got three quotes to fence 10 acres for horses: $11,800, $16,200, and $19,500. Instead of grabbing the low number, she made each contractor break out posts, wire, spacing, and braces. The $11,800 bid had t-posts on 20-foot centers and no top rail. The $19,500 bid included an entrance gate she didn’t ask for. The $16,200 bid matched exactly what she wanted, with a written two-year workmanship warranty. She signed it, the fence went up in six days, and her only regret is not asking for line items on the first two bids sooner. If you’re pricing a similar project, our guide on the cost to fence 10 acres walks through the math.

The lesson from both: the total tells you almost nothing. The line items tell you everything.

## Make the Bids Match, Then Pick the Contractor

Once you’ve got itemized quotes, force them onto the same spec so the comparison is fair.

Call each contractor and say: “Bid me 5-strand, 12.5 gauge class 3 barbed wire, treated posts on 12-foot centers set 3 feet deep, H-braces at all corners and gates, old fence torn out and hauled off.” Now every number describes the same fence. County extension programs, like Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension’s fencing workshops, teach this same spec-first approach, and the University of Georgia Extension publishes a solid free reference on fence construction basics in Fences for the Farm if you want to study up on materials before those calls.

With matching specs, pick on these four things, in order:

- Completeness of the paperwork. Contract, insurance, warranty, payment schedule.

- Quality of the answers. A pro explains why they space posts the way they do. A pretender gets annoyed that you asked.

- Local track record. Ask for two or three fences they built nearby that you can drive past. Around here, work from three years ago is visible from the road.

- Price. Last, not first. Between two qualified contractors, sure, take the better number.

And know when the decision isn’t about quotes at all. If a fence is down and cattle are on the road tonight, you don’t need three bids, you need a crew. That’s why we run a 24/7 emergency line for storm damage and cattle-out situations. For everything else, a couple of days spent comparing bids properly will save you thousands.

One more thing: never let a low bid talk you out of the fence you actually need. A barbed wire fence built right beats a cheap net wire job, and a fence matched to your stock beats both. If you’re not sure what spec to put out for bid in the first place, tell us about your place and we’ll write you a free, fully itemized estimate you can compare against anybody’s.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How many fence quotes should I get?

Three is the sweet spot for most ranch fencing jobs. One quote gives you no context, and five starts wasting everybody’s time, including yours. Make sure all three are bidding the exact same spec, footage, and scope, or the comparison is worthless.

### Is the cheapest fence quote always a bad sign?

Not always, but a quote far below the others usually means something is missing: lighter materials, wider post spacing, no braces, no insurance, or no plan to finish. If the low bidder can show you an itemized spec that matches the others and local fences you can go look at, the price may be honest. If they can’t explain the gap, believe the other two bids.

### How much deposit is normal for a fence job in Texas?

Expect somewhere between 10% and about a third down, mostly to cover materials, with the balance due when the work is done and you’ve walked the line. Be very cautious of anyone wanting half or more up front, and never pay a large deposit in cash without a signed contract and a physical business address.

### What should a written fence quote include?

At minimum: measured footage, price per foot, post type and spacing, wire gauge and galvanizing class, brace and gate counts, who handles clearing and old fence removal, a start window, a payment schedule, and a workmanship warranty. It should also come with proof of liability insurance. If a contractor can’t put those things on paper, keep looking.

## How to Fix a Sagging Barbed Wire Fence and Keep It Tight (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/fix-sagging-barbed-wire-fence/)

> Learn how to fix a sagging barbed wire fence the right way. Re-tension wire, reset posts, and rebuild braces with real tips from a Waco ranch fence pro.

Fence Repair

# How to Fix a Sagging Barbed Wire Fence and Keep It Tight
Published July 24, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A loose bottom strand is an open invitation to a 1,200 pound cow. Give her a sagging wire and a reason, and she'll have her head through it by Tuesday and be standing on the county road by Friday...

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A loose bottom strand is an open invitation to a 1,200 pound cow. Give her a sagging wire and a reason, and she’ll have her head through it by Tuesday and be standing on the county road by Friday night.

If you’re wondering how to fix a sagging barbed wire fence before that happens, you’re in the right place. We build and repair barbed wire fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and slack wire is the number one complaint we hear. The good news is that most sag is fixable in an afternoon with basic tools. The catch is that sag is a symptom, not the disease. Fix the wire without fixing the cause and you’ll be back out there in six months doing it again.

This guide walks you through finding the real problem, tightening the wire correctly, and keeping it tight through Central Texas heat, storms, and cattle pressure.

## Why Barbed Wire Fences Sag in the First Place

Wire doesn’t loosen itself. Something in the system gave up, and it’s almost always one of these five things.

Failed corner or end braces. This is the big one. Every ounce of tension in your fence pulls against the corners. When an H-brace leans, rots, or was never built right to begin with, the whole run goes slack. If you can push your corner post and see it move, that’s your answer.

Rotted or heaved posts. Wood posts rot at the ground line, especially in our bottomland clay that stays wet all spring. T-posts get shoved sideways by cattle scratching on them. Either way, a line post that’s leaning stops holding the wire at height. We covered this in detail in our post on leaning fence posts.

Wire stretch and metal fatigue. Barbed wire relaxes over time, especially cheaper Class 1 galvanized wire in Texas heat. A fence stretched in January will run measurably looser by August. Older wire that’s gone brittle stretches worse and snaps sooner.

Animal and tree damage. A steer leaning over the top strand to reach grass, hogs rooting under the bottom strand, or a live oak limb dropping across the line will all put permanent slack into the wire in one afternoon.

Loose or popped staples. Staples work out of wood posts over years of wire vibration. Once three or four posts in a row lose their staples, the wire’s carrying its own weight over a 50 foot span and it shows.

Walk your line before you touch a tool. Figure out which of these five you’ve got, because the fix is different for each one.

If you’d rather have somebody who does this every day take a look, request a free written estimate or call us at (254) 870-8898. We’ll tell you straight whether it’s a two hour repair or time to talk replacement.

## How to Fix a Sagging Barbed Wire Fence, Step by Step

Here’s the process we use on repair calls, in order. Don’t skip ahead to tightening. Tension applied to a fence with a bad brace just pulls the brace over faster.

### 1. Gear up first

Barbed wire under tension stores real energy. When a strand snaps, it whips. Wear leather gloves, long sleeves, and eye protection every time. Keep kids and dogs away from the work area, and never stand in line with a wire you’re stretching.

### 2. Check your corners and braces

Push hard on each corner and end post. Any movement at all means the brace needs attention before you tighten anything. Look for rotted brace posts, loose brace pins, and diagonal brace wire that’s gone slack. More on brace repair in the next section.

### 3. Fix the posts

Reset leaning T-posts by driving them plumb, or pull and re-drive them a foot down the line if the original hole is blown out. Replace rotted wood line posts. In our clay, tamp new posts in with dry dirt or crushed base in 3 to 4 inch lifts. Concrete around a wood line post usually traps water and speeds up rot, so we skip it except on gates and corners.

### 4. Splice any breaks properly

Don’t just twist broken ends together with pliers. Use a figure 8 knot or, better, crimp sleeves rated for your wire gauge. A proper splice holds close to the full strength of the wire. A hand twist holds maybe half, and it’s the first thing to fail when a cow hits the fence.

### 5. Re-tension each strand

Use a fence stretcher or a come-along with wire grips. Pull from mid-span or from an end, take up the slack, then cut out the extra wire and splice. Tension until the strand is snug and sings a little when you pluck it, but stop before the barbs start straightening or the wire visibly thins. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension has good general fencing guidance if you want to go deeper on tension specs, at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu.

### 6. Re-staple and re-clip

On wood posts, drive new 1.75 inch barbed staples at a slight angle to the grain, and leave a hair of play so the wire can slide during temperature swings. On T-posts, replace any missing wire clips. A strand should touch every single post at the correct height, top strand around 48 to 54 inches for cattle.

### 7. Walk it again

Sight down the line from each end. Every strand should run straight and level. If one span still dips, you’ve got a low post or a missed staple.

Dale Hoffman, who runs about 40 momma cows outside Crawford, spent a whole summer chasing slack this way, about $180 in wire, clips, and splice sleeves across three separate Saturdays. The wire wasn’t his problem. His northeast corner post had rotted below grade and was slowly laying over. We rebuilt that one corner as an H-brace for $650, re-tensioned the two runs pulling off it, and the fence has stayed drum tight for two years since.

## Fixing a Sagging Barbed Wire Fence at the Corners: Braces Do the Heavy Lifting

If there’s one thing to take from this article, it’s this: 8 out of 10 chronically saggy fences we see have a brace problem, not a wire problem.

A proper H-brace is two posts set 8 feet apart, a horizontal cross member between them, and a diagonal brace wire twisted tight. The horizontal member pushes the posts apart while the twisted wire pulls the assembly square, so the corner can resist thousands of pounds of pull without leaning. We break down the geometry in our post on H-brace fence corners.

Signs your brace has failed:

- The corner post leans toward the fence line

- The diagonal brace wire is slack or broken

- The horizontal cross member has dropped or rotted out

- Wire tension disappears within weeks of every re-stretch

You can rebuild an H-brace yourself if you’re handy, but it takes a post hole digger or auger, proper 6 inch or larger posts set 3.5 feet deep, and getting the diagonal wire wrapped in the right direction. Wrap it the wrong way and the brace actually pulls itself apart under load. If that sentence made you squint, this is a good spot to hand it off. Corner work is where most DIY fence repairs go sideways.

We rebuild corners as standalone repairs all the time. Call (254) 870-8898 and we’ll usually have a crew out within the week, same day if you’ve got cattle out.

Here’s what typical repairs run in the Waco area, both if you do it yourself and if you hire us. Your numbers will move with rock, access, and how far gone the fence is.

Repair Typical DIY cost (materials) Typical hired cost

Re-tension one strand, one run $10 to $25 $75 to $150

Replace a T-post $8 to $12 each $15 to $25 each installed

Notice the jump on that last line. Once wire has been re-stretched two or three times, or it’s rusted through its galvanization, repair money starts chasing a fence that’s done. Our rule of thumb: if more than a third of the posts need work or the wire snaps during re-tensioning, put the money toward new fence instead. Our barbed wire fence installation page has current per-foot pricing, and if you’re weighing repair against replacement, the numbers in our rusted barbed wire, repair or replace guide will help you decide.

Marcy Vlasek, north of West, learned that math the honest way. A spring storm dropped a big hackberry limb across her east line and flattened about 60 feet of it. The emergency repair to get her heifers contained ran $480. But the re-stretch showed her 30 year old wire snapping at every splice point, so she put in a quarter mile of new 5 strand that fall for about $3,900 instead of feeding another decade of repair calls.

## How to Keep Barbed Wire Tight Year Round

Tightening the fence is half the job. Keeping it tight is a habit, and it’s a cheap one compared to chasing cattle at midnight.

Walk or ride your lines twice a year. Spring after storm season and late fall before winter is the minimum. You’re looking for leaning posts, slack strands, popped staples, and rubbed spots. Ten minutes per quarter mile.

Keep trees and brush off the line. Limbs are the number one cause of sudden fence damage in our area. Trim anything overhanging the wire.

Watch your water gaps. Creek crossings blow out in every big rain and put slack into the adjoining runs. Check them after every gully washer.

Fix small slack immediately. One loose strand teaches cattle to test the fence. Once they learn a fence gives, they never unlearn it, and you inherit a herd of fence testers.

Control hogs where you can. Feral hogs root under bottom strands and shove through fences, and the damage compounds fast. USDA’s Wildlife Services program tracks the problem and offers control resources at usda.gov.

Mind the seasons. Wire contracts in cold and relaxes in heat, so a fence stretched banjo tight in a January cold snap can overload your braces, and one stretched in August will hang loose come winter. Aim for firm and singing, not violin string.

Make those checks a habit and most sag never gets past the ten minute stage.

## When to Stop Patching and Call a Pro

Plenty of fence work is honest DIY territory. Re-clipping T-posts, driving new staples, splicing a break, tightening a strand or two. Have at it.

But call in help when you hit any of these:

- Corner and brace rebuilds. Bad geometry here undoes everything downstream.

- Full re-stretches of old wire. Brittle wire under tension is genuinely dangerous. It snaps without warning and it does not care where your face is.

- Fence along a road. In most of Texas outside open range areas, a stock law county puts the liability on you if your cattle get onto the highway. That fence needs to be right, not close.

- Storm damage with livestock loose. Speed matters more than pride. Get the animals contained.

- Anything involving rock. If your post holes need a breaker bar or a hydraulic auger, your weekend is better spent elsewhere.

We’re a Waco crew that builds and repairs farm and ranch fence for a living, licensed and insured, with a 24/7 emergency line for storm damage and cattle-out calls. If your fence is more sag than steel, get a free written estimate or call (254) 870-8898. If barbed wire has you rebuilding every few years and you’re ready for something that shrugs off cattle entirely, take a look at our pipe fence options while you’re at it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How tight should barbed wire fence be?

Snug enough that each strand runs straight between posts with no visible dip, and gives a light ring when you pluck it. You should be able to deflect it an inch or so with firm hand pressure. Tighter than that starts straightening barbs, thinning wire, and overloading your corner braces, which shortens the life of the whole fence.

### Can I re-tighten old rusty barbed wire, or does it need replacing?

You can usually get one more stretch out of wire with surface rust if the metal underneath is still sound. But if the wire snaps during tensioning, flakes when you bend it, or breaks at old splices, it’s done. At that point every repair dollar is borrowed time, and new Class 3 galvanized wire is the cheaper path over the next 20 years.

### How much does it cost to fix a sagging barbed wire fence?

Small fixes are cheap: $75 to $150 to have a strand professionally re-tensioned, and $450 to $800 to rebuild a failed corner brace, which is the most common root cause. A full re-stretch of a quarter mile of 4 strand fence typically runs $500 to $900 around Waco. If the wire or a third of the posts are shot, replacement at $2.50 to $4.50 per foot usually beats repeated repairs.

### How often should I check my fences for sag?

Walk or ride every line at least twice a year, spring and fall, plus a quick check after any major storm. Catching one loose strand early is a ten minute fix. Missing it for a season teaches your cattle to push fences, and that habit costs far more than the wire ever will.
