## How to Fix a Sagging Gate That Drags or Won't Latch (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/fix-sagging-ranch-gate/)

> Gate dragging or won't latch? Learn how to fix a sagging gate step by step, from hinge fixes to resetting posts, with real costs from a Waco fence pro.

Fence Repair

# How to Fix a Sagging Gate That Drags or Won't Latch
Published August 17, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

You know the move. Lift the gate with your hip, drag it through the dirt, then fight the chain for ten seconds before it finally catches.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

You know the move. Lift the gate with your hip, drag it through the dirt, then fight the chain for ten seconds before it finally catches. Every rancher in Central Texas has done that dance, and most of us have done it for two years longer than we should have.

Here’s the good news. Learning how to fix a sagging gate is one of the easiest wins in ranch maintenance. Most sagging gates come down to one of three problems: loose hinges, a leaning post, or a bent gate. Two of those you can usually fix yourself in an afternoon for under $50. The third one depends on how bad it is.

We build and repair ranch gates all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, so we’ve seen every version of this problem there is. This guide walks you through diagnosing your gate, fixing what you can, and knowing when it’s time to put the wrenches down and call somebody.

## Why Ranch Gates Sag in Central Texas

A gate is basically a lever hanging off a post. A 16-foot tube gate weighs 90 to 130 pounds, and all of that weight pulls sideways on the hinge post every minute of every day. Add a few thousand swings, some kids riding it like a carnival ride, and a bull scratching his neck on it, and something’s going to give.

Around Waco, our soil makes it worse. Most of the ground here is expansive blackland clay. It swells when it rains and shrinks hard in a drought, and that movement works posts loose the same way it cracks slab foundations. The Natural Resources Conservation Service maps most of McLennan County as clay or clay loam, and if you’ve ever dug a post hole in August, you don’t need a map to believe it.

So before you touch a wrench, figure out which of these is your actual problem:

- Hinge trouble. The hinge pins have worked loose, worn out, or were never adjusted right. The post is still plumb.

- Post trouble. The hinge post is leaning toward the gate. Put a level on it and you’ll see it fast.

- Gate trouble. The gate frame itself is racked or bent, usually from an animal or a tractor bumping it.

Stand back 20 feet and look at the gate closed. If the post is straight but the latch end droops, it’s hinges or the gate. If the whole post tilts, that’s your answer, and it’s a bigger job.

If you’d rather have somebody else sort it out, that’s what we’re here for. Request a free written estimate or call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll take a look, usually within a couple of days.

## How to Fix a Sagging Gate at the Hinges First

Always start with the hinges, because it’s the cheapest fix and it solves the problem more often than people expect. Standard tube gates hang on J-bolt hinges: a lag-thread or bolt-through pin on the post, with a hinge strap on the gate that drops over it. There’s adjustment built into that system that most folks never use.

Step 1: Tighten everything. Grab a wrench and snug up every hinge bolt on the post and both hinge straps on the gate. Loose hardware alone causes a surprising amount of sag. Five minutes, zero dollars.

Step 2: Adjust the bottom hinge. Here’s the trick most people miss. On a typical setup, the top hinge pin points down and the bottom pin points up, which keeps the gate from being lifted off. To raise a drooping latch end, you usually want to move the bottom hinge pin outward, away from the post, or move the top pin in tighter. That tips the whole gate back and lifts the far end. Turn the lag-style pins a few rotations at a time and check your latch height as you go.

Step 3: Replace worn pins. Hinge pins wear egg-shaped over the years, and the gate settles into the slop. New J-bolt hinge pins run $8 to $15 apiece at any farm store in Waco. Swap them and you’ve often bought yourself another decade.

Step 4: Check the hinge spacing. Hinges mounted too close together give the gate less leverage to resist sag. If yours are less than about two-thirds of the post height apart, spreading them out helps more than any other single adjustment.

Kenny Braswell out in Crawford called us last spring convinced he needed a whole new entrance because his 16-foot gate was dragging a trench in the caliche. His post was dead plumb. We replaced two worn hinge pins, re-tensioned the bottom hinge, and squared the latch. Total bill was $165, and he’d been quoted $1,100 by somebody else for a full rebuild he didn’t need.

## Fixing a Sagging Gate Post That Leans

If the level shows your hinge post tipping toward the gate, no amount of hinge tweaking will hold for long. The post is the foundation, and you fix foundations first.

Check for rot or rust at the ground line. Wood posts fail where they meet the soil, not at the bottom. Shove a screwdriver into the post right at grade. If it sinks in easy, the post is done and needs replacing, not straightening. We cover the warning signs in our post on fence post rot. Steel pipe posts can rust through at the same spot, so give them a hard look too.

Straighten and re-tamp a sound post. If the post is solid but leaning, dig out one side, pull the post plumb with a come-along anchored to your truck hitch or a solid tree, then pack the hole in 3 to 4 inch layers of damp soil or crushed base, tamping each layer hard. Tamped properly, that post will hold better than a sloppy concrete pour. Our guide on leaning fence posts walks through this in more detail.

Upgrade the post if it keeps failing. A gate post is not a line post. For a 14 to 16 foot gate, you want at least a 2 7/8 inch steel pipe post or a 6 to 8 inch treated wood post, set 36 to 48 inches deep in concrete. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension’s fencing guidance (agrilifeextension.tamu.edu) makes the same point: braced, deep-set gate and corner posts are what keep a fence system standing. In our blackland clay, we also bell the bottom of the hole slightly so the seasonal shrink-swell can’t jack the post up. If your soil turns to concrete every summer, our article on fence posts in clay soil explains what’s happening underground.

Lisa Hutyra near Valley Mills had a gate post that leaned a little more every year no matter how many times her son straightened it. It was a 4-inch wood post carrying a 16-foot gate, way undersized. We pulled it, set a 2 7/8 inch pipe post 4 feet deep in concrete with an H-brace tie-back, and rehung her gate. That job ran $425 and the gate hasn’t moved an inch since, through one wet winter and one brutal August.

## When the Gate Itself Is Bent or Racked

Sometimes the post is plumb, the hinges are tight, and the gate still droops. Sight down the top rail from the hinge end. If it curves or the frame looks like a parallelogram instead of a rectangle, the gate is racked.

You’ve got three options:

Cable and turnbuckle kit. An anti-sag kit runs $15 to $30. Run the cable from the top hinge corner down to the bottom latch corner, then crank the turnbuckle until the latch end lifts. This works well on wood gates and lightly sagged tube gates. It will not fix a gate with a crushed or kinked rail.

Weld it back square. A racked tube gate can sometimes be pulled square and reinforced with a welded diagonal brace. If you or a neighbor can weld, it’s an hour of work. If you’re paying a mobile welder around Waco, expect $125 to $250.

Replace the gate. A new 16-foot tube gate costs $140 to $260 depending on gauge. If your gate has been run over, wallowed out at the hinges, and welded twice already, replacement is usually the cheaper path over the next ten years. Heavier 2-inch pipe gates cost more but shrug off cattle abuse, which is why we build them onto most of our pipe fence projects.

One more thing worth saying: a gate that sags open is how cattle end up on the county road, and in Texas that can become your legal problem in a hurry. We’ve written about what happens when cattle keep getting out, and a bad gate latch is one of the top causes we find.

## What Sagging Gate Repairs Cost: DIY vs Hiring It Out

Here’s what the common fixes run in the Waco area right now. DIY numbers are parts only. Pro numbers are our typical range, parts and labor, and every job gets a free written estimate first.

Repair DIY Parts Cost Pro Cost (Typical) Time

Two honest notes on that table. First, the cheap fixes at the top solve most sagging gates, so start there. Second, if you’re fixing the same gate for the third time, the math flips. Sink money into the foundation once instead of the band-aid three times. Our ranch fence cost guide breaks down where repair money goes furthest across a whole place.

Danny Kolar, who runs cows on 60 acres outside West, kept a tally one year: three trips to the farm store, two Saturdays, and about $190 in parts fighting a gate on a rotted post. He finally had us replace the post and hang a new heavy gate for $780, and his words were “should’ve called you the first Saturday.”

## When to Stop DIY and Call a Fence Pro

Most of what’s in this article is safe, sensible work for anyone comfortable with hand tools. But there are lines worth respecting.

Call a professional when:

- The post needs replacing and it’s tied into a brace or corner. Cut the wrong thing and you can drop tension on a quarter mile of wire.

- You’re dealing with heavy pipe gates. A 16-foot pipe gate can weigh 250 pounds or more. That’s a two-man lift with pinch points that will take a finger.

- Welding is involved and you don’t weld. Galvanized coatings give off toxic fumes when burned, and gate repairs are not the place to learn.

- The gate is part of an entrance with masonry columns or an automatic opener. Openers have force settings and safety requirements that matter, especially with kids and livestock around.

- Utilities might be in the ground. Any time you’re digging a new post hole near your entrance, call 811 first. It’s free and it’s the law in Texas.

And if the sag is really a symptom of a whole entrance that’s past its prime, it might be time to think bigger. A properly built entrance with concreted pipe posts and a heavy gate is a 30-year fix, not a 3-year one. Take a look at our ranch entrance gates page to see what that looks like on places around Central Texas.

Either way, you don’t have to guess. Call (254) 870-8898 and we’ll tell you straight whether your gate needs a $15 part or a new post. If it’s a $15 part, we’ll say so.

## Keep It From Sagging Again

A few habits make gate repairs stick:

- Latch it every time. A gate left swinging in the wind works its own hinges loose.

- Don’t let anybody ride it. One kid swinging on the latch end applies more leverage than a year of normal use.

- Add a gate wheel on long spans. For 16-foot gates that only open one direction on firm ground, a $30 gate wheel carries the latch-end weight and takes nearly all the load off the hinge post.

- Check hinge bolts twice a year. Add it to your spring and fall walk-around along with your wire and braces. Our ranch fence maintenance checklist has the full routine.

- Grease the pins. A shot of grease on each hinge pin once a year cuts wear and keeps the swing smooth.

Ten minutes of prevention twice a year beats an afternoon with a come-along every time.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I fix a sagging gate without taking it off the post?

Usually, yes. Hinge tightening, hinge pin adjustment, and cable anti-sag kits can all be done with the gate hanging. You’ll only need to lift the gate off if you’re replacing hinge pins entirely or resetting the post, and even then a floor jack or a helper makes it a quick job.

### How much does it cost to fix a sagging ranch gate?

Most sagging gates in the Waco area cost between $95 and $350 to fix professionally, depending on whether it’s a hinge adjustment or a post reset. DIY parts for the common fixes run $15 to $50. A full post replacement with a new heavy gate typically lands between $500 and $1,000.

### Why won’t my gate latch in summer but works fine in winter?

That’s our blackland clay talking. Expansive clay soil shrinks in dry heat and swells when it rains, which moves your posts enough to throw off latch alignment by an inch or more. A deeper-set post in concrete with a slightly belled hole rides out the movement, and an adjustable latch gives you seasonal wiggle room.

### Is a gate wheel a good fix for a sagging gate?

It’s a good assist, not a cure. A gate wheel carries the latch-end weight and works well on firm, level ground where the gate swings one direction. It won’t help on rough or muddy ground, and it doesn’t fix the underlying hinge or post problem, so do the diagnosis first and add the wheel as insurance.

## Buying a Ranch? How to Inspect Fences Before Buying Land (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/inspect-fences-before-buying-land/)

> Learn how to inspect fences before buying land in Central Texas. Spot rotted posts, rusted wire, and bad corners, then use real repair costs to negotiate.

Maintenance

# Buying a Ranch? How to Inspect Fences Before Buying Land
Published August 20, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

The prettiest 100 acres in McLennan County can hide $40,000 in fence problems behind one nice entrance gate.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

The prettiest 100 acres in McLennan County can hide $40,000 in fence problems behind one nice entrance gate. Most buyers walk the house, kick the barn door, test the well, and never look at the one improvement that runs the entire perimeter of the property.

That’s why you should inspect fences before buying land, every time, before you sign anything. Fence on a working ranch isn’t decoration. It’s infrastructure, and it’s priced like infrastructure. New barbed wire runs $2 to $4 per foot installed around here, and a mile of fence is 5,280 feet. Do that math on a quarter section and you’ll see why a “small fence issue” can swing a deal by five figures.

This guide walks you through exactly what to check, what it costs to fix, and how to use what you find at the negotiating table. It’s the same walk-through we do for buyers all over Central Texas.

## Why Fence Condition Should Change Your Offer Price

Sellers and listing agents love the phrase “fenced and cross-fenced.” It sounds complete. It tells you nothing about condition.

A property can be fenced and cross-fenced with 60-year-old rusted wire on rotted cedar posts, and the listing reads exactly the same as a place with five-year-old fence on steel pipe corners. One of those properties is ready for cattle the day you close. The other one needs a six-figure rebuild before you can safely turn out a single cow.

Here’s the frame we give buyers: fence is either an asset or a liability, and it’s never neutral. Good fence adds real value because you don’t have to build it. Bad fence subtracts value twice. You pay to tear it out, then you pay to build new. Removal alone often runs $1 to $2 per foot before the first new post goes in the ground.

There’s a liability side too. In most of Texas, if your cattle get onto a highway and cause a wreck, you can be on the hook if you knew your fence wouldn’t hold them. The Texas Agriculture Code, Chapter 143, covers fencing and stock law rules, and most of McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties operate under local stock laws that put the burden on the livestock owner. Buying a place with failing perimeter fence means buying that risk on day one.

If you’re under contract on a place right now and the clock is ticking, we can walk it with you. Call Brazos Ridge Fence Co. at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll give you a free written estimate you can take straight into negotiations.

## How to Inspect Fences Before Buying Land: The Perimeter Walk

You can’t inspect fence from the truck. Plan to walk or ATV the full perimeter, and budget about an hour per mile if you’re actually looking. Bring gloves, a camera, and something to take notes on. Here’s what to check, in order of what matters most.

Corners and braces first. The corners carry the whole fence. Look for H-braces at every corner and gate: two solid posts, a horizontal rail, and a diagonal wire. If corners are single posts leaning toward the pull of the wire, the fence is failing from the inside out no matter how straight the line looks today. Our post on H-brace fence corners shows what a correct corner looks like.

Grab the posts. Push hard on every tenth line post. A sound post barely moves. A post that wobbles like a loose tooth is rotted at the ground line, and rot rarely hits just one. Kick the base of wood posts and probe at soil level with a screwdriver. Soft, punky wood means the clock’s already run out.

Read the wire. Surface rust is normal on older galvanized wire. Deep rust, flaking, and wire that snaps when you flex it is dead wire. Check tension by pressing down on the top strand between posts. More than a few inches of give means stretching at minimum, replacement more likely.

Walk every water crossing. Creeks and draws are where fences die first. Look for water gaps, the sacrificial fence sections built across drainages. Missing or blown-out water gaps are open doors for your cattle and the neighbor’s.

Check the gates. Swing every gate. Dragging, sagging, or wired-shut gates tell you how the whole place was maintained.

## Red Flags That Cost Central Texas Buyers Real Money

We’ve walked a lot of pre-purchase properties around Waco, and the same handful of problems shows up over and over. Three quick stories from folks we’ve worked with show what’s at stake.

The Crawford wire that looked fine from the road. Dale Hutchins was under contract on 160 acres outside Crawford last spring. From the county road, the perimeter looked straight and tight. Walking it, we found about two miles of barbed wire so rusted it snapped by hand, hung on cedar posts from the 1970s. Replacement bid came to $38,000. Dale took our written estimate to the seller and negotiated $18,500 off the purchase price. One afternoon of walking fence paid him more per hour than most people make in a year.

The Valley Mills buyer who skipped the walk. A young couple bought 90 acres near Valley Mills without ever checking the fence, trusting “fenced and cross-fenced” in the listing. Six weeks after closing, their cattle pushed through a rotted stretch and ended up on FM 56 at night. Nobody got hurt, and they were lucky. They ended up spending about $31,000 replacing the worst 1.4 miles of perimeter, money they could have negotiated off the price if they’d found it first. If you’ve ever dealt with cattle getting out of a fence, you know that phone call is the worst one a rancher gets.

The Lorena water gap. Maria Salazar was looking at 45 acres south of Lorena with a creek through the back. The listing photos never showed the creek crossing, and there’s a reason. Both water gaps were gone, washed out years earlier, and the erosion had taken two line posts on each bank with it. That was a $4,800 fix, and she got the seller to cover it at closing because she asked before she signed.

The pattern in all three: the fence problems were findable in an afternoon, and every dollar identified before closing was a dollar of leverage.

## What Fence Repairs Actually Cost Around Waco

Numbers make negotiations. Here’s what common fixes and replacements run in our area right now. These are typical installed ranges for McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and your terrain, rock, and brush can move them.

Problem Found Typical Fix Cost Range

Loose or sagging wire, posts sound Re-stretch and re-staple $0.50 to $1.00 per ft

Scattered rotted posts Replace posts, reuse wire $25 to $45 per post

Failed corner or gate brace Rebuild H-brace $250 to $450 per corner

Blown-out water gap Rebuild water gap $800 to $2,500 each

Rusted, brittle wire on sound posts Re-wire 5 strands $1.50 to $2.50 per ft

To put that in acreage terms, a square 100-acre tract has about 5,280 feet of perimeter. Full barbed wire replacement on that tract lands somewhere between $13,000 and $24,000. A square 500-acre place has roughly 2.2 miles of perimeter, and full replacement can clear $50,000 before you touch a single cross fence.

For deeper breakdowns, our ranch fence cost guide covers pricing by fence type, and if the place needs new perimeter wire, our barbed wire fence installation page explains exactly what a properly built fence includes. When you’re deciding whether old wire is worth saving, read rusted barbed wire: repair or replace before you commit either way.

## Fence Inspection Before Buying Land: The Legal Questions

The physical walk is half the job. The paperwork is the other half, and it trips up more buyers than bad posts do.

Is the fence on the property line? Old ranch fences wander. Some were built along the easiest ground, not the surveyed line, and some have been “fence line” boundaries for so long that nobody remembers where the deed line runs. Compare the survey to the fence on the ground. If they disagree by more than a few feet, get it resolved in writing before closing, not after. Texas has specific rules on boundary fences, and our post on who pays for a fence between neighbors in Texas covers how shared fences work here.

Who maintains shared fences? Ask the seller directly about any agreements with neighbors, written or handshake. A neighbor who has “always kept up the south fence” may feel differently about a new owner.

Does the fence support the ag exemption? If the property carries an agricultural valuation, the fence has to actually hold livestock for the grazing use to be real. A perimeter that can’t turn a cow can put an ag exemption at risk, and losing one can mean thousands per year in extra property taxes plus rollback exposure. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid guidance on ag land management and is worth a read before you buy.

Are there easements through the fence? Pipeline, utility, and access easements often come with gates or gaps that third parties can open. Know where they are and who has keys before you stock the place.

## When to Stop Guessing and Bring in a Fence Contractor

You can do the basic walk yourself, and you should. But bring in a professional before closing when any of these are true.

First, the numbers are big. If your walk turns up more than a few hundred feet of questionable fence, you need a real bid, not a guess, because your negotiation is only as strong as the estimate behind it. Second, the terrain is rough. Creek crossings, rock, and heavy cedar change costs fast, and eyeballing them gets expensive. Third, you’re planning a different operation than the seller ran. Fence that held gentle cows won’t necessarily hold goats, horses, or keep feral hogs out, and it definitely won’t hold deer if you’re thinking high fence.

And know your own limits after you buy. Re-stapling loose wire is a fine weekend job. Rebuilding corners, stretching new wire, and setting posts in creek banks is hard, dangerous work where wire under tension can cut you badly. When a repair involves a failed brace, a washed-out crossing, or anything near a road where livestock could get loose, stop and call a pro.

We do free pre-purchase fence walk-throughs and written estimates all over Central Texas, from China Spring to West to McGregor. Reach out here or call (254) 870-8898, and if you ever close on a place and wake up to cattle on the road, that same number is our 24/7 emergency line.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How long does it take to inspect the fences on a property?

Plan on about an hour per mile of fence if you’re checking posts, wire, corners, and water crossings properly. A square 100-acre tract has roughly a mile of perimeter, so most small tracts are a half-day job including cross fences. Larger ranches are usually a full day, and it’s worth every hour given what’s at stake.

### Can I use fence problems to negotiate the purchase price?

Yes, and it’s one of the most effective negotiation tools rural buyers have. Get a written repair or replacement estimate from a licensed contractor, then present it as a price reduction or a seller-paid repair credit at closing. Sellers respond to documented numbers far better than to “the fence looks rough.”

### What’s the biggest fence red flag when buying ranch land?

Failing corners and braces, because everything else hangs on them. Rusted wire on solid corners can sometimes be re-wired affordably, but leaning corners mean the fence’s skeleton is gone and a full rebuild is usually coming. Rotted posts across long stretches are a close second.

### Should the seller fix the fence before closing, or should I take a credit?

Take the credit or price reduction in most cases. A seller fixing fence on their way out the door has every reason to do it as cheaply as possible, and you’ll live with the result for decades. With cash in hand you control the materials, the contractor, and the quality of the build.

## No Climb Horse Fence: What It Costs and When It Is Worth It (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/no-climb-horse-fence/)

> What no climb horse fence costs per foot in Central Texas, where it beats pipe or barbed wire, and when it is not worth the money. Free on-site estimates.

Cost Guide

# No Climb Horse Fence: What It Costs and When It Is Worth It
Published September 8, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A horse can put a front hoof through a loose field fence at midnight and turn a cheap roll of wire into a vet bill that runs into four figures.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A horse can put a front hoof through a loose field fence at midnight and turn a cheap roll of wire into a vet bill that runs into four figures. That is the whole argument for no climb horse fence, and it is why 2x4 inch woven mesh ends up on most of the horse jobs we bid around Waco.

The question is not whether it works. It works. The question is whether it is worth the extra dollars per foot on your place, or whether your horses would be just as safe behind something cheaper.

This article gives you the real per-foot range in McLennan, Bosque and Falls counties, three jobs we have priced and what moved the numbers, and an honest read on where no-climb is overkill. If you would rather skip to a number for your own fence line, call (254) 870-8898 and we will come walk it with you. On-site estimates are free.

## What No Climb Horse Fence Costs Per Foot Around Waco

No-climb belongs to the net wire family, so we price it against our net wire fence band of $3.50 to $8 per foot installed. Horse-grade 2x4 mesh sits at the upper end of that band, and there is a reason for it.

Horse mesh is heavier wire, tighter spacing, and usually a taller roll than the field fence a cattleman puts up. It also gets built differently. Horse fence gets more posts, better corners, and almost always a top rail or a sight board, because bare mesh at nose height is close to invisible to an animal at a dead run.

So when we talk about no-climb on a horse place here, we are usually talking about the $6 to $8 end of that range, and the low end of the band is field fence for goats and cattle, not a finished horse fence.

Fence type Installed cost per foot Where it fits

5-strand barbed wire $2.50 to $5.50 Cattle on acreage. Not a horse fence.

Net wire / field fence $3.50 to $8 Horse-grade 2x4 no-climb sits at the top of this band

Welded pipe fence $12 to $28 Pens, arenas, road frontage, stud runs

Custom ranch entrance $5,000 to $25,000 and up The gate at the road

Those are our installed numbers, materials and labor together, for this three-county area in 2026. You will see rolls of 2x4 no-climb on the shelf at farm stores for somewhere around $400 to $700 for a 330-foot roll, and that is worth knowing, but treat it as a general materials-only figure and not as a quote from us. It leaves out posts, braces, gates, clips, fuel, and the two or three days it takes to build the thing straight and tight.

Full pricing for everything else we build is on our ranch fence cost page.

## Why the 2x4 Mesh Is the Whole Point

Everything expensive about this fence comes back to one measurement. A 2 inch by 4 inch opening is smaller than a hoof. That is it. That is the feature you are paying for.

Standard field fence has openings that get wider as you go up the roll, and a horse pawing at grass on the other side can slide a foot through and then panic when it will not come back out. Hinge-joint field fence also mashes down when a 1,100 pound animal leans on it, and once it is bellied out it stays bellied out. If you want the detail on wire construction, our guide to fixed knot versus hinge joint covers how the two behave under pressure.

The other half of a horse fence is visibility, and mesh alone does not solve it. We put a wood rail, a pipe rail, or a wide sight board on top of nearly every no-climb fence we build. It gives the horse something to see and it keeps the top of the mesh from getting rolled over by a horse reaching across.

This is not just our opinion. Penn State Extension’s fence planning guide for horses walks through the same reasoning on mesh size and visibility, and the University of Georgia Extension horse fencing material comparison lays out the tradeoffs by material if you want a second read before you spend the money.

One more thing worth saying plainly. No fence makes a horse injury-proof. A horse that is determined enough will find a way to hurt itself on the safest fence ever built. What no-climb does is take the two most common wrecks, a leg through the fence and a run-through, and make them a lot less likely.

## Three Jobs, Three Very Different Numbers

The per-foot range only tells you so much. Here is how it actually lands on real ground in this area.

A 12-acre horse place outside Lorena. Two mares and a gelding on flat blackland, roughly 2,900 feet of perimeter. Wood corners, treated line posts on 10-foot spacing, 60-inch 2x4 no-climb with a treated top rail, one 12-foot gate and one walk gate. That job prices at the top of the net wire band, call it $20,000 to $23,000, because the top rail and the tighter post spacing are doing real work. Straight field fence with no rail on the same line would have come in several thousand dollars lower and would have been a worse fence for those horses.

A limestone hill section near Valley Mills where every post has to be drilled. Only about 600 feet of new fence, but the auger will not touch it. Every hole gets a rock drill, and some posts get set in concrete because there is nothing to backfill with. Short runs like this land at the ceiling of the band, around $8 per foot, so roughly $4,800 for a stretch that would have cost half that on soft ground a mile away. Rock is the single biggest surprise on bids in the Bosque County hills, and it is why we walk the line before we quote. More on that in our notes on setting fence posts in rocky ground.

A 40-acre place west of Crawford with a split approach. Pipe on the two working pens and the 300 feet of road frontage where the horses crowd the gate, no-climb on the rest of the perimeter. At $12 to $28 per foot, the pipe sections alone can run from about $5,000 to $12,000 depending on pipe size and rail count, so putting pipe everywhere was never on the table. Concentrating it where the horses push and where traffic goes past is how most people around here get the safety they want without doubling the budget. Our pipe fence page covers that comparison in more depth.

If you want a number for your own place rather than somebody else’s, call (254) 870-8898. We will walk the line with you and price what is actually there.

## When a No-Climb Horse Fence Is Worth the Money

There are four situations where we will push hard for no-climb, and we will say so on the walk.

Small acreage with real stock density. Five to twenty acres with two or more horses on it means the horses are in contact with the fence every day. They will lean on it, paw at it, and reach through it for the neighbor’s grass. On a small tract you also have more corners per foot of fence, which raises the per-foot price on any fence type, so the gap between cheap and good is smaller than people expect.

Foals and young stock. A foal will find the one gap you did not think about. A 2x4 mesh does not have one.

Road frontage. A horse loose on a farm-to-market road at dusk is somebody’s worst day. Where a pasture touches pavement, we want either no-climb with a rail or pipe, and we would rather build pipe.

Boarders, lesson horses, or anything you do not own. When somebody else’s horse is behind your fence, the calculation changes. That is a business decision as much as a fencing one.

## When It Is Not Worth It

We would rather tell you to spend less than sell you a fence you do not need.

If you are running two quiet, older horses on 60 acres of open pasture, no-climb around the whole perimeter is a lot of money spent on wire those horses will never touch. A well-built smooth wire or field fence on the back sections, with no-climb only around the barn trap and the lots where the horses actually spend their time, gets you most of the safety for a fraction of the total.

If you run cattle and horses together, no-climb still works, but a lot of folks here are better served by a good field fence with a hot wire offset at chest height. The offset keeps horses off the fence entirely, which protects both the animal and the wire. It is not free, and an electric fence is only as good as the ground rods and the weekly habit of checking it, but it is cheaper per foot than rebuilding a mile of mesh.

And if the budget genuinely is not there yet, do not build half a bad fence around everything. Fence the small lot properly, run the perimeter in something economical, and upgrade in sections as money allows. Our ranch fence cost breakdown is honest about what each compromise actually costs you.

Everything we install for horses, mesh, pipe, rail, gates and pens, is on the horse fence page.

## What Moves Your Price Up or Down

Two horse places a mile apart can get bids that differ by 30 percent on the same footage. Here is what does it.

Rock. Limestone and caliche mean drilling instead of augering. That is time, wear, and sometimes a second machine on site.

Brush. A clean line is a cheap line. Heavy cedar or mesquite along the route has to come out before the first post goes in, and it will show up as its own item on the estimate.

Corners, gates and braces. Every corner and every gate opening needs a proper H-brace or a pipe corner. A square 12-acre tract has far more corners per foot than a mile of straight perimeter, which is why small jobs cost more per foot than big ones.

Top rail choice. Treated wood, pipe, or none at all. This is often the single biggest lever you control on a horse fence bid.

Access. Line we can drive a truck along costs less than line we have to carry material into by hand.

Water crossings. Any creek or draw needs a water gap built so it fails safely in a flood instead of taking out 200 feet of good fence with it.

None of that gets settled over the phone. Call (254) 870-8898 or ask for a free on-site estimate, and we will walk your fence line, look at what is in the ground, and give you a number you can build a budget around. We cover McLennan, Bosque and Falls counties.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does no climb horse fence cost per foot in Central Texas?

Installed, it falls in our net wire band of $3.50 to $8 per foot, and horse-grade 2x4 mesh sits at the upper end of that range. Most finished horse fence with a top rail lands around $6 to $8 per foot on normal ground. Rock, heavy brush, and a high number of corners and gates push it toward the ceiling.

### Is no-climb fence better than pipe for horses?

Pipe is tougher and more visible, and it is the better answer for pens, arenas and road frontage at $12 to $28 per foot. No-climb costs a fraction of that and is safer than any wire fence with gaps a hoof can fit through. Most horse places here end up with both, pipe where the horses crowd and mesh on the rest of the perimeter.

### Do I need a top rail on a no climb horse fence?

We recommend one on nearly every horse fence we build. Mesh alone is hard for a horse to see at speed or in poor light, and the top edge takes a beating from horses reaching over it. A wood or pipe rail solves both problems and adds a few dollars per foot.

### How long will a no-climb fence last around Waco?

A class 3 galvanized mesh on sound posts is a long-term fence here, and we expect to see two decades or more out of one that is built tight and kept clear of standing water. Lifespan depends on your soil, your drainage, and how hard your stock uses it. Posts almost always fail before the wire does, so post choice and how they are set matter more than the brand on the roll.

## What Pipe Fencing Really Costs Per Foot in the Waco Area (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/pipe-fence-cost/)

> What pipe fencing really costs per foot in Waco and Central Texas: real job prices, new vs used oilfield pipe, labor, and smart ways to trim your quote.

Cost Guide

# What Pipe Fencing Really Costs Per Foot in the Waco Area
Published July 24, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Call five fence companies around Waco and you'll get five different numbers for the exact same stretch of pipe fence. One guy says $14 a foot, another says $28, and nobody explains why.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Call five fence companies around Waco and you’ll get five different numbers for the exact same stretch of pipe fence. One guy says $14 a foot, another says $28, and nobody explains why. That gap isn’t dishonesty. It’s the difference between pipe sizes, new steel versus used oilfield pipe, and how much welding your layout actually needs.

So let’s put real numbers on it. In McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, pipe fence cost per foot typically runs $12 to $28 installed, depending on the style. That’s a wide range, and this article breaks down exactly where your project will land inside it. We build pipe fence every week around Waco, China Spring, Crawford, and Lorena, so these are the numbers we quote off our own trucks, not something scraped from a national calculator.

## Pipe Fence Cost Per Foot: The Short Answer

Here’s what the common pipe fence styles run installed in Central Texas right now. These prices include materials, labor, welding, and paint. They assume decent access and normal soil, which we’ll get into later.

Pipe Fence Style Installed Cost Per Foot Best For

Pipe top rail with T-posts and net wire $12 - $16 Perimeter fence with a clean look

Pipe posts with 4 or 5 strands of barbed wire $12 - $16 Cattle perimeter that outlasts wood posts

Pipe posts with cable (3 to 5 runs) $14 - $18 Horse-safe pastures on a budget

Full pipe fence, used oilfield pipe, 3 rail $16 - $22 Working pens, arenas, road frontage

Full pipe fence, new steel, 4 to 5 rail $22 - $28 Show-front fencing, horse facilities

A quick gut check on totals. At $20 a foot, a quarter mile (1,320 feet) of pipe fence runs about $26,400. A 300 foot road frontage at the same rate is $6,000. Pipe fence isn’t cheap, but it’s the last fence most people ever build on that line.

If you want a number for your specific place instead of a range, that’s what we’re here for. Call us at (254) 870-8898 or request a free written estimate. We’ll walk the line with you and price it foot by foot, no pressure and no rounding up.

## What Drives Pipe Fencing Cost Up or Down

Two neighbors on the same road can get quotes $8 a foot apart and both quotes can be fair. Here’s what actually moves the number.

Pipe size and wall thickness. Most fence around here uses 2 3/8 inch pipe for posts and top rail, with 1 to 1 1/4 inch for fill rails. Step up to 2 7/8 inch posts for a heavy cattle setup and you add $2 to $4 a foot in steel alone. Wall thickness matters just as much as diameter. We covered the tradeoffs in our guide to what size pipe to use for a pipe fence.

New steel vs used oilfield pipe. This is the single biggest lever on price, and it gets its own section below.

Number of rails. Every rail you add is more pipe, more welding time, and more paint. Going from 3 rails to 5 rails typically adds $4 to $8 a foot.

Corners, gates, and short runs. A long straight run is efficient. A layout with six corners, four gates, and three short segments means more setting, more welding, and more mobilization per foot. Gates are priced separately, and a good pipe entrance can run $1,500 to $6,000 or more. See our ranch entrance gates page for what those setups involve.

Ground conditions. Most pipe posts around Waco get set 3 feet deep in concrete. In the blackland clay east of I-35 that’s routine. Get into the rocky ground around Crawford and Valley Mills and we may be coring rock, which adds drilling time and cost.

Total footage. Setup and mobilization get spread across the job. A 2,000 foot job almost always prices lower per foot than a 250 foot job, sometimes by $4 to $6.

Tearout and brush. If there’s an old fence coming down or a fence line grown up in mesquite and cedar, budget for removal and clearing on top of the build. Old fence tearout typically adds $2 to $5 a foot depending on what’s tangled in it, and heavy brush work is usually billed by the hour with a skid steer. It’s worth doing right, because a clean line makes the new fence faster to build and easier to maintain.

## New Pipe vs Used Oilfield Pipe: Where the Savings Are Real

Used oilfield pipe, often called structural pipe, is drill stem and tubing that’s done its service in the oil patch. It’s heavy, it’s plentiful in Texas, and it usually costs 30 to 40 percent less than new steel of the same size.

Ruben Salazar, who runs cattle on 40 acres outside West, is a good example. He wanted 900 feet of 3 rail pipe along his county road frontage. New steel priced out at $24 a foot, about $21,600. We quoted the same fence in good used 2 3/8 inch drill stem at $18 a foot, or $16,200. That’s $5,400 back in his pocket for a fence that will still outlive both of us.

The catch is that “used pipe” covers everything from excellent to junk. Good drill stem has thick walls with surface rust you can wire brush and paint. Bad pipe has wall loss, splits, and internal scale that bleeds rust through paint for years. We inspect and reject pipe before it ever gets welded on your place. If you’re weighing this choice, read our full breakdown on used oilfield pipe fence before you buy a trailer load off a classified ad.

One more note. New pipe comes with mill specs, so if you want a uniform, dark-painted showpiece along your entrance, new steel gives the cleanest result. For working pens and pasture fence, used pipe is usually the smarter spend.

## Real Pipe Fence Cost Per Foot on Three Local Jobs

Ranges are helpful, but real jobs are better. Here are three from the past year, with numbers.

Crawford: 1,300 feet of cattle fence with pipe posts and barbed wire. Gary Whitlock had cedar posts rotting off at the ground line on his east fence, and his cows knew it. We pulled the old fence, set used pipe posts on 10 foot centers, welded a pipe top rail, and strung 5 strands of new barbed wire. Cost came to $15 a foot, $19,500 total including tearout. That fence will hold cattle for 40 years or more with almost no maintenance.

Valley Mills: 480 feet of pipe and cable for a horse paddock. Dana Kirkpatrick keeps two barrel horses and wanted something safer than barbed wire near the barn. Barbed wire and horses are a bad mix, and vets will tell you the same. We built pipe posts and top rail with 4 runs of smooth cable at $17 a foot, $8,160 total. If you’re fencing for horses, our guide on the best fence for horses walks through why cable and pipe beat wire every time.

West: Ruben’s 900 feet of 3 rail used pipe from the section above, at $18 a foot. Six months in, he’s already asked us to price the next stretch. The road frontage looks sharp, and he told us the fence has already survived one neighbor’s loose bull leaning on it without so much as a bent rail.

Notice the spread: $15, $17, and $18 a foot for three different jobs, all fairly priced. Style and materials set the number, not the zip code.

Want to know where your project lands? Get a free written estimate and we’ll give you a firm per-foot price on paper, broken out so you can see exactly what you’re paying for.

## Where the Money Actually Goes: Materials vs Labor

On a typical $20 per foot pipe fence, here’s roughly how the dollar splits.

Steel is the biggest line, usually 40 to 50 percent of the job. Pipe prices track the broader steel market, which is why quotes from two years ago don’t hold today.

Labor and welding run 30 to 40 percent. Pipe fence is a welded product. Every post gets cut, set, plumbed, and every rail gets fitted and welded on both sides. A crew that hurries the welds leaves you with rails that pop loose the first time a bull leans on them.

Concrete, paint, and consumables take the rest. Every post gets concrete. Paint matters more than people think, because primer and a proper topcoat are what keep used pipe from streaking rust.

That’s also why the cheapest bid deserves a hard look. If a quote comes in $5 a foot under everyone else, the money is coming out of pipe wall thickness, weld time, or paint. Ask every bidder the same three questions: what size and wall of pipe, new or used, and how deep the posts are set. If the answers are vague, keep shopping. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid fence planning and cost research at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu if you want a university-backed second opinion on materials and construction.

## How to Bring Your Pipe Fence Price Down

You can’t change the price of steel, but you can control the design. A few honest ways to trim the quote:

Use pipe where it counts, wire where it doesn’t. A lot of our customers put full pipe fence on the road frontage and around pens, then run pipe posts with barbed wire on the back perimeter. You get the strength and the look where people see it, at half the cost on the rest.

Choose used pipe for working fence. As Ruben’s job showed, that’s 25 to 35 percent off with no real loss in service life.

Drop from 4 rails to 3. Three rails hold cattle fine in most setups. Save the 4 and 5 rail builds for horses and show frontage.

Fence more at once. Combining this year’s and next year’s phases into one mobilization usually beats doing them separately.

Check your ag exemption. If your land qualifies for an agricultural appraisal, fencing is part of qualifying ag use in Texas, and materials may qualify for the sales tax exemption. The Texas Comptroller explains the ag/timber exemption at comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/ag-timber.

A word on DIY. Plenty of ranchers can weld, and if that’s you, you already know what your time is worth. But pipe fence is unforgiving work. It means hundreds of overhead and vertical welds in the heat, trenching and coring near buried utilities, and handling 30 foot joints of steel that can hurt you fast. If you don’t weld regularly, or your line involves rock, slopes, or a water gap, stop and call a professional. A failed weld on a corner post can let a whole stretch of fence go slack, and loose cattle on a road is a liability you don’t want. Our pipe fence installation page covers how we build them and what’s included in every quote.

If cattle are already testing a weak spot, don’t wait on it. Our emergency line runs 24/7 for cattle-out and storm damage calls: (254) 870-8898.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does pipe fence cost per foot in the Waco area?

Most pipe fencing in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties runs $12 to $28 per foot installed. Pipe top rail with wire sits at the low end, full 4 or 5 rail new steel at the top. The most common builds we do land between $16 and $22 a foot.

### Is used oilfield pipe good enough for a fence?

Good used drill stem is excellent fence material and saves 25 to 35 percent versus new steel. The key is inspection, because wall loss and splits hide under surface rust. We check every load before it’s welded, and we reject pipe that doesn’t measure up.

### How long does a pipe fence last?

A properly welded and painted pipe fence set in concrete will last 40 to 70 years in Central Texas, and often longer. Compare that to wood posts that can rot out in 15 to 25 years in our clay soils. Repaint every 10 to 15 years and it’ll outlast the mortgage.

### Is pipe fence worth the cost compared to barbed wire?

For pure pasture perimeter, barbed wire on T-posts is cheaper up front at $2.50 to $5.50 a foot. Pipe wins where strength, safety, or looks matter: pens, horse areas, entrances, and road frontage. Many owners split the difference with pipe up front and wire on the back fence, and that combination is what we quote most often.

## Ranch Entrance Gate Cost: From Basic Pipe to Custom Iron (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/ranch-entrance-gate-cost/)

> Real ranch entrance gate costs in Central Texas, from $1,200 pipe gates to $30,000 custom iron entries. See what drives the price and where to save money.

Cost Guide

# Ranch Entrance Gate Cost: From Basic Pipe to Custom Iron
Published August 21, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A ranch entrance gate can cost you $400 or $40,000, and both numbers are real. The gap between a plain tube gate hung on two posts and a custom iron entry with stone columns and a solar opener is...

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A ranch entrance gate can cost you $400 or $40,000, and both numbers are real. The gap between a plain tube gate hung on two posts and a custom iron entry with stone columns and a solar opener is enormous, and most landowners around Waco have no idea where their project falls on that line until the quotes come in.

This guide breaks down ranch entrance gate cost the way we quote it here in Central Texas. You’ll see real prices for basic pipe gates, welded entrances, automated systems, and full custom iron builds, plus the factors that push a bid up or down. By the end you’ll know what a fair number looks like before a contractor ever steps on your place.

## What a Ranch Entrance Gate Costs in Central Texas

Here’s the short version. Most working ranch entrances in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties land between $1,200 and $8,500 installed. That covers a quality gate, two properly set posts or columns, and the labor to hang it so it swings true for decades.

Below that range you’re looking at a farm-store tube gate on T-post hinges, which works fine for interior pastures but tends to sag at a main entrance that sees daily traffic. Above that range you’re into automation, masonry columns, overhead signs, and custom ironwork, where $15,000 to $30,000 builds are common on larger properties along the Bosque River and out toward Crawford.

Three things set the price more than anything else:

- Gate type and width. A 12 foot single swing is cheap. A 20 foot double swing with a cantilever slide option is not.

- What holds it up. Two pipe posts in concrete might run $600. Two rock columns with lighting can run $9,000 by themselves.

- Power and automation. Openers, solar panels, keypads, and safety sensors add $2,500 to $7,000 to almost any entrance.

If you want a number for your specific driveway instead of a range, call us at (254) 870-8898 or request a free written estimate. We measure, we quote in writing, and the price doesn’t wander after you sign.

## Basic Pipe Gates: The Workhorse Option

For most ranches, a welded pipe gate is the right answer. It handles cattle pressure, survives a bump from the stock trailer, and doesn’t rot. A basic pipe entrance around Waco typically runs:

- 12 foot single swing gate, installed: $1,200 to $2,200

- 16 foot single swing, installed: $1,600 to $2,800

- 20 foot double swing (two 10 foot leaves), installed: $2,400 to $4,200

Those numbers include heavy-wall pipe posts set 3 to 4 feet deep in concrete, which matters more than the gate itself. A 16 foot gate hanging on a shallow post will drag the ground within two years in our clay soils. That’s the single most common problem we get called out to fix, and we wrote a whole guide on it: how to fix a sagging ranch gate.

Danny Kolar, who runs cows on 90 acres outside Crawford, is a good example of the basic build done right. He’d been fighting a rusted-out farm-store gate that dragged so badly he had to lift it to latch it. We set two 4 inch heavy-wall posts in concrete, hung a 16 foot welded pipe gate with adjustable hinges, and added a chain latch he can work from horseback. Total: $2,650. That gate will outlive his truck.

A lot of our pipe gates are built from used oilfield pipe, which keeps material cost down without giving up strength. If you’re curious how that works, read our breakdown of used oilfield pipe fence, because the same economics apply to gates. And if you’re pricing the whole perimeter at the same time, our pipe fence installation page covers per-foot numbers for matching fence.

Entrance Type Typical Installed Cost Best For

Two notes on reading that table. First, “installed” is doing heavy lifting. ## Custom Iron and Automated Ranch Entrances

This is where ranch entrance gate cost climbs fast, and where the money either shows every day or disappears into mistakes.

Custom iron gates run $6,000 to $15,000 installed for the gate itself, depending on size, design complexity, and finish. Plasma-cut silhouettes, your brand or ranch name worked into the panel, and powder coating over galvanizing all add cost. Powder coat over bare steel without proper prep is the classic corner-cut, and it’ll be peeling in three Texas summers.

Stone or brick columns add $3,500 to $9,000 per pair around here, more if you want lighting inside them. Columns need real footings. We’ve torn out leaning columns that were set on 8 inches of concrete like a mailbox post.

Automation adds $2,500 to $7,000 depending on power. If grid power is near the entrance, you’re at the low end. If the nearest outlet is 800 feet up the driveway, solar is usually cheaper than trenching wire, and modern solar openers handle a heavy iron gate fine.

The Machacek family, west of West off the Tokio Road area, went the full route last spring: 20 foot custom iron double gate with their brand cut into the panels, limestone columns, solar opener with keypad and exit sensor. Final invoice was $24,800. That sounds like a lot until you price what a comparable build runs in the Hill Country, where the same entrance quotes closer to $35,000.

On the smaller end, Karen Delgado in Valley Mills kept her existing 16 foot pipe gate and just added automation. Solar opener, keypad post, and a fire department access switch came to $3,900. Same daily convenience, fraction of the cost, because her gate and posts were already plumb and heavy enough to automate.

One safety note that isn’t optional. Automated gates are machines that can trap and crush. Openers need properly adjusted force limits and obstruction sensors, especially with kids and livestock around. This is not the place for a bargain opener and a YouTube install. If you’re adding automation, have it done by someone who installs them weekly. Get a free automation quote here and we’ll tell you straight whether your existing gate can carry an opener or needs new posts first.

## What Drives Your Gate Price Up or Down

When two neighbors get quotes that differ by thousands for “the same gate,” these factors usually explain it.

Post depth and soil. Central Texas clay swells and shrinks with moisture, and it will heave a shallow post out of plumb. Proper entrances get posts 3 to 4 feet deep with real concrete footings. The USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service has good soil survey data for our counties at nrcs.usda.gov if you want to see what you’re building on. Hit rock instead of clay and drilling cost goes up, not down.

Gate width. County fire codes and common sense both favor wide entrances. A 16 foot minimum opening handles trucks and trailers. Go 20 feet if hay equipment or a gooseneck comes through regularly. Wider gates weigh more, need heavier posts, and cost more per foot than fence ever will.

Setback from the road. A gate set 30 to 50 feet off the county road lets you pull a truck and trailer fully off the pavement while the gate opens. That setback means wing fencing on both sides, which adds cost but prevents the daily hazard of a trailer hanging out in traffic.

Power distance. Every foot of trench for electrical service costs money. Past a few hundred feet, solar almost always wins.

Matching fence. An entrance rarely stands alone. If you’re fencing the front of the property at the same time, combining the work saves mobilization cost. Our ranch entrance gates page covers full entrance packages, and if the whole perimeter is on the table, start with what it costs to fence 10 acres to frame the budget.

Who builds it. A welding shop can build a beautiful gate and still hang it wrong. A handyman can hang it cheap and have it dragging by fall. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid fencing and ranch infrastructure guidance at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu that’s worth reading before you compare bids.

## DIY or Hire It Out?

Plenty of ranchers can hang a gate, and we won’t pretend otherwise. Here’s an honest split.

Reasonable DIY: hanging a tube gate on existing sound posts, replacing hinges and latches, adding a wheel to support a long light gate, painting and greasing. If your posts are plumb and deep, swapping a gate is a Saturday job.

Call a professional: setting entrance posts in expansive clay or rock, hanging anything over 16 feet or over about 250 pounds, any masonry columns, and all automation. Heavy gates hurt people during installation, and a main entrance that fails blocks your only way in and out. If cattle are getting through a failed entrance onto a road, that’s a liability problem on top of a fence problem, and it’s exactly what our 24/7 emergency line exists for.

The math usually favors doing the main entrance right once. We see it constantly: a $900 self-install becomes a $2,400 repair three years later, which is more than the professional install would have cost on day one.

### Is a custom iron entrance worth the money?

It depends on what the property is for. On a working cattle place, a heavy pipe gate does the same job for a fifth of the price. A basic pipe gate takes one day plus concrete cure time, so figure two short visits. Automated entrances usually take two to three days including electrical or solar setup and safety testing. Custom builds with masonry columns run one to three weeks depending on stonework and fabrication lead time, which is often the longest part of the wait.

## Rusted Barbed Wire Fence: When to Repair It and When to Replace It (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/rusted-barbed-wire-repair-or-replace/)

> Is your rusted barbed wire fence worth fixing? A Waco fence contractor explains how to tell surface rust from dead wire, with real repair and replacement costs.

Fence Repair

# Rusted Barbed Wire Fence: When to Repair It and When to Replace It
Published August 20, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Grab a strand of your oldest wire and twist it hard with a pair of pliers. If it snaps like a dry twig instead of bending, you already have your answer, and it's not the cheap one.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Grab a strand of your oldest wire and twist it hard with a pair of pliers. If it snaps like a dry twig instead of bending, you already have your answer, and it’s not the cheap one.

That test settles more arguments than anything else we do on ranch calls around Waco. A rusted barbed wire fence isn’t automatically a dead fence. Plenty of wire out here in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties turned brown twenty years ago and still holds cattle just fine. But there’s a point where rust stops being cosmetic and starts being structural, and guessing wrong costs real money in vet bills, liability, and midnight phone calls about cows on the highway.

This article walks you through how to tell the difference, what repairs actually cost per foot, and when replacement is the smarter spend. If you’d rather have a second set of eyes on it, call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk your fence line with you. The written estimate is free.

## Why Barbed Wire Rusts Faster in Central Texas

All barbed wire rusts eventually. The zinc galvanizing on the wire sacrifices itself to protect the steel underneath, and once the zinc is gone, the steel starts eating itself. How fast that happens depends on three things: the quality of the original coating, your local conditions, and what’s touching the wire.

Cheap Class 1 galvanized wire carries roughly a third of the zinc that Class 3 wire does. In our climate, Class 1 can show red rust in 8 to 12 years. Class 3 often runs 25 to 30 years before serious corrosion sets in. We covered the full breakdown in our post on Class 3 galvanized wire, but the short version is that the coating you can’t see is the biggest factor in how long your fence lasts.

Central Texas conditions pile on from there. Creek bottoms and low spots along the Brazos and Bosque hold humidity that eats zinc. Livestock rubbing on wire wears the coating off at pressure points. Brush and grass growing up into the fence line trap moisture against the strands, which is one more reason clearing your fence line pays for itself. And anywhere wire touches bare dirt, a rock, or an old steel post with no coating left, you get a corrosion hot spot.

One more culprit people miss: wildfire and old burn piles. Heat from a grass fire cooks the galvanizing right off wire, even wire that looks fine afterward. If a pasture burned in the last few years, check that wire first.

## How to Tell Surface Rust From Wire That’s Failing

Brown wire scares landowners more than it should. Here’s how we actually judge a rusted barbed wire fence in the field, and you can do every one of these checks yourself with gloves and a pair of fencing pliers.

The look test. Uniform light brown or orange surface rust with the wire still full thickness is mostly cosmetic. What you’re looking for is pitting, flaking, scale that comes off in chunks, or spots where the wire is visibly thinner than the rest of the strand. Thinning means the steel itself is going, not just the surface.

The twist test. Grip a strand mid-span and bend it back and forth with pliers. Good wire bends and springs. Brittle wire snaps after one or two flexes. If wire snaps in three or four random spots along a stretch, that whole stretch is done.

The tension test. Try to tighten a strand with a fence stretcher. Healthy rusted wire takes tension and holds it. Far-gone wire breaks the moment you put a real pull on it. If you can’t tension it, you can’t fence with it, period.

The barb test. Wiggle a few barbs. On badly corroded wire, barbs rust through at the wrap point and spin loose or fall off. A barbed wire fence without barbs is just wire, and cattle figure that out fast.

Check the hot spots first. Water gaps, creek crossings, shaded creek bottom stretches, splices, and anywhere wire wraps a corner post. Wire almost never fails evenly. It fails at the wet spots and the stress points, sometimes ten years before the rest of the fence.

While you’re out there, look at what’s holding the wire up. Rusted wire on rotten posts is a replacement conversation no matter what the wire says. Our posts on fence post rot and leaning fence posts cover how to check those.

## When Repairing a Rusted Barbed Wire Fence Makes Sense

Repair is the right call more often than people think. If the twist test passes on most of the fence and the failures are localized, you can buy years for hundreds of dollars instead of thousands.

Repair makes sense when:

- Rust is surface-level and the wire still takes tension

- Breaks are clustered in one or two spots, like a water gap or a shaded bottom

- Posts and braces are still solid

- The fence is under 20 years old with Class 3 wire, or under 12 with cheap wire

- You need the pasture holding cattle this week, not next month

The standard fix is cutting out the bad section, splicing in new wire with a proper figure-eight or Western Union splice, and re-tensioning the strand. Done right, a splice is as strong as the original wire. Done with a granny knot and a prayer, it’s the first thing that pops next time a bull leans on it.

Here’s what that looks like in real dollars. Last fall, Danny Kolar, who runs about 40 cow-calf pairs outside Crawford, called us convinced he needed a full quarter mile of new fence because the whole stretch had gone brown. We walked it with him. The wire passed the twist test everywhere except a 90-foot run through a creek crossing where the bottom two strands had rusted through. We rebuilt the water gap, spliced in new Class 3 wire on all five strands through the low spot, and re-tensioned the rest. Total bill: about $640. The quote he was bracing for was north of $4,000.

That’s the value of diagnosing before you spend. If your problem is slack wire rather than broken wire, our guide to fixing a sagging barbed wire fence walks through re-tensioning step by step.

One honest warning about repairs on old wire: every splice you add is a future weak point, and stretching brittle wire to tension often snaps it somewhere new. If you find yourself splicing the same stretch three times in a year, the fence is telling you something. Ready for a straight answer on yours? Request a free written estimate and we’ll tell you plainly whether it’s worth patching.

## When Replacement Is the Smarter Money

At some point, patching a rusted barbed wire fence is like putting new tires on a truck with a cracked frame. Here’s where we draw the line after years of these calls.

Replace when:

- Wire snaps the twist test in multiple random spots, not just wet areas

- Barbs are rusting off or spinning loose along whole stretches

- You’ve made more than three or four repairs on the same run in two years

- Wire is 25 to 30 plus years old, which you can often date by the fence style and splice pattern

- Posts and braces are failing along with the wire

- You’re switching livestock, running goats or horses, or leasing to someone who needs a fence that actually holds

There’s also the liability math nobody likes to think about. Under Texas law, if your cattle get onto a highway through a fence you knew was failing, you can be on the hook for the wreck. The cost difference between patching dead wire and replacing it looks a lot smaller next to one collision claim. We broke down the legal side in cattle on the road liability in Texas.

Marcy Duron learned the math the expensive way on her place near Lorena. She’d spent roughly $1,100 over three years on piecemeal repairs to a half mile of 1980s-era wire, and it still let two heifers out onto Old Lorena Road one night last spring. No wreck, thank God, but two hours of flashlight cowboying convinced her. We pulled the old wire and rebuilt the half mile with new Class 3 barbed wire on a mix of T-posts and treated wood line posts for about $8,700. Her words afterward: she wished she’d skipped the $1,100 in patches and put it toward the rebuild two years sooner.

Full replacement is also your one chance to fix everything at once: post spacing, corner braces, gates, and strand count. If you’re rebuilding anyway, look at our posts on H-brace fence corners and how many strands of barbed wire you actually need before you buy materials.

## Repair vs. Replace: The Real Numbers

Prices below reflect what we’re seeing on jobs across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties in 2026. Your terrain, access, and old fence removal can move these up or down.

Situation Typical Fix Ballpark Cost

Slack but healthy rusted wire Re-tension strands, replace clips $0.25 to $0.75 per foot

Broken strands in one spot Cut out and splice new wire $75 to $200 per repair visit

Bad 100 to 300 ft section (water gap, burn area) Replace wire in that section only $2 to $4 per foot

A mile of fence is 5,280 feet, so a full rebuild runs roughly $13,000 to $26,000 per mile depending on terrain and materials. That number makes some folks sit down, which is exactly why catching wire early, when re-wiring on good posts is still an option, matters so much. Frank Villareal, who runs stockers on leased ground near Valley Mills, used that early window to his advantage in March. His wire was going brittle but his 15-year-old T-posts and cedar corners were solid. Re-wiring 2,600 feet on the existing posts ran him about $5,200. Waiting five more years, until the posts followed the wire, would have pushed the same stretch past $9,000.

## How to Keep the New Wire From Rusting Early

Whether you repair or replace, a few habits stretch the life of every foot of wire you own.

Buy Class 3 galvanized from the start. It costs maybe 10 to 15 percent more per roll and routinely doubles the life of the fence. It’s the cheapest insurance in fencing.

Keep wire off the ground and out of the brush. Vegetation holds moisture against strands and shortcuts the coating. Shred or spray your fence lines once a year.

Walk your fences twice a year, spring and fall, and after every big storm. Catching one rusted-through splice in October beats chasing cattle in January. Our ranch fence maintenance checklist gives you a simple routine, and Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid fencing guidance for landowners at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu.

And a safety note that comes from experience: wear heavy gloves and eye protection every time you handle old wire. Rusty barbed wire under tension can snap and whip, and a puncture from a dirty barb is a genuine tetanus risk. The CDC recommends adults keep their tetanus booster current every 10 years, and doubly so for anyone working fence lines. Details are at cdc.gov/tetanus. If a stretch of old wire is under heavy tension, tangled in brush, or woven through trees, stop and call a pro. That’s not a DIY situation, and we’ve pulled wire out of more than one landowner’s forearm story.

Some folks rebuilding high-traffic areas skip wire corrosion worries entirely by going to pipe fencing around pens and entrances, then running new barbed wire on the perimeter. That combination handles Central Texas weather about as well as anything.

The bottom line: brown wire that bends is a repair, brown wire that snaps is a replacement, and the twist test costs you nothing. If you want a straight answer on your fence with numbers attached, call (254) 870-8898 or request your free written estimate. And if cattle are already out through a failed stretch, that same number reaches our 24/7 emergency line.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is rusted barbed wire still safe to use?

Often, yes. Surface rust alone doesn’t kill wire, and plenty of brown fences hold cattle for another decade. The test that matters is whether the wire still bends without snapping and holds tension when stretched. If it passes both, it’s serviceable. If it snaps or the barbs are rusting off, it’s a hazard to livestock and people and should come out.

### How long does a barbed wire fence last before rust wins?

Cheap Class 1 galvanized wire typically gives you 15 to 20 years in Central Texas, sometimes less in creek bottoms. Class 3 galvanized commonly runs 25 to 40 years. Posts, brush contact, and livestock pressure move those numbers a lot, which is why two fences built the same year can age completely differently. See our full breakdown in how long a barbed wire fence lasts.

### Can I splice new wire into old rusted wire?

Yes, if the old wire still takes tension. A proper figure-eight splice joining new Class 3 wire to sound older wire is a standard, reliable repair. The catch is that stretching brittle wire often snaps it somewhere else, so if you get two or three new breaks while fixing one, the strand is telling you it’s done. At that point, replace the whole run instead of chasing breaks.

### What does it cost to replace a rusted barbed wire fence per foot?

If your posts are still good, re-wiring five strands usually runs $1.50 to $2.50 per foot in our area. A full tear-out and rebuild with new posts runs about $2.50 to $5 per foot, plus $0.50 to $1.50 per foot if you want the old fence removed and hauled off. Terrain, gates, and access move the price, which is why we put every number in a free written estimate before work starts.
