## Safest Fence for Horses: Injury Risk Ranked by Fence Type (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/safest-fence-for-horses/)

> Which fences cut, trap or spook a horse, ranked by injury risk, with installed cost per foot for horse fence around Waco, McLennan, Bosque and Falls counties.

Well Care

# Safest Fence for Horses: Injury Risk Ranked by Fence Type
Published September 10, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A horse can be grazing quietly at dusk and tangled in wire before full dark. The fence does not have to fail for that to happen. It only has to be the wrong fence for the animal standing behind it.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A horse can be grazing quietly at dusk and tangled in wire before full dark. The fence does not have to fail for that to happen. It only has to be the wrong fence for the animal standing behind it.

Picking the safest fence for horses is really a question about injury risk. Every fence type carries a different kind, and the difference between a bad night and a routine one usually comes down to what the fence is made of, whether the horse can see it, and whether a leg fits through it.

We build ranch fence around Waco, in McLennan, Bosque and Falls counties, and we build plenty of barbed wire for cattle people. We do not put horses behind it. What follows is how the common fence types rank on risk, what each costs per foot installed, and where the money is worth spending on a horse place.

If you already have horses standing behind old wire and it worries you, do not wait on an article. Call (254) 870-8898 and we will come walk the line with you. On-site estimates are free.

## The Four Ways a Fence Injures a Horse

Almost every fence injury we get called out to look at falls into one of four buckets. Knowing which bucket a fence puts you in tells you more than anything printed on the wire tag.

Laceration is the one everybody pictures. Barbs and cut wire ends slice hide. A horse that hits barbed wire at speed does not bounce off it. The wire wraps, the horse fights it, and the barbs work like a saw against a moving leg. Serious wire cuts run into the thousands of dollars in vet work, and that is a general figure from the horse world, not anything we can quote.

Entrapment is the quiet one. A hoof goes through a 6 inch mesh opening, or under a slack bottom wire, or over a low top wire while the horse is reaching for grass on the neighbor’s side. The horse pulls back, the wire tightens, and most of the damage happens in the fight rather than the first contact. That is why cheap field fence hurts horses even though the wire on it is perfectly smooth.

Then there is impalement and blunt trauma. Uncapped T-post tops, broken wood rails and open pipe ends all punch instead of cutting. This is what turns an ordinary spook into a chest wound.

The fourth one is simple impact. Thin wire disappears at dusk, in rain and against tall grass, and a horse running from something it fears will go straight through a fence it never saw. Visibility is a safety feature. That is the whole argument for a top rail or a sight board on an otherwise ordinary wire fence.

## Injury Risk by Fence Type: How the Common Options Rank

Here is how the fence types we see on Central Texas horse places compare. Cost columns are our installed price bands for this market, and they move with terrain, brush, and how much of the line is corner and gate work.

Fence type Worst injury risk Visibility to a horse Installed cost per foot

5-strand barbed wire Deep laceration, wire wrap Poor $2.50 to $5.50

Hinge-joint field fence, 6x6 openings Hoof and leg entrapment Fair $3.50 to $8

No-climb 2x4 horse mesh with top rail Bruising, little laceration risk Good with a rail $3.50 to $8, horse-grade mesh at the top of that band

Fixed-knot game fence, 8 ft Entrapment where openings are large Fair $4.50 to $10

Welded pipe Blunt impact, scrapes Very good $12 to $28

Electric poly tape or rope Tangling if a line breaks Good with wide tape Added to another fence and priced with the job

Wood or vinyl rail Splinters, broken rail edges Very good Not a line we build, so treat any figure you see as a general estimate

Two things stand out on that table. The safest fences are not the cheapest ones, and the gap between a cattle fence and a horse fence is roughly the difference between $3 per foot and $8 per foot on the same run of line.

The other thing worth saying plainly: cost per foot on any of these depends on the ground. Blackland clay that a post driver walks through prices very differently from limestone that has to be drilled.

## Why No-Climb Mesh Is the Safest Fence for Horses on Pasture

For most horse places under 50 acres around here, 2 inch by 4 inch woven mesh with a top rail is the honest answer. The openings are too small for a hoof to pass through, there is nothing sharp on it, and the top rail gives the horse something to see from a dead run.

The specification matters more than the brand. We build these at 48 to 60 inches tall, with the bottom of the mesh set close to the ground so a horse that rolls near the fence cannot get a leg under it. Class 3 galvanizing is worth the small upcharge in our humidity. Wood or pipe posts on the corners and a real H-brace at every pull, because a horse fence that sags is a horse fence with a gap in it.

A 12-acre horse place outside Lorena is a fair example. Roughly 3,000 feet of perimeter in tired 5-strand barbed wire, two mares, and an owner who had already paid for one wire cut. Horse-grade no-climb with a top rail put that job at the top of our net wire band, around $7 to $8 per foot, so about $21,000 to $24,000 for the whole perimeter.

That was more than the owner wanted to spend in one season, so we phased it. The horse trap and the paddock nearest the barn went first, about 900 feet at roughly $6,300 to $7,200, and the back line stayed barbed wire until the following year with the horses kept off it. Phasing a horse fence is normal and it beats doing the whole thing in the wrong material. More on the mesh itself is in our no-climb horse fence guide, and the service page for this work is horse fence in Waco.

## Pipe Fence: The Safest Option Where Horses Get Crowded

Injury risk is not evenly spread across a property. Most horse wrecks happen where horses are gathered, sorted, fed, or worked, which is exactly where wire is least appropriate.

Welded pipe is the safest thing we build for pens, alleys, round pen walls, and stallion runs. A horse that hits pipe slides along it instead of tangling in it, there is nothing to cut with, and the fence does not deform when a 1,100 pound animal leans on it. It also does not care about a horse cribbing, pawing or kicking at it.

The price is the tradeoff. Welded pipe runs $12 to $28 per foot installed depending on pipe diameter, rail count and how much gate work is in it. That is real money on a perimeter, which is why the usual layout on a horse place is pipe where horses are handled and no-climb on the pasture line.

A small place near China Spring did exactly that. About 220 feet of pipe around the working pens and the alley to the trailer, then mesh on the pasture perimeter. The pipe section landed in the middle of that band, in the neighborhood of $4,000 for the pens, and it will outlive everything else on the property. Details are on our pipe fence and corrals and working pens pages.

If you are trying to decide where pipe earns its price on your place, that is a walk-the-fence-line conversation rather than a phone quote. Ask for a free on-site estimate and we will price it in sections so you can see what the safety is costing you per foot.

## The Fences Behind Most of the Wrecks

Barbed wire is a good cattle fence. A 300-acre cattle lease west of Crawford is exactly where it belongs: five strands, T-posts on 12 foot spacing, wood corners, $2.50 to $5.50 per foot or roughly $13,200 to $29,000 per mile depending on the ground and the brush. Cattle are thick hided and slow to panic, and the barbs teach rather than injure.

Horses are the opposite animal. They run first, they run into things, and their skin tears. Penn State Extension says it plainly in its fence planning guide for horses, and University of Georgia Extension reaches the same conclusion in its bulletin Fences for Horses. This is not a fencing contractor’s opinion, it is the standing recommendation from the extension services.

The second common problem is cattle-grade hinge-joint field fence used on a horse pasture. It looks like the right idea, and it is smooth wire, but 6 inch by 6 inch openings in the upper part of the roll are big enough for a hoof and small enough to trap it. Cattle fence and horse fence come off different rolls for a reason, and the roll is where the safety difference lives.

Third is a single strand of hot wire on step-in posts used as a real fence rather than as a training aid. Electric is a psychological barrier, not a physical one. It works well on top of a solid fence to keep horses off it, and it fails badly as the only thing between a spooked horse and a county road. We cover the details, including grounding problems in dry ground, in electric fence for horses.

Fourth, and the cheapest to fix, is uncapped T-posts. Caps or post sleeves are a few dollars per post and they remove an impalement risk entirely. If nothing else on this page gets done this month, do that one.

## Where Safe Fences Still Fail

A well-specified fence still hurts horses if the details are wrong, and the details are where corners get cut on a low bid.

Gates are the first place to look. A tube gate with wide horizontal spacing is a leg trap for a horse that paws at it, and the gap between the gate end and the post is where hooves get caught. On horse gates we either fill the gate with mesh or keep the frame tight to the post. Corners are the second place, because a horse that gets pushed into a sharp corner by a pasture mate has nowhere to go.

Ground conditions drive both cost and safety here. A limestone hill section near Valley Mills is a good example: about 1,400 feet where nearly every post had to be drilled rather than driven. Rock work put that run at the top of the net wire band at roughly $8 per foot, where the same fence on flat blackland clay would have come in nearer $5.50. Shortcutting post depth in rock is how you get a fence that leans in two years, and there is more on that in fence posts in rocky ground.

Our clay does its own damage. It shrinks in drought, opens cracks around posts, then swells when the rain comes back, and a fence that was tight in May can be loose in September. On horse fence that matters more than on cattle fence, because a sagging top rail or a slack mesh is exactly what a leg goes over or through.

Walk your fence line twice a year with a pair of fencing pliers and look for three things: slack in the mesh, wire ends that have worked loose, and posts that have started to lean. Anything you can move with one hand, a horse can move with its chest. Full price bands for every fence type we build are on the ranch fence cost page, and if you want a number for your own place, call (254) 870-8898 and we will come look at it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is barbed wire ever safe for horses?

No, and the extension services have been consistent about this for decades. Barbed wire is a proper cattle fence and we build a lot of it, but on horses it causes wrapping lacerations that are expensive at best and career-ending at worst. If barbed wire is what you have, the practical step is to fence the horses off it with a safer interior line rather than trusting the horses to respect it.

### How tall should a safe horse fence be?

For most riding horses, 54 to 60 inches at the top wire or rail. Ponies and minis can be kept in lower fences, but the risk is a horse getting a leg over a low top wire, so we would rather build to 60 inches on any line a horse can reach across at a neighbor’s pasture. Height matters less than the size of the openings and whether the horse can see the fence.

### Can I make my existing fence safer without replacing it?

Often, yes. Capping T-posts, adding a visible top rail or a wide electric tape at chest height, tightening slack mesh, and filling gate openings all reduce risk for a fraction of a rebuild. Whether that is enough depends on what the fence is made of, so it is worth having someone walk the line with you before you spend money on either option.

### What does the safest horse fencing cost per foot around Waco?

Horse-grade no-climb mesh with a top rail sits at the upper end of our net wire band, $3.50 to $8 per foot installed, with most horse jobs landing at the top of that range. Welded pipe runs $12 to $28 per foot and is usually reserved for pens and working areas. Final numbers depend on terrain, brush, corner and gate count, so we quote after walking the line, not before. If you are comparing options first, the best fence for horses guide sets them side by side.

## Setting Fence Posts in Clay Soil: A Central Texas Blackland Guide (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/fence-posts-in-clay-soil/)

> Blackland clay swells, shrinks, and heaves fence posts out of line. Here's how Central Texas ranchers set posts in clay soil so they stay put for decades.

Ranch Fencing

# Setting Fence Posts in Clay Soil: A Central Texas Blackland Guide
Published August 13, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Ever set a corner post plumb and tight in March, then come back in August to find it leaning like it had a rough night? That's not bad luck.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Ever set a corner post plumb and tight in March, then come back in August to find it leaning like it had a rough night? That’s not bad luck. That’s Blackland clay doing what Blackland clay does, and if you’re setting fence posts in clay soil anywhere around Waco, Crawford, or West, the dirt itself is the biggest variable in whether your fence lasts 30 years or 3.

We build fence in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, which means almost every hole we dig goes into some of the most expansive soil in the country. Houston Black clay, the stuff most of the Blackland Prairie sits on, can swell and shrink enough to crack slab foundations. A fence post doesn’t stand a chance against it unless you set it right.

This guide covers how deep to go, when concrete helps and when it hurts, why corners fail first, and what all of it costs. Real numbers, real jobs, no fluff.

If you’d rather skip the digging altogether, call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll come look at your place. Written estimates are free.

## Why Fence Posts in Clay Soil Lean, Heave, and Snap

Blackland clay is what soil scientists call expansive. It’s loaded with clay minerals that soak up water and swell, then give that water back in a drought and shrink. The ground around your post isn’t sitting still. It’s breathing, slowly, a few inches at a time.

Here’s what that does to a fence:

It heaves posts up. When wet clay swells, it grabs whatever’s in it and pushes. A post set 24 inches deep can get jacked up an inch or two per season. Over five years, your wire goes slack, your post wobbles, and your fence line looks like a picket of drunks.

It lets posts lean. In a dry summer, clay shrinks and pulls away from the post, leaving a gap around it. Then a wet norther blows through, water runs down that gap, softens the bottom of the hole, and the post tips the first time a 1,300 pound cow scratches on it.

It snaps rigid assemblies. Clay doesn’t push evenly. One side of a braced corner swells more than the other, and something has to give. Usually it’s a rail weld or a brace pin.

The zone doing all this movement is roughly the top 8 to 15 feet of soil, but the worst action is in the top 3 to 4 feet. That’s exactly where your fence post lives. You can’t stop the clay from moving. You can only build so the movement doesn’t matter, and that’s what the rest of this guide is about.

We wrote more about diagnosing tilted posts in our post on leaning fence posts, so if your fence is already crooked, start there.

## Know Your Dirt Before You Dig

Not every acre in Central Texas is the same. Head west of the Bosque River toward Crawford and Valley Mills and you start hitting shallow limestone. Stay east and south, around Lorena, West, and most of the flat farmland in McLennan and Falls counties, and you’re in deep black clay.

You can check your exact soil for free using the USDA Web Soil Survey. Type in your property, and it’ll tell you whether you’re on Houston Black, Heiden, Branyon, or something friendlier. If the report says “very high shrink-swell potential,” everything in this article applies to you double.

Here’s why it matters in dollars. Dale Kubacek runs about 60 cows outside West, and he set his own corner posts three separate times over four years. Tamped earth the first time, a bag of sackcrete the second, a bigger post the third. Every spring the corner leaned again and his wire went slack. He finally had us rebuild both corners with deep-set pipe and proper H-braces for $2,800, and those corners haven’t moved through two wet winters and one brutal drought since. He spent close to $900 in posts, concrete, and weekends before that, all of it wasted because the holes were never deep enough for that dirt.

Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension has good general guidance on livestock fencing if you want the academic version at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu. The short version for our area: know whether you’re fencing clay or rock before you buy a single post, because the two call for completely different setting methods.

## How Deep to Set Fence Posts in Clay Soil

Depth is the whole ballgame in clay. The movement is worst near the surface, so the deeper your post goes, the more of it sits in soil that stays relatively stable. Shallow posts ride the clay like a cork on water. Deep posts anchor below the worst of it.

Here’s what we run on our own jobs in Blackland clay:

Post type Line or corner Depth in clay Typical installed cost

Steel T-post Line post 18 to 24 in driven $6 to $9 each

4 in wood post Line post 30 to 36 in $20 to $32 each

5 to 6 in wood post Corner or brace 42 to 48 in $85 to $150 per assembly post

2 7/8 in pipe Corner or brace 48 in in concrete $150 to $250 per assembly post

4 in pipe Gate or heavy corner 48 to 60 in in concrete $250 to $400 each

A few rules of thumb behind those numbers:

Line posts: a third in the ground, minimum. A 6.5 foot wood line post should have at least 30 inches buried in clay. In sandy loam you might get away with 24. In Houston Black, you won’t.

Corners: half again deeper than you think. Corner and gate posts carry all the wire tension, so they take the movement hardest. We don’t set a corner in clay shallower than 42 inches, and on heavy game fence or long pulls we go to 60.

T-posts are surprisingly good in clay. A driven T-post disturbs almost no soil, so there’s no loose backfill for water to work through. Clay grips the anchor plate tight. That’s part of why the classic Central Texas setup is steel T-post line posts between pipe corners. We compared the options in detail in t-post vs wood post.

Post spacing matters too. In clay we’d rather see posts at 10 to 12 feet than stretched to 15, because when one post heaves, its neighbors carry the load. Our fence post spacing article breaks that down by fence type.

Not sure what your soil needs? Request a free written estimate and we’ll bring the auger out and show you exactly what your dirt looks like at 4 feet.

## Concrete, Gravel, or Tamped Earth: What Actually Holds

This is where most DIY fences in clay go wrong, because the standard internet advice is written for people with normal dirt.

Tamped earth or crushed base. For wood line posts, dry-tamped crushed limestone or the native clay itself, tamped hard in 4 inch lifts, works well. Tamping in lifts is the part everyone skips. Dumping loose dirt in the hole and stomping it twice is how you get a post you can wiggle by hand in a year.

Concrete done wrong. Here’s the trap. A shallow concrete collar in expansive clay makes things worse, not better. The clay grabs that fat concrete ball and heaves the whole thing like a piston. Worse, if you pour a mushroom cap of concrete at the surface, you’ve given the swelling clay a handle to lift with. We pull out heaved concrete footings every month that failed exactly this way.

Concrete done right. For corners, gates, and pipe fence, concrete is still the answer, but it has to be deep and shaped right. The hole should go 48 inches or more, be straight-sided or slightly wider at the bottom than the top, and the concrete should stop 2 to 3 inches below grade with soil over it. That shape resists uplift instead of inviting it. This is standard practice on our pipe fence installations in Waco, and it’s why a properly set pipe corner in clay will outlive the wire strung on it.

Drainage helps everything. A few inches of gravel at the bottom of a wood post hole gives water somewhere to go and slows down rot. In clay, water that gets in a post hole stays there, which is why wood posts rot faster in Blackland soil than the bag label suggests. Pair good drainage with the right post material, because clay plus trapped water will find out quick whether you cheaped out on posts.

Marcy Tullos, who runs goats on 30 acres near Lorena, learned the concrete lesson the expensive way. A handyman set her corner posts with one 50 pound bag each, about 8 inches of concrete sitting near the surface of a 24 inch hole. Two wet springs later, every corner had lifted and her net wire sagged enough that the goats treated it like a suggestion. Redoing six corner and gate assemblies correctly cost her $3,900. The original job had “saved” her about $1,200.

## Bracing and Corners: Where Clay Punishes Shortcuts

In stable soil, a mediocre corner might limp along for years. In expansive clay, the corner is the first thing to fail, because it’s fighting both wire tension and soil movement at the same time.

Every corner and every gate opening in clay needs a true H-brace: two deep-set posts, a horizontal rail, and a diagonal tension wire. The H-brace spreads the pull across two posts and a bigger block of soil, so seasonal movement can’t tip a single post over. We walk through the build step by step in h-brace fence corners.

A few clay-specific bracing notes:

- Make the brace span at least 8 feet. A longer H resists overturning better in soft, wet clay.

- Pipe braces beat wood in heavy clay. Welded pipe H-braces move as one unit, so uneven swelling can’t rack them apart.

- Re-tension in the fall. Clay moves seasonally, so plan to snug your diagonal wires and wire stays once a year. It takes an hour and adds years.

Bracing matters most on long pulls of barbed wire, where a quarter mile of tensioned wire is all anchored to two corners. If those corners creep even a couple inches, you’ll feel it in every strand. That’s the fence style we build most around here, and you can see how we handle it on our barbed wire fence page.

## Drought Cracks, Wet Winters, and When to Call a Pro

Clay problems come in seasons. In a wet winter, posts heave and lean. In a drought, the ground opens up cracks you can drop a hammer into, posts loosen in their holes, and wire tension sags across the whole line.

Last August, Roy Hendricks near Crawford called our emergency line at 6 a.m. because three heifers were standing on FM 185. A drought-loosened line post had given up, the wire dropped, and the cattle walked over it. We had the gap closed that morning and rebuilt 200 feet of line for about $900. The fix that would’ve prevented it, resetting two loose posts the previous fall, would’ve cost him maybe $150.

So walk your fence twice a year, spring and fall. Push on posts, watch for concrete footings showing at the surface, and look for gaps opening around post bases in dry weather.

And know when to stop DIYing. Call a professional when:

- Corners or gate posts are moving. Rebuilding a braced corner right takes an auger that can reach 4 feet, and doing it wrong means doing it twice.

- You’re fencing more than a few hundred feet. Hand-digging 48 inch holes in dry Houston Black clay is genuinely miserable, and a skid steer auger turns a week of pain into a morning.

- Cattle are getting out. That’s a liability problem, not just a fence problem. In most of McLennan County you’re under stock law, and a cow on the highway is your cow. Our emergency line runs 24/7 for exactly this.

- You’re near utilities. Call 811 before any digging, every time. It’s free and it’s the law.

We’re licensed, insured, and we set posts in this dirt every working day. Call (254) 870-8898 or request your free written estimate and we’ll spec the right depth, post, and footing for your exact soil.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How deep should fence posts be in clay soil?

Line posts need 30 to 36 inches in Blackland clay, and corner or gate posts need 42 to 60 inches. That’s deeper than standard advice because the top 3 to 4 feet of expansive clay moves with the seasons. Getting below the worst of that movement is what keeps posts from heaving and leaning.

### Should I use concrete for fence posts in expansive clay?

Yes for corners, gates, and pipe posts, but only if the hole is deep and the concrete stops a few inches below the surface. A shallow concrete collar or a mushroom-shaped cap at grade gives swelling clay something to grab and lift. Deep, straight-sided footings with soil over the top resist heave instead of inviting it.

### Why do my fence posts keep heaving out of the ground?

Expansive clay swells when it’s wet and grips the post or its concrete footing, pushing it upward a little each cycle. Shallow posts and surface-heavy concrete make it worse. The fix is depth, proper footing shape, and in many cases driven T-posts for line posts, since they disturb the least soil.

### Do T-posts work well in Blackland clay?

They work very well as line posts. Driving a T-post leaves no loose backfill, so the clay grips the anchor plate tightly and there’s no easy path for water. Just don’t ask T-posts to do a corner’s job. Corners and gates in clay still need deep-set wood or pipe with H-braces.

## Setting Fence Posts in Rocky Ground West of Waco: What Actually Works (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/fence-posts-in-rocky-ground/)

> Hitting limestone a foot down? Here's how we set fence posts in rocky ground west of Waco, real per-hole costs, and when to quit renting augers and call a pro.

Ranch Fencing

# Setting Fence Posts in Rocky Ground West of Waco: What Actually Works
Published August 14, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Ten inches. That's about how far most rented augers get west of Waco before they hit solid limestone and stop dead, smoking and screaming, with 200 more holes to go.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Ten inches. That’s about how far most rented augers get west of Waco before they hit solid limestone and stop dead, smoking and screaming, with 200 more holes to go.

If you’re trying to set fence posts in rocky ground anywhere around Crawford, Valley Mills, or McGregor, you already know the dirt out here is a thin blanket over rock. Sometimes it’s 18 inches of decent soil. Sometimes it’s 4 inches of caliche over a limestone shelf that laughs at your digging bar.

We build fence in this ground every week. This article covers what’s actually under your pasture, the methods that work in rock, what rock adds to the bill in real dollars, and the point where DIY stops making sense.

## Why the Ground West of Waco Fights Back

Drive west out of Waco on Highway 84 or 6 and you’re climbing onto limestone country. The soils get shallower as you head toward Crawford, Valley Mills, and the Bosque County line. A lot of that ground is mapped as shallow, stony clay sitting right on top of limestone bedrock.

That’s not bad luck on your particular place. It’s the whole region. You can look up your exact tract for free on the USDA Web Soil Survey and see the mapped depth to rock before you ever rent a machine. Ten minutes on that site has saved plenty of our customers a wasted weekend.

The practical problem is simple. A fence post needs depth to hold. For a 5 foot barbed wire fence, we want wood posts about 3 feet in the ground, and corner posts deeper than that. When rock shows up at 10 inches, you can’t get that depth by digging harder. You either go through the rock, into the rock, or you build the fence a different way.

Here’s the part that surprises folks: rock isn’t all bad news. A post drilled and grouted into solid limestone holds better than a post in 4 feet of loose sand. The rock is only your enemy while you’re fighting it. Once the post is in, that same rock is the best anchor in Texas.

If you’d rather skip the fight entirely, we’ll come look at your ground and give you a free written estimate with the rock work priced line by line. Call us at (254) 870-8898 or request an estimate here.

## How the Pros Set Fence Posts in Rocky Ground

There’s no single trick. There are four main methods, and on a typical half-mile job west of Waco we’ll usually use two or three of them on the same fence line.

1. Heavy rock auger on a skid steer. Our first move is a hydraulic auger with carbide rock teeth, running a lot more torque than anything at the rental yard. In fractured or layered limestone, which is most of what’s around Crawford and China Spring, this chews through. It’s slower than dirt digging, maybe 5 to 15 minutes a hole instead of 1, but the hole comes out clean and full depth.

2. Rock drill and pin. When we hit solid, unfractured rock, we switch to drilling a smaller diameter hole into the rock itself. For steel posts and pipe fence, we drill, set the post, and grout it in. A pipe post grouted 12 to 18 inches into solid limestone is about as permanent as fencing gets. This is standard practice on our pipe fence jobs in the western part of the county.

3. Breaker and hand work. Some holes need a hydraulic breaker or a gas-powered jackhammer to bust a ledge, then hand cleanup with a rock bar and spoon. Nobody enjoys it. It’s the right call when a shelf sits at 14 inches with decent digging under it.

4. Above-grade anchoring. On solid caprock where drilling every hole would blow the budget, there are legitimate workarounds: rock cribs at corners, driven pins with welded post plates, and letting the wire spans run longer between anchored posts. These need to be engineered right or the fence sags in a year, but done right they’re a smart money saver.

Which method wins depends on what the rock is doing at each hole, and that changes every 50 feet out here. That’s the honest reason experience matters more in rocky ground than anywhere else.

### A quick story from Crawford

Last spring, Dale H. out past Crawford called us after two ruined weekends. He’d rented a two-man auger twice, $340 total in rental fees, burned up a set of teeth, and had 9 holes to show for a quarter mile of planned barbed wire fence. Rock at 8 to 12 inches the whole run.

We brought the skid steer with the rock auger and the drill. Full-depth holes where the rock was fractured, drilled and pinned posts across about 300 feet of solid shelf. The rock work added roughly $1,100 to what a same-length fence would cost in soft ground, and the whole quarter mile was done in three days. Dale’s words: “I spent $340 learning what y’all charge $1,100 to actually finish.”

## What Rocky Ground Adds to Your Fence Cost

Straight answer: rock usually adds 20 to 50 percent to the post-setting portion of a fence job, and post setting is roughly a third of total cost on a wire fence. Here’s how the per-hole math typically shakes out in our area. These are ballpark 2026 numbers for planning, not a quote.

Method Best for Typical cost per hole Time per hole

Standard auger in soil Normal dirt, no rock $10 to $20 1 to 2 min

Skid steer rock auger Fractured or layered limestone $25 to $50 5 to 15 min

Breaker plus hand digging Rock ledge over diggable soil $40 to $80 20 to 45 min

Core drill, pin, and grout Solid limestone shelf $60 to $120 15 to 30 min

Gate or corner post drilled in rock Entrances, H-braces $150 to $300 each 45 min plus

On a real job, that means a quarter mile of 5-strand barbed wire that runs about $4,500 to $6,500 in friendly dirt might land between $5,500 and $8,500 in rock, depending on how much of the line sits on shelf. For the bigger picture on wire fence pricing, our barbed wire fence cost guide breaks down the full per-foot numbers.

Two things keep rock costs from getting away from you. First, an honest site walk before the quote. We probe the line, mark where the rock starts, and price it by section instead of slapping a blanket “rock fee” on the whole job. Second, smart post layout. Sometimes shifting a corner 20 feet puts it in a pocket of deep soil and saves a $250 drilled corner.

### Valley Mills gate posts, done once

Marcy T. near Valley Mills had a contractor from out of the area set her entrance gate posts in 2024. They hit rock at a foot, shrugged, and set the posts shallow in concrete “mushrooms” sitting mostly above the rock. By late 2025 both posts leaned and her 16 foot gate dragged.

We pulled both posts, core drilled 18 inches into the limestone, grouted in heavier pipe, and rehung her gate. That fix ran $1,850. Drilling them into the rock correctly the first time would have cost her maybe $600 over a standard install. Shallow posts in rock country are the most expensive shortcut there is, and it’s the same failure we walk through in our post on leaning fence posts.

## DIY Fence Posts in Rocky Ground: When to Push On and When to Quit

Plenty of our customers are handy, and if you’ve only got a handful of holes, doing it yourself can make sense. Here’s what actually works with tools you can rent or buy.

T-posts are your friend in shallow rock. A T-post only needs about 18 to 24 inches, and a heavy driver will seat one through caliche and fractured rock that stops an auger. If your line posts can be steel, you’ve solved most of the problem cheap.

Rent the rotary hammer, not just the auger. A big rotary hammer or gas breaker with a spade bit, about $90 to $130 a day, will break a thin ledge the auger can’t. Drill a ring of relief holes, then bust out the middle.

Try moving the hole first. Rock depth changes fast. Probing 2 feet either direction with a digging bar often finds a softer pocket. Your post spacing doesn’t have to be perfect to the inch, so use the soft spots the ground gives you.

Use dry-pack or gravel correctly. In a rock-bottomed hole that’s slightly shallow, tight-tamped crushed rock around the post holds better than a soupy concrete pour. Tamp in 3 inch lifts and check plumb every lift.

Now the quit signals. Stop and call a pro when: your corners and gate posts can’t reach at least 30 inches or solid rock anchorage, because everything else hangs off those; you’re facing more than 15 to 20 rock holes, where rental fees and your weekends pass our per-hole price fast; or you’re renting demolition-class tools you’ve never run. A 60 pound breaker kicking off a hidden ledge can break a wrist, and no fence is worth an ER visit. Same rule if the line crosses anywhere utilities might run: call 811 and wait for locates before any drilling.

One more from China Spring: a customer there spent $610 across three weekends of rentals fighting 14 holes before calling us. We drilled all 14 in one morning for $780. He told us he’d have paid double just for the Saturdays back.

If you’re staring down a long line of rock, get a free written estimate before you burn another weekend. Worst case, you’ll know exactly what the pro option costs and can make a real comparison.

## Bracing and Post Choice When You Can’t Go Deep

Shallow ground changes what a strong fence looks like. Two rules carry most of the weight.

First, corners decide everything. In rock country we either drill corner posts into the limestone or build wider H-brace assemblies so the pull spreads across more anchor points. A wire fence is really just corners with wire stretched between them, and our H-brace corners guide shows why a shallow corner will slowly walk out of the ground under tension no matter how pretty the rest of the line looks.

Second, match the post to the anchorage. Grouted pipe beats wood where rock is solid, because you can drill a small hole for steel where a 10 inch wood-post hole is impractical. Where soil pockets allow full depth, treated wood line posts are still fine. Mixing post types along one line isn’t sloppy out here. It’s how a fence gets built to the ground it’s standing on, and Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension’s fencing resources back up the same principle: design to your site, not to a catalog picture.

Get the corners anchored in rock, put steel where the shelf is solid and wood where the dirt is deep, and a fence west of Waco will outlast one built in soft ground. The rock that fought you going in is the thing holding it all together for the next 30 years.

Ready to fence rocky ground without the guesswork? Call Brazos Ridge Fence Co. at (254) 870-8898 for a free written estimate anywhere in McLennan, Bosque, or Falls County. We probe the line, price the rock honestly, and put it all in writing.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How deep should fence posts be in rocky ground?

Aim for the same holding power, not the same number. In soil we want line posts around 30 to 36 inches and corners deeper. If solid rock stops you short, a post drilled and grouted 12 to 18 inches into limestone holds as well as or better than a full-depth post in dirt. What fails is the middle ground: a post sitting 12 inches deep in loose material on top of rock.

### Can you drive T-posts into rock?

Into fractured limestone and caliche, usually yes, with a heavy manual or gas-powered driver. Into a solid unbroken shelf, no, and forcing it just bends the post. If a T-post refuses after a few solid hits, move it a couple feet and try again, or drill that spot instead.

### Should I use concrete for fence posts in rocky ground?

Only where it does real work. Grout or concrete bonding a steel post into a drilled rock socket is excellent. A shallow blob of concrete poured on top of rock around a short post is the classic failure we get called to fix, because the whole mushroom tips as a unit. In partial-depth dirt holes, well-tamped crushed rock often beats concrete.

### How much does rocky ground add to fence cost near Waco?

Plan on roughly 20 to 50 percent added to the post-setting portion of the job, which usually works out to $1 to $4 more per foot on barbed wire fence. Drilled gate and corner posts run $150 to $300 each. The spread depends on how much of your line sits on solid shelf versus fractured rock, which is why we probe before we quote.

> Fencing 5 to 20 acres near Waco? Get real per-foot prices, layout tips, and the right wire for horses, goats, and cattle from a Central Texas fence crew.

Ranch Fencing

# Small Acreage Fencing Around Waco: What Hobby Farms Really Need
Published August 20, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Five acres and two horses will teach you more about fencing than a thousand acres of open ranch ever will. On a big place, a fence just has to hold cattle. On a small place, it has to hold horses, goats, a donkey, and a dog, look decent from the road, survive your neighbor's hunting lease traffic, and fit a budget that doesn't have a ranch operation behind it.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Five acres and two horses will teach you more about fencing than a thousand acres of open ranch ever will. On a big place, a fence just has to hold cattle. On a small place, it has to hold horses, goats, a donkey, and a dog, look decent from the road, survive your neighbor’s hunting lease traffic, and fit a budget that doesn’t have a ranch operation behind it.

That’s why small acreage fencing is its own conversation. The math is different, the animal pressure is different, and the mistakes cost more per acre. We build fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and a big share of our calls now come from folks on 5 to 20 acres outside Waco, China Spring, Lorena, and Crawford. This guide covers what actually works on a hobby farm, what it costs in real numbers, and where people waste money.

## Why Fencing 5 to 20 Acres Is Its Own Animal

Here’s the part that surprises new landowners: small places have more fence per acre than big ones. A square 10 acres needs about 2,640 feet of perimeter fence. A square 1,000 acres needs about 26,400 feet. That’s ten times the fence for a hundred times the land. Per acre, the small place pays way more.

Small acreage also concentrates animal pressure. Two horses on 8 acres walk the same fence line every single day. Goats on 5 acres test every low spot and every gap by lunchtime. On a 2,000-acre ranch, a cow might not touch a given stretch of fence for a month. On a hobby farm, your fence gets leaned on, rubbed on, and chewed on constantly.

Then there’s the neighbor factor. On small tracts, your fence is usually shared on at least two sides, your entrance is close to the county road, and any escaped animal is on pavement in minutes. Under Texas stock law in most of McLennan County, if your cow or horse causes a wreck on the road, you can be held liable if you were negligent about your fence. That raises the stakes on doing it right the first time.

So the small acreage fencing job has three goals: contain mixed animals under heavy pressure, keep them off the road, and do it without spending ranch money. Everything below flows from those three. If you’d rather just talk it through on your own fence line, call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk it with you.

## What Small Acreage Fencing Costs Around Waco

Let’s talk real numbers, because this is where most folks start. Prices below are typical installed ranges in our area as of 2026, materials and labor, for straightforward ground. Rocky ridges near Valley Mills or tight clay bottoms along the Brazos can push these up.

A few things jump out of that table. First, barbed wire is cheap but it’s a cattle fence. It won’t hold goats and it’s a bad idea around horses, which we cover in barbed wire vs net wire. Second, nobody pipes a whole 10 acres. The smart play is pipe or a nice entrance across the front where you see it every day, then net wire down the sides and back. You can dig into full-perimeter math in our cost to fence 10 acres breakdown.

Budget rule of thumb for a mixed-animal hobby farm around Waco: plan on $10,000 to $20,000 for a solid perimeter on 8 to 12 acres, plus $2,500 to $7,500 if you want a pipe entrance with a gate that’ll still swing straight in ten years.

If you’d rather skip the guesswork, we’ll walk your property line and put a written number on it for free. Call us at (254) 870-8898 or request your free estimate here. Takes about an hour, and you’ll know your real cost instead of a blog range.

## Match the Fence to the Animals, Not the Catalog

The single most expensive mistake on small acreage is building for the animals you have today instead of the animals you’ll have in two years. Almost every hobby farm ends up with more species than it started with. Plan for that.

Horses need visibility and smooth wire. A horse that hits barbed wire at a run can do thousands of dollars of vet damage in one night. Go with 2x4 “no-climb” net wire, a top rail or a hot wire on top, and posts on the outside of the wire. More detail in best fence for horses.

Goats and sheep are escape artists and predator bait in the same body. You want net wire with 4x4 or smaller openings, stretched tight, with the bottom close to the ground. Horned goats will hang themselves in cheap large-mesh field fence, so mesh size matters more than brand. Our fence for goats and sheep guide covers spacing and predator strategy.

A few cows or a steer for the freezer are the easy case. Five strands of barbed wire holds them fine, and if the rest of your fence is net wire for other animals, cattle respect it too.

Pigs and feral hogs are the wildcard. Domestic pigs root under anything that isn’t tight to the ground. Feral hogs around the Middle Bosque and Tonk Creek bottoms will flat tear a light fence open, and they don’t ask first.

Real example from last spring. Dana Whitlock bought 8 acres off Cooksey Lane in Lorena with an older barbed wire perimeter and brought home six Boer goats. The goats were out in nine days. We replaced 1,850 feet of the worst two sides with goat-height net wire and a barbed top strand for $11,300, and she kept the decent barbed wire on the side shared with a neighbor’s cattle. That’s the small acreage move: spend where your animals actually push, keep what still works.

## Layout Tricks That Stretch a Small Acreage Fence Budget

On a small place, layout decisions swing your cost by thousands. Here’s what we tell folks on every walk-through.

Fence the perimeter right, cross-fence cheap. Your perimeter is your liability line and your predator line, so build it stout. Interior cross fences just sort animals, so they can be lighter: a couple strands of electric on t-posts makes a fine paddock divider for a fraction of net wire cost.

Put your money where the pressure is. Road frontage and the sides facing neighbors’ animals need your best fence. The back line along a wooded creek can often be a grade lower.

Plan gates before you build, not after. You need at least one 16-foot gate a truck and trailer can actually swing into from the road, plus a man gate near the barn. Cutting a gate into a finished stretched fence later costs more than framing it in now, because every gate needs braced posts on both sides. Corner and gate bracing is where cheap fences fail first, and our h-brace fence corners post shows why.

Don’t fence tight to the survey line without checking. On small tracts the pins matter. Six feet off on a 300-foot line is a real fight with a neighbor later.

The Kolar family in West learned the gate lesson the expensive way. They fenced 12 acres themselves in 2024 with a single 12-foot gate at the house. First hay delivery, the truck couldn’t make the turn, and they were hand-carrying round bale netting in the mud. We came back, cut in a 16-foot double gate with proper h-braces on the field side for $2,400. Framing that same opening during original construction would’ve run them around $900. Sequence matters.

One more layout note: leave yourself a working pen. Even two head of anything eventually needs to be caught, doctored, or loaded. A small cattle-panel pen in a corner, tied into the perimeter, costs $1,500 to $3,000 and saves you a rodeo every time the vet comes.

## Posts, Wire, and What Central Texas Ground Does to Both

Material choices matter more here than the catalogs let on, because Central Texas ground is hard on fences. Blackland clay east of I-35 swells and shrinks with every wet-dry cycle, which heaves posts and slacks wire. West of Waco toward Crawford and Valley Mills, you’re fighting rock a foot down.

For posts, the honest answer for most hobby farms is a mix: treated wood or pipe at corners, gates, and braces, with t-posts between. Wood corner posts should be 6 inches or bigger, set 3 feet deep or more, and concreted at gates. In clay, deeper beats wider. In rock, we’re often drilling or driving pipe, which changes the bid, so tell your contractor what your ground is like before they price it.

For wire, buy class 3 galvanized, not class 1. It costs maybe 10 to 15 percent more and roughly doubles the life of the wire. On a fence you’re paying real money to install, cheap wire is a false economy. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid fence construction guidance if you want the research side of post depth and bracing; it’s worth a read at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu.

And if part of your plan is grazing or a wildlife plan to qualify for an agricultural appraisal, know that fencing itself doesn’t earn the exemption, but your county appraisal district will expect infrastructure that matches a real ag use. The state’s ag-timber rules live at the Texas Comptroller site, and we break down how fences fit into it in ag exemption fencing in Texas.

Here’s what shortcuts look like a few years on. Marcus Trejo bought 6 acres near China Spring in 2023 with a fence the seller’s crew had thrown up fast: light t-posts, class 1 wire, no real braces. By early 2026 the corners were leaning and the top wire had a foot of sag. Patching it was going to run $3,800 and still leave bad bones. Rebuilding the two worst runs with proper h-braces and class 3 net wire ran $9,600, and the rest of the fence tightened up fine off the new corners. He got the itemized version of both options in writing first, which is exactly what you should demand from anybody bidding your place.

## DIY or Hire It Out? An Honest Answer

Plenty of hobby farm fence work is genuinely DIY-friendly, and we’ll tell you so. Driving t-posts, stringing a hot wire cross fence, hanging a gate on existing posts, stapling wire on a repair: if you’ve got a weekend and a helper, go for it.

Where we see DIY go sideways is the structural work. Corner and gate braces carry the entire tension of the fence, and a brace that’s undersized or shallow fails slowly, then all at once. Stretching net wire takes equipment and technique; wire stretched by hand goes slack the first summer. Post holes in our rock and clay can turn a one-weekend project into a three-weekend fight that ends with a rented skid steer and a sore back.

The safety lines are simpler. Stop and call a professional if the fence borders a road where an escaped animal becomes a liability, if you’re working anywhere near buried utilities, if the job involves old wire under tension, or if you’re taking out an existing fence with unknown junk in the line. Rusty high-tensile wire under load can snap and whip, and it does not care how careful you feel.

A hybrid approach works great on small acreage: we set the corners, braces, and gates and stretch the wire, and you handle tear-out of the old fence and cleanup. That can shave 15 to 25 percent off the bill. There’s a fuller breakdown in DIY fence vs professional.

### How much does it cost to fence 5 acres near Waco?

A square 5 acres has roughly 1,870 feet of perimeter. In our area that runs about $6,500 to $11,000 in net wire for goats or mixed stock, and $4,700 to $8,400 in 5-strand barbed wire for cattle only. ### What’s the best fence for a hobby farm with mixed animals?

Net wire with a barbed or electric top strand is the workhorse answer, because it holds goats, sheep, cattle, and donkeys in one build. ### Do I need a fence to keep my ag exemption?

Fencing alone doesn’t qualify land for an agricultural appraisal, but appraisal districts expect infrastructure that supports a genuine ag use, and grazing without a stock-tight fence is a hard sell. Check your county’s degree-of-intensity standards and the Texas Comptroller’s ag-timber guidelines. A functional perimeter fence is usually part of a credible grazing operation on small acreage.

### How long does it take to fence a small place?

For a typical 5 to 12 acre perimeter, plan on 3 to 7 working days once materials are on site: a day or two for tear-out and clearing, a day for corners and braces, then stretching wire and hanging gates. Weather, rock, and brush along the line are the usual things that stretch a schedule. Most of our hobby farm jobs around Waco are done within a week.

## Storm Damaged Fence Repair: What to Do in the First 24 Hours (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/storm-damaged-fence-repair/)

> Storm damaged fence repair starts the minute the wind dies down. Here's your first 24 hours, step by step, with real Central Texas costs and safety tips.

Pump Repair

# Storm Damaged Fence Repair: What to Do in the First 24 Hours
Published August 22, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

The wind finally dies down, you step outside, and there's a 60-foot live oak laying across 200 feet of your barbed wire.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

The wind finally dies down, you step outside, and there’s a 60-foot live oak laying across 200 feet of your barbed wire. Your cows are already eyeballing the gap like somebody left the gate open on purpose.

What you do in the next 24 hours decides whether this is a $600 fix or a $6,000 headache with a highway liability problem stacked on top. We’ve handled storm damaged fence repair all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties for years, and the ranchers who come out of a storm cheapest all follow the same basic playbook. Here it is, hour by hour.

## Hour One: Find Your Cattle Before You Worry About the Fence

Fences can wait a few hours. Loose cattle can’t wait ten minutes, especially if your place fronts a farm-to-market road.

Before you touch a single wire, do a head count. Drive or ride your pastures and confirm every animal is where it belongs. If something’s missing, check the obvious escape routes first: water gaps, corners near downed trees, and any stretch of fence that was already sagging before the storm. We wrote a whole guide on what to do when cattle get out, but the short version is simple. Get them contained first, in any pen or pasture that still holds, even if it’s not where they normally live.

This matters more than most folks realize. Texas is technically open range, but most of Central Texas sits under local stock laws, and a jury can still find you negligent if your cattle cause a wreck and you knew your fence was down. We break down the legal side in our post on cattle on the road and liability in Texas. The one-sentence takeaway: once you know the fence is open, the clock is running on you to do something about it.

If you’ve got cattle out and fence down right now, don’t finish reading this article. Call our 24/7 emergency line at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll get a crew moving while you round up stock. That’s exactly what the emergency line is for.

## Hours Two to Four: Walk the Line and Assess the Storm Fence Damage

Once your animals are secure, walk or drive every foot of affected fence line. Not just the spot where you can see the downed tree from the house. Straight-line winds do sneaky damage a quarter mile from the obvious mess.

Bring three things: your phone for photos, a notepad or notes app, and flagging tape or spray paint to mark trouble spots. You’re building two lists at once. One for the repair work, one for the insurance claim.

Here’s what to look for:

Downed trees and limbs on wire. The big obvious stuff. Note whether the wire underneath is snapped or just pinned. Wire that’s pinned but intact often survives once the tree comes off. Wire that’s stretched past its limit won’t hold tension again.

Leaning or snapped posts. Push on every post near the damage. Saturated ground plus 60 mph wind rocks posts loose even where nothing fell on the fence. A post that wiggles now will lean worse in a month. Our guide on fixing leaning fence posts covers which ones can be reset and which need replacing.

Blown-out water gaps. If you got the kind of rain that usually rides along with Central Texas storms, check every creek and draw crossing. Water gaps are built to give way in a flood, which means they’re usually the first thing gone.

Damaged braces and corners. An H-brace that shifted even a couple inches will let the whole stretch go slack. Sight down your fence lines and look for wire that’s lost its snap.

Debris you can’t see past. Don’t climb through or over tangled brush to inspect. If a tree is under tension on top of stretched wire, it can shift without warning. Mark it, photograph it from a safe distance, and move on.

One safety note that’s not optional: if any fence wire is touching a downed power line, or even close to one, stay away from the entire fence. Wire carries current a long way down the line. Call your electric co-op first and let them kill the line before anyone touches that fence. The National Weather Service has a good rundown of post-storm electrical hazards at weather.gov/safety/thunderstorm.

## Hours Four to Eight: Temporary Fixes That Actually Hold

You don’t have to rebuild anything today. You just have to make the fence hold cattle until a proper repair happens. Here’s what works.

Cattle panels are your best friend. A few 16-foot panels wired to solid posts on either side of a gap will hold most cattle for weeks. Keep four to six panels on hand year-round. At roughly $25 to $35 apiece they’re the cheapest insurance on your place.

Splice snapped wire with a figure-eight knot or crimp sleeves. For a clean break in barbed wire, a proper splice restores most of the strength. Twist splices done in a hurry pull apart the first time a cow leans on the fence. If the wire is old and rusty enough that it snaps while you’re splicing it, that stretch was on borrowed time anyway. Take the time to do the splice right and re-tension the whole stretch while you’re at it.

T-posts and a couple strands. For longer gaps, drive temporary t-posts every 10 to 12 feet and run two strands of barbed or smooth wire. It’s not pretty, but cattle respect it if it’s tight.

A strand of electric over the damage. If you’ve got a solar charger, one hot wire on step-in posts across a damaged section changes cattle behavior fast. They’ll quit testing the weak spot.

What not to do: don’t try to chainsaw a large tree off tensioned wire by yourself. When the weight comes off, stretched wire can whip back hard enough to take out an eye, and the trunk can roll onto your legs. Trees under tension kill people every storm season. If the tree is bigger around than your thigh and it’s laying on tight wire, that’s a job for a crew with the right equipment.

## Before Dark: Document Everything for Insurance

Most farm and ranch policies cover fence damage from named perils like wind, hail, and falling trees, but the adjuster wasn’t there when the oak came down. Your photos are the whole case.

Take wide shots that show the full damaged stretch, close-ups of broken posts and snapped wire, and photos of whatever caused the damage while it’s still sitting on the fence. Get pictures before you do temporary repairs if you can do it safely, then more photos after. Note the date, time, and location of each damaged section.

Then call your agent and report the claim within a day or two. Ask specifically what your policy covers on fencing, because coverage varies a lot. Some policies pay replacement cost, some pay depreciated value, and some cap fence payouts at a number that won’t touch a long rebuild. FEMA’s guidance at ready.gov/severe-weather recommends documenting all storm damage before cleanup for exactly this reason.

A written repair estimate from a contractor gives the adjuster a real number to work with instead of a guess. We provide free written estimates, and after big storms we prioritize them for folks with open claims. Reach us through the contact form and mention you’ve got an insurance claim going.

Real numbers, because that’s what you actually want to know. These are typical ranges we see on storm work around Waco. Your exact price depends on access, terrain, and how much material survived.

A few real jobs from the last couple of storm seasons. Names changed, numbers real.

He penned the cattle with panels that afternoon, called us the next morning, and we ran temporary wire the same day. The full rebuild in new barbed wire came to $2,700, and honestly the storm did him a favor. That net wire was 40 years old and due to fail anyway.

## When to Stop DIY and Call a Storm Fence Repair Pro

Plenty of storm damage is a Saturday morning fix for a handy rancher. Some of it isn’t. Here’s the honest line between the two.

Handle it yourself if: the damage is a few broken strands or a couple of leaning t-posts, no trees bigger than a fence post are involved, and nothing is near a road or a power line. Splice it, tighten it, move on.

Call a professional if any of these are true:

- A tree larger than your leg is resting on tensioned wire

- Corner posts or H-braces are broken or shifted, because everything downstream depends on them

- The damaged stretch borders a public road, where the liability math changes completely

- More than about 100 feet needs full rebuilding

- Any wire is anywhere near a downed power line

- You’re facing an insurance claim and need a documented, written repair estimate

There’s no shame in the second list. We carry the hydraulic post drivers, wire stretchers, and skid steer with a grapple that turn a dangerous two-weekend job into an afternoon. We’re licensed and insured, so if something goes wrong on the job, it’s on our policy, not yours.

Storm season in Central Texas isn’t going anywhere. Cattle-out and storm emergencies get answered 24/7, because cows don’t check the clock before they walk through a gap.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does insurance cover storm damaged fence repair?

Usually yes, if you carry a farm and ranch policy that lists wind, hail, or falling objects as covered perils. Standard homeowners policies often exclude agricultural fencing or cap it at a low limit, so read your declarations page. Photograph everything before cleanup and get a written repair estimate to give the adjuster a real number.

### How fast can a storm damaged fence be repaired?

Temporary containment can happen the same day with panels or a couple strands of wire. Most repair jobs, like resetting posts and splicing wire, take one to two days once a crew is on site. Full rebuilds of a quarter mile or more typically run three days to a week depending on clearing and terrain.

### Can I just splice broken barbed wire back together?

For a clean break in decent wire, yes, a figure-eight splice or crimp sleeves will restore most of the original strength. If the wire snaps again while you’re tensioning the splice, the whole stretch is too far gone and splicing is throwing good time after bad. Wire that’s badly rusted or stretched past its limit needs replacing, not patching.

### Am I liable if my cattle get out through a storm damaged fence in Texas?

Not automatically, but you’re on thin ice once you know the fence is down and do nothing. Most Central Texas counties operate under local stock laws that require you to keep cattle fenced, and knowing about an open gap and ignoring it looks like negligence to a jury. Contain your cattle first, patch the gap the same day, and document what you did and when.

## T-Post vs Wood Post: Where Each One Belongs on Your Fence Line (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/t-post-vs-wood-post/)

> T-post vs wood post for Central Texas ranch fencing. Real costs per post, spacing rules, when to mix both, and mistakes that let cattle out. Waco pros.

Materials

# T-Post vs Wood Post: Where Each One Belongs on Your Fence Line
Published August 20, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

About half the fence repair calls we run in McLennan County trace back to one decision somebody made years ago: they put a t-post where a wood post belonged, or paid wood-post money where steel would've done the job. The t-post vs wood post question isn't really a question of which one is better. It's a question of where each one belongs, because a good barbed wire fence around Waco uses both, and the ranchers who get the mix right spend a lot less on repairs over the next 25 years.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

About half the fence repair calls we run in McLennan County trace back to one decision somebody made years ago: they put a t-post where a wood post belonged, or paid wood-post money where steel would’ve done the job. The t-post vs wood post question isn’t really a question of which one is better. It’s a question of where each one belongs, because a good barbed wire fence around Waco uses both, and the ranchers who get the mix right spend a lot less on repairs over the next 25 years.

We build and repair ranch fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, so we’ve seen every version of getting this wrong. All-steel fences with corners leaning into the pasture. All-wood fences that cost double what they needed to. This article lays out where each post type earns its keep, what they actually cost in 2026, and how to combine them so your fence stays tight.

If you’d rather skip the reading and just get a straight answer for your place, call us at (254) 870-8898. Estimates are free and in writing.

## What T-Posts Do Well (and Where They Fall Short)

A steel t-post is a line post. That’s its whole job. It holds wire at the right height and keeps strands spaced along the run. Driven 18 to 24 inches into decent soil, a 6.5-foot t-post does that job for decades at a fraction of the cost of wood.

Here’s what steel gives you:

- Speed. A two-man crew with a driver can set 150 to 250 t-posts a day. Wood posts in augered holes go in at maybe a third of that pace.

- Price. A 6.5-foot, 1.25 lb/ft t-post runs $6 to $9 at Central Texas farm stores. A comparable treated wood line post runs $15 to $25 before you dig a single hole.

- Rocky ground. In the chalky limestone west of Crawford and out toward Valley Mills, driving steel beats augering rock every time. We cover that fight in detail in our post on setting fence posts in rocky ground.

- Fire and rot. Steel doesn’t rot at the ground line and a grass fire won’t take out a mile of it.

Now the other side of the ledger. A t-post has almost no resistance to pull along the fence line. Stretch five strands of barbed wire to proper tension and anchor them to a t-post, and that post will lean, then pull, then fail. Steel also bends and stays bent. A cow that leans on a wood post gets bored and walks off. A cow that leans hard on a t-post can leave it kinked at 30 degrees, and it never stands straight again.

T-posts also make poor gate hangers, poor corner posts, and poor ends. Anywhere the fence changes direction or the wire terminates, steel line posts are the wrong tool.

## Where Wood Posts Earn Their Keep

Wood posts handle the loads t-posts can’t. Every place your fence starts, stops, turns, or crosses something is a wood post location.

Corners and ends. A properly built corner is two or three 6-inch treated posts set 36 to 48 inches deep in concrete or tamped tight, tied together with a horizontal brace and a diagonal wire. That assembly is what actually holds your wire tension. Without it, the whole fence is loose no matter how many t-posts you drive. We walk through the build in our guide to H-brace fence corners, and it’s the single most important 20 feet of any fence.

Gates. A 12-foot tube gate weighs 90 to 120 pounds and swings on two hinges all day. Hang it on anything less than a deep-set 6-inch or 8-inch wood post (or pipe) and you’ll be lifting that gate to latch it within two years.

Stretch posts. On long runs, a wood post every 300 to 600 feet gives you a place to tie off and re-tension wire in sections. When a limb drops on the fence, you fix one section instead of re-stretching a half mile.

Dips, rises, and water gaps. Wherever the wire wants to pull up out of a low spot or down over a rise, the vertical load will lift a t-post right out of the ground. Wood holds.

Livestock pressure points. Working pens, alleyways, feed areas, anywhere cattle bunch up and push, wood posts (or better, pipe) take the abuse. For heavy-pressure areas a lot of our customers step up to a pipe fence, which outlasts everything.

The catch with wood is cost, labor, and rot. A treated pine post in the black clay east of Waco can last 20 to 30 years. A bargain post with thin treatment can rot at the ground line in 8. Post choice matters as much as post placement, and we compare the options in cedar vs treated pine posts.

## T-Post vs Wood Post Cost: Real 2026 Numbers

Here’s what the two actually cost around Waco right now, materials and typical installed price. Prices move with steel and lumber markets, so treat these as planning numbers and get a written quote before you budget a whole project.

Item Material cost Installed (typical) Best use

T-post, 6.5 ft, 1.25 lb/ft $6 to $9 $12 to $18 Line posts on straight runs

T-post, 8 ft heavy duty $10 to $14 $16 to $24 Taller net wire, game fence lines

Treated pine line post, 4 in $15 to $25 $35 to $55 Stretch posts, dips, pressure spots

Treated pine corner post, 6 in $30 to $45 $85 to $150 Corners, ends, gate posts

Full H-brace corner assembly $90 to $150 $250 to $450 Every corner and end

Run the math on a quarter mile (1,320 feet) of five-strand barbed wire with posts every 12 feet. All wood, you’re looking at roughly 110 line posts at $35 to $55 installed each, which is $3,850 to $6,050 in posts alone. Swap the line posts to steel and keep wood only at the corners, ends, and a couple of stretch points, and the post budget drops to around $1,600 to $2,400. Same fence height, same wire, and honestly a straighter-looking fence, for less than half the post cost.

That’s why nearly every barbed wire fence we build follows the same recipe: wood where the fence works hard, steel where it just stands there. You can see how posts fit into total project pricing on our ranch fence cost page.

Last fall we rebuilt a fence for Dale Kubacak, who runs about 40 cows outside Crawford. The previous owner had fenced the whole place with t-posts, corners included, sometime in the 2000s. Every corner had crept inward 8 to 14 inches, the wire sat slack enough to step over in places, and his cows had figured that out twice that summer. We didn’t replace the fence. We built him nine new H-brace corners and ends at about $340 apiece, re-stretched the existing wire, and replaced 60-odd bent t-posts. Total came in just under $4,100. A full rebuild would’ve run him north of $16,000. The lesson: the steel was fine. The missing wood is what failed.

## Mixing Wood Posts and T-Posts: The Layout That Works

Here’s the standard layout we use on barbed wire and field fence across Central Texas. It’s not fancy, and that’s the point.

- Wood H-braces at every corner, end, and gate. No exceptions. This is the skeleton.

- Wood stretch assemblies every 300 to 600 feet on long runs, and at the bottom of every significant dip.

- Steel t-posts on 10 to 12 foot centers between them for cattle on barbed wire. Tighten to 8 feet for goats, sheep, or heavy hog pressure. Our fence post spacing guide covers the spacing question by animal and wire type.

- Wood or pipe at water gaps and creek crossings, because that’s where floodwater loads hit.

Some folks ask about the old-school pattern of one wood post every fourth or fifth post down the line. It looks stout, and on show-front fencing along a county road it does dress things up. Structurally, though, a 4-inch wood line post driven or tamped 24 inches deep doesn’t add much that a good t-post doesn’t, and it triples your line post budget. Put that money into deeper, bigger corner posts instead. Corners are what keep wire tight, and tight wire is what keeps cattle home.

Texas A&#x26;M and other land-grant extension programs publish the same basic guidance if you want a second opinion. The University of Georgia’s extension bulletin Fences for the Farm is one of the better free references on brace construction and post depth, and USDA NRCS publishes fence standards used in cost-share fencing programs if you’re fencing under an EQIP contract.

One more real-world example. In March, Marcy Villanueva near Valley Mills called our emergency line at 6 a.m. with cattle on FM 56. A dead post oak had dropped across her fence overnight, and because the old fence had no stretch posts, the falling tree slacked the wire for a full quarter mile in both directions. We got the cattle penned and the gap closed that morning for $650, then came back the next week to add four wood stretch assemblies down that line for another $1,400. The next limb that falls will slack one 400-foot section, not 1,300 feet. If you’re getting those dawn phone calls yourself, our post on cattle getting out of the fence walks through finding the weak point fast.

If you’re staring at a fence line right now trying to figure out which posts failed and why, send us a couple of photos through the contact form and we’ll give you an honest read on repair versus rebuild.

## Central Texas Soil Changes the Answer

The t-post vs wood post math shifts with what’s under your boots, and around here that changes fast.

Blackland clay east of I-35, around Lorena and out toward West, swells when wet and shrinks hard in drought. That movement heaves shallow posts and opens gaps around them. In clay we set wood corners deeper, 42 to 48 inches, and we expect some t-post straightening after a wet winter. Deep-set wood is cheap insurance in that ground.

Limestone and caliche west of Waco, out through Crawford, McGregor, and Valley Mills, is the opposite problem. You can’t drive deep, and augering means rock bits and patience. Steel pilot points and rock drills earn their keep, and sometimes the right answer for a corner is drilling and setting pipe in concrete instead of fighting a 48-inch hole for wood.

Sandy river bottoms along the Brazos and Bosque hold posts loosely. T-posts wobble, so we tighten spacing to 8 or 10 feet and upsize wood posts.

Drought years are their own problem. In cracked, dried clay a t-post that drove tight in April can rattle loose by September. That’s part of why fences that stood fine for a decade suddenly start leaning during a dry stretch.

Frank Mynar, who runs stockers on leased ground outside West, learned the sandy-soil lesson the expensive way in 2025. He’d fenced a 30-acre bottom trap himself with t-posts on 15-foot centers to save money. Feral hogs went through it like it was string, and he lost roughly $2,200 in a busted fence, an escaped-cattle gathering fee, and a neighbor’s flattened oat patch before he called us. We rebuilt the pressure side with net wire, 8-foot t-post spacing, and wood posts every 100 feet for about $5,800. He’s had zero breakouts since.

## When to Stop DIYing and Call a Pro

Plenty of fence work is fair game for a capable landowner. Driving t-posts, splicing wire, swapping a bent post, stapling loose strands. If you’ve got a post driver and a good pair of gloves, have at it.

But know where the line is. Call a professional when:

- Corners or braces need rebuilding. A corner that’s set wrong fails slowly and takes the whole fence’s tension with it. This is the highest-skill part of the job.

- You’re stretching long runs of wire. Barbed wire under tension stores real energy. A snapped strand or a slipped stretcher can cut you badly. Wear eye protection and never stretch wire alone.

- The fence is on a property line. Texas fence law has quirks worth understanding before you build, and a misplaced fence is an expensive argument.

- There’s a water gap, road frontage, or utility easement involved. Call 811 before any post holes near buried lines. It’s free and it’s the law.

- The project is more than you can finish before livestock test it. A half-built fence is an invitation.

We’re licensed and insured, our estimates are free and written, and our emergency line answers 24/7 for storm damage and cattle-out calls. Call (254) 870-8898 or reach us at brazosridgefence.com and we’ll walk your line with you, whether you need the whole job done or just the corners set so you can run the wire yourself.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I build a barbed wire fence with only t-posts?

You can, but it won’t stay tight. T-posts can’t anchor wire tension, so an all-steel fence goes slack as the corners lean, usually within a few seasons. At minimum, put wood H-braces at every corner, end, and gate, then run steel between them.

### How many t-posts should go between wood posts?

On a typical Central Texas cattle fence, we run t-posts on 10 to 12 foot centers with wood stretch posts every 300 to 600 feet, plus wood at every corner, end, gate, and major dip. For goats, sheep, or hog pressure, tighten steel spacing to about 8 feet. There’s no structural need for a wood post every fourth or fifth post unless you want the look.

### How long do wood fence posts last in Central Texas?

A quality treated pine post rated for ground contact typically lasts 20 to 30 years here, and good steel t-posts often outlast them. Cheap, lightly treated posts can rot at the ground line in under 10 years, especially in wet bottomland. Buy posts with a.40 CCA (or equivalent) ground-contact treatment rating and you’ll only do this job once.

### Which is cheaper, t-posts or wood posts?

Per post, steel wins big: $12 to $18 installed for a t-post versus $35 to $55 for a wood line post and $85 to $150 for a corner post. On a quarter mile of fence, using steel for line posts and wood only where the fence needs anchoring usually cuts the post budget by more than half. Get a written quote though, since steel and lumber prices both move around.
