## Texas High Fence Regulations for Deer and Exotics: What to Know (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/texas-high-fence-rules/)

> Texas high fence regulations surprise most landowners. Learn what permits deer and exotics really require, fence height specs, and real Central Texas costs.

Well Care

# Texas High Fence Regulations for Deer and Exotics: What to Know
Published August 23, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Texas has more high-fenced acreage than any other state in the country, and here's the part that surprises most landowners: the state never inspects the fence itself.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Texas has more high-fenced acreage than any other state in the country, and here’s the part that surprises most landowners: the state never inspects the fence itself. There’s no high fence permit, no state inspector, and no minimum legal height written into the game code.

So why do so many high fence projects around Waco end up tangled in paperwork, dead deer, or lawsuits with the neighbors? Because Texas high fence regulations aren’t really about the fence. They’re about what’s inside it. The wire is your business. The animals behind the wire are a whole different story, and that’s where folks get burned.

We build game fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and we’ve watched smart people make expensive mistakes because nobody explained the rules in plain English. This article fixes that.

## What Texas High Fence Regulations Actually Cover

Let’s clear up the biggest misunderstanding first. In Texas, you can build an 8 foot fence around your property tomorrow without asking anyone’s permission, as long as it’s on your own land and outside any road right of way or utility easement. No state agency signs off on the fence.

What the state does regulate, and regulates hard, is deer. Native white-tailed deer and mule deer are property of the State of Texas, even when they’re standing inside your high fence. Building the fence doesn’t make them yours. You can’t sell them, you can’t trap them and haul them to your buddy’s place, and you can’t buy “some deer” off Craigslist to stock your new pen.

Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) controls everything involving native deer through a permit system:

- Deer Breeder Permit: lets you hold and sell captive-bred whitetails from a registered facility. These are the only whitetails that can legally be bought and sold.

- Triple T Permit (Trap, Transport, Transplant): lets qualified landowners move wild deer between approved properties. It’s not a purchase program, and TPWD has tightened it in recent years because of chronic wasting disease.

- Deer Management Permit (DMP): lets you temporarily pen wild deer for breeding purposes on your own place.

- Managed Lands Deer Program (MLDP): not required for a high fence, but most serious high-fenced operations enroll because it gives you extended seasons and custom harvest quotas tied to a management plan.

Current rules and season details live in TPWD’s Outdoor Annual, and they change often enough that you should check before every project and every season.

If you’re planning a high fence and want real numbers before you talk permits, call us at (254) 870-8898. Estimates are free and written, and we’ll tell you straight what your ground needs.

## High Fence Rules for Native Whitetail: Where Landowners Get Burned

Here’s a story we tell every new high fence customer. Rachel Dunn bought 90 acres outside Valley Mills in 2024 and had us quote a high fence so she could “buy a dozen good does and a nice buck” and build her own herd. She’d budgeted about $5,000 for deer.

Then she learned the rules. Wild whitetails can’t be purchased at any price. The only legal route was buying breeder deer from a permitted facility, and pen-raised bred does were running $2,500 to $4,000 each, with quality bucks a lot higher. Her $5,000 stocking budget turned into a $30,000 line item, plus release requirements and disease testing paperwork on every animal that came through the gate.

She still did the project, but she did it two years slower than planned. That’s the pattern with native deer: the fence is the easy part.

A few more rules that catch people off guard:

- Hunting inside a high fence is still hunting. Seasons, bag limits, and license requirements all apply to native deer unless you’re enrolled in MLDP with its own tag system.

- Chronic wasting disease (CWD) rules follow the deer, not the fence. If you bring in breeder deer, the source facility’s testing status matters, and a CWD trace can freeze movement on and off your property.

- A high fence can change your neighbors’ hunting too. Deer that used to cross four properties now live on one. That’s legal, but it’s the number one source of hard feelings, so talk to the folks next door before the first post goes in.

## Texas High Fence Laws for Exotics: Axis, Blackbuck, and Friends

Exotics play by a completely different rulebook, and it mostly works in your favor. Axis deer, blackbuck antelope, fallow deer, aoudad, and other non-native hoofstock are legally livestock in Texas. They’re your private property, there’s no closed season, and no bag limit. You still need a valid hunting license to hunt them, but that’s about it from the state’s side.

The catch is the flip side of ownership: exotics are only yours while they’re on your land.

Marcus Teague learned that one the hard way near Crawford. He stocked 14 axis does at about $800 a head before his fence was fully finished. One stretch along the creek was still old 6 foot net wire from the previous owner. Axis are strong jumpers, and within a month, 11 of those does had cleared that low section and scattered. Two got taken legally by a neighboring hunter, because a free-ranging exotic on someone else’s land is fair game for anyone with a license and permission to hunt there. Marcus was out roughly $9,000 in animals plus the cost of fixing the fence he should’ve finished first.

Two more things to know on exotics:

- The Texas Animal Health Commission (TAHC), not TPWD, handles disease rules for exotic livestock. CWD-susceptible exotics like elk, red deer, and sika have their own movement and testing requirements. Check tahc.texas.gov before you buy or move those species.

- Escaped exotics can create liability. If your aoudad ends up causing a wreck on a county road, you’ll want to show you maintained a fence adequate to contain them. That’s the same standard logic we cover in our post on who’s responsible when livestock hit the road, and it applies double to animals that can clear a cattle fence without breaking stride.

## Fence Specs That Actually Hold Deer and Exotics

Since the law doesn’t set a height, the animals do. The industry standard in Central Texas is 8 feet, built with 96 inch fixed knot wire on line posts, with taller pipe posts at corners and gates. A healthy whitetail can clear 7 feet from a standing start when it’s motivated. Axis are worse. Nilgai and elk push the strength requirements more than the height.

Here’s how a true game fence compares to the other fencing on a typical ranch:

Fence type Typical height Installed cost per foot (Central TX) What it holds

5-strand barbed wire 48 to 54 in $3 to $5 Cattle

Net wire (field fence) 48 in $5 to $8 Cattle, goats, sheep

8 ft fixed knot game fence 96 in $15 to $25 Whitetail, axis, most exotics

Game fence with apron or hot wire 96 in plus $18 to $30 Adds hog and dig-under protection

A few spec points that matter more than most people think:

- Fixed knot beats hinge joint for high fence, period. The solid knot keeps vertical stays from shifting when a 200 pound animal hits the wire. We break down the difference in fixed knot vs hinge joint wire.

- Corners and gates carry the whole fence. An 8 foot fence puts serious leverage on corner assemblies. Skimp there and the whole run sags inside five years.

- Feral hogs will test the bottom. Hogs don’t jump, they root under. A buried apron or a low hot wire saves you from the constant repairs we describe in feral hog fence damage.

- Gates have to match the fence. A beautiful 8 foot fence with a 6 foot gate is a 6 foot fence. We build matching tall gates as part of our ranch entrance gate work in Waco.

Ready to get a real spec for your place? Request a free written estimate and we’ll walk the property lines with you.

## Property Lines, Neighbors, and County Rules Around Waco

The state may not permit your fence, but geometry and neighbors still can wreck a project. Three local issues come up on almost every high fence job we quote in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties.

First, the property line itself. Texas law doesn’t force your neighbor to pay for any part of a fence, high or low, and it doesn’t give you the right to set posts on their side. Best practice is building 6 to 12 inches inside your own line so every post, brace, and inch of concrete is unquestionably yours. Get a survey if there’s any doubt. A fence built even slightly over the line is a problem that only gets more expensive with time. Our post on fence on the property line in Texas covers the details.

Second, right of way and easements. County road rights of way, pipeline easements, and utility easements all restrict where an 8 foot fence can go. Most easements allow fencing but require gates or specific clearances. Read your easement documents before you order 300 rolls of wire.

Third, water crossings and floodplains. High fence across a creek needs engineered water gaps that swing or break away in a flood. If you’re in a mapped floodplain, check with the county floodplain administrator before building a solid barrier across a drainage. A washed-out quarter mile of game fence is a five-figure repair.

## What a High Fence Really Costs in Central Texas

Now the numbers, because everybody asks. At $15 to $25 per foot installed, a mile of 8 foot game fence runs roughly $80,000 to $130,000 depending on terrain, rock, brush clearing, and gate count. That’s not a typo. High fence is the most expensive wire fence you can build, and it’s priced like it.

Danny Kolar runs 210 acres a few miles west of West, and in 2025 we built him 1.3 miles of 8 foot fixed knot, two 16 foot tall-frame gates, and three water gaps. Rocky ground on the north line meant drilling instead of driving posts. His final invoice landed just under $140,000. He’d gotten a lowball bid at $95,000 from an outfit that planned to use hinge joint wire and T-post corners, and he was smart enough to ask why the bids were so far apart. The cheap version would’ve been a very expensive cattle fence, not a deer fence.

Budget honestly, and budget for the whole system: fence, gates, water gaps, clearing, and stocking if you’re going that route. Our game fence cost guide breaks the per-foot math down line by line.

One safety note before you grab an auger and a pallet of wire. Stretching high-tensile fixed knot wire stores enormous energy, and 8 foot fence work means heavy posts, tall ladders, and hydraulic equipment. A snapped stretch of high-tensile wire can cut you badly. Small repairs on existing fence are fine DIY territory. Building a mile of high fence is not. If any part of the job involves stretching full-height game wire or setting pipe corners in rock, call a professional crew.

That’s what we do all day. Our game fence installation team in Waco handles permits questions, surveys, specs, and the build itself, and our estimates are always free and in writing. Call (254) 870-8898 or reach us here, day or night. The emergency line runs 24/7, because deer don’t wait for business hours and neither do storm-flattened fences.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Do I need a permit to build a high fence in Texas?

No state permit is required to build the fence itself on your own property. What requires permits is holding, moving, buying, or breeding native white-tailed deer, all of which run through TPWD. Check easements, road rights of way, and floodplain rules with your county before you build.

### How tall does a Texas high fence have to be?

The law sets no minimum height, but 8 feet is the working standard because whitetails can clear 7 feet and axis deer jump even better. Most builds use 96 inch fixed knot wire with taller pipe posts at corners and gates. Going shorter to save money usually means paying for the fence twice.

### Who owns the deer inside my high fence?

Native white-tailed and mule deer belong to the State of Texas no matter whose fence surrounds them, so seasons, licenses, and bag limits still apply. Exotics like axis and blackbuck are your private property while they’re on your land. Once an exotic escapes onto a neighbor’s place, anyone hunting there legally can take it.

### Can I make my neighbor split the cost of a high fence on the property line?

No. Texas law doesn’t obligate a neighboring landowner to contribute to any fence, and you can’t set posts on their side of the line without permission. Build inside your own boundary, get a survey if the line is uncertain, and have the cost conversation before construction, not after.

## Texas Open Range Law: What Stock Laws Mean for Your Fences (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/texas-open-range-law/)

> Texas is still open range by default, but county stock laws flip the rules. Here's what Texas open range law means for your fences, liability, and wallet.

Texas Law

# Texas Open Range Law: What Stock Laws Mean for Your Fences
Published August 20, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Here's something that surprises almost every new landowner we meet: in most of Texas, the law doesn't require you to fence your cattle in. It expects your neighbor to fence them out.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Here’s something that surprises almost every new landowner we meet: in most of Texas, the law doesn’t require you to fence your cattle in. It expects your neighbor to fence them out.

That’s the heart of Texas open range law, a rule that goes back to the trail-drive days and still shapes who pays when a bull walks through a hayfield or a heifer ends up on a farm-to-market road at midnight. But the rule has big exceptions. County stock laws, highway statutes, and plain old neighbor disputes can flip the whole thing on its head.

We build fence for a living in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and we’ve seen what happens when folks guess wrong about these rules. It usually costs real money. So let’s walk through what open range actually means, where stock laws change it, and what kind of fence keeps you out of trouble either way.

Quick note before we start: we’re fence builders, not lawyers. This article explains the general rules so you can ask better questions. For a legal opinion on your land, talk to an attorney.

## Texas Open Range Law Starts With “Fence Out,” Not “Fence In”

Texas inherited its livestock rules from a time when cattle grazed free across unfenced prairie. The courts settled it more than a century ago: under the common law of Texas, livestock owners have no general duty to prevent their animals from roaming.

That’s called being an open range or “fence out” state. If you don’t want your neighbor’s cows eating your coastal bermuda, the default rule says it’s on you to build a fence that keeps them out. If a cow wanders onto unfenced land and grazes it down, the cow’s owner usually owes nothing, because the animal wasn’t trespassing in the legal sense.

Compare that to “fence in” states, where the animal’s owner must contain their stock and is on the hook for damage when they don’t. Most of the country works that way now. Texas kept the old rule as its starting point, then let counties opt out of it piece by piece.

That opt-out system is where stock laws come in, and it’s why the honest answer to “is Texas open range?” is always the same: it depends on where your land sits and sometimes on which animal we’re talking about.

If your fences wouldn’t stop a determined cow today, don’t wait for the legal question to answer itself. Call Brazos Ridge Fence at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk your lines with you and give you a free written estimate.

## How County Stock Laws Close the Range

Starting in the late 1800s, the Legislature let local voters hold elections to adopt “stock laws.” A stock law makes it unlawful to let certain animals run at large in that county or precinct. Where a stock law passed, the range is “closed” and the rule flips to fence in.

The details live in Chapter 143 of the Texas Agriculture Code, which you can read yourself on the Texas Legislature’s statutes site. A few things worth knowing about how these laws work:

- Stock laws are adopted by local election, sometimes countywide, sometimes for a single precinct or an area described by old survey lines.

- They’re animal specific. An election might cover cattle and horses but not sheep or goats, or hogs but nothing else.

- Many of these elections happened between the 1890s and 1930s. The records sit in county clerk archives, and some are handwritten.

That last point trips people up constantly. There’s no clean statewide map of which counties are closed range. Most of the settled parts of Central Texas voted in stock laws for cattle generations ago, but the only way to know for sure what applies to your pasture is to ask the county clerk or sheriff’s office, or have a title company or attorney pull the records.

Here’s the practical takeaway. If a valid stock law covers your land and your animals, you have a legal duty to keep them off other people’s property and off the roads. Your fence stops being a courtesy and becomes your liability shield.

## The Highway Rule Catches Everybody, Open Range or Not

Even in a true open range area, there’s one exception with teeth. Texas Agriculture Code Section 143.102 makes it illegal to knowingly permit cattle, horses, mules, donkeys, sheep, goats, or hogs to roam at large on the right-of-way of a U.S. or state highway.

That means the fence along a highway frontage matters everywhere in Texas, stock law or not. If your bull has been getting out onto Highway 6 for weeks and you knew about it, “we’re open range out here” is not going to save you. The word “knowingly” does a lot of work in these cases, which is exactly why courts look at the condition of your fence, how often the animal escaped before, and what you did about it.

County roads are a different story, and farm-to-market roads have their own wrinkles that lawyers argue about. The Texas State Law Library keeps a plain-language guide to these rules in its animal law research guide, and it’s worth twenty minutes of your time.

The pattern we see in real wrecks is simple: a loose cow on pavement at night is a disaster for everyone, including the cow. Which brings us to what this looks like when it goes wrong.

## What Texas Open Range Law Looks Like When It Goes Wrong

Three quick stories from our service area, with the numbers attached.

The bull in the hayfield. Dale runs about 60 head outside Crawford. His east line was a tired three-strand fence with rusted wire and leaning cedar posts. His bull pushed through it into the neighbor’s fertilized coastal field and spent two days doing what bulls do. The neighbor claimed $2,400 in hay and reseeding damage. Whether a stock law made Dale liable or not, the relationship was worth more than the argument, so he paid it. Then he called us. We rebuilt 1,300 feet of five-strand barbed wire with steel corners for about $4,225. The fence cost less than two more incidents would have.

The heifer on the FM road. A couple near Valley Mills lost a 750-pound heifer when a pickup hit her on the farm-to-market road after dark. The heifer was worth around $1,900 at the sale barn, the truck was totaled, and the driver’s insurance company came asking hard questions about a washed-out water gap that had been down for a month. It settled quietly, but the stress of six months of letters cost more than the water gap ever would have. A proper water gap rebuild on that crossing ran them about $850.

The line fence standoff in West. Leon bought 42 acres north of West and assumed the sagging boundary fence was the neighbor’s problem. Texas law generally doesn’t force either neighbor to build or pay for a shared line fence, which surprised him. After six months of cows trading pastures in both directions, the two of them split a 1,900-foot rebuild at $3.50 a foot. That’s $6,650 total, $3,325 each, and the calls about loose cattle stopped completely. We wrote about how those cost-share talks usually go in our guide to who pays for a fence between neighbors in Texas.

Notice the theme. In every case, the legal question mattered less than the fence. A sound fence prevents the fight instead of winning it.

## Open Range vs. Closed Range: What Changes for You

Here’s the side-by-side, keeping in mind that highway frontage rules apply in both columns.

Question Open range area Closed range (stock law) area

Must I fence my livestock in? No general duty, except along U.S. and state highways Yes, letting them run at large is unlawful

Neighbor’s cattle eat my crops Usually my problem if my land wasn’t fenced Usually the cattle owner’s problem

Cow hit on a U.S. or state highway Owner liable if they knowingly let it roam Owner liable if they knowingly let it roam

Cow hit on a county road Often no owner liability Owner may be liable under the stock law

Who builds the boundary fence? Whoever wants protection builds it Livestock owner needs it, but cost-sharing is voluntary

What your fence does for you Keeps trouble out Keeps liability in

Two more things every landowner should file away.

First, a fence on the line is usually a shared question but not a shared obligation. If you build entirely on your own side, it’s yours, and a survey before you set the first post is cheap insurance against moving a half mile of fence later.

Second, if your cattle are already getting out, treat it as urgent. Every escape builds the “knowingly” record against you. Our post on cattle getting out of the fence walks through the usual escape points, and if you’ve got animals out near a road right now, our emergency line answers 24/7 at (254) 870-8898.

## What a Legal, Cattle-Tight Fence Costs in Central Texas

Neither the open range rule nor a stock law spells out one required fence design for every situation, but the practical standard around here has been settled for decades: a tight five-strand barbed wire fence on good posts, or net wire where you run small stock too.

Real numbers we quote every week in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties:

- Five-strand barbed wire: $2.50 to $4.50 per foot installed, which works out to roughly $13,000 to $24,000 per mile depending on terrain, brush, and corners.

- Net wire with a barbed top strand: $3.00 to $6.00 per foot, the right call for goats, sheep, and mixed operations.

- Pipe fencing for pens, highway frontage, and high-pressure areas: $10 to $25 per foot. See our pipe fence installation page for what drives that range.

- Water gaps, the number one escape point in this county: $400 to $1,200 per crossing depending on span and flow.

Strand count matters more than people think. Three strands is a suggestion to a cow. Five strands, stretched tight on well-braced corners, is a fence. We break down the why in how many strands of barbed wire you really need.

Where your land fronts a highway, spend the extra money. That’s the stretch where the law is strictest everywhere in Texas, and it’s where a failure costs the most. Plenty of ranchers around Waco run barbed wire on the interior and upgrade the road frontage. Our barbed wire fence crew builds both, and we’ll tell you straight where the upgrade is worth it and where it isn’t.

A word on DIY. Patching a strand or resetting a t-post is a fine Saturday job. But corner braces, highway frontage, water gaps, and anything involving a survey dispute are places to stop and call a professional. A corner brace that fails takes a quarter mile of tension with it, and a bad fence on the wrong side of a line can turn into a legal problem no amount of wire fixes.

## How to Find Out What Applies to Your Land

Don’t guess. Here’s the checklist we give buyers and new landowners:

- Call the county clerk and ask whether stock law elections cover your precinct, and for which animals. In McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, expect to do some digging in old records.

- Ask the sheriff’s office how they handle loose livestock calls in your area. Their answer tells you a lot about how the county treats the question in practice.

- Note every foot of U.S. or state highway frontage on the property. That fence has to hold no matter what the county records say.

- Walk the fences before you close on land, and budget honestly for what you find. Old wire hides a lot of sins.

- When real money or a real dispute is on the table, spend a few hundred dollars on an hour with an ag law attorney. It’s the cheapest thing on this list.

Then look at your fences the way an insurance adjuster would. Would they hold a motivated bull tonight? If the answer is “probably,” that’s a no.

If you’d rather have a professional set of eyes on it, request a free written estimate and we’ll walk your lines, flag the weak spots, and price the fixes by the foot so you can plan it in stages. Licensed and insured, and we work these three counties every single week.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is all of Texas open range?

No. Texas is open range by default, but most populated counties and precincts adopted local stock laws long ago that close the range for some or all animals. The only reliable way to know your land’s status is to check stock law records with your county clerk or an attorney, because there’s no official statewide map.

### If my county is open range, can my cattle legally roam anywhere?

Not quite. Even in open range areas, state law makes it illegal to knowingly let livestock roam on the right-of-way of a U.S. or state highway. Repeated escapes and a known bad fence are exactly the kind of evidence used to prove “knowingly,” so a sound fence protects you even where no stock law applies.

### Who pays if my neighbor’s cattle damage my property?

In a closed range area, the cattle owner is generally responsible for damage their loose animals cause. In a true open range area, you usually can’t recover for grazing damage unless your land was fenced and the animals broke in. Either way, documenting the damage with photos and dates helps, and a solid perimeter fence prevents the fight entirely.

### What kind of fence do I need to meet the law?

There’s no single statewide spec for every situation, but the practical standard for cattle in Central Texas is a tight five-strand barbed wire fence on braced corners, or net wire if you also run goats or sheep. Plan on $2.50 to $4.50 per foot for barbed wire and more for net wire or pipe. Put your best fence on highway frontage, where the legal duty is strictest.

## Texas Stock Laws by County: Who Has to Fence, and Where (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/texas-stock-law-by-county/)

> Texas stock laws by county decide who fences stock in and who fences them out. How to check your county and precinct, and what it means for the fence you build.

Regulations

# Texas Stock Laws by County: Who Has to Fence, and Where
Published September 12, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A fellow west of Crawford called us one March after his neighbor's cows spent three nights in his winter pasture. He wanted to know who owed him a fence.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A fellow west of Crawford called us one March after his neighbor’s cows spent three nights in his winter pasture. He wanted to know who owed him a fence. The answer started with a question he had never once thought about in twenty years of owning that place: does the stock law where his land sits cover cattle, or does it not?

That is the whole game with Texas stock laws by county. Texas starts from open range, where the burden is on you to fence animals out. A county stock law flips that and makes the animal’s owner keep them in. Which rule applies to your dirt depends on an election that probably happened before your grandfather was born.

We build fence in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, not law. Nothing here is legal advice. Talk to an attorney about your specific tract before you rely on any of it, because these records are old and they are local.

## Open Range Is the Default and a Stock Law Is the Exception

Texas never adopted the fence-in rule that most states use. Under Texas common law, a livestock owner has no general duty to keep animals from wandering off. If you want your neighbor’s cattle out of your hay meadow, the default rule says build a fence that keeps them out.

Then the Legislature gave local voters a way out of that. Under Chapter 143 of the Texas Agriculture Code, a county or a subdivision of a county could hold an election to make it unlawful for certain animals to run at large. Where one of those passed, the range is closed and the burden moves to the animal’s owner.

Most of the settled counties in Central Texas closed the range on cattle generations ago. That does not mean yours did, and it does not mean it covers every animal. You can read the statute yourself on the Texas Legislature’s site, which is a short read and worth twenty minutes if you run stock.

If your perimeter would not stop a determined cow today, the legal question is secondary. Call (254) 870-8898 and we will walk the line with you and put a free written estimate in your hand.

## Texas Stock Laws by County Are Not Something You Can Download

Landowners ask us for a map. There isn’t one, at least not one you should bet a lawsuit on. What exists is a pile of county-level records going back to the 1890s, some of them handwritten in a clerk’s minute book.

Three things make the county-by-county picture messier than people expect.

The elections were animal specific. One vote might cover cattle and horses and say nothing about hogs, sheep, or goats. Plenty of counties held separate elections years apart for different animals.

They were not always countywide. The law allowed subdivisions, so a stock law can apply to one commissioner precinct, or to an area described by old survey lines and roads that no longer exist by that name.

And they stayed on the books. A stock law adopted in 1912 is still the rule unless a later election repealed it, so age tells you nothing about whether it applies.

Every online list of closed-range counties we have seen carries a disclaimer, and it should. Treat those lists as a starting point and nothing more.

## How to Check the Stock Law in Your County and Precinct

This is a phone call and a courthouse visit, not a research project. Here is the order that works.

Start with the county clerk. Ask for the commissioners court minutes and any recorded stock law elections for your precinct, and ask which animals each one covered. Some clerks have this indexed and will read it to you over the phone.

Call the sheriff’s office next. Deputies handle loose-stock calls every week and they generally know how the county treats them, which is useful even though it is not a legal opinion.

Then check your deed and survey against the precinct boundaries. If your tract straddles a line, you can genuinely have two answers on one piece of property.

If money or liability is on the table, pay an attorney or a title company to pull the records and give you a written answer. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife’s Texas Agriculture Law blog is the best free plain-English resource on this subject, and it will save you time before you ever call a lawyer.

We cover this same ground from the other direction in our post on Texas open range law, which explains the fence-out rule itself.

## Highways Have Their Own Rule, Stock Law or Not

Here is the part that catches people. Separate from any county stock law, the Agriculture Code makes it an offense to knowingly permit livestock to run at large on a highway. That applies whether the range around you is open or closed.

The catch is the definition. For that section, the code defines highway narrowly, as U.S. and state highways. Numbered farm-to-market roads and county roads are treated differently, and Texas courts have declined to read a general duty to fence into those roads for open-range areas.

So the honest summary is this. Frontage on a U.S. or state highway carries a duty that does not depend on your county’s stock law. Frontage on an FM road or a county road depends on the local stock law and on the facts of the wreck. Either way, a jury looking at a night-time collision will hear about the condition of your fence.

That is a fence conversation more than a legal one. We go deeper on the wreck side in our post on cattle on road liability in Texas.

## What a County Stock Law Changes About the Fence You Build

A stock law does not build fence and it does not decide who pays for a boundary fence. That is a separate question with its own rules, covered in who pays for the fence between neighbors in Texas.

What the stock law changes is your exposure. In closed range, an animal of yours out on the road or in a neighbor’s crop is your problem from the first minute. That moves the fence from a grazing tool to a liability line, and it changes what we recommend on the frontage side of a place.

Here is what those choices cost in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties in 2026.

Fence type What it holds Installed cost Where it earns its keep

5-strand barbed wire Cattle on open pasture $2.50 - $5.50 per foot Back and side perimeter, cross fencing

Net wire / field fence Goats, sheep, calves, mixed stock $3.50 - $8 per foot Small acreage, roadside, horse mesh at the top of the range

8-ft game fence Deer and exotics $4.50 - $10 per foot High-fence operations, whole-tract perimeter

Welded pipe fence Anything, permanently $12 - $28 per foot Road frontage, corrals, entrances

Cattle guard, installed Keeps stock in at an open gate $3,500 - $8,000 Drives and interior crossings

On big tracts, think in miles. Barbed wire runs roughly $13,200 to $29,000 per mile and game fence $25,000 to $50,000 per mile, with rock and brush driving the spread. Our ranch fence cost page breaks down what moves a bid up or down.

A 12-acre horse place outside Lorena runs about 2,900 feet of perimeter. ## What We Tell People to Do About It

Find out which rule applies before you need to know. It costs a phone call, and the answer usually arrives the same week.

Then fence to the risk, not to the statute. Open range is a defense in a lawsuit, not a fence, and it does nothing for the calf that is already on the highway. Put your money on the frontage and the corners first, then work back. Loose stock nearly always comes out of the same weak spots, which we listed in why cattle keep getting out of the fence.

Write down what you find. If a wreck or a crop claim ever happens, being able to show which stock law applies and when your fence was last inspected puts you in a much better position than a hazy memory of what somebody at the feed store said.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do I find out if my county has a stock law?

Call the county clerk and ask for recorded stock law elections covering your precinct, and ask which animals each one named. The sheriff’s office can tell you how loose-stock calls are handled in practice. For anything with money on it, have an attorney or title company pull the records and put the answer in writing.

### Does a stock law mean my neighbor has to pay for the boundary fence?

No. A stock law governs whether animals may run at large. Who pays for a shared fence is a separate matter that usually comes down to agreements, prior use, and what the two of you work out. Get any cost-sharing arrangement in writing before the first post goes in.

### Is Texas open range or closed range?

Both, depending on where you stand. The statewide default is open range, and counties or precincts that passed stock laws are closed for the animals those elections named. That is why there is no single reliable map for the whole state.

### What fence do I need if my county is closed range?

The law does not specify a fence type. It says keep your animals in, so build what your stock actually respects: five-strand barbed wire at $2.50 to $5.50 a foot for cattle on pasture, net wire at $3.50 to $8 for small stock and horses, pipe at $12 to $28 where the pressure is highest. ## Used Oilfield Pipe for Fencing: Pros, Cons, and What to Check (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/used-oilfield-pipe-fence/)

> Thinking about a used oilfield pipe fence? Real Central Texas prices for drill stem, the problems to watch for, and how to check pipe before you pay for it.

Well Care

# Used Oilfield Pipe for Fencing: Pros, Cons, and What to Check
Published August 24, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Drive any ranch road between Waco and Crawford and you'll see it. Rust-brown pipe fence running straight as a rifle shot, and most of that pipe pumped oil out of a West Texas well before it ever held...

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Drive any ranch road between Waco and Crawford and you’ll see it. Rust-brown pipe fence running straight as a rifle shot, and most of that pipe pumped oil out of a West Texas well before it ever held back a cow.

A used oilfield pipe fence is the standard around here for a reason. Drill stem costs about half what new structural pipe runs, it’s heavier walled than most new fence pipe, and a bull can lean on it all day without moving it. But “used” covers everything from nearly perfect pipe to junk that’ll rust through in ten years, and the difference isn’t always obvious sitting in a stack at the pipe yard.

We build pipe fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and we’ve bought a lot of used pipe over the years. Here’s what it really costs, where it goes wrong, and exactly what to check before you hand anybody money.

## Why a Used Oilfield Pipe Fence Makes Sense in Central Texas

Start with what the stuff actually is. Drill stem is the threaded pipe that turns the drill bit downhole. Once it’s been through enough trips in and out of a well, it gets retired from drilling and sold off as structural pipe. The most common size you’ll see for fencing is 2 3/8 inch outside diameter, followed by 2 7/8 inch for posts and heavier corners.

Here’s why ranchers keep choosing it:

- Price. Used 2 3/8 drill stem runs about $1.60 to $2.50 per foot around Waco right now. Comparable new pipe runs $3.50 to $5.00 per foot. On a corral or a long stretch of fence line, that gap adds up to thousands of dollars.

- Wall thickness. Drill stem was built to survive thousands of feet downhole under torque. Typical wall thickness is around 0.19 inch, which is thicker than a lot of new “fence grade” tubing. Thicker wall means more years before rust wins.

- Strength. It’s high-grade steel. A pipe corral built from sound drill stem will outlast the person who built it, and it shrugs off cattle, horses, and the occasional tractor bump.

- Looks. That uniform rust patina is part of the ranch look in Central Texas. Plenty of folks skip paint entirely and let it brown out even.

For working pens, arena rails, entrance ways, and corner braces on wire fence, it’s hard to beat. If you’re pricing a full project, our pipe fence installation page breaks down what we build and how we build it.

Want a real number for your place instead of internet ranges? Call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll walk your fence line and put a written estimate in your hand for free.

## The Downsides Nobody Mentions at the Pipe Yard

Used pipe isn’t free money. There are four real drawbacks, and you should know them before you commit.

It’s inconsistent. New pipe comes with a spec sheet. Used pipe comes with a history you can’t see. One joint in a load might have thin spots from downhole corrosion while the joint next to it is near perfect. You’re buying a mixed bag unless you inspect piece by piece.

Inside scale and gunk. Pipe that carried oil or produced water often has paraffin, scale, or cement inside. That matters when you weld. Burning through paraffin makes ugly, contaminated welds and a lot of nasty smoke. Cement-lined joints are miserable to cut and nearly worthless for fencing.

NORM contamination. Some oilfield pipe picks up naturally occurring radioactive material, called NORM, from scale that builds up inside during production. Reputable yards test and reject hot pipe, but it’s a real thing the EPA documents in its overview of oil and gas production wastes. The Railroad Commission of Texas also regulates how NORM-contaminated oilfield equipment gets handled in this state (rrc.texas.gov). Buy from a yard that can tell you their pipe has been surveyed. Don’t buy mystery pipe off a trailer at a gas station.

Hard on tools and welders. Drill stem is high-carbon steel. It cuts slower, eats blades, and it’s less forgiving to weld than mild steel. Welds on high-carbon pipe can crack if they cool too fast, which is one reason a cheap DIY pipe fence sometimes starts popping welds after the first hard freeze.

Here’s what that last point looks like in real life. Gary Hoelscher, who runs a small cow-calf place outside Valley Mills, called us in March after the corral he’d welded up himself over two summers started failing. He’d bought bargain pipe at auction, some of it thin-walled tubing mixed in with the drill stem, and his welds were cracking at the rail joints. We ended up cutting out and rebuilding about 60 feet of it for $4,200. Good pipe from the start would’ve cost him maybe $900 more than the auction load.

## What to Check Before You Buy Used Oilfield Pipe

This is the part that saves you money. Whether you’re buying pipe yourself or checking a contractor’s material, run through this list on the actual pipe, not the photo in the listing.

1. Ring it. Tap each joint with a hammer. Sound pipe rings clear like a bell. A dull thud means heavy scale inside, internal cement, or a wall so thin it can’t ring. This one test catches more bad pipe than anything else.

2. Look down the bore. Hold one end up to the light and look through. You want to see daylight. Heavy paraffin, scale buildup, or blockage means welding headaches and hidden wall loss.

3. Check the wall at the cut ends. Fresh-cut ends show you true wall thickness. On 2 3/8 drill stem you want to see roughly 3/16 inch of steel. If the wall looks like a soup can at the ends, walk away, because it’s worse somewhere in the middle.

4. Hunt for pitting, not surface rust. Uniform orange surface rust is fine and normal. Deep pitting, flaking layers, or holes near the tool joints mean the pipe corroded downhole. Drag a gloved hand along the joint and feel for rough, cratered sections.

5. Watch for crooked and worn joints. Sight down each pipe like a rifle barrel. Slight bows are workable for rails. Banana pipe is not. Also check the upset ends where the tool joints are, since heavy wear there means the pipe had a hard life.

6. Ask about NORM surveys. A legitimate pipe yard will answer this question without blinking. If the seller gets cagey, that tells you what you need to know.

7. Confirm what you’re actually buying. Drill stem, tubing, casing, and sucker rod are different products at different prices. More on that below, but don’t pay drill stem money for thin-wall production tubing.

Kyle Determan, who runs cattle northwest of China Spring, called us last fall before buying a $3,800 load of 2 7/8 pipe he’d found online. We looked at it with him and rang every joint. About a third of the load thudded dead, and two joints had visible pitting you could catch a fingernail in. He passed, bought a cleaner load from a yard in West for $4,300, and got pipe that’ll still be standing when his grandkids run those pens.

If you’d rather skip the pipe-yard homework entirely, request a free estimate and we’ll source inspected pipe, build the fence, and warranty the welds.

## Drill Stem, Tubing, Casing, and Sucker Rod: Know What You’re Buying

Sellers throw these terms around loosely, and the differences matter to your wallet.

Drill stem is the workhorse. Thick wall, high strength, threaded tool joints on the ends. It’s what you want for posts, top rails, and braces. The 2 3/8 and 2 7/8 sizes cover almost everything on a ranch.

Production tubing looks similar but usually runs thinner walled because it just carried fluid instead of turning a bit. It’s fine for middle rails where loads are lighter, and it’s cheaper. It’s not what you want holding a corner under a quarter mile of stretched wire.

Casing is the big-diameter pipe, 4 1/2 inch and up, that lines the wellbore. It makes outstanding corner posts, H-brace posts, and entrance columns. If you’re planning a headgate entrance off the county road, casing uprights are the standard look, and our ranch entrance gates page shows how we build them.

Sucker rod is the solid steel rod, usually 3/4 or 7/8 inch, that ran the downhole pump. It’s the classic material for continuous-rail fence and top rails on wire fence. It’s springy, strong, and cheap, but it’s also high-carbon and snaps welds if it’s not welded right.

One more real example. Maria Villarreal bought 12 acres outside Lorena last year and wanted pipe corners and an H-brace layout for a new net wire perimeter. She’d been quoted a load of “heavy pipe” that turned out to be thin production tubing when we rang it. We sourced true 2 7/8 drill stem for the corners instead, set them in concrete, and her whole corner and brace package came to $2,650. Her wire will still be tight in twenty years because the corners won’t move. If you want to understand why corners decide everything, read H-brace fence corners.

## When to DIY and When to Call a Pro

Plenty of ranchers around here are handy with a welder, so let’s be straight about where the line is.

Reasonable DIY territory: hauling and inspecting pipe, cutting and painting rails, and welding non-structural stuff like a hay ring repair. If you’ve got a good machine, real hood time, and patience for preheating high-carbon steel, a small pen is doable.

Call a professional when any of these apply:

- Corners and braces on stretched wire. A failed corner weld lets a whole quarter mile of wire go slack, and then the cattle get out. That’s a liability problem on a public road, not just a fence problem.

- Entrance gates and anything overhead. A pipe header over a driveway is hanging steel above people’s vehicles. Cracked welds up there aren’t a someday problem.

- Horse fencing. Horses find every sharp edge and every gap. Rail spacing and smooth finishes matter more than with cattle.

- Long runs on a deadline. A crew with a pipe trailer, welders, and an auger will set in three days what takes a solo weekend warrior all summer.

Also know your limits on the buying side. If you can’t confidently tell drill stem from tubing, or you can’t inspect a load in person before paying, let somebody who buys pipe every week do it. The most expensive pipe fence in the county is the cheap one you build twice.

We’re happy to be that somebody. Call (254) 870-8898 or hit our contact form for a free written estimate anywhere in McLennan, Bosque, or Falls county. We answer the phone, we show up when we say, and our welds hold.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does used oilfield pipe cost for fencing?

Around Central Texas in 2026, used 2 3/8 inch drill stem runs about $1.60 to $2.50 per foot, and 2 7/8 inch runs about $2.25 to $3.25 per foot. Casing for corner posts is usually priced per joint rather than per foot. A fully installed 5-rail pipe fence built from used pipe typically lands between $28 and $40 per foot including labor and concrete.

### Is used oilfield pipe safe, or is radiation a real concern?

NORM contamination is real but manageable. It shows up as radioactive scale inside some production pipe, and reputable pipe yards survey their inventory and pull hot joints before resale. Buy from an established yard that can confirm their pipe has been checked, and skip private sellers who can’t answer the question.

### How long will a used oilfield pipe fence last?

Sound drill stem with good wall thickness will last 40 years or more as a fence, and often much longer in our dry Central Texas climate. The failures you see are almost always thin-wall pipe that should’ve been rejected, or cracked welds from poor technique on high-carbon steel. Buy good pipe, weld it right, and it’s a one-time fence.

### Should I paint used pipe fence or let it rust?

Either works, and it’s mostly a looks decision. Surface rust on thick-wall pipe advances very slowly here, so plenty of ranchers let it brown out naturally. If you want paint, a rust-converting primer plus an oil-based enamel holds up best, and dark colors hide future rust bleed. Paint adds roughly $3 to $6 per foot if a crew does the prep and spraying.

## Water Gap Fences: Crossing Creeks Without Losing Your Fence (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/water-gap-fence/)

> Learn how a water gap fence lets your creek crossing flood without wrecking your whole fence line. Real costs, designs, and repair tips from Waco fence pros.

Ranch Fencing

# Water Gap Fences: Crossing Creeks Without Losing Your Fence
Published August 20, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

One hard rain on Hog Creek can tear out more fence in ten minutes than a whole herd of cattle can wreck in ten years. We've seen it happen over and over across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties. The fence that crosses the creek gets loaded up with brush, limbs, and floodwater, and the current rips out not just the crossing but fifty, a hundred, sometimes three hundred feet of good fence on either side.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

One hard rain on Hog Creek can tear out more fence in ten minutes than a whole herd of cattle can wreck in ten years. We’ve seen it happen over and over across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties. The fence that crosses the creek gets loaded up with brush, limbs, and floodwater, and the current rips out not just the crossing but fifty, a hundred, sometimes three hundred feet of good fence on either side.

That’s why every fence that crosses moving water needs a water gap fence. A water gap is a short, sacrificial section of fence built across a creek, draw, or drainage that’s designed to give way or swing open when floodwater comes through, then go right back to holding cattle when the water drops. Build it right and a flood costs you an hour of cleanup. Build it wrong, or skip it entirely, and a flood costs you a week of rebuilding and cattle scattered down the county road.

We build and repair water gaps all over Central Texas, from the Bosque River bottoms up around Valley Mills down to Cow Bayou near Lorena. Here’s how they work, what they cost, and how to keep yours from becoming next spring’s headache.

## Why Creek Crossings Destroy Fences

Water is patient and it’s strong. When a creek rises after a Central Texas gully washer, it’s not just water coming down that channel. It’s tree limbs, cedar brush, hay net wrap, and sometimes whole trees.

All that debris hangs up on your wire, and now your fence isn’t a fence anymore. It’s a dam. Water piles up behind it, the force multiplies fast, and something has to give.

Here’s the part that stings. A solid fence doesn’t fail neatly at the creek. The wire is stretched tight for hundreds of feet in both directions, so when the crossing rips out, it drags the line with it. Posts snap, braces lean, and wire ends up wrapped around trees a quarter mile downstream.

The National Weather Service ranks flash flooding as one of the deadliest weather hazards in Texas, and our creeks can rise several feet in under an hour (weather.gov flood safety). Your fence has to live with that reality. A water gap is how it does.

If you’ve got a crossing you’re worried about, don’t wait on the next storm. Call us at (254) 870-8898 and we’ll take a look and give you a free written estimate.

## How a Water Gap Fence Works

The idea behind a water gap fence is simple. You end your permanent fence on solid ground on each bank, anchored with stout braced posts that floodwater can’t reach or move. Then you span the channel itself with a separate, lighter section that’s built to fail on purpose.

That sacrificial section holds cattle just fine in normal conditions. When the creek rises and debris starts pushing, it breaks away, swings up, or lays down instead of fighting the current. The flood passes through, your permanent fence stays put, and you’re repairing a 20 foot gap instead of 300 feet of line fence.

Three things make the whole system work:

- Strong anchors on the banks. Heavy braced posts set above the normal flood line. These take the strain of the permanent fence so the gap section carries none of it.

- A weak link in the channel. The gap panel or wires attach with light wire, smooth wire loops, or hinges, never with the full-strength connections you’d use on line fence.

- Nothing for debris to grab. The fewer strands and posts in the channel, the less the water can load up on.

Get those three right and you’ve got a crossing that shrugs off high water. Get them wrong and you’ve built a debris trap with your name on it.

## Types of Water Gaps We Build in Central Texas

There’s no single right water gap design. The right one depends on how wide the channel is, how hard the water comes through, and what kind of stock you’re holding. Here are the four we build most.

Breakaway wire gap. The simplest version. Barbed wire strands cross the channel attached to the anchor posts with light tie wire designed to snap under load. Cheap, quick, easy to rebuild after a rise. Best for narrow draws and seasonal creeks. Pairs naturally with a standard barbed wire fence.

Swinging or floating panel. A cattle panel, pipe frame, or row of vertical stays hung from a cable or pipe stretched high across the channel. Water and debris push the panel downstream and it swings up out of the flow, then gravity drops it back into place when the water falls. Great for creeks that rise often, because there’s often nothing to rebuild at all.

Hinged flap gap. Similar idea but hinged at the top from a rigid pipe header, usually built from drill stem. This is the heavy-duty option for crossings that see real current. If you’ve already got a pipe fence, a pipe-framed water gap matches it in both strength and looks.

Electric water gap. One or two hot wires across the channel on breakaway connections. Almost nothing for debris to catch, and cattle respect it. The catch is it only works if your charger and grounding are solid, and it needs checking after every rise.

Here’s how they compare on cost and upkeep for a typical 20 to 30 foot crossing:

Water gap type Installed cost (typical) Flood survival Rebuild after a big rise Best for

Breakaway wire $250 to $600 Sacrificial, breaks away 1 to 2 hours, cheap materials Narrow draws, seasonal creeks

Swinging panel $600 to $1,200 Swings clear, usually survives Often none, just clear debris Creeks that rise several times a year

Hinged pipe flap $1,000 to $2,500 Toughest option Rarely needed Wide crossings, strong current

Electric gap $200 to $500 Minimal debris load Reconnect wires, test charger Managed pastures, gentle cattle

Those are typical ranges for our area. A wide crossing, rock excavation, or a long haul to the site can push numbers up, which is why we always quote off a site visit, not a phone guess.

## What a Water Gap Costs Compared to Not Having One

The cheapest water gap we build costs less than a single flood repair. That’s the whole math, and it’s not close.

Roy Kettler runs cows outside Valley Mills, with a North Bosque tributary cutting through his east pasture. His old fence crossed the creek dead solid, five strands bank to bank with no gap. The May storms two years back loaded that crossing with cedar and took out 260 feet of fence. Our repair bill was $2,850. We rebuilt the crossing with a swinging panel gap for $875, and it’s been through four good rises since without costing him a dime.

Down near Lorena, Dana Fuchs had it worse. Her crossing on a Cow Bayou drainage blew out overnight and eleven pairs went through before sunup. She spent the morning horseback getting them off a neighbor’s wheat, and cattle getting out is a liability problem on top of a fence problem. The repair ran $1,600. The breakaway wire gap we built her afterward cost $425, and now when the bayou rises, the gap pops loose like it’s supposed to and she resets it herself in an hour.

And out west of Crawford, Tom Villarreal called us after his third blowout in two years on the same Middle Bosque crossing. He’d been rebuilding it solid every time, roughly $900 a pop, so he was almost $2,700 in before we ever showed up. A hinged pipe flap gap cost him $1,850 once. It’s outlasted every rise since.

Add it up across a few storm seasons and the water gap is the cheapest insurance on the ranch. If you’re doing the math on your own crossing, our ranch fence cost guide covers what full fence rebuilds run per foot, and it’ll make the gap look even better.

Want a real number for your crossing instead of a range? Request a free written estimate and we’ll walk the creek with you.

## Building a Water Gap Fence the Right Way

Whether we’re building it or you’re handy enough to tackle a simple one yourself, the same rules apply.

Set your anchors high and heavy. The braced posts on each bank are the foundation of the whole crossing. Put them above the debris line from past floods. Look for the rafts of sticks and grass hung in the brush; that’s your creek telling you how high it gets. Use a full H-brace on each bank, because these posts are holding the tension of your entire line fence.

Dead-end the permanent fence at the banks. Never run your line fence wire continuously across the channel. Tie it off at the anchor braces so the gap section is structurally separate. That separation is what saves the rest of your fence when the gap lets go.

Make the weak link actually weak. The most common mistake we see is a water gap wired in so tight it can’t release. Light gauge tie wire, smooth wire loops, or a proper hinge at the top. If it takes fence pliers and a fight to remove the gap section by hand, the flood is going to take your braces instead.

Keep the channel clean. Fewer strands, fewer stays, no old wire or T-posts left lying in the creek bed. Every extra piece of steel in that channel is a debris hook.

Match the gap to the stock. Cows need less than calves, and calves need less than goats and sheep. A two-strand gap that holds mature cows will not hold a weaned calf that’s walked the creek and found daylight under the bottom wire. Build the gap for the smallest animal in the pasture.

Think about the neighbors. If the creek is a boundary line, talk to the landowner across the fence first. A shared water gap split two ways is cheaper for both of you.

One safety note that outranks all of this. Never work in a creek channel while water is rising or heavy rain is falling upstream. Central Texas creeks come up fast enough to trap you. The gap can wait a day.

## Water Gap Maintenance After Every Rise

A water gap isn’t a build-it-and-forget-it item. It’s a build-it-and-check-it item. The whole design assumes you’ll walk the crossing after high water, because a gap that released in the last flood isn’t holding anything today.

After every significant rise, do four things:

- Walk the crossing and confirm the gap is back in place or rehang it.

- Pull off any debris hung on the panel, wires, or anchor braces.

- Check the bank anchors for scour. Water cutting under a brace post is a slow failure you can catch early.

- If it’s an electric gap, test the wire with a fence tester, not the back of your hand.

Twice a year, give the crossing a harder look. Erosion moves creek banks, and an anchor post that sat five feet from the edge can end up two feet from it after a wet spring. Wire living in a creek bottom also rusts fast, and our guide on rusted barbed wire will help you decide whether to patch or replace.

The USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service publishes fencing practice standards that treat stream crossings as their own engineering problem, and some cost-share programs through NRCS can even help pay for fence work on grazing land (nrcs.usda.gov). Worth a conversation with your local office if you’re refencing a place with a lot of water on it.

## When to Call a Pro on a Water Gap

Plenty of ranchers build and maintain their own breakaway wire gaps, and we’ll never talk you out of work you can do well. But some crossings are past DIY territory.

Call a professional when the channel is wider than about 20 feet, when the creek carries real current and big debris, when you’ve rebuilt the same crossing more than once, or when the banks are eroding around your anchors. Those situations need engineered anchors and pipe work. Sometimes moving the crossing 50 feet to a straighter, shallower stretch of creek solves a problem that no amount of rebuilding ever will.

We’ve built water gaps on just about every creek, draw, and bayou in the Waco area, and we know which designs survive which water. We’re licensed and insured, estimates are free and in writing, and if a storm just took your crossing out and there are cattle on the wrong side of it, our emergency line answers around the clock.

Call (254) 870-8898 or request your free estimate online, and let’s make the next flood a non-event.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is a water gap fence?

A water gap fence is a short, sacrificial section of fence built where a fence line crosses a creek, draw, or drainage. It’s designed to break away, swing up, or lay down when floodwater and debris push on it, so the flood passes through without tearing out the permanent fence anchored on each bank. After the water drops, you rehang or rebuild the small gap section instead of hundreds of feet of line fence.

### How much does a water gap fence cost?

For a typical 20 to 30 foot crossing in Central Texas, a simple breakaway wire gap runs about $250 to $600 installed, a swinging panel gap runs $600 to $1,200, and a heavy hinged pipe gap runs $1,000 to $2,500. Wide channels, rock, and hard access add to that. Compare that to flood repairs on a solid crossing, which routinely run $1,500 to $3,000 per blowout, and the gap pays for itself in one storm.

### Will cattle get out through a water gap?

Not if it’s built and maintained right. A properly hung gap holds stock just like the rest of the fence in normal conditions, and it only opens under flood load. The risk comes after a rise, when a released gap sits open until someone resets it. Walk your crossings after every high water event, and build the gap tight enough for the smallest animal in that pasture.

### Do I need a water gap on a creek that’s dry most of the year?

Yes, and dry creeks are honestly where we see the worst damage. A draw that runs twice a year still moves serious water and debris when it does, and a solid fence across it becomes a dam the first time it flows hard. If a channel shows signs of flow, like scoured rock, bent grass, or debris hung in brush, it needs a water gap.

## What Size Pipe for a Pipe Fence: 2 3/8 vs 2 7/8 Explained (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/what-size-pipe-for-pipe-fence/)

> Choosing what size pipe for a pipe fence? We compare 2 3/8 and 2 7/8 oilfield pipe by cost, strength, and use so your Central Texas fence lasts decades.

Well Care

# What Size Pipe for a Pipe Fence: 2 3/8 vs 2 7/8 Explained
Published August 25, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A half inch of steel can be the difference between a fence that shrugs off a 1,400 pound bull and one that folds like a lawn chair.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A half inch of steel can be the difference between a fence that shrugs off a 1,400 pound bull and one that folds like a lawn chair. That’s really what you’re deciding when you ask what size pipe for pipe fence work makes sense, because in Central Texas the choice almost always comes down to two numbers: 2 3/8 and 2 7/8.

Those are the outside diameters, in inches, of the two most common sizes of used oilfield tubing sold around Waco. Between China Spring, Crawford, and Valley Mills, we’d bet 9 out of 10 pipe fences are built from one or both of them.

Here’s the short version. 2 3/8 pipe handles line posts and top rails on most cattle and horse fences. 2 7/8 pipe belongs at corners, gates, H-braces, and anywhere heavy animals lean, rub, or crowd. The rest of this article explains why, what each size costs in real dollars, and exactly where cheaping out ends up costing you more.

## The Quick Answer: What Size Pipe for a Pipe Fence

If you just want the answer so you can go order pipe, here it is.

For a standard perimeter or cross fence holding cows or horses, use 2 7/8 pipe for corner posts, gate posts, and brace posts. Use 2 3/8 pipe for line posts set every 8 to 10 feet, and 2 3/8 or 1.9 inch pipe for the top rail. That combination is what we install on most ranches in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and it’s the setup that holds up decade after decade.

Why not just build the whole thing from 2 7/8? You can, and for bull pens, working corrals, and arenas we often do. But 2 7/8 weighs about 6.5 pounds per foot compared to roughly 4.7 for 2 3/8. On a quarter mile of fence, that’s thousands of pounds of extra steel you’re paying for, hauling, and welding, mostly in places that don’t need it.

Why not all 2 3/8? Because corners and gates take loads that line posts never see. A 300 pound gate hanging off a post is a lever working on that post every single day. A corner post takes the pull of every stretched wire tied to it, which can add up to thousands of pounds on a long run. That’s where the bigger pipe earns its keep.

If you’d rather skip the math and the welding altogether, we build pipe fence in Waco and the surrounding counties every week. Request a free written estimate and we’ll spec the right pipe sizes for your land and your animals, no guesswork and no upselling.

## 2 3/8 Pipe: The Workhorse for Line Posts and Top Rails

2 3/8 inch pipe is the most common size on Central Texas ranches for good reason. It’s strong enough for line duty, light enough for two people to handle, and cheap enough that fencing a whole pasture doesn’t require a second mortgage.

Set 30 to 36 inches deep in concrete on 8 to 10 foot spacing, a 2 3/8 line post will hold barbed wire, net wire, or continuous fence panels for decades. Most used 2 3/8 tubing runs a wall thickness around 0.190 inches. That’s real structural steel, not the flimsy fence tubing you’ll find at big box stores.

Where 2 3/8 shines:

- Line posts on cattle and horse fences

- Top rails over barbed wire or net wire

- Stays and verticals in continuous fence

- Light walk gates and trailer gates

Where it falls short is exactly where you’d guess: anywhere the fence takes concentrated load. Roy, who runs about 60 cow-calf pairs outside Crawford, learned that one the expensive way. His previous fence builder set 2 3/8 corners on 1,200 feet of new fence to shave a few dollars off the bid. Two summers of bulls leaning through the shade line and both corner assemblies were tipped 6 inches out of plumb, with every wire on the fence gone slack. We rebuilt both corners with 2 7/8 posts and proper braces for $2,800. The original savings from the smaller pipe was about $190.

If your existing fence is already doing that lean, our article on leaning fence posts covers what’s fixable and what needs to come out of the ground.

## 2 7/8 Pipe: Corners, Gates, and Anywhere Cattle Push

2 7/8 inch pipe is the muscle of a pipe fence. The extra half inch of diameter doesn’t sound like much, but stiffness in a round pipe climbs fast as diameter grows. Combined with a heavier typical wall, a 2 7/8 post resists bending roughly half again better than 2 3/8 under the same load.

Use 2 7/8 for:

- Corner posts and end posts

- Gate posts, especially anything hanging a gate 12 feet or wider

- H-brace and pull posts on long wire runs

- Bull pens, working pens, and alleyways

- Entrance columns and cattle guard wings

Gate posts deserve special mention. A 16 foot pipe gate can weigh 250 to 350 pounds, and every time it swings, sags, or catches a tractor bucket, that load works on the hinge post. A 2 7/8 post set 4 feet deep in concrete shrugs it off for a lifetime. A 2 3/8 post slowly rolls toward the gate until nothing latches anymore. If your entrance is already doing this, read our guide on how to fix a sagging ranch gate, or have us build the entrance right the first time. Our ranch entrance gates in Waco crew handles everything from hinge posts to overhead signs.

For fences that see serious abuse, some ranchers step up to 3 1/2 or even 4 1/2 inch pipe at gates and main corners. That’s rarely necessary on a family ranch, but it’s standard on feedlots and heavy commercial operations, and it’s cheap insurance on a wide entrance gate.

## Wall Thickness Matters as Much as Pipe Size

Here’s the part most pipe sellers won’t volunteer: two sticks of 2 7/8 pipe can differ wildly in strength. Outside diameter is only half the story. Wall thickness is the other half.

Common used tubing walls run from about 0.190 up to 0.217 inches and heavier. Structural grades and drill stem can run thicker still. A thin-wall, heavily pitted 2 7/8 can actually be weaker than a clean, heavy-wall 2 3/8. The quick check is weight. Honest 2 7/8 at 0.217 wall weighs about 6.5 pounds per foot. If a yard is selling “2 7/8” that weighs 4.5 pounds per foot, you’re buying a big diameter wrapped around thin steel.

Danny, who bought 25 acres near Valley Mills in 2023, found a deal on 2 7/8 at about 60 cents a foot under market. He saved roughly $600 on the load. The pipe turned out to be badly pitted from years of downhole service, with walls rusted paper thin in spots you couldn’t see under the scale. Within a year, 14 of his posts had rusted through at ground level and snapped in a spring storm. Cutting them out and replacing them ran $1,900, three times what the cheap pipe saved him.

When you’re buying used pipe, check for:

- Deep pitting or scale flaking off in sheets

- Split seams or crushed ends

- Walls you can dent with a hammer blow

- Heavy internal scale that hides thin spots

Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid guidance on fence planning and materials for Texas landowners at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu, and it’s worth a read before you spend real money on steel. For a deeper dive on sourcing, grades, and fair prices, our post on used oilfield pipe fence covers what to buy and what to walk away from.

Not sure what you’re looking at on a trailer full of rusty pipe? Call us at (254) 870-8898 before you pay for it. A five minute conversation is free. A load of junk pipe is not.

## Cost Comparison: 2 3/8 vs 2 7/8 Pipe

Prices move with the scrap and oil markets, but here’s what used oilfield pipe has been running around Waco in 2026, along with where each size belongs on your fence.

Spec 2 3/8 Pipe 2 7/8 Pipe

Outside diameter 2.375 in 2.875 in

Typical weight About 4.7 lb/ft About 6.5 lb/ft

Used price per foot $1.60 to $2.50 $2.25 to $3.50

Cost per 8 ft post $13 to $20 $18 to $28

Best use Line posts, top rails, stays Corners, gates, braces, pens

Set depth 30 to 36 in 36 to 48 in

Concrete per post About 1 bag 1.5 to 2 bags

On a typical 1,320 foot quarter mile of fence, the difference between an all 2 7/8 build and a smart mixed build usually lands between $800 and $1,500 in pipe alone, before you count the extra concrete, welding wire, and labor the heavier pipe demands.

Flip it around, though, and upsizing only the posts that matter is cheap. Corners, gates, and braces might account for 10 or 15 posts on that quarter mile. Upgrading just those from 2 3/8 to 2 7/8 costs maybe $75 to $120 in pipe. That’s the best hundred dollars you’ll spend on the whole project.

Installed pipe fencing in Central Texas generally runs $22 to $45 per foot depending on rail count, pipe size, and terrain. We break the whole budget down, materials and labor both, in our pipe fence cost guide.

## When to Mix Pipe Sizes on the Same Fence

Almost every fence we build mixes sizes, and yours probably should too. Here’s how we spec jobs across our service area, from China Spring to Lorena.

Perimeter fence with wire. 2 7/8 corners, gates, and H-braces. 2 3/8 line posts every 8 to 10 feet with a 2 3/8 top rail, then 4 or 5 strands of barbed wire or net wire below. This is the standard Central Texas ranch fence. If you’re stretching wire between pipe posts, our h-brace fence corners guide explains why those brace assemblies carry the whole fence.

Horse fence. Same post layout, but we tighten spacing and often add a second rail or continuous fence panels. Horses lean, chew, and spook into fences, so smooth, stout, and visible wins. Karen, who keeps three barrel horses on 10 acres south of Lorena, had us build about 600 feet of paddock fence with 2 7/8 gate and corner posts, 2 3/8 lines and rails, and net wire below the rail. The total came to $9,600, and after two springs of storms and one gelding that tests everything, it hasn’t moved an inch.

Bull pens and working pens. All 2 7/8 posts, sometimes heavier, with 2 3/8 rails stacked 5 or 6 high. A 2,000 pound bull hitting a fence at a trot is not a load you engineer down to a price.

Entrances. 2 7/8 minimum on gate posts, and often 4 1/2 inch or larger on main entrance columns that carry a heavy swinging gate or an overhead sign.

One more sizing note: depth beats diameter. A 2 7/8 post set 18 inches deep will fail before a 2 3/8 post set 3 feet deep in concrete. The USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service fence practice standards, available through nrcs.usda.gov, lean hard on proper embedment and bracing for exactly this reason. Our blackland clay around Waco and West swells and shrinks with the weather, so shallow posts walk out of plumb faster here than almost anywhere.

A word on DIY before you fire up a welder. Cutting and joining used oilfield pipe means grinding scale, breathing weld fumes, and running a hot arc over dry Texas grass. If you’re not set up with proper gear, a fire watch, and water on hand, this is the point to stop and call a professional. Burns and grass fires cost a lot more than a fence contractor does. And if the pipe has any coating or galvanizing on it, don’t weld it at all without real ventilation. Zinc fumes will put you on your back.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is 2 3/8 pipe strong enough for fence corner posts?

For a short garden fence, maybe. For a stretched wire fence holding livestock, no. Corner posts take the combined pull of every wire plus animal pressure, and undersized corners are the most common pipe fence failure we see around Waco. Spend the extra few dollars on 2 7/8 at corners, ends, and gates.

### How deep should pipe fence posts be set?

Line posts should go 30 to 36 inches deep in concrete, and corner and gate posts 36 to 48 inches. In the blackland clay around Waco and West, deeper is better because that soil swells and shrinks with moisture and can work shallow posts loose. In rocky ground near Crawford or Valley Mills, you may need a rock auger, and that’s usually a job worth hiring out.

### What size pipe is best for a top rail?

Most top rails are 2 3/8 or 1.9 inch pipe. The rail mostly keeps animals from leaning over the wire and gives the fence a straight, finished look, so it doesn’t need corner-post strength. On horse fences and working pens where animals hit the rail hard, stay with 2 3/8 or heavier.

### Is used oilfield pipe safe to buy for fencing?

Yes, and it’s what most Central Texas pipe fences are built from, but quality varies a lot from load to load. Inspect for deep pitting, thin walls, and split seams before you pay, and weigh a stick if you can, since weight per foot tells you the true wall thickness. If a price looks too good to be true, the wall thickness usually explains why.
