## Who Pays for a Fence Between Neighbors in Texas? (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/who-pays-for-fence-between-neighbors-texas/)

> Texas law rarely forces neighbors to split fence costs. Learn who pays for a fence between neighbors in Texas, real prices, and how Waco ranchers handle it.

Texas Law

# Who Pays for a Fence Between Neighbors in Texas?
Published August 20, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

Here's the answer most landowners don't want to hear: in Texas, nobody has to pay for that fence. Not you, and not the fella on the other side of the line.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

Here’s the answer most landowners don’t want to hear: in Texas, nobody has to pay for that fence. Not you, and not the fella on the other side of the line.

The question of who pays for a fence between neighbors in Texas comes up on almost every boundary job we quote around Waco, and the honest answer surprises people. Texas has no statute that forces one landowner to chip in on a fence the other one builds. Some states have “fence viewer” laws that split costs down the middle by force of law. Texas isn’t one of them.

That doesn’t mean you’re stuck paying the whole bill every time. Plenty of neighbors in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties split fence costs fairly, and there are smart ways to make that happen. There are also a few situations where the law does put money on the other side of the table. We’ll walk through all of it, with real numbers from real jobs.

## The Short Answer on Who Pays for a Fence Between Neighbors in Texas

Under Texas law, a boundary fence is treated like any other improvement. If you build it, you pay for it. Your neighbor has no legal duty to contribute, even if the fence sits right on the property line and even if his cattle benefit from it every single day.

The flip side is just as true. If your neighbor builds a fence on the line, he can’t send you a bill for half and take you to court when you don’t pay. There’s no Texas statute that lets him do that.

The relevant law lives in Chapter 143 of the Texas Agriculture Code, which covers fences and range restrictions. Read it front to back and you won’t find a single line requiring cost sharing between neighbors. What you will find is a rule that matters a lot in practice: it’s illegal to attach your fence to your neighbor’s fence without their written permission. More on that below, because it’s the closest thing Texas has to a “you use it, you pay for it” rule.

So the default answer is simple. The person who wants the fence pays for the fence. Everything beyond that comes down to agreements, and that’s where most of the good and bad neighbor stories start.

If you’re staring at a bare property line right now and wondering what a fence would actually run, we’ll walk the line with you and put a real number on paper. Request a free written estimate or call us at (254) 870-8898. No pressure, no games, just footage and a price.

## What Texas Law Actually Says About Boundary Fences

A few pieces of Texas law touch boundary fences, and it helps to know each one before you knock on your neighbor’s door.

Open range is still the default. Texas is an open range state at the state level, which means livestock owners generally aren’t required to fence animals in. Most counties, including McLennan and the counties around it, have passed local stock laws that flip that rule and require owners to keep livestock off roads and off other people’s land. We break down how that works in our post on the Texas open range law, because it changes who’s liable when cattle get where they shouldn’t be.

No forced cost sharing. As covered above, no Texas statute makes a neighbor pay for a boundary fence he didn’t ask for. Courts have held this position for well over a century.

No attaching without permission. Agriculture Code Section 143.121 makes it unlawful to attach a fence to someone else’s fence without written consent. If your neighbor ties his cross fence into your line fence without asking, you can require him to take it down. In practice, this is your leverage. A neighbor who wants to use your fence has a reason to help pay for it.

Fences and property lines are separate questions. A fence is not automatically the legal boundary. Old fences wander off the line all the time, and a fence built in the wrong spot for long enough can create adverse possession headaches. Before you spend money on a line fence, know where the line actually is. Our article on building a fence on the property line in Texas covers surveys, setbacks, and why we sometimes build a foot inside the line on purpose.

HOAs and deed restrictions are a different animal. If your land sits in a subdivision with deed restrictions, those documents can require fences, dictate materials, and sometimes address cost sharing. Rural acreage around Waco usually isn’t restricted, but small ranchette subdivisions near Lorena and China Spring often are. Read your deed before you build.

## When Your Neighbor Might Actually Owe You Money

There’s no automatic cost split, but a few situations do put real money on your neighbor’s side of the ledger.

A written agreement exists. If you and your neighbor sign an agreement to share fence costs, that contract is enforceable like any other. Some older deeds in Central Texas even carry fence maintenance covenants that run with the land. Check your title documents.

Your neighbor damaged the fence. If his bull went through your fence, his dozer operator clipped a corner post, or his hunting lease guests drove through a water gap, he’s liable for the damage he caused. That’s basic negligence law, not fence law. Document it with photos and dates before anything gets repaired.

His livestock are using your fence in a stock law county. In a county with a local stock law, your neighbor has a duty to keep his cattle contained. If the only thing containing them is your fence, he doesn’t owe you rent, but he does carry the liability if they get out through a gap on his side. Our post on what happens when cattle get out explains why that liability motivates a lot of neighbors to pay their half without a fight.

He attached to your fence. If he tied into your fence without written permission, you can demand removal. Most neighbors would rather write a check for a share of the fence than tear out their own cross fencing. It’s not a court-ordered split, but it gets to the same place.

Here’s how that played out near Crawford last spring. Dale Hutchins runs cows on 180 acres, and his neighbor tied three cross fences into Dale’s aging line fence without asking. Instead of lawyering up, Dale showed him the statute and offered a deal: help fund a rebuild and the attachments stay. We rebuilt the half mile of 5-strand barbed wire for $9,240, they split it clean at $4,620 each, and both men got a tight fence and kept the peace.

## How to Split Fence Costs Between Neighbors the Right Way

Most boundary fences in our area do end up cost shared, not because the law requires it but because it’s fair and everybody knows it. Here’s the process that keeps it friendly.

Talk before you build. Nobody likes finding out about a fence project from the sound of a skid steer. Walk the line together, talk about what the fence needs to hold, and find out what matters to each side. One of you runs goats and needs net wire. The other just wants the line marked. That conversation shapes the price.

Get a survey if there’s any doubt. A boundary survey on rural acreage typically runs $500 to $1,500 around here. That’s cheap insurance against building a $15,000 fence on the wrong dirt.

Get the quote in writing, then split it in writing. A one-page agreement that names the fence line, the total cost, each party’s share, and who handles future maintenance will prevent 90 percent of fence feuds. Sign two copies. You don’t need a lawyer for this, though it never hurts to have one look it over.

Splits don’t have to be 50/50. Common arrangements we see: one party pays for materials and the other pays labor, one party pays extra to upgrade from barbed wire to net wire because they’re the one running sheep, or one party covers the brush clearing because the overgrowth crept in from their side. Fair beats equal.

Put maintenance in the deal. The old Central Texas custom is the “right hand rule”: stand at the middle of the shared line facing the fence, and you maintain the half to your right. It’s not law, but it’s a handy convention worth writing into your agreement.

Robert Kalich and his neighbor west of West did it about as well as it can be done. They shared 2,600 feet of line where an old fence had rotted out. Robert wanted net wire for his Boer goats, the neighbor only needed barbed wire for cows. Total for the net wire build came to $15,600. They split the barbed wire equivalent 50/50 at $5,200 each, and Robert paid the $5,200 net wire upgrade himself. Both signed a one-page maintenance agreement. Five years from now there won’t be an argument, because it’s all on paper.

Real numbers make these conversations easier. Here’s what boundary fencing runs installed in the Waco area, and what a clean 50/50 split looks like per quarter mile.

Fence type Installed cost per foot Per 1/4 mile (1,320 ft) Your half at 50/50

For a deeper breakdown of what drives the price, see our barbed wire fence cost guide, and if you’re pricing the stouter option, our pipe fence installation page covers what oilfield pipe construction runs and why it lasts 40 plus years.

For most shared cattle boundaries in McLennan and Bosque counties, 5-strand barbed wire is still the workhorse. It’s the cheapest split, it holds cattle, and both sides understand exactly what they’re getting.

Want a firm number for your specific line? Call (254) 870-8898 and we’ll measure it, flag the trouble spots, and hand both you and your neighbor the same written estimate. A neutral third-party number makes the split conversation a whole lot easier.

## When One Neighbor Refuses to Pay

Sometimes the conversation goes nowhere. The neighbor doesn’t run livestock, doesn’t care about the line, or just doesn’t want to spend the money. In Texas, you can’t force him. So here’s how to protect yourself when you’re building alone.

Build it entirely on your side. Set the fence 6 to 12 inches inside your line. The fence is then 100 percent your property. Your neighbor can’t attach to it without written permission, can’t claim any ownership of it, and if he ever wants to tie in, you’re holding all the cards for a buy-in conversation.

Document everything. Keep the survey, the invoice, and dated photos of the completed fence. If a cost dispute or a boundary question ever surfaces, paper wins.

Don’t touch his side. Clearing brush or old wire on your neighbor’s side of the line without permission can create trespass liability, even with good intentions. Clear your side and stop at the line.

Skip the retaliation moves. We’ve been called out to look at fences built out of spite, and they never end well. A fence built in anger gets built fast and cheap, and it fails fast too.

Marcy Templin in Lorena ran into the refusal problem last fall. Her 22 acres shared 1,900 feet with an absentee owner who wouldn’t return calls, and her horses kept testing the collapsing old wire. She stopped waiting. We built 1,900 feet of net wire with a top rail, set a foot inside her surveyed line, for $12,350. It’s her fence, on her land, under her control. When the absentee owner eventually sells, the new buyer will have to come to her if they want to use it.

One safety note that matters here. Tearing out an old shared fence is where DIY boundary projects go sideways. Rusted wire under tension can snap and whip, old corner posts hide rot, and pulling wire near a disputed line can turn a cold disagreement hot. If the old fence is in bad shape or the line is contested, stop and bring in a professional. The Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid landowner resources on fence law and liability, and a local contractor who works boundary lines every week can keep you out of both physical and legal trouble.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I legally force my neighbor to pay half for a fence in Texas?

No. Texas has no statute that requires a landowner to share the cost of a boundary fence, so courts won’t order your neighbor to contribute to a fence he never agreed to. Your options are a voluntary written agreement or building the fence yourself on your own side of the line. If he later attaches to your fence, you can require written permission, which is your best leverage for a buy-in.

### Can my neighbor attach his fence to mine?

Not without your written permission. Texas Agriculture Code Section 143.121 makes it unlawful to attach a fence to someone else’s fence without consent, and you can require unauthorized attachments to be removed. Many landowners trade that permission for a share of the fence cost or a signed maintenance agreement. Get any deal like that in writing.

### Who pays when my neighbor’s cattle damage the boundary fence?

If his livestock or equipment caused the damage, he’s responsible for it under ordinary negligence rules. Take dated photos before you repair anything and send him a written repair estimate. Most disputes settle once there’s a clear number on paper, and if he won’t pay, small claims court handles amounts up to $20,000 in Texas.

### Does the fence on the line belong to both of us?

Only if you both paid for it or agreed it’s shared. A fence built and paid for by one owner belongs to that owner, even if it sits on the boundary. That’s why we recommend building 6 to 12 inches inside your own line when you’re paying alone, so ownership stays clean and there’s no argument later.

## Winter Fence Preparation: Getting Ranch Fences Ready for Texas Ice Storms and Hard Freezes (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/winter-fence-prep-texas/)

> Winter fence preparation for Central Texas ranches. Tighten wire, brace corners, and trim ice-heavy limbs before the freeze. Free estimates: (254) 870-8898.

Maintenance

# Winter Fence Preparation: Getting Ranch Fences Ready for Texas Ice Storms and Hard Freezes
Published August 26, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

One night of ice in February 2021 tore up more fence in Central Texas than the previous five years of cattle rubbing, hog damage, and rot put together.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

One night of ice in February 2021 tore up more fence in Central Texas than the previous five years of cattle rubbing, hog damage, and rot put together. Here’s the part that still stings: most of the fences that went down that week had weak spots a rancher could’ve found and fixed in one Saturday afternoon.

That’s what winter fence preparation is really about. It’s not some big project. It’s a focused walk of your lines in November or early December, a short list of cheap fixes, and a little chainsaw work before the first Arctic front rolls down I-35. Do it right and an ice storm is an inconvenience. Skip it and you’re chasing cows down a farm-to-market road at 2 a.m. in freezing rain.

We build and repair ranch fence all over McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, and every January we see the same failures. Here’s what actually breaks in a Texas freeze, what to check, what fixes cost, and when to call for help.

If you’d rather have a second set of eyes on your lines before winter, we’ll walk them with you. Call (254) 870-8898 and ask for a free written estimate on any repairs we find.

## Why a Hard Freeze Hits Central Texas Fences So Hard

Fences up north are built for winter. Ours mostly aren’t, because for eight months of the year the enemy is heat, drought, and hogs. Then a freeze shows up and attacks the fence in three ways at once.

First, ice load. Freezing rain coats every wire, every limb, and every cedar top with a layer of ice that can triple the weight hanging on your fence. A quarter inch of ice adds roughly 500 pounds of weight to a 100-foot span of loaded tree limbs. Wire itself usually holds. The trees above the wire don’t.

Second, soil movement. Most ground around Waco is blackland clay, and clay moves with moisture and temperature. A hard freeze after a wet spell can heave posts upward or tip marginal posts past the point of no return. Posts that were already loose in October end up leaning at 30 degrees by March. If your corners were weak going in, the whole line loses tension. We covered why corners carry the entire fence in our guide to H-brace fence corners.

Third, livestock pressure. Cold cattle bunch along fence lines for windbreak, and hungry cattle lean on wire to reach grass on the other side. A five-strand fence at proper tension shrugs that off. A saggy fence with rusted wire doesn’t, and along a highway, loose cattle can become your liability problem fast.

The National Weather Service office that covers our area keeps winter storm data and safety guidance at weather.gov/fwd. Central Texas averages at least one significant freeze most winters. The question isn’t whether ice is coming. It’s whether your fence is ready.

## Your Winter Fence Preparation Checklist

Here’s the walk-through we recommend to every customer, in the order that catches the most problems for the least effort. Budget half a day for a typical 50 to 100 acre place.

Walk every line, don’t drive it. From the truck you’ll see the fence. On foot you’ll see the fence’s problems. Grab every third or fourth post and push. Solid is fine. Wiggle means the post is on borrowed time.

Check tension on every stretch. Barbed wire should feel tight enough to hum when you pluck it. If you can push two strands together easily, that stretch needs restretching before ice and cattle pressure find it. A couple of hours with wire stretchers now beats a blown-out stretch in January.

Test your corners and braces. Push hard on every corner post and gate post. Any movement at all is a red flag, because the corner holds the tension for the entire run. A failed corner in an ice storm can drop a quarter mile of fence at once.

Mark rotted and broken posts. Kick each wood post at ground line. A soft, punky thud means rot. Flag it with tape and replace it before winter, not after. Rotted posts snap under ice load like matchsticks.

Trim the trees. More on this below, because limbs are the number one killer.

Check water gaps and low crossings. Winter rain events blow out water gaps, and a blown gap is an open door for cattle.

Test electric fence now. Cold, wet weather is hard on chargers, connections, and insulators. Walk hot wire lines with a fence tester and fix weak spots before you need them.

Stock a repair kit. Wire, a stretcher, fence pliers, steeples, T-posts, and clips. When the storm hits, the co-op will be sold out.

None of this takes special skills. It takes an honest afternoon and a willingness to fix what you find instead of telling yourself it’ll hold one more season.

## Trees and Ice Load: The Fence Killer Nobody Budgets For

Ask any fence builder in Central Texas what wrecks the most fence in an ice storm and you’ll get the same answer: trees. Not wind, not cattle, not the ice on the wire itself. Limbs and whole trees coming down across the top strand.

Roy Slovacek runs about 60 cows off FM 933 north of West. In the January 2024 ice event, a big hackberry limb he’d been meaning to trim for two years came down across his east line and flattened 180 feet of five-strand barbed wire, snapped two wood posts, and let 14 pairs out toward the road. Our crew got there the next morning. The repair ran him $1,850, and he burned a full day of his own time gathering cattle in the sleet. The trimming that would’ve prevented it? About $200 of chainsaw work in November.

Here’s the rule of thumb we give customers: anything hanging over the fence that’s bigger around than your wrist needs to go, and any dead tree within falling distance of the line needs to come down entirely. Live oaks and cedars hold ice worst because they keep their leaves and needles, which gives the ice more surface to grab.

Fall and early winter are the right time for this work. The brush is easier to see through, the ground is firm enough for equipment, and you’re ahead of the storm instead of behind it. If your lines have gone full jungle, we offer line clearing as part of repair jobs.

One safety note we mean sincerely: limbs under ice load and leaning trees store energy like a loaded spring. That kind of chainsaw work hurts people every single winter. Call a professional for anything you can’t drop cleanly from the ground.

## Posts, Braces, and What Freezing Clay Does Underground

The damage you can’t see coming is below the ground line. Blackland clay shrinks all summer, cracks open around your posts, then swells shut when fall rain arrives. Add a hard freeze and the moisture in that clay expands, shoving posts upward and sideways. It’s the same reason sidewalks buckle, just slower.

The posts that survive this are the ones set deep, in good soil contact, with sound wood or heavy pipe. The ones that fail were already compromised: shallow-set posts, posts rotted at the ground line, and T-posts driven into loose fill. Some moving posts can be reset, but posts rotted at the ground line need replacing outright.

This is also where pipe fence earns its keep. A properly cemented pipe fence simply doesn’t care about frost heave or ice load the way wood does. We’re not saying replace your perimeter with pipe. We are saying that corners, gate openings, and high-pressure areas like pens and alleys are worth upgrading to pipe, because those are exactly the spots winter attacks first.

Martha Kolar has a horse place outside Valley Mills, and she learned this one the expensive way. A wood gate post on her main entrance had been leaning slightly for a year. The December 2022 freeze heaved it another few inches, the gate dropped and jammed, and then a spooked mare shouldered the whole assembly over. Between resetting the opening with pipe posts and rehanging the gate, she spent $1,400. Resetting that one leaning post the summer before would’ve been about $300.

If you’re not sure whether a wobbly corner will make it through winter, don’t guess. Request a free written estimate and we’ll tell you straight which posts need work and which ones are fine.

## Gates, Water Gaps, and Hungry Cattle

Gates fail in freezes for a simple reason: they’re the only part of the fence with moving parts. Hinges seize, latches ice shut, and heaved posts throw the whole gate out of level so it drags or won’t close. Before winter, grease every hinge, check that each gate swings and latches with one hand, and shim or reset anything that’s dragging. A gate that won’t latch is a gate a cow will find.

Water gaps deserve their own line on the checklist. Winter storm systems in Central Texas often bring two or three inches of rain ahead of the cold front, and creeks come up fast. A water gap that’s already half-wrecked from fall rains will wash out completely, and cattle follow creek bottoms like highways. Rebuild weak gaps before winter with breakaway construction so the gap gives instead of the fence. Our water gap fence guide shows the setups that survive Central Texas creeks.

Finally, think about feed placement. Cattle congregate where you feed them, and 30 cows packed against one stretch of fence in an ice storm will test it hard. Feed hay away from fence lines, especially your oldest wire and road frontage. Texas A&#x26;M AgriLife Extension publishes solid cold-weather livestock guidance at agrilifeextension.tamu.edu.

## What Winter Fence Prep Costs Compared to Storm Repairs

Prevention is cheaper than repair in every trade, but fencing might be the most lopsided example we know. Here’s what the numbers look like on jobs we see every winter.

Danny Urbanovsky, who runs a stocker operation between Crawford and China Spring, put real numbers on this for us. In fall 2023 he had us do a prep pass on about a mile and a half of older fence: eight posts, one corner rebuild, restretching, and limb work, for right at $2,100. His neighbor across the county road skipped prep that year. The January ice took out roughly 900 feet of the neighbor’s fence in three separate tree strikes, and the rebuild cost him about $6,400. Same storm, same road, one fence bill three times the size of the other.

The pattern holds on nearly every job we quote after a storm. Repairs cost three to five times what prevention would have, before you count lost time and the risk of cattle on a public road. If a storm beats you to it, our storm damaged fence repair guide covers triage and insurance.

## When to Put Down the Pliers and Call a Pro

Plenty of winter fence prep is honest DIY work: walking lines, greasing hinges, driving a few T-posts, splicing a break, trimming small limbs. Do all of that yourself and pocket the savings.

But some jobs should end with a phone call, not a trip to the barn for more tools. Call a professional when:

- A tree or heavy limb is down on tensioned wire. Stored energy in stretched barbed wire can whip when it’s cut, and it does real damage to hands and faces.

- A corner or H-brace has failed. Rebuilding one properly takes equipment and know-how, and everything downstream depends on it.

- Posts need to go into frozen or saturated ground. Wrong technique now means redoing it in spring.

- The damage runs hundreds of feet. At that scale you’re not repairing, you’re rebuilding, and it pays to price new construction. Our barbed wire fence crews can usually quote a rebuild within a couple of days.

- Cattle are already out. Get the herd secured first with temporary electric or panels, then fix fence. We run a 24/7 emergency line for exactly this situation.

Winter fence preparation comes down to one idea: find the weak spot before the ice does. Walk your lines in November, spend a few hundred dollars on the obvious fixes, and you’ll spend February by the stove instead of in a ditch with a flashlight in your teeth.

If you’d rather have us handle the walk-through, the trimming, and the repairs in one visit, we do winter prep packages across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties every fall. Call (254) 870-8898 for a free written estimate, or reach us here and we’ll get you on the schedule before the first front.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### When should I start winter fence preparation in Central Texas?

Start in November and aim to finish by early December. Our first real freeze usually lands in late November or December, and ice events cluster in January and February. Starting early leaves time to schedule a contractor for the bigger fixes before everyone’s calling about storm damage at once.

### Does barbed wire actually break in a hard freeze?

Cold alone rarely breaks healthy wire, because good galvanized wire handles Texas winter temperatures fine. What breaks fences is weight and impact: iced limbs coming down, trees falling, and cattle pressure on wire that was already slack or rusted. That’s why prep focuses on trees, tension, and posts rather than the wire itself.

### Is ice storm fence damage covered by insurance?

Sometimes, depending on your farm and ranch policy. Many policies cover fence damage from falling trees or named storm events, often subject to a deductible and a per-foot or per-structure limit. Photograph everything before you repair, save receipts, and call your agent early, because adjusters get backed up after a big ice event.

### What should be in a winter fence repair kit?

Keep a roll of barbed wire, wire stretchers, fence pliers, gloves, steeples, T-posts with clips, and a few insulated splice sleeves in the barn before the first storm. Add a fence tester if you run electric. Supply stores sell out fast after ice hits, so stock up while the shelves are full.

## Wood vs Vinyl 3 Rail Horse Fence: What Each One Costs to Own (https://brazosridgefence.com/blog/wood-vs-vinyl-horse-fence/)

> Compare wood and vinyl 3 rail horse fence in Central Texas: real per-foot costs, what blackland clay and limestone do to each, and upkeep over 20 years.

# Wood vs Vinyl 3 Rail Horse Fence: What Each One Costs to Own
Published September 15, 2026 · Brazos Ridge Fence Co.

A three-rail fence looks finished the day the last board goes up. What it looks like in year seven is the part the brochure leaves out.

Get a Free Estimate Call (254) 870-8898

A three-rail fence looks finished the day the last board goes up. What it looks like in year seven is the part the brochure leaves out. If you are pricing a 3 rail horse fence around Waco right now, the decision that matters is not which one photographs better on install day. It is which one you are still happy with after eight Texas summers, a couple of ice storms, and a gelding who has decided the top rail is a scratching post.

We get asked about wood and vinyl rail fence most weeks, usually by somebody who just bought 10 or 20 acres and wants the front pasture to look like the places along the FM road. That is a fair thing to want. It is also the fence type where the gap between the bid and the twenty-year cost is widest, so it is worth understanding before you sign anything.

This article compares the two honestly, including where each one fails in blackland clay and limestone, and what we actually build for horse people in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties. If you would rather skip to real numbers on your own place, call (254) 870-8898 and we will walk the line with you. On-site estimates are free.

## The Real Numbers Behind a Three-Rail Horse Fence

Start with the honest disclaimer, because this matters. Wood and vinyl rail are not the fences we price off our own cost sheet. Our published bands cover ranch fence cost for wire, mesh, pipe, entrances and cattle guards. So the wood and vinyl figures below are general market estimates for Central Texas, not a Brazos Ridge Fence quote, and you should treat them that way.

As a general estimate, installed wood three-rail with treated pine boards and set posts runs somewhere in the $9 to $18 per foot range in this market. Vinyl three-rail with a reputable extruded rail and routed posts generally runs $14 to $28 per foot installed. Materials only, before anybody sets a post, a vinyl three-rail kit commonly lands around $9 to $16 per foot and treated wood rail around $4 to $8 per foot. Those spreads are wide for a reason. Corner count, gate count, and what is under your topsoil move the number more than the rail material does.

For comparison, here is what we do quote from our own cost sheet. Horse-grade no-climb mesh prices against our net wire band of $3.50 to $8 per foot, and horse mesh sits at the upper end of that band because 2 inch by 4 inch woven wire costs more than field fence. Welded pipe fence runs $12 to $28 per foot. Those are firm ranges from real jobs, not averages pulled off the internet.

## Wood Three-Rail: Cheap to Buy, Never Quite Finished

Wood is the cheaper fence to build and the more expensive fence to own. That is the whole story in one sentence, and everything below is detail.

The good part is real. A wood rail fence is visible from a dead run, which is the single most important safety property a horse fence has. A horse sees three solid boards. It does not always see wire. Both Penn State Extension and the University of Georgia Extension rank board fence highly for horses on visibility alone.

Wood also fails gracefully. A board that gets hit breaks, and a broken board is a $30 part and twenty minutes with a cordless drill. Compare that with a bent steel panel or a torn mesh section.

The costs show up later. Treated pine boards in Central Texas sun will need stain or paint on a three to five year cycle if you want them to keep looking like the day they went in. On a 1,500 foot run that is a real weekend, or a real invoice, every few years. Posts are the other clock. Ground contact rot at the soil line is what eventually takes a wood fence down, not the rails, and our shrink-swell clay pumps water in and out of that zone twice a year.

Then there are horses. Cribbers chew rails. Pasture-mates lean on them. A horse that has learned it can push a board off will keep testing it. Wood handles all of that better than vinyl does, but it does not handle it for free.

## Vinyl Three-Rail: No Painting, Different Problems

Vinyl solves the paint problem completely. That is not a small thing when you are looking at 2,000 feet of white fence along a county road. There is no stain cycle, no rot at the rail, and it looks the same in year ten as year one if the product was any good.

Be careful about that last condition. Quality varies a lot between vinyl products, and the difference is mostly UV package and wall thickness. Rail that is thin or short on UV inhibitor will chalk, yellow, and get brittle in this climate faster than the warranty language suggests. Ask what the rail wall thickness is and read the warranty for what it actually covers, because most cover the material and not the labor to swap it.

Cold is the other thing people underestimate in Texas. Vinyl gets more brittle as temperature drops, and our winter is not mild every year. A rail that would flex in July can crack in a February freeze when a horse hits it. Heat runs the other direction: vinyl expands and contracts through the year, so it has to be installed with room to move or it will bow between posts.

The safety picture is genuinely mixed. Most vinyl rail systems are designed so the rail pops out of the routed post under impact rather than shattering. That is good for the horse. It also means a horse that leans hard enough will pop a rail out and walk through, which is why vinyl rail on a horse pasture is usually run with a hot wire or backed with mesh. Vinyl alone is a boundary. It is not a containment fence for a horse that has decided to leave, and any vinyl salesman who tells you otherwise has not stood in a pasture at 6 a.m. looking for a mare.

Vinyl also does not fix your post problem. Most vinyl posts are hollow, and the fence still depends on how deep and how well those posts are set. In blackland clay, that is the whole ballgame.

The row that decides most jobs is the containment row. If your only fence is rail, you are relying on the horse respecting it. That works for a lot of horses and fails badly for a few. Our page on the safest fence for horses works through that trade in more detail.

## Three Central Texas Jobs and What Decided Them

A 12-acre horse place outside Lorena wanted white vinyl three-rail on 1,850 feet of perimeter, and priced it out at roughly $22 a foot as a general market estimate, call it $40,000. Two mares and a pony, one of them a known fence-tester. We built 1,850 feet of horse-grade no-climb with a treated wood top rail instead, and it came in inside our net wire band at the upper end. Same clean look from the road, a fence a hoof cannot go through, and the money left over paid for the gates and a run-in shed pad.

A limestone hill section near Valley Mills is the opposite lesson. On 600 feet of that line, every post had to be drilled rather than augered, and rock drilling is specialist equipment with an operator, not something you rent for a Saturday. Post setting on that run cost more than the rails would have, whichever material we used. When the ground is rock, the rail material stops being the main variable, and anybody quoting a flat per-foot price over the phone for a line they have not walked is guessing.

A 40-acre place west of Crawford already had 900 feet of 20-year-old wood three-rail along the drive. The owner assumed the whole thing needed replacing. It did not. The rails were sound. Eleven posts had rotted at grade and were leaning, which made the entire fence look finished. Reset the posts, replace nine boards, restain, and that fence has another decade in it. That is the argument for wood in one story: the failure was cheap to find and cheap to fix.

## What We Usually Build for Horses Around Waco

Here is the straight answer, and it is not the answer a rail fence salesman gives.

On small acreage with horses, the fence that does the most work per dollar in this part of Texas is 2 inch by 4 inch no-climb woven wire with a wood or pipe top rail. The mesh keeps hooves out and foals in. The rail gives the horse something to see and keeps the top of the fence from getting mashed down. It prices against our net wire band of $3.50 to $8 per foot, with horse-grade mesh sitting at the upper end, and it reads clean from the road. We cover the build in detail on our horse fence page and in our guide to no-climb horse fence.

Where somebody wants the fence to be permanent and the budget allows, welded pipe at $12 to $28 per foot is the last fence you will build on that line. Pipe is what we run on road frontage, around corrals and working pens, and anywhere horses crowd a gate.

Rail alone still has its place. Around a house, along a drive, on a dry lot where the horses are handled daily, wood three-rail is a good-looking, safe, repairable fence. Just budget for the paint cycle and set the posts properly, because in blackland clay the posts are what fails. Our notes on fence posts in clay soil cover depth and backfill.

What we will not do is tell you the material choice matters more than the ground it sits in. It does not. Two identical fences, one on flat clay pasture and one on a limestone slope, will not cost the same and will not age the same.

If you are weighing wood against vinyl on your own place, the useful next step is not another article. Call (254) 870-8898 and we will walk the line with you, look at the soil, count the corners and gates, and put a number in writing. No charge for the visit.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does a 3 rail horse fence cost per foot in Central Texas?

As a general market estimate, installed wood three-rail runs about $9 to $18 per foot and vinyl three-rail about $14 to $28 per foot in this area. Those are not our quoted prices, and the spread depends almost entirely on your ground, your corner count and your gates. The fences we do price from our own cost sheet are horse-grade no-climb mesh at $3.50 to $8 per foot, top of that band for horse mesh, and welded pipe at $12 to $28 per foot.

### Is vinyl horse fence safer than wood?

It depends on the failure you are worried about. Vinyl rails are designed to pop out of the post under impact rather than splinter, which is easier on a horse than a broken board. But vinyl gets more brittle in a freeze, and a horse leaning on it can push a rail out and walk off, so it is usually run with a hot wire or backed with mesh. Neither rail fence on its own stops a foal or a dog.

### Will a three-rail fence hold up in blackland clay?

The rails will. The posts are the question. Shrink-swell clay around Waco moves through the year and works posts loose over time, which shows up as leaning posts and bowed rail lines. Set depth, backfill and bracing decide how long that takes, which is why we look at the soil on site before we quote a rail fence.

### Can you repair an old wood three-rail fence instead of replacing it?

Often, yes. On rail fences we look at 20 years old, the boards are frequently still sound and the failure is a handful of posts rotted at grade. Resetting the bad posts, swapping the broken boards and restaining is a fraction of the cost of a rebuild. We will tell you honestly on site if the fence is worth saving or if you are better off starting over.
